Ministry's dispute with the butchers in

officer, Mr. Adams.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The answer to all
parts of the hon. Member's question is
in the negative.

opinion, not a matter of fact.

to the hon. Member that there is a large

4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

Pigs Marketing Board is in the process
of being transferred to my Ministry for

CONTROL.
8. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of
the plight of men displaced by the Meat
Control Scheme; whether the Government will pay compensation in view of
loss of employment; whether the displacement of men engaged in shipping
of SOWS to England is only of a
temporary nature caused by the war;
and whether men employed under the
Meat Control hold dual jobs under his
Department, and, if so, how many are.
so engaged.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am fully
and sympathetically aware of the fact
that the operation of the Meat and Livestock Control Scheme has in certain
cases occasioned loss of employment. So
far as I have power, however, I have
endeavoured to reduce such cases. For
instance, in engaging staff for the operation of the scheme preference has been
given in the first place to those who
have been, or would be, displaced by the
scheme, and, secondly, to unemployed
persons. I may say here that in the
staffing of the slaughter-houses, which
have been authorised in Northern Ireland for the purpose of the scheme, my
Ministry has been, and is in close touch.
with workers' organisations.
The hon. Member will be aware of the
fact that the scheme is a United
Kingdom scheme, and is operated in Northern Ireland by my Ministry as agents
of the Ministry of Food. It is a decision
of the Imperial Government that no
compensation such as that visualised by
the hon. Member can be considered.
The scheme is not of a permanent
character. It has its foundation in the
Emergency Powers (Defence) Act, 1939,
which is framed to expire subsequent to
the passing of the war emergency.
I am not aware of any employment in
a dual capacity such as that mentioned
by the hon. Member, but I am not

NORTHERN IRELAND SCUTCH
MILLS.
9. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can give any
information as to the state of scutch
mills in Northern Ireland, and if
financial aid will be given to put them
in a fit state to cope with extra flax
grown; and whether he can give an
assurance that as the price of flax is now
higher than pre-war, a similar increase
in wages will be paid.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: A survey will
very shortly be made of the scutch mills
in Northern Ireland to indicate those
that require renovation, and financial
aid for this purpose will be given by way
of loan in approved cases; we hope very
shortly to discuss the wages of scutchers
with the interests concerned, but without
such consultation I cannot, of
course, give an assurance such as is
desired.
ULSTER PUBLICITY OFFICER.
10. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the salary
and allowance paid or to be paid to Mr.
F. M. Adams, late editor of the

The Press Officer took up duty on the
1st January, 1940; he is drawing at
present remuneration at the rate of £700
per annum and is attached to the offices
of the Cabinet Secretariat at Stormont
Castle.
The PRIME MINISTER: The Government have had under consideration since
the outbreak of the war the necessity for
making more effective use of existing
facilities for publicity, and they decided
early in November last that the appointment of a Press Officer should be made.
Hon. Members were informed of this
decision at the first available opportunity
during the Debate on the Address.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I did not think it necessary to
advertise the position as I considered that
the present holder of the post possessed
in the highest degree the necessary
qualifications for the successful conduct
of publicity work.

Commerce in January, 1939, advertise

economical, and if it was satisfactory and

The PRIME MINISTER: I can only
say I saw the advertisement that was
inserted. I studied the question as to the
best
I could find for this parperson
ticular work, and I think I have found
the best man.

at all?
Mr. HENDERSON: I understand
that Mr. Adams is a very competent
officer.

Mr. HENDERSON: But does the
noble Lord think that he was justified in

no Ulsterman was competent to fill the
job? Personally, I think an Ulsterman
could have been got.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must not give expression to his own

Mr. BEATTIE: Is it fit and proper
that any job of this description should not

Minister whether he can state if Government advertisements are now transmitted
for publication through the Publicity

WAR SAVINGS COMMITTEE STAFF
AND OFFICES.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the rent,
rates, taxes and other expenses of the
offices in Royal Avenue taken over by his
Ministry for the use of the newlyappointed "War Savings Committee";
whether he can give the names, salaries,
and allowances of the Secretary and staff
appointed to the Committee, the number
of persons on the Committee, the allowance paid or payable to the members of
the Committee the number of meetings
held by the Committee, and the periods
at which such meetings are held; and
whether the advertisements issued on behalf of the Committee are transmitted
for publication through the Publicity
Officer.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews) The offices and furniture of
the Ulster Savings Committee in Royal
Avenue, Belfast, were taken over for the
duration of the war from the Ulster
:
Tourist Development Association and involve an annual expenditure of £540 in
respect of rent, rates and heating. Of
this sum the rent accounts for £375 per
annum, heating £15 per annum, rates
£141 per annum, and water rate £9 per
annum.
The staff consists of four in all; three
of whom have been lent from other
departments; namely the secretary of the
Committee, Mr. Siggins, in receipt of a
salary of £500 per annum; his assistant,
Mr. Maxwell, at a salary of £260 per
annum, and one shorthand typist. The
fourth member of the staff, Mr. C. W. S.
Magill, whose salary is £550 per annum,
was appointed as organiser by the
Minister of Finance in a temporary
capacity on the recommendation of the
Ulster Savings Committee.
The Committee consist of a chairman
and 44 members appointed by the
Minister of Finance, and six additional
members have been co-opted on subcommittees. All members act in an
honorary capacity, and though my
Ministry have agreed to meet out-ofpocket travelling expenses, if claimed, no
such expenses have been claimed as yet.
The Committee is responsible for its own
procedure, and the frequency of its meetings is a matter for the Chairman's discretion. The advertisements issued on
behalf of the Committee are placed direct
by the Ministry of Finance, but the cost
thereof is not paid out of money voted by
this House, being met by the Imperial
authorities as part of the Savings Campaign covering the United Kingdom as a
whole.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Minister's idea of
saving to spend money and create new
jobs and new posts all over the country?
Mr. ANDREWS: Frequently money
well spent has an advantage, and on this
occasion I think it has been well spent.
The returns which have already accrued
through this effort are very creditable to
Ulster.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister says the
money is well spent. Is not that only a

in that respect only expressing his own.
opinion?

DRAINAGE SCHEMES.
13. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state if the
Drainage Advisory Committee have made
any report to him showing how drainage
schemes could be made more effective.
than at present; and whether, in view
of the immense acreage of arable land
which is still subject to flooding, he is
prepared to ask the Government to take
some steps to utilise the unemployed in
carrying out necessary drainage schemes.
Mr. ANDREWS: I appreciate. the
interest that my hon. Friend has always
shown in the problem of drainage. The
Drainage Advisory Committee have made
a report, stating among other things that
there would be little good in their continuing to investigate the problem while
war conditions prevail, as any recommendations they might make would
almost certainly involve additional financial burdens to the Exchequer and the
County Councils. The Government is in
agreement with this view and has decided
that new drainage schemes cannot be
embarked upon during the period of the.
war.
The Committee's report will be presented to the House in due course.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the Minister whether there is any hope of the
people residing in areas such as Caledon
getting any relief in the near future?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am afraid not
during the period of the war.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is it true to say
that the men engaged on this work are
now unemployed and are practically
receiving the same amount in unemployment benefit as they did in wages?
Would the Minister not think that bad
economy?

indvidual cases of hardship do not, as

I am sure that in many cases, where the
family income is low in relation
to the number of persons dependent upon
it, unemployed parents must find it
difficult themselves to provide school
books for their children.
In reply to the second part of the
question, the Education Act of 1923
provides that local education authorities
may, at their discretion, provide, or
assist in the provision of, books,
stationery and other school requisites for
the use of children attending any public
elementary school in their education area.
Eleven of the education committees
have made some provision for this service in their Financial Schemes for
1939-40, the total provision amounting to
£5,217 and ten of these committees have
continued this provision for 1940-41, the
total amount for the latter year being
£3,767.
In the case of a number of schools,
funds for the purpose of supplying books
to the children attending them are available from local endowments or trusts,
which in some cases are administered by
local education authorities. The Ministry is not in possession of information
which would give the total available from
such sources.

19. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is a fact that the
Unemployment Assistance Board disallowed a number of girls (minors) relief,
for not accepting work in Dorset; whether

Tribunal, whether such treatment will be
continued; whether the Minister can give
any information as to the amount of
available labour in Britain for the class of
work offered to girls from Armagh; and
whether parents are entitled to direct
their girls to take employment in England
in view of existing war conditions and
dangers.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The facts in this case are as
follows:
Towards the end of December work at
a spinning mill in Bridport, Dorset, was
offered to a number of young women
applicants in the Armagh district. The
wages offered were 30s
week for
per
workers of eighteen years of age, though
spinners, reelers, winders and warpers
were to be paid 34s 4d per week, and
an increase of 10 per cent. on the wages
was promised to take effect in February.
The prospective employer is an Armagh
man who is anxious to help people from
his own locality. He took nine girls from
Armagh at the beginning of January,
and reports received indicate that these
girls are quite happily placed. Lodgings
are provided in a hostel at 10s per week.
In twenty-four cases girls who were
drawing unemployment assistance refused
this offer of work. Each case was considered individually, and it was thought
that in eleven of them there were home
circumstances which justified refusal. In
six other cases, disallowances were imposed for short periods, and in seven cases
an open disallowance was imposed.

UNEMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of

receipt of unemployment

Mr. GORDON: In answer to the hon.
Member I may state that about 93 per
cent. of the persons in receipt of unemployment assistance were given increases

made towards the end of last year. The

figures are available, was 83,655. Of

PLOUGHING IN 1939-40.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if a
subsidy of £2 per acre will be paid to
Written Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Written Answers
[Mr. Nixon]
farmers in Northern Ireland for ploughing in 1939 and 1940, and when the
actual payment will be made.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: A grant at the
rate of £2 per acre is payable in respect
of all old pasture land, which has been
under grass for seven years or more,
ploughed before the 31st March, 1940.
Farmers must make application to the
Ministry, on a statutory form, stating

payment is made as soon as possible

inspected.
DESTRUCTION OF PESTS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
progress, if any, made in connection
with the promised scheme for the destruction of pigeons, rats, rabbits, and
other pests in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
very carefully considering this matter
since replying to the hon. Member's
question on 1st November last, and have
arrived at the conclusion that, unless in
very exceptional cases, the Ministry
would not be justified in exercising its
powers under the Defence Regulations.
In the Ministry's opinion these are
matters in which concerted action by
farmers themselves is likely to give the
best results.
A leaflet relating to the destruction of
rats and rabbits has been prepared and
copies are being circulated to local
authorities and farmers' organisations.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The cost of the
van, staff and appliances referred to by

approximately.
SPAHLINGER EXPERIMENTS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

approximately two-thirds of their normal

in Northern Ireland.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Building Societies Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The measure, the Second
Reading of which I now commend to the
House, is of considerable public interest
since it concerns a form of house purchase which has become increasingly
popular, especially in the post-war years.
Hon. Members will be aware of the
nature of the business carried on by
building societies. Such societies, despite
The rapid and widespread development
of the building society movement in
Northern Ireland occurred within the
last decade when a number of crosschannel societies commenced operations
in this area.
I think there, can be little
doubt that the activities of these societies
have resulted in a substantial increase in
the number of the smaller type of
privately-owned dwelling-houses.
Some idea of the progress made by the
building society movement in Northern
Ireland can be gleaned from the figures
available. In 1922 the amount outstanding on loans made by building societies
operating in Northern Ireland was
£253,000. By December, 1938, the latest
date for which figures are available, the
comparable figure was £3,510,000. Over
the same period the amount invested with
building societies operating in Northern
Ireland increased from £251,000 to
£1,591,000.
Hon. Members will have observed from
the explanatory memorandum circulated
with the Bill that the law relating to
building societies is at present to be found
in the Building Societies Acts of 1874
and 1894. They may reasonably ask,
therefore, why a legislative code which
has stood the test of time should now be
amended. They may have observed that
the step we now propose to take follows
closely that taken by the Imperial Parliament which placed on the Statute Book
some six months ago an amending Building Societies Act. The justification for
our following such a step will be obvious
when I explain that the great bulk of
building society business in Northern
Ireland is in the hands of the large
societies with headquarters in England or
Scotland.
The course of administration indicated
the desirability of the amendment of
existing Building Societies Acts, but the
221 Building Societies Bill-

13 FEBRUARY 1940
Second Reading
immediate cause of the British Act of
1939 was a case in the Courts where the
question was raised whether building
societies had legal power to make any
larger advances than they would have
made on the security of the property only,
or whether they could advance a larger
sum in consideration of some additional
security given to them. I shall not weary
hon. Members by describing at length the
course of the proceedings, beyond mentioning that the learned Judge, who
heard the case in the first instance, expressed the view that building societies
had the necessary powers not only to lend
money on the security of property but
also, if they so thought fit, to lend additional money beyond what they would
have lent on the security of a house if
additional security were not offered.
It is obvious that there can be no objection to any lender obtaining collateral
security for his loan and that, in the case
of a person with small means, there is an
advantage in an arrangement which enables a building society to advance a high.
percentage of the cost of the building. In
the course of the debates in the Imperial
Parliament, however, it was alleged that
one of the prejudicial effects of the
existing system, under which a builder
could enter into an arrangement with a
building society for the provision of
collateral security against a number of
houses to be mortgaged with the society
by private individuals, was that the
prospective house-owner might be led to
believe that the house was of a higher
value than might prove to be the case.
The legislation now before the House is
designed to provide additional security
for buyers.
advancing. The special feature of the
arrangement is that the builder's guarantee to the society is paid into a central
pool which provides security covering not
only one house, but a whole series of
houses, and the actual houses covered by
the arrangement may change from time
to time as the loans on some are paid off
and as new houses are built. Although
this is a fluid arrangement, it would, if
worked in accordance with safeguards
such as those we propose in this Bill,
prove to the advantage of the purchaser,
who could not otherwise afford to buy a
house on the security of the property
alone.

In order that hon. Members may
appreciate the nature of these
tinuing arrangements, or builder's pools,
which are a common means of providing
additional security, let me give a typical
example. A purchaser wishes to buy a
house priced at £1,000. The building
society, on its part, is prepared to
advance him £750 on the security of the
property alone. The would-be house
owner, however, has only £50 of ready
money, and the building society agrees
to advance to him a further £200 under a
guarantee by the builder. Usually what
happens is that the builder agrees to pay
into a pool a cash deposit covering the
additional £200 which the society is
Turning now to the detailed provisions
of the Bill itself, hon. Members will
observe that the Measure is really in two
parts. While the position of societies is
safeguarded, their activities are also
regulated with a view to the protection
of members.
Clause 1 is declaratory in nature and
puts into legislative form the legal position as enunciated by the courts in the
recent ligitation.
Clause 2 limits the additional security
which may be taken by the society to
certain classes, and prescribes a limit of
75 per cent. of the purchase price as the
basic advance, with a maximum of 20
per cent. as the limit of the excess
advance.
Where a society takes additional
security in respect of the advance to a
member for the purpose of defraying
the purchase price, Clause 6 requires the
society to give the member a notice in
writing stating the maximum amount
which the society would consider proper
to advance upon the security of the
property if no other security were taken
by the society for the advance; and also
the amount, if any, by which the advance
exceeds this maximum amount. The
notice in question is required to be given
before any contract for the repayment of
the advance is entered into. If the
society fails to do this, no
recoverable in respect of the advance
except by leave of the court.

:-
The psychological effects of diet are
of the first importance in war. Malnutrition tends to be accompanied by
listlessness and apathy alternating
with hyper-excitability. There is a
gradual loss of power of concentration
on either physical or mental work.
Nervous debility and a feeling of despondency are common symptoms of
faulty diets.
These are psychological
factors which make for a spirit of
defeatism. In the present war the
whole nation is subjected to the strain
of war conditions. The dislocation of
our lives, the black-out, the separation
of families, the worries and anxieties
and emotional disturbances all put a
heavy strain on health. The diet of
our people must be such that they can
endure the strain and preserve
the
courage and power of endurance which
will be needed to secure victory.
The object of our food policy in war
time must be to provide (a) sufficient
energy-yielding foods, and (b) sufficient
"protective" foods.

something about Comber.
The DEPUTY SPEAKER: Let there
be no personalities.
Mr. BEATTIE: Personalities do not
worry me.
The DEPUTY SPEAKER: But they
worry me.
Mr. BEATTIE: You should sit there
and look pleasant.
It must be hard for
those in the Front Bench to sit and listen
to someone pointing out the conditions
under which the people suffer after the
Government has been 18 years in power.
I know it is hard for the Minister of
Labour and it must require a very firm
grip to remain in his seat while I am
delivering this oration of condemnation
against him for his failure to live up to
the needs and requirements of the people
who returned him. I will finish on this
note if I am allowed. Sir John Boyd Orr
further states:
Food is already rationed by price.
The poor eat the cheap foods, the
wealthy eat the expensive foods. To
superimpose a system of rationing by
amount on top of a system of rationing
by price involves an additional elaborate
and expensive administration
and
creates inconvenience and confusion.
It would be easier to continue the
principle of rationing by price and
adjust the supply and the price of the
essential foodstuffs referred to at such
a level that every person could get
sufficient without coupons.
There are many other suitable quotations which I could fling at the Government, but if I take up too much time I
would cut out others who may wish to
speak. I would have them shelled out
of their positions if I continued quoting
Sir John Boyd Orr, who has ably put
down in book form the conditions under
which the people of this and other
countries are living. Therefore, thanking the Members of the House for their
indulgence during my presentation of the
facts in a brief way, I will conclude. I
know there will be weeping and wailing
in the rooms of the Government on this
question. It will be said, "He is at it
again. He will be quoted by Lord
Haw Haw.' This fellow will ruin this
part of the world. We must put a stop
to it. We will have to get a candidate
to challenge him at the next election."
My advocacy to-day is on behalf of those
who are not able to come here and speak
for themselves, and, if I have driven any
wedges home, I hope they will have the
desired result and be in accordance with
my wishes.

Mr. AGNEW: The problem of unemployment has been often brought before
this House. It is one which is not put
forward for the purpose of political
propaganda; it is a question which, in
my opinion, the Government of Northern Ireland has neglected. In 1940
we, who belong to the working-class

unless the Government take action at

future in regard to unemployment and
the alarming figures which have been put

the matter from the point of view of the
breadwinner. Just endeavour to consider
the position of a man who, although willing to work, has suffered through prolonged unemployment. He is denied the
right to work through no fault of his
own, and after many years unemployment he is physically incapable of working because no effort has been made to
bring about a state of society whereby
his labour could be used in something
productive.
Take the wife of an unemployed man.
Her burden is even more heavy. She has
to look very carefully at the little
income she gets from unemployment
benefit, unemployment assistance or outdoor relief. She has to be very careful
to spend the money to the best advantage
in accordance with the needs of her
family. Before she can purchase any of
the necessities of life she must, first of
all, face up to the reality that rent, coal,
light and clothing have to be provided.
With meagre incomes seriously affected by
war conditions and by control and rationing there is bound to be poverty in the
homes of our unemployed owing to the
fact that their purchasing power has been
curtailed. I am certain the Government
must realise that point.

Unemployment
Unemployment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Professor Corkey]
There are a number of things which
the mover and seconder of the motion
have ignored in their speeches. They
have ignored the fact that there has been
a distinct fall in the figures for unemployment since this time last year. This
time last year the actual figure stood at
about 94,000 unemployed. During the
early months of 1939 the figure fell
steadily, until in the month of August
it stood at about 63,000. The figure thus
fell by about one-third. I am bound to
say that since the war started, in spite
of the need for men and munitions, the
figure for unemployment in Northern
Ireland has continued to rise until to-day,
when it stands at about 80,000.
Neither the mover nor seconder of the
motion called any attention at all to the
immense steps taken already by our
Government to mitigate hardships on
those who are unemployed. According to
calculations I saw not very long ago this
Government is spending in social services
every week between £90,000 and £100,000.
There has not been a word said about that;
no notice taken of it at all, but attention
was wholly concentrated on the number
of cases of hardship that still exist. My
colleague for the University has referred
to the fact that we have set ourselves a
very high standard in attempting to
maintain our social services at the same
level as the social services in England, and
if we can do that we shall have done
very well.
Complaints have been made regarding
the rationing schemes in force, but, after
all, these schemes are in the interests of
the poor people. A number of commodities now available to poor people owing
to rationing would otherwise simply be
off the market owing to the selfishness of
people in a better position. They would
very speedily become beyond the purchasing power of the poorer people. These
rationing schemes are being constantly
modified in accordance with the supply to
enable producers to have a fair return
and also to maintain prices within the
reach of the poorer people.
I remember long ago an incident of an
Irishman who was a little bit inebriated.
He was noticing the whirring of the
wheels of a rather old-fashioned phaeton
that was passing by. The front wheels
were very small and the rear wheels were
large, and he was heard to say, "Is it not
wonderful that the little wheels can keep
up with the big wheels." It is rather
wonderful that we in Northern Ireland
have had the audacity, shall I say, to set
before ourselves the task of maintaining
our social services on a level with those
in Great Britain. That is all the more
remarkable by reason of the fact that
within the next few weeks we shall have
a new level to reach by reason of the
enunciation of the policy at Westminster
to increase old-age pensions where they
are most needed, and also to reduce the
age of eligibility for widows' pensions.
A further complaint I would like to
make about the mover and seconder of
the Motion is that there was nothing very
constructive in their Motion. They did
not suggest any particular way in which
these evils they have cited are going to
be remedied. If they had suggested, for
example, the subsidising of Ulster-made
goods for the purpose of export there
would have been something in that idea
and it might have been workable. If
Ulster linen could in some way be subsidised by an amount which would make
it more saleable abroad it might pay the
country as a whole to operate the industry
along. those lines. Again, if they had
suggested the policy of extending guaranteed loans, or the policy of family allowances there would have been something in
the Motion of a constructive and positive
nature.
I believe the policy of family allowance
is one that will come. From references
to it which I have observed in leading
articles in the London "Times" and
other newspapers I believe it is on the
way.
It came in France in the last war,
and I believe it will have to be put into
force in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland to mitigate some of the evils
pointed out to-day. What a feather in
the cap it would have been for the Member for Pottinger if he had enunciated
these family allowances as his policy
instead of allowing me to mention it.
When it does come along he would have
some of the credit for popularising this
scheme, which I believe is inevitable, and
which I think might be put into force in
Northern Ireland.
I think it is possible that in some ways
and at times we might give a lead to
Great Britain. We like to keep in step

with Great Britain, and that is a wise
policy. We have a small area here, and

In regard to the rationing scheme
itself, the seconder of the Motion seemed
to think there was no reason why we in
Ulster should ration ourselves at all. He.
seemed to suggest that the people in
Ulster should retain for their own consumption everything, and in particular
the best, that is produced in Northern
Ireland. That is all right from his point
of view, because he does not at all realise
there is a war on. He is one of those
people who have never yet awakened to
the fact that there is a Hitler in the
world, and that we are threatened with
the loss of our independence and a great
many other things.
We are rationing ourselves voluntarily,
because we desire to co-operate with
Great Britain in resisting this menace to
ourselves at the present time, and really
I do not think that the actual rationing
that has been so far imposed bears very
heavily upon the average member of the
community. Speaking for myself, I find
that the 4 oz. of butter satisfied me quite
well. Possibly at times I could use more,
and did use more, but perhaps I am all
the better for being rationed in this way.
The other members of my family, since
being rationed, have discovered that they
actually use a good deal less each week,
whether it is right or wrong, than the
4 oz. As far as bacon is concerned, I
discovered that at my time of life the
less of it I use the better. I am sorry

issued a regulation under which a

us who are familiar with this matter know
that one cannot go round a large number
of sheep with a light of that kind. I
suggest that the Minister of Agriculture
should ask the Minister of Home Affairs
to get into communication with the
authorities across the water with a view
to getting this relief for the purpose of
sheep lambing.

power to do anything in regard to

turned down. The ordinary drainage
schemes run by the Ministry will be continued provided it is possible to show that
they will bring in extra acreage.

PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
PREVENTION OF FRAUD
(INVESTMENTS) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BARBOUR: This Bill is one
which will, I am sure, commend itself
to all members of the House. It has
been drafted with one object in view,
namely, the protection of the public
against the activities of unscrupulous
share-pushers.
I should like at the outset to make it
perfectly clear that the introduction of
this Measure implies no criticism of those
regular dealers in securities who are such
an essential element in the financial life
of Northern Ireland. Indeed, by combating fraudulent practices against the
public interest the Bill automatically
protects honest and reputable dealers and
safeguards the good
the good name of their
profession.
-
The plundering of the public by misrepresentation of the value of shares or
by dishonest forecasts of their prospective
value is, unfortunately, by no means unfamiliar. There is great truth in the
saying that although you cannot fool all
the people all of the time you can, if your
intentions are dishonest, fool some of the
people. In spite of constant warnings to
the public and exhortations to consult
competent advisers before buying any
stocks or shares, the confidence tricksters and adventurers who prey upon the
public have generally not found it difficult to persuade a number of imprudent
people to part with their money under
the delusion that it will return to them
with substantial accretions.
The tragedy of the situation is that the
victims of this form of exploitation are
not only ignorant of financial matters,
281 Prevention of Fraud Bill-

20 FEBRUARY 1940
Second Reading
but are also as a rule in no position to
afford the loss of their hard-earned
savings.
The plight of victims of share-hawking
and share-pushing is one which has stirred
legislators in the past to attempt the difficult task of devising practicable means
for their protection. This Bill, it is
hoped, will do much to further that aim.
It closely follows the Act recently passed
at Westminster, which was based on the
recommendations of a Committee presided over by Sir Archibald Bodkin in
1937. In Northern Ireland, I am glad
to say, we have had little experience of
the frauds upon the public which in the
past have provided sensational headlines.
for newspapers in Great Britain; but it
will be realised that our contact with
Great Britain is so close that we cannot
ignore the possibility that fraudulent
share-pushers, whose livelihood has been
threatened by legislation in Great Britain,
may turn their attention to the comparatively unexploited field of Northern
Ireland. Generally speaking, the Ulsterman is not the type who believes he can
get something for nothing; but there
may be amongst us those who might
succumb to the temptation offered by a
prospect of easy riches.
The method proposed in the Bill for
the prevention of this type of fraud
includes, first of all, a system of licensing
of dealers in securities. Licences will be
granted under Ministerial authority, and
before they are granted a deposit of £500
will usually be required. It will be an
offence punishable by heavy penalties for
a person to carry on the business of dealing in securities unless he holds such a
licence. In order to make provision for
the overwhelming majority of honest
dealers in securities, there will be exemption from this requirement in favour of
certain classes of persons-for example,
members of recognised stock exchanges,
municipal corporations, industrial and
provident societies, building societies, and
persons acting in the capacity of manager
or trustee under authorised unit trust
schemes.
The Bill also contemplates imposing
limitations upon the registration of
industrial and provident societies, and
giving wider powers of control and supervision to the Registrar of Friendly
Societies. The industrial and provident
society has been termed the poor man's
company, but nevertheless it has been
used elsewhere to carry on business which
would more fittingly be undertaken by companies registered under the Companies
Act. Although difficulties of this nature
have not arisen in Northern Ireland, hon.
Members will, I think, agree that it is
desirable to keep in line with English law
in this respect.
Certain transactions will also be regarded as outside the scope of the restrictions imposed by this section of the Bill,
such as the issuing of a prospectus which
complies with the requirements of the
Companies Act.
The Bill also follows the British Act
by imposing restraint on any building
society whose practices appear to the
Registrar likely to give cause for serious
complaint. Subject to the approval of
the Ministry, the Registrar will be able
to take action to protect the interests of
such a society's investors and depositors
by suspending the activities of the society.
I should, perhaps, explain that this Clause
has been retained in this Bill, and not
included in the Building Societies Bill
which is still before the House, since this
is a provision concerned with that form
of unorthodox financial practice which it
is the purpose of this particular Bill to
prevent.
The Bill also contains general provisions
directed towards the prevention of fraud.
Clause 12 prescribes the penalty of penal
servitude for anybody who induces a person to part with his money under the
conditions of misrepresentation which

being submitted to the Corporation.

Hospital Committee, subject to the

confirmed by the Council. There is,

In moving this Resolution I should like
to explain to the House that in December
last the Unemployment Assistance Board
decided that owing to the increased cost
of living the existing rates of unemployment assistance required revision.
Between the 1st September, 1939, and
the 1st December, 1939, the cost of living
had increased by a little over 11 per
cent. After taking all the circumstances
into account, the Board reached the conclusion that an increase should be made
in the rates of unemployment assistance
and draft regulations were prepared
accordingly and submitted to the Ministry of Labour. The draft was approved
and the substantive regulations, of
which a copy is now before you, were
made by the Ministry and came into
force on the 18th December last.
Briefly, the changes made by the
regulations, which correspond with
changes made by similar regulations in
Great Britain, provide for increases in
the rates amounting to 2s a week in the
case of a man and wife, 1s in the case of
a member of the household who is 16
years old and over, and 6d in the case
of a child under 16. The increase for a
person living alone, including a person
living as a lodger or boarder, will be

ing rent the amending regulations preserve this position in the applicant's

Let us take some of the prices fixed by
the Ministry of Food. Steak has advanced
from 1s to 2s per lb. A whole tongue
used to cost 2s 9d, but it is now sold at
ls 2d per lb. Therefore if a tongue
weighs 4lb. it now costs 4s 8d as against
2s 9d previously. An ox tail could be
procured for 10d or 1s, but it is now ls 2d
per lb. If the average weight of an ox
tail is 3 lb. it means that what previously
cost the consumer 10d or is now costs him
3s 6d, or an increase of over 300 per
cent. The price of kidneys has been

brought into agricultural economics, the
whole fertility of the land would disappear.
I should like hon. Members to
realise that that is not a mere dream.
It has happened already. It has happened in America, and it has happened
in Australia. If you remove all the
organic matter, all the humus, from the
soil, you will destroy the fertility of the
land. If you drive flax production in
this country to an absurd and unreasoning extent you would get a loss of
fertility.
Therefore from the agricultural
economic point of view, you must build
your policy on a livestock policy; that is
what is going to keep up the fertility of
the land. There is the probability, indeed the certainty, that if you did anything else, the fertility of the land would

they find themselves. The position I

should go in for research and an educational and demonstrational campaign.
We left the matter largely to a committee composed of representatives of all
the contributing factors to the raising of
flax. A certain number were to be

number by the spinners, the Linen Industry Research Association and the
scutchers. We left it to each of these
different branches of the trade to select

which had been confided to them. I admit
it may seem to some hon. Members or to
the outside public that the progress made
has been disappointingly slow; but I, on
the other hand, commend them for the
caution with which they approached this
most difficult subject. After all the
growing of flax and the preparation of it
is centuries old. They are dealing with a
subject which has been tried out in
different ways by many different
countries throughout the world, but as
yet the perfect system has not been
found.
It is the intention of the committee to
follow that work up and make such improvements as they may be able to
devise on the flax as turned out by these
turbine scutchers. I think it will improve
very materially the cleaning of Irish flax.
The Irish fibre is quite good. Irish flax
has been at a disadvantage in its irregularity and the poor handling it receives.
Our soil is not as uniform as the soil in
Belgium. You might find one cart load
of flax, consisting of two or three different
qualities, for which the spinner would be
ready to pay different prices. It will
thus be seen that there are disadvantages
in our climate. It is open to doubt
whether our fibre would bring as high a
price as the Belgian, but still Irish fibre
is far ahead of Russian flax and commands a higher price. By efficient
methods of handling we might be able to
add to the value of the Irish crop. Unfortunately, as the hon. Member is aware,
we have to wait a year between our experiments. We may work on this season's crop, and if what we try out is not
a success we have to wait twelve months
until the next experiment can be made.
What this committee did was to go
over to Belgium-the finest flax is produced there and make a study of the
methods pursued there. They engaged
experts there and brought them over here
to put up a plant similar to that in vogue
in Belgium. That was done in order to
demonstrate the Belgian system of
handling flax. Then the matter of
scutching-handling flax is the technical
term-requires a great deal of skill. We
require to be flax-minded and almost to
devote our lives to the handling of flax in
order to get the fibres properly laid
alongside each other so that there is no
waste. That is a matter which I am
afraid our people in Northern Ireland
are not as well up in as they are out in
Courtrai. They have also got one or two
Belgian turbine scutchers at work. Even
that turbine, although it is the latest
machine brought out in Courtrai, is not
perfect; it requires to be worked in conjunction with other processes.
I should be sorry if this Committee or
the money at its disposal were in any way
diverted from the main objects-research,

important that we should do all we can to
stimulate the growth of flax and increase
the sowing as much as we can. I should
be very sorry, indeed, if that necessity
should in any way distract the Committee from improving the methods of

PRICE OF ELECTRICITY.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I presume the hon.

Board. As he will be aware, the board

tariffs on such a basis as will ensure the
balancing of income and expenditure each
year.
The recently announced increases were
rendered necessary by the increase in the
costs of materials as well as in the wages
of labour at a time when lighting restrictions have led to curtailment of revenue.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply, is it a fact that the Electricity
Supply Board purchase their electricity
at the cost of production and is it also
a fact that the producers, who are largely
the Belfast Corporation, have not increased their charges, and if the producers do not increase their charges why
is it that the retailers, the Electricity
Supply Board, do?
Mr. BARBOUR: The circumstances
are hardly similar. In Belfast we have
a compact area and in Belfast the consumption of industrial electricity is far
more than an offset to the decrease in
electricity for lighting purposes while
there is no corresponding offset in the
country districts.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister unintentionally did not reply to the principal
part of my supplementary question. Is
it not a fact that the board purchase their
electricity at the cost of production and
the cost of production has not been increased?
Mr. BARBOUR: I admit the Electricity Board purchase from the Corporation
at the cost of production, but whether
the cost of production has not been increased I do not know.

aware that the public air-raid shelters

Sir DAWSON BATES: As regards

responsibilities of local authorities under
the Air Raid Precautions Act are permanent, and not confined to preparations
for the present war.
In reply to the second part of the

overriding consideration of ensuring that
the provision of air-raid shelter accommodation for the public proceeds as expeditiously as possible, my Department
is always willing to consider proposals
for the construction of buildings which

in such cases the percentage grant would
be related only to that portion of the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: As the hon.
Member is aware, we have as yet done
nothing to stimulate recruiting for a
branch of the Women's Land Army in
Northern Ireland. Our policy has been
to train for the present only those
women who have a reasonable prospect
of obtaining farm jobs, and who are,
therefore, likely to be of immediate
assistance in the food production campaign. Twenty-four such girls have so
far been trained, and all but 3, who
have found employment in other occupations, have gone back to their homes,

present being trained is 8. The cost of
training, including board and lodging,
is approximately 18s 6d per head per
week.

AND KIDNEYS.
16. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
price per lb. at which the following are
sold by his Ministry, acting on behalf of
the Minister of Food, to retail butchers,
viz., ox tails, livers, kidneys, tongues;
whether in view of the high prices
charged for such, many of those people
who formerly purchased them are no
longer able to do so, and whether large
quantities of these commodities have to
be disposed of to Newforge, Ltd., and, if
so, at what price.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The wholesale
prices fixed by the Ministry of Food for
the edible offals to which the hon. Member refers are as follow:-Ox tails, 101d
per lb; ox livers, 10d per lb. ; ox kidneys,
ls 2d per lb., and ox tongues, 101d per lb.
It is a fact that at the start of the
meat and livestock scheme there was a
reluctance on the part of butchers to buy
edible offals. However, purchases of
offals by butchers are now being much
more freely made.
Edible offals have been sold at the
appropriate wholesale prices to Messrs.
Newforge, Limited. In addition, the
Ministry has arranged with Messrs.
Newforge, Limited, for the handling and
storing of any surplus edible offals and
for their disposal as opportunity offers
on a commission basis. All offals so far
disposed of by the firm have been sold
by them at the appropriate wholesale
prices.

INCONVENIENT
RECEIVING
DEPOTS FOR LIVE PIGS.
Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that extreme dissatisfaction is being caused
amongst the farmers of Ballyroney and
surrounding townlands owing to their
having to take their live pigs to receiving
depots at either Newry or Banbridge, a
distance of over fifteen miles in many
instances; whether he would consider
opening a receiving depot at Ballyroney
station, which is in the centre of this
pig producing district, and whether he
will take into account the saving of petrol
in the haulage of these pigs a much
shorter distance and the time saved by
the farmer, who has to accompany his
pigs to the receiving depot.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not aware
of the dissatisfaction to which the hon.
Member refers. I might explain that
the collecting depots at which live pigs
are being purchased from producers by
Government buyers are those which have
been operated for a number of years by
the Pigs Marketing Board. In selecting
these depots the Board had regard to the
supplies of live pigs forthcoming in the
various districts, and it has been found
that the existing disposition of depots has
proved satisfactory from the point of
view of producers generally. On the
grounds of economy and efficiency it is
essential that the number of depots should
be kept down to a minimum. The
position will be reviewed from time to
time, and changes may be found desirable
in the light of experience. I shall see
that the representations of the hon. Member for the establishment of a collecting
depot at Ballyroney station are not overlooked.

to be made in the constitution of the

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill
follows closely the precedent presented by
the Chartered and Other Bodies (Temporary Provisions) Act, passed by the
Imperial Parliament in November last.
It is designed to enable such amendments
The Bill is purely an enabling one and
in general no action will arise on its provisions unless and until application has
been made by a body concerned for
powers under the Act. In response to
such application his Grace the Governor
may, if satisfied that it is necessary and
desirable, give the powers asked for
within the limits laid down in the Bill.
Clause 1 provides that in the case of
chartered bodies the powers sought may
be given by a direction of the Governor.
This process, I think the House will
agree, is less cumbersome and better
suited to purely temporary provisions
than the alternative method of issuing an
amending Charter.
Clause 2 makes similar provision for
bodies incorporated or constituted by
Act, Order in Council, or by a Minister
of the Crown. In this case the powers
will be given by means of Order in
Council.
Clause 3 makes the necessary provision
for Queen's University. The remaining
clauses are supplementary.
Clause 4 makes it possible to give retrospective effect as from September 1
last to the powers given by any direction
or Order in Council, and provides for
variation or revocation of directions and
Orders in Council.
By Clause 5 all local authorities, for
which provision is being made elsewhere,
are excluded, and chartered bodies and
corporations are also excluded if their
activities extend throughout the United
Kingdom, provision for these bodies being
made in the United Kingdom Act.
In Clause 6 the overruling authority
of Parliament, so far as bodies established
under the authority of Parliament are
concerned, is maintained. The Order in
Council will have to lie on the Table of
the House.

Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The main
object of this Bill is to provide for the
suspension of the elections of local government bodies during the war. I think it
will be generally admitted that such a
time as this is not a suitable time for
holding elections or for introducing
matters of local controversy. Candidates, electors, and officials are fully
occupied with work of national importance, and the time which it would be
necessary to spend on local elections,
apart altogether from the difficulties
which the electors would experience in
having to travel to the polling booths,
would, I think, be wasted unnecessarily.
On the other hand, I recognise that to
postpone elections indefinitely might lead
to stagnation, and might not be good for
local government administration. Accordingly, the Bill is limited for one year, so
that the position can be reconsidered and
the period of postponement either extended or curtailed. A similar measure
was passed during the last war, and a
corresponding Act has already been passed
in Great Britain.
option, and I propose to make this the
rule for all local government bodies. It
will be necessary, of course, to hold annual
meetings for the elections of chairmen
and vice-chairmen, and Clause 2 provides.
for the continuance of the usual procedure
for these meetings.
Clause 1 gives effect to the proposal,
as I have said, to postpone the elections,
and provides in addition that casual

by co-option and not by election. At the
present time in the case of certain bodies

On the experience of recent months it
appears probable that the amount will
not be sufficient, and I have accordingly
to ask the House for a further sum of
£10,000. As pensions under this Act to
persons over the age of 70 amount to
£16,000 a week, the House will
appreciate that the sum I am asking for
represents little more than half a week's
requirements for these pensions and that
the original Estimate has turned out to
be very close to the mark. The actual
expenditure on pensions of this class depends on many factors, such as the
number of new claims made in the year,
the average level of means of the
applicants, and the rate of mortality,
which might easily upset our calculations.
I beg to move.

Adjournment.
LOANS TO FISHERMEN.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Lord Glentoran.)
Mr. BROWN: I have no desire to spoil
your chance of getting away early for
once, but I merely desire to say one word.
In the present crisis our admiration goes
out more to fishermen and seamen generally than to anybody else, because they
are carrying on very valuable work in
maintaining the food supplies of the
nation. I have been informed that the
County Down fishermen if they get a loan
are charged by the Government 5 per
cent. I say that the Government, in order
to encourage these County Down fishermen, should give them these loans free of
interest, at least for the duration of the
war. This rate of 5 per cent. is totally
prohibitive. I could say a lot more today, but the appropriate Ministers are
not present. In the meantime, I hope
what I have said will sink in and that
we will eventually get this concession for
our fishermen, who are carrying on very
important and valuable work.
Question put and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at
Ten Minutes after Five
o'clock until Tuesday
next, pursuant to the
Resolution of the House
of this day.

spectively, in which the Pigs Marketing'

FOOD MINISTRY'S PRICE
FOR SOWS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
price charged by his Ministry, acting for
the Ministry of Food, to curers for sows
for which the producer receives 51s per
live cwt., and who gets the advantage of
any difference in price.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The prices
charged by the Ministry, on behalf of
the Ministry of Food, to curers in
Northern Ireland for sows for manufacturing purposes are 86s 4d per dead
cwt. for sows with heads on, and 88s 8d
per dead cwt. for sows with heads off.
The difference between these prices and
the price of 51s per live cwt. paid to
producers accrues to the Ministry of
Food.
The price payable to producers has
been deliberately fixed at the present
level in order to discourage producers
from disposing of their sows, which
should be retained for breeding.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
sows are not the only class of pigs in
which producers are penalised in this way
and whether it is the considered policy of
his Ministry to prevent producers from
getting fair prices for their produce?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think so far
as this particular question is concerned
it is obviously the right policy not to
encourage the destruction of breeding
SOWS.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
BACON CURERS' CONTRIBUTION
TO THE EXCHEQUER.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state what
contribution (if any) the curers have
made to the Exchequer under the terms
of the Bacon Industry Act.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No contributions have been made to the Exchequer
by curers under the provisions of Section
12 of the Bacon Industry Act (Northern Ireland), 1939. Between 1st September, 1939, and 31st January, 1940,
approximately £5,900 was paid in levies
by curers under the Act to the Pig
Industry Fund.
GOLF COURSES FOR SHEEP
GRAZING.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that many of the golf courses in
Northern Ireland which have been
exempted from the operation of the
Tillage Order are not now to be available
for sheep grazing as formerly, owing to
the action of the committees controlling
same; and whether, in view of the fact
that grazing for livestock will be very
materially curtailed owing to the increased tillage, he will take steps to
render available such exempted lands for
sheep grazing.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I was not
aware of any action, such as that indicated by the hon. Member, having been
taken by committees in control of golf
courses. I understand that there are
certain difficulties with which golf clubs
are confronted, such as the provision of
adequate fencing, damage to greens, etc.,
and for these reasons the more general
use of golf courses for sheep grazing may
be impracticable. I welcome the opportunity, nevertheless, to urge golf clubs,
wherever possible, to allow their lands to
be utilised for food production.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware of the fact that at least
six golf clubs in the vicinity of Belfast
absolutely refuse to allow their courses to
be used for grazing sheep, and will he
take steps to see that these lands are made
available for that purpose?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not aware
of that.
NEGLECTED GRANITE INDUSTRY.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he approved of a
booklet issued jointly by his Ministry and
the Industrial Development Council set
up by his Ministry for distribution across
the Channel listing the industries of
Northern Ireland, in which they mentioned cement manufacture and gave a
photograph of the cement-making works
at Magheramorne, but omitted any reference whatever to the competing and more
important granite industry; and whether
in the event of further copies of the booklet being printed he will see that the older
and more valuable granite industry receives the prominence to which it is
entitled.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
The hon. Member will appreciate, however, that the booklet was not designed
to present a detailed account of industrial
activities of Northern Ireland and that
the photograph to which the hon. Member
refers had no descriptive title to indicate
the location, being intended to do no
more than suggest that factories could be
established here in ideal surroundings.
It is unlikely that there will be a reprint of the booklet under present circumstances, but the suggestion in the latter
part of the hon. Member's question will
be borne in mind.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Minister
agree that apart from the photograph the
booklet did mention specifically cement
and not granite? Does he agree that
that is so?
Mr. BARBOUR: That is obvious.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising further out
of the right hon. Gentleman's reply will
he take steps to see that the brickworks
in County Tyrone are also suitably advertised?

MEAT AND LIVESTOCK CONTROL
SCHEME.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state in
what way the meat and livestock control
scheme referred to by him in the House
on 31st October last differs from that
which is now in operation.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Meat and
Livestock Control Scheme, as at present
in operation, has the following main
points of difference from the scheme
originally contemplated:-
(1) All public abattoirs may now be
included in the scheme, and
(2) The rationing of meat to consumers has been excluded, although,
as the hon. Member is no doubt aware,
meat will be rationed to consumers as
from the 11th of this month.
It is probably necessary that I should
add that in the interval between the
postponement of the original scheme and
its coming into operation in its modified.
form, on the 15th of last month, circumstances had arisen which necessitated increases in the different price structures
for the purposes of the scheme. Furthermore, in that interval the original idea
of having one schedule of prices, according to cuts, for all classes of meat, was
abandoned, with the result that the
prices fixed for first-quality meat were
naturally in excess of the "pooled"
prices originally contemplated.
I shall be dealing in more detail with
prices under the scheme in my reply to
another question which the hon.
Member has on the Order Paper to-day.

PURCHASE OF SEED BARLEY.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is now in a position
to make any statement implementing the
assurance given in his personal letter to
all farmers at the beginning of January
that the necessary supplies of seed
barley for sowing this year would be
forthcoming at prices within the farmers'
reach.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir.
Thanks to the assistance of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
the Ministry has been able to buy several
thousand tons of seed barley in England.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, has agreed with me that the
barley shall be made available to our
farmers at our country merchants'
stores at the price at which we have purchased it in England-approximately
17s 9d a cwt. Our farmers will thus
get seed barley at the same price as
English farmers can buy one from another. Full particulars of the arrangements will be in the hands of all local
merchants who deal in seeds to-day. I
am most anxious that farmers should
place their orders for seed barley at once.
Supplies will reach these merchants in
a few days, but we must be in a position
to know what quantities to send out to
the various districts.
to
I think it necessary to warn farmers
that they cannot expect the present
favourable position with regard
supplies of maize meal to continue. The
situation next winter with regard to
maize may be even more difficult than it
was this winter, and every farmer who
hopes to be able to maintain his pig and
poultry stock must SOW barley this
spring. I cannot emphasise this fact too
strongly, and I am most anxious that
every possible help will be given me in
driving the fact home. There is a
certain reluctance to grow barley, but if
farmers will lime their land before sowing they should experience no difficulty
in growing a good crop.
There are two very vital factors. We
need every possible acre under the plough,
and every acre suitable for growing barley
sown to barley. The next six weeks will
determine our success or otherwise.
Farmers in England and Scotland are
ploughing day and night. I am counting
on our farmers utilising to the full every
possible hour and being thoroughly alive
to the necessity in their own interests of
growing barley.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): With your
permission, I will deal with the four sup-
The details of the additional sum required are very fully set out in the Estimate. The additional sum of £700 for
legal charges is mainly required for meeting a contribution towards costs of litigation in a case where the situation of
property for the purpose of Estate Duty
gave rise to important issues affecting our
revenue from Estate Duty. The case
was taken to the House of Lords by the
solicitors acting for the executors in a
particular case. In view of the desire
of the Government to obtain a judicial
decision and of the financial issues in
question, it was agreed to make a contribution towards the legal costs involved. Unfortunately a decision adverse
to Northern Ireland interests was given,
and as the Ministry had agreed to pay a
sum of £600 towards the legal costs involved additional provision under Subhead D becomes necessary.
The sum required for the expenses of
administration of the Ulster Savings
Committee is provision for part of a year
only. In view of the fact that 75 per
cent. of the proceeds of the new War
Issue of our Ulster Certificates is being
lent to the Imperial Government the
latter have undertaken to make a substantial contribution towards meeting
these expenses, and consequently the net
amount only is required to be voted.
With regard to the Stationery and
Printing Estimate, additional provision
on Subhead B is required to meet the cost
of various reports issued by committees
held last year.
On Subhead C there has
been an increased purchase and sale of
Imperial publications largely occasioned
by new publications which have appeared
as a result of the war. With regard to
the supplies to public departments
additional provision has been required
for the printing of Ulster Savings Certificates, and for various supplies of firstaid books, etc., to the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
In addition, owing to the expansion of
departments due to the war an extra
supply of typewriters and similar
machines has been purchased. In some
cases these supplies are for Agent Departments, from some of which it is not
anticipated that repayment will be received until next year. The increases in
the receipts are self-explanatory.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In reply to
the points raised by the hon. Member
for Woodvale, I will deal first with the
£1,000 payable to the registrars of stock
in respect of management expenses of
Northern Ireland 33 per cent. stock,
1950-54. The hon. Gentleman asked
why this item was not included in the
original estimate. The explanation is
that the estimates came out last March,
and the loan was not issued until the
summer. The amount named is paid to
the Government's bankers as registrars of
stock for keeping a record of all the
transactions. As to the £5,000 item in
Receipts Appropriated in Aid, this is a
deficiency owing to the programme of
works being put off as a result of the
war. The agency work is not being
carried out, and we receive £5,000 less.
The hon. Member referred to the
administration of the Ulster Savings
Committee. In this connection I think
the House will realise that it is quite
impossible to run a national savings
campaign without a staff to encourage
the people to save and to supervise the
work. It is quite true that anybody can
buy these war savings certificates through
the banks, but there are many small
people who do not deal with banks, and
they are the people whom we wish to
encourage to save for the purpose of
winning the war. For the staff employed
the total amount payable since this committee was set up comes to £800.
When the House considers that the
actual sum received up to 24th February
was £648,381, and that the actual cost
was only £800, I do not think they will
agree with the hon. Member that the expenditure has been extravagant. There
must be an organisation to encourage
the people to save. The Post Office is
also engaged in this work, and we pay
it £3,000 for agency expenses. The Imperial Government will receive 75 per
cent. of the proceeds, and, as I have said,
the amount recoverable from the Imperial
Government in respect of administration
is £3,320.
it was quite true that bonds could be

£200,701, and an additional gross provision of £26,250 is now required. With

Stationery, Superannuation, etc. I beg

The second Clause of the Bill will, I

any local

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not at

been moved and seconded, but I do
Hon. Members are aware that Parliament has long ago laid down a certain
procedure to be followed by local
authorities who may desire to promote a
Bill for private purposes of their own.
A great many Members have sat on such
committees. This procedure provides
very stringent safeguards to ensure that
a local authority shall not embark upon
special legislation for its own purposes,
without the ratepayers of that authority
being given a full opportunity to decide
whether the local authority shall proceed
with this Bill or not. As soon as a local
authority decides to promote a Bill by
way of a private Measure the proposals
contained in that Bill must be approved
of by a special resolution of the local
government electors for that particular
area. I rather suggest from what I know
that the hon. Member opposite wishes to
avoid having such a meeting. Further,
if at that meeting a resolution approving
of the Measure has been passed, and if
any five persons demand a poll, then a
plebiscite must be taken of all the electors
in that particular area.
I only want to dwell on this to show
that Parliament feels that the electors
must be protected against anything in
the way of ram-stam legislation. I feel
that hon. Members will agree that this
is a safeguard from the point of view
of the ordinary elector who has not the
privilege of being a member of the local
authority. I suggest that this safeguard
should not be lightly done away with at
the present time. I have never known
a case where an attempt has been made
to adopt the course proposed by the hon.
Member.
The hon. Member has given a history
of this Measure. Let me give my version

For the past fifty years it has been
the pratice of Parliament to require local
authorities who are proposing to introduce legislation affecting their own area,
to comply with certain regulations laid
down in the Borough Funds Act. That
is done for the protection of the

electorate, to avoid the possibility of
Parliament having foisted upon it
measures introduced at the instance of
individuals, and to avoid taking up the

procedure laid down under such circumstances is that there shall be in the local
authority promoting the Bill an absolute
majority of all the members. A second
meeting has to be held at which their
action has got to be confirmed, and when
that is done it is required by the Borough
Funds Act that there shall be a meeting
of the electorate.
In connection with this matter the
Belfast Corporation, in the year 1928,
called a meeting of the electors for the
purpose of promoting a Private Bill.
The electors on the only occasion upon
which this matter was presented to them
turned it down, and the Belfast Corporation were not allowed to proceed with
the Bill in this House. This matter
having already been considered by the
electorate of the city in the manner laid
down by Parliament, I suggest it would
not be proper for the House to pass this
Bill. It should compel the Corporation
to introduce this as a Private Bill and
compel them to go through the procedure
laid down by Parliament and which has
been uniformly adhered to since the year
1888 in the Imperial Parliament and
since this Parliament was established.
As a matter of constitutional practice
I do suggest to the House that every
Member who respects Parliamentary
procedure should vote against the Bill on
that ground. I might say that so far
as the Bill is concerned I am entirely in

Private Bill I am prepared to do so in

You may rely upon us giving you all
the assistance, official and unofficial,
within our power.
There is an alternative way, and I think
it would be a great pity if we departed
from our Parliamentary procedure in
connection with a matter which has been
under consideration since 1924 and which
only reaches us now in this particular
way.

At the outset I wish to say that I am
not in any way proposing a vote of
censure on the Government. No one
realizes more than I do what has already
been done by our Government towards
providing work for the unemployed in
Northern Ireland. We all know and
appreciate the number of new industries
that have already been started during
the last year or two, and which will grow
and become more important units of industry as the years go by. But we have
only begun to tap the resources of our
Province. Much more can still be done.
are

getting more than perhaps most

make use of the great facilities which we
are most anxious to offer. We want to
train our men at home and fit them for

here instead of sending them to England.
In order to do this we require at least

people.

Such a

In summing up, the conclusion of the
whole matter is-We want more employment. My suggestions are:-(1) Additional factories; (2) increased orders for
existing small workshops; (3) utilisation.
of our youth movements to mobilise the

Member for Ballynafeigh has said,

I want to see more work going to the

I have asked about work here, but

I would like to see things booming at

to go even further than that. I want

an owner
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I cannot claim
that there are no complaints in individual cases as to the grading of cattle
under the Meat and Livestock Scheme,
but I certainly have no reason for believing that in general farmers are not
quite satisfied with such grading.
Cattle are purchased on a live weight
basis at a price fixed having regard to
the estimated killing out percentage of
the individual beast.
As I have explained in reply to another question which the hon. Member
has on the Order Paper to-day,
my
Ministry is precluded from giving particulars of the nature indicated by him.
All letters addressed to my Ministry
and seeking information receive replies,
although for the reason which I have
given requests for information of this
particular character cannot be acceded
to.
Mr. MINFORD: I would like to ask

weight brought about from the live
weight. How is the conclusion arrived
at? I think it is an impossibility for anyone to estimate the dead weight from the
live weight.

weight, because it would educate the

up to? I think there is no reason why

to educate the farmers as to what is the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am sure the
House would be surprised if they saw
the extreme accuracy of these officers.
Unfortunately I cannot give the exact
figures. But I have watched them personally, and they are accurate to within
a very small margin.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do not think
there is any real necessity to educate the

and the Ministry are looking after his

6 MARCH 1940
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Owners of
butter which my Ministry requisitioned
in October on behalf of the Ministry of
Food, have in general already received
an advance on compensation of 100s per
cwt. The amount of the balance which
is payable under the Compensation
(Defence) Act, 1939, is at present under
consideration in the British Treasury, who
are the responsible Department in this
matter.
My Ministry is in close touch with
them, and I am pressing for a settlement which will be both speedy and as
favourable to Northern Ireland interests
as is possible within the terms of the
Compensation Act. I have been promised
by the Ministry of Food that this settlement will soon be made, but special difficulties have arisen owing to the wide
variety of types, grades and qualities of
butter taken over.
I can
assure the hon. Member that
Northern Ireland owners will not be
behind owners in Great Britain in obtaining the balance due to them. In the
meantime, interest on this balance is
accruing and will accompany the final
payment of compensation.

A further point why we considered it

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes. The real
reason is this, and it is an important one
to notice. We have in this country a

shipped to Birkenhead it might be a long

cattle deteriorating and have the farmer

Member might argue "Why do you not
kill the beasts and send them across?"
The difficulty is that there are not enough
ships to carry so many carcases across
every week. You come down to the one
way of grading and that is the estimation
of live weight. Here I think the producers have got to have confidence in me
and in the Ministry's staff. So far as I
am concerned the only thing I am
interested in seeing is that the farmers
can get the best I can give them. The
