resulted in savings on the original
Estimate of £18,000, or £9,000 a month.
The Force remained in the drill category
for two months only, for upon the out-
By reason of the lengthy period for
which most members of the Force have
been performing the usual nightly
patrols and the consequent absence of
facilities for the usual drills and training, it has also been considered desirable
to organise courses of intensive training
for the sub-district commandants and
non-commissioned officers of the Force
for which purpose these are being
mobilised at full-time rates of pay for
a period of a fortnight in each case.
The basic rate of pay for members of
the Force engaged on full-time duties
has been raised from 7s per day to 9s
per day. It was realised that, while the
former rate was probably adequate to
cover short periods of mobilisation such
as, for instance, during the Twelfth July
celebrations, which did not interfere with
the men's usual employment, it was not
adequate in respect of periods of wartime mobilisation which would entail
acceptance of service with the Special
Constabulary as an alternative to civilian
employment. The total amount of additional expenditure involved by the
mobilisations for protective and training
purposes at the increased rates is
estimated to amount to £37,000 in all
in the current financial year.
Vote No. 4 will be dealt with by my
right hon. and learned Friend the
Attorney-General.
The fifth Vote relates to prisons. The
additional provision is required because
the number of prisoners in custody was
greater than was anticipated, and the
cost of feeding has risen owing to the
general rise in the cost of foodstuffs. The
employment of additional staff at Belfast
Prison and subsequently at Londonderry
Prison was due to the number of persons
interned under the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Acts. Incidental expenditure for travelling and subsistence
allowances in respect of staff transferred,
and for the purchase of bedding was also
involved. I will be happy to answer any
Supplementary Estimates-

Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
questions on these Estimates. I have
dealt with them fairly fully, and I beg to
move.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Since I became a
Member of this House I have consistently supported every Estimate put
forward by the Ministry of Home Affairs
and I intend to support this Estimate as
well. I do not always agree with every
little detail of the Ministry, but I want
to pay a tribute to the Minister and his
officials for the way in which they discharge the very onerous duties placed
upon them.
I would like to say in regard to the
Road Fund, to which reference has been
made by the hon. and learned Parliamentary Secretary, that I intended to
say a great deal more about this Road
Fund grant were it not for the fact that
a very influential deputation waited upon
the Minister of Finance and the Minister
of Home Affairs some time ago, and the
Minister of Finance, in that very persuasive way in which he can deal with
deputations, issued to us a memorandum,
in which he said that when there was anything in the Road Fund he would guarantee that we would get it out. With that
we had to be content. I hope, seeing
that the motorists are contributing very
largely to this Fund, that in the near
future we will get it restored.
There are just one or two other items
in the Estimates to which I would like
to refer sympathetically. First of all
there is the Prisons Vote. As a Visiting
Justice to His Majesty's Prison in
Belfast, I would like to pay a tribute to
the sympathetic and tactful way the
governor, his deputy, and all the officials
discharge their duties in that prison.
They have sometimes a very difficult task
to perform, and I think they do it as
efficiently as the members of any staff
could do it. The Visiting Justices are
perfectly satisfied that the Ministry of
Home Affairs are giving them and the
officials all the help they can, so that those
people who are unfortunately thrown into
prison, when they have served their
sentences and come out, have an opportunity of starting a useful life again.
that the Minister and the Ministry ought
to get all the financial assistance they can
in these difficult times, in order not only
to deal with the offenders who are put
into prison, but to see that all who are
cast in there are dealt with fairly and
squarely. There should be a sufficient
staff employed in the prisons, and that
staff should be protected in every possible
way. I hope that if those in charge call.
for extra assistance during troublous
times the Minister will not be too parsimonious, but will listen to those appeals.
As one of the Visiting Justices and as a
Member of this House, I can assure
him that I will support even an increased
Vote in connection with this Estimate.
The increase in the Estimate to-day is
due to the increased cost of foodstuffs
and other things to which I do not want
to refer. I do, however, want to say
I should like to say a word about the
Constabulary. They are doing good
work, and though, as in the case of
Members of Parliament, there may be
black sheep amongst them, I think as a
force we have a right to be proud of our
Royal Ulster Constabulary and the work
they are doing. I would like to pay a
tribute to them. I come across them
very often throughout the length and
breadth of County Tyrone and other
places. For the Special Constabulary I
want to say a special word. In County
Tyrone we look to the Constabulary, but
we look a little more, I may say, to the
Specials to protect us along the Border.
I hope the Ministry will see to it that
a sufficient force of Constabulary and
Special Constabulary are there in order
to quell any trouble that may arise and
to preserve the peace, which I am glad
to say reigns in the Border counties
to-day.
no
There may be influences at work in
different parts, but I am glad to say that
in the two Border counties of Tyrone
and Fermanagh there has been
trouble for quite a considerable period of
time. I believe that that is due to two
things; first of all, to the sound commonsense of the people who reside in those
two counties, and then to the fact that
we have a strong police force and a
strong Special police force whom I see
on the roads nightly. They give a great
deal of confidence to the law-abiding
people and also deter those who would
do ill. I support this Vote wholeheartedly, and as the Member for South
Tyrone I pay a tribute to those very
efficient bodies of men.
Question put, and agreed to.

7 MARCH 1940
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 7th March, 1940.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PROHIBITION OF BAG-NETS.
1. Rev. R. MOORE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
difficulties of those engaged in the coastal
fisheries of Northern Ireland owing to
their being compelled to use drag-nets
instead of bag-nets; whether, in view of
the need for obtaining all possible supplies of home food during war time, the
shortage of skilled men to operate the
drag-nets and the unsuitability of many
of the sites around our northern coasts
for the use of these nets, he will agree
to the substitution for the period of the
war, of one bag-net for every two dragnets, and whether it is the policy of his
Ministry that the vested interests in the
inland fisheries of Northern Ireland
should have preferential consideration
over those engaged in the precarious business of coastal fishing.
The considerations underlying the Committee's suggestion and the policy of the
Government in reference to this matter
do not appear to me to be affected by
war-time circumstances. Even under
present conditions, when it is in the
national interest to increase our supplies
of food as much as possible, the Government must have regard to the continuing
conservation of our valuable salmon
fisheries. I am satisfied that the substitution of bag-nets for fixed draft-nets in
the proportion suggested by the hon.
Member would have the effect of depleting the salmon stocks to a dangerously low
level.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am aware of the
difficulties outlined by the hon. Member,
but I regret that I am unable to accede
to his request for the substitution of one
bag-net for every two fixed draft-nets.
The hon. Member is, no doubt, aware
that this problem has engaged my attention on several occasions during the past
10 years. A committee was appointed in
1930 to enquire into the whole subject,
and their report, while sympathetic to
the difficulties under which the owners
of the fixed draft-nets are obliged to
operate, made a recommendation somewhat on the lines of what the hon.
Member suggests, but that recommendation was evidently not acceptable to the
fishing interests concerned. The practical
application of that recommendation would
have entailed the formulation of a COordinated scheme by the owners themselves, and, as the hon. Member will be
aware, no such scheme has yet been formulated.
With reference to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I cannot accept
the suggestion that the Government is
according preferential consideration to
any vested interest, in maintaining the
position which was established by the
Legislature in 1863, after an exhaustive
investigation of the causes which had
brought about the depleted stocks of
salmon in Irish rivers.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have a brief in
this matter and I hope the Minister will
not mind my asking this. It says that
Mr. Barbour and the river interests were
totally disagreed on the change. Is it a
fact that the right hon. Gentleman himself has any river interests? That is
what I want to know.
Mr. BARBOUR: None whatever.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thanks very much.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement, I think I am right
in saying he said that the decision was
based on something that happened in
1863. I may have made a mistake, but
if that is the Minister's statement does
he think the world has not advanced
since 1863 and that what was proper in
the matter of vested interests in 1863 is
still proper so far as Northern Ireland
is concerned?
Mr. BARBOUR: I have carefully
watched so far as I could the exports and
catches of salmon since then, and unfortunately the catch of salmon does not
seem to have been increasing during that
time. In very many rivers salmon is
seasonal and goes in cycles, and the
results vary from year to year. For the
Oral Answers

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.]
last two or three years the catch of
salmon seems to have been small and not
such that it would have been judicious to
increase the nets of the catchers.
EXTRA SUGAR FOR JAM MAKING.
2. Rev. Mr. MOORE (on behalf of Sir
Norman Stronge) asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he will make representations to the Ministry of Food for an
extra allowance of sugar to be made to
householders for the purpose of making
apple jam or jelly on a similar basis to
that allowed for marmalade; and
whether, in view of the fact that marmalade is largely made from imported fruit,
and that large quantities of home-grown
apples are going to loss in the country,
his Ministry does not consider that this
would be in the interests of fruit growers
and householders in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BARBOUR: I understand that
the divisional food officer has already
brought to the notice of the Ministry of
Food the position with regard to the
Northern Ireland apple crop, and that
he recently suggested to the Ministry the
desirability of issuing permits to householders for the purpose of making jam
from fruits other than bitter oranges. It
appears, however, that the balance of
sugar available after the needs of consumers, trade users, and industry have
been met, is not sufficient to warrant an
extension of the scope of the present
scheme beyond marmalade-making from
bitter oranges, and that it has not been
possible to make a concession even in
respect of closely allied fruits such as
sweet oranges and grape-fruit.
INTEREST ON LOANS TO
FISHERMEN.
Mr. BARBOUR: The present rate of
interest chargeable on fishery loans repayable within five years is, as stated by
the hon. Member, 5 per cent. This rate
applies to loans made on and since 6th
October last and, from the borrower's
point of view, is the most favourable rate
applicable to loans made from the
Government Loans Fund. Although,
owing to the war, the rate is higher than
at any time since 1932, I do not consider
that, in comparison with the terms available from other sources, to-day's rate can
be regarded as excessive, nor that it is
having the effect suggested in the hon.
Member's question. On the contrary,
the total amount of loans applied for by
fishermen during the last few months is
greater than that applied for during the
corresponding period for a number of
years past. I regret that I can hold out
no hope of the granting of the concession
referred to in the final part of the
question.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware that
the interest of five and one-eighth per
cent. charged on loans to fishermen is
regarded as grossly excessive, and is preventing such loans being availed of to
any appreciable extent, and whether, in
view of the increased importance and
hazards of the industry in war time, his
Ministry will, for the duration of the
war at least, grant such loans free of
interest.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's admission, does he think it
does not savour of profiteering to borrow
money at 33 per cent. and lend it to poor
people at 5 per cent.?
Mr. BARBOUR: The rate is applicable no matter what the means of the
borrower may be.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister
tell us why this rate should be higher
in Northern Ireland than in Great
Britain?
KILKEEL AND ANNALONG
HARBOURS.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether, in view of the valuable part played by the fishing industry
in maintaining food supplies and the increasing extent and importance of the
potato exporting trade, the Government
is prepared to give grants for the carrying out of much needed improvements at
the harbours of Kilkeel and Annalong.
Mr. BARBOUR: I regret that in the
present state of financial stringency due
to the war I can hold out no hope of
grants being made available for the purpose referred to by the hon. Member.

Mr. BROWN: Is there any more

DERRY LABOUR PARTY'S
RESOLUTION.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he has received the
following resolution: "This mass meeting of Derry citizens, called by the
Derry Labour Party, demands that the
practice of sending unemployed citizens
away to England or to Scotland to work
be stopped at once, and that there be no
victimisation of either unemployed who
refuse to go, or of those who return
unable to stand the intolerable conditions. Further, this meeting demands
the immediate abolition of the means
test; increases in benefit and assistance
to meet the rising cost of living, and
work schemes at Trade Union rates of
pay for Derry's unemployed," and, if
so, can he state why these conditions are
being imposed upon our workers.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon) I have received a copy of the
Resolution to which the hon. Member
refers. The facilities provided by the
Northern Ireland Exchange Service for
the transfer of applicants to employment
in Great Britain, free of expense to
themselves, have proved of great value.
to our unemployed workers, who, I am
glad to say, are usually not only willing,
but anxious, to take up work in Great
Britain. The withdrawal of these
facilities would, I am convinced, be most
detrimental to the interests of our people.
As regards the other matters referred
to in the Resolution, the hon. Member
is aware that it is the declared policy of
this Government, for reasons well known
and repeatedly approved by Parliament,
to keep our social services identical in
conditions and standards with those in
Great Britain.
Furthermore, I must remind the hon.
Member that under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts a claimant is disqualified
for benefit if he refuses to accept suitable
employment offered to him. No question
of victimisation arises. An applicant
who refuses employment is given every
opportunity of stating his reasons, and
it is for the statutory authorities to
decide whether these are sufficient to
justify his refusal. I should add that
the umpire has held in many instances
that the fact that the employment
offered was in Great Britain did not
make it unsuitable for persons in Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Minister aware
that I had an unemployed man here
yesterday-an able-bodied man-who has
a job to go to in Glasgow and wants
nothing from the Ministry except £1 to
take him over? Will the Minister give
him that £1.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is he not aware
there are 1 millions unemployed in
Great Britain, and in view of that
situation why is it necessary to send unskilled labour from Northern Ireland to
the Orkneys and other isolated districts
at 1s 2d per hour? In view of the unsatisfactory answer of the Minister I will
raise this whole question on the
adjournment of the House.

of the programme for Mr. Burgin's visit.
Time will not permit of his visiting

The answer to the last part of the

Mr. BROWN: May I ask the noble
Lord to bear in mind, while I thank
him for his reply, that in addition to
many sites for new factories in the
provincial areas, we have also many dis-

were
The officer in question was recruited
into the Civil Service in 1921 in the
usual way, regard being had to the
duties he was then called upon to perform. He was transferred to my
Ministry in 1936, and last September,
shortly after the outbreak of war, I
selected him to become my Private
Secretary. This is in accordance with
the usual practice of Ministers, the only
consideration being suitability for the
post, and I have had no reason to
regret my choice.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The total remuneration of my Private Secretary is
£480 per annum, and no part of that
remuneration is attributable to the
tillage campaign.
With regard to my speeches I may be
allowed to point out to the hon. Member
that I do not, as a rule, speak from
manuscript. In respect of the few formal
speeches which I recollect making between
the outbreak of war and the 19th

summaries of those speeches or my own
notes were supplied to the local Press
representatives in attendance at the
various meetings, as well as to the Belfast
Press.
With regard to the tractor demonstration at Stormont, invitations were sent to
the four Belfast papers, but the demonstration was also extensively advertised
and any representatives of the provincial Press who cared to attend would have
been very welcome. Copies of the statement which I made to the Press on the
occasion were circulated to all papers in
Northern Ireland.

credit facilities in the shape of interestfree advance payments as are to be given
by the Ministry of Supply in Great
Britain, and whether the Government
will grant interest-free advance payments
of £10 per acre to farmers growing flax
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not aware
that credit of the nature referred to, free
of interest, is given by the Ministry of
Supply to flax growers in Great Britain.
The requirements of farmers in Northern
Ireland in this respect are adequately met
by the Ministry's scheme of loans, under
which advances are made to farmers for
the purchase of all classes of seeds and
fetilisers. This scheme has recently been
revised and the conditions made still
easier in that sureties for the loans are
no longer necessary. There is, therefore,
no need to make arrangements such as
those referred to in the latter part of the
question.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister tell
us why the same facilities are not given
to flax growers here as in Great Britain?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think the
hon. Gentleman is under a misapprehension. There are no credit facilities
given to flax growers in England.
MIXED FEEDING STUFFS.
10. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to a letter signed "Oppressed
Farmer" in the "Northern Whig" of
1st March, 1940, stating that cattle, pigs
and poultry are refusing to eat the
present mixed feeding stuffs, that 80,000
stock-owners in Northern Ireland are
having the same trouble, and warning
the Ministry that if they do not stop
the present mixture and supply straight
feeding stuffs the writer will take the
shortest route to clear out his entire
stock; and whether he can hold out any
hope of this request being granted.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have seen the
letter to which the hon. Member refers.
As I think I have already indicated to
the hon. Member, it was necessary, in
order to secure anything like equitable
distribution, to allocate available supplies of feeding stuffs to importers,
millers, mixers, merchants and farmers
alike strictly on the basis of pre-war consumption. In view of the shortage of
feeding stuffs prevailing during the earlier
months of the war, the Ministry had no
Oral Answers
Vote on Account
7 MARCH 1940
alternative to the prescription of mixtures
in order to make the best possible use
of the limited supplies then available.
As I announced in the House on 13th
February, however, my Ministry has now
made arrangements whereby millers and
mixers are prohibited from using as
mixtures more than one-third of the supplies allocated to them, and also from
including in certain mixtures any ingredients which are not included in the
Maximum Prices Order. The effect of
the new arrangement is that approximately two-thirds of available supplies
are now issued to farmers in the form of
straight meals, and reports reaching my
Ministry indicate a consequent considerable improvement in the position which
is still being closely observed.
Mr. NIXON: Does the House understand from the Minister's reply that he
takes serious notice or any notice of
anonymous letters ?

The PRIME MINISTER: I only rise
really to deal with one particular point
in the hon. Member's speech. Since the
Government was established in 1921 my
colleagues and I have been extremely
anxious to get the farming community
out of what we might almost call the rut
of borrowing. As the years went on one
became more and more acquainted with
the life which the farmers led in the
country districts, how much they owed
to the banks and, I am sorry to say, to
the gombeen men. It was the desire and
anxiety of my colleagues and myself to
try to tackle this problem from the very
bottom. We began in those days under
Sir Edward Archdale to tackle the small
farmers first, because they were in those
days in a parlous condition. From that
day to this, by taking a more personal
interest in the smaller farming community, we have, I think, accomplished
a good deal in the way of relieving them
from many of the burdens which were unnecessary, and which generally
through their own carelessness and bad
farming. By the encouragement given
to them by the Ministry from those days
up to the present we have been enabled
to elevate the farmer, and I think he is
to-day in the position I would rather like
to describe as a yeoman farmer. The
yeoman farmer has confidence in himself
and is now in a position which he was
richly entitled to claim.
arose
All through the motive, if I may use
the term, was to try to keep the farming
community out of debt. The local banks
are very convenient to the farmers. They
get good terms from those banks which
do their best to assist them in any way
they can. With that co-operation,
coupled with the sincere desire of the
Government for their welfare, the
farmers have got themselves into a very
much better position than ever they
were before. The tone of the hon. Member's speech was to the effect that the
Government ought to, as it were, force
upon the farming community a loan in
order that they may buy seed to sow flax,
oats and barley or whatever crop it may
be.
They are getting the £2 per acre for
cutting up land, and this will put
them in a certain amount of funds.
Bankers to my knowledge-some if not
all-have certainly through their
managers shown it to be their desire, as
it is the desire of the Government, to
foster the growing of flax as much as
possible in order to facilitate the export
of our linens to foreign countries with a
view to securing dollars abroad. That
shows that the banks will be able to give
any little temporary assistance individual farmers may require without our
forcing on them to take a loan from the
Government, which only means that
when they are paid for the crop in the
end the loan will be deducted from the
result. I think most of them, indeed
practically all, would much prefer to
finance these things in their own way
locally and get the full reward for the
crop when it is paid for.
There are two or three explanations
which I would like to make. The hon.
Member suggested that there was a
differentiation in the rate of interest
charged, because in England it is 5 per
cent. and here it is 5 per cent. As my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Commerce, explained to the House to-day in
answer to a question, the fact that
interest has risen does not curtail the
desire or the demand where it arises for
help when help is really needed. May
I give the comparable figures for the
past three years, not for agricultural but
for fishery loans? The same thing
naturally applies. In 1938 loans amounting to £1,129 were granted and the rate
was 3 per cent.; in 1939 there were five
loans amounting to £1,071 at 3 per
cent., and in the first two months of this
year there were nine loans-that is,
double the number last year-amounting
to £1,712 when the rate was 5 per cent.

[The Prime Minister]
That shows that it is only when there
is real pressure the demand is made, and
what the interest may be on these small
amounts does not make much difference.
Of course, as far as I remember, there
has always been a slight differentiation
between the rates ruling in Great Britain
and the rates ruling here, although I
may say that the actual borrowing of the
short-dated bonds for the Government
here is practically the same as in the
London market. I think I am right in
saying there is hardly a fraction between
the rates of interest for short loans in
England and short loans here. That
shows the extraordinarily fine credit
which Ulster has for raising money in
the London market.

time.

We hear a lot about the policy of the
Government in regard to the growing of
flax. You know what happened; you
know it better than I do. At the time
of the Ottawa Conference, which was
composed of representatives from all
parts of the British Empire, you sent
over delegates with specific instructions to
oppose any move to put a tax on foreign

the Prime Minister congratulated the

in succeeding in having foreign flax,

when the Import Duties Committee was

foreign flax, including Russian flax.

made in the courts is because there is no
right to do so in the civil courts against
the Crown as to any moneys due. I
would ask the Minister in this case of
Miss Florence Glass why it was she was
not given the right to say yes or no to
her case being heard before a full court.
No full court was constituted on the
occasion. A decision was given against
her in the absence of members of the
court on the first occasion as having left
her work voluntarily, and on a previous
occasion as not being available for work.
She is now suffering the penalty of
unemployment insurance benefit by
decisions which, in my opinion, could not
be justified before any fair or reasonable
court. On that ground Miss Glass has
a right to a re-hearing of her case. I
think the correspondence speaks for itself.
The Parliamentary Secretary being the
gentleman who was dealing with the case,
I prefer to hand it to him, and hope he
will re-examine it in the light of the
circumstances I have given. I think he
will agree with me that there could be
no justification for disallowance. Availability must be wiped out by one thing
only. You must, by getting a period of
employment, prove that you are available
for work. She cannot prove that on these
grounds. She cannot get a period of employment in her own town at the moment
as things are not suitable. Therefore,
availability will continue on the Kathleen
Mavourneen style. That is unfair to this
young lady, who went to England on two
occasions and found work. She suffers a
continuity of disallowance.
I come now to the Orkney Island cases. I
claim that this labour should be recruited
from England, Scotland and Wales.
There are upwards of 14 million unemployed in those areas. That refers mainly
to unskilled labour, because all the skilled
labour is used up there. England, Scotland and Wales, therefore, should have
at command a supply of labour equal to
the demand for the Orkney Islands job.
Englishmen and Scotsmen are not so

Then the Minister thought “We cannot be too severe in this one district, we
will change our tactics." He made an
attack on Londonderry. He proceeded
to Derry City, the loyal town, one of
the towns which helped to place the
Minister where he is at the moment.
The workers of Derry City were
pelled under the threat of stoppage of
benefit payments to go to the Orkney
Islands. The same thing happened as in
Strabane-disallowance and persecution
not of the individuals alone but of their
families. When he found failure in that
area he came back to the City of Belfast.
You can take it from me you are not
going to get off so easily in Belfast as in
Strabane and Derry. At the moment
there are 30 returns from the Orkney
Islands. These men made a reasonable
effort to carry on the work. When they
were being sent they agreed to go for
a period of three months. They went
for that period, but the conditions during
the three months were intolerable and
the hardships severe. The lodging conditions at their command were bad and
inhuman. Their homes here were being
broken up as they could not afford a
decent amount out of their wages to keep
their families. The men at the end of
three months decided "We will return
home, it is better to go home and starve
than starve in the Orkney Islands."
The men returned home, and what
does the Minister do? He puts the
charge about them leaving their work
voluntarily. The men are now home;
they have no money, although they
did three months there. As one of
them said to me: "Jack, I would prefer
to do three months in Crumlin Road
any time to doing one month in the employment we were compelled to take
across the Channel." I do not think
those men are laggards or lazy or unwilling to take up reasonable employment. I believe they are anxious and
willing to take it, but let the employment be decent and let the return be
equal to the demands made upon them
by their wives and families.
To ask any
man, who has a wife and
family, to
proceed from here to Great Britain at
ls 2d an hour is outrageous and unreasonable. It never was done in
normal times. It was never expected
that unskilled men would be asked to
go to Great Britain and live on the rate
of wages applicable to the district he was
sent to. It was never thought that that
class of labour would ever be transferred.
The only labour that ever was asked in
normal times was skilled labour, and we
did agree that it was reasonable and
just for that class of labour to be transferred to the areas where employment
was suitable and their labour was required. We put up no objection to that
class of labour being transferred, because
the rates applicable to it were as high
if not higher than those at home.
To treat unskilled labour in this way
is to deal with a very dangerous element.
Desperation sometimes adopts desperate
remedies, and I advise the Minister of
Labour to go down to the labour exchange and separate the married men
from the single. He should then withdraw the married men from this test.
A married labourer should not be asked
to go to Britain. If a man is willing
and has no family responsibility then
it should be up to himself, but there
should be no compulsion on him to go
across the Channel. I presume we will
be told that this is a job of national
importance. Do I say that men should
go unemployed here while their labour
is required in Great Britain? I say
nothing of the sort. I say that when
labour is available in Great Britain it
should be used. They have the
the same
labour in Great Britain that we are
exporting from here.

I have often heard the hon. Member

When examining requests for men
from across the Channel we find out the
wage to be paid, and also inquire if the
conditions of employment are such as we
would expect a relative of our own to
work under. No claim to provide men
is ever received by any labour exchange
without its being looked into by our
officials. They make inquiries as to the
wages to be paid, and the conditions
under which the men are to be employed
before I agree to any men being sent
across the Channel. From Belfast alone
73 labourers were sent to the job referred
to by the hon. Member. We were
anxious that Londonderry should also
have an opportunity of sending men.
When this matter was raised on a previous occasion in this House, the hon.
Member for Woodvale drew my attention
to the fact that there were many people
in his constituency anxious to have the
opportunity of taking up the jobs, for
which they would receive 1s 2d per hour.
While I am referring to the question
of wages I should also like to deal with
the point raised by the hon. Member for
South Down. He asked two questions.
He wanted to know whether the fares of
these men were paid, and also whether
they received any subsistence allowance.
Not only do we pay the fares of these
men right to the job, but the firm allows
them 21s per week subsistence allowance.
In addition they have a great deal of
overtime. The hon. Member for Pottinger
during the course of his speech said the
lodgings were bad and that the conditions
under which the men were living were inhuman. I have fortified myself to meet an
argument of that kind. As I informed the
hon. Gentleman earlier in my reply, I
always make inquiries. I found that
one of the men who returned from the
job complained that the conditions were
not as they should be, and that they
were exactly as stated by the hon. Member-inhuman.
I got into touch with the firm carrying
out the work, and what did I find? The
camp conditions are such that they have
been the subject of favourable comment
in the local Press. Who will challenge
the Press? In my long and intimate experience of the Press I have always felt
that no organisation or body of men were
more ready to focus attention on bad
conditions, and that no body of men
were more anxious to laud good conditions. The Press, with all the wisdom
and genius at its disposal, sent men for
the purpose of investigating the conditions. What did they find? They
found that the food was of the finest
quality obtainable. There is a wet and
dry canteen in the camp. I am sorry
about the wet canteen, but there it is.
There is attached to the camp a well
equipped hospital, which the local doctor
visits three times per week or oftener if
required.
The twenty-one shillings per week subsistence allowance is paid to all men in
the camp who complete a full week's
work, and to men, who through no fault
of their own, are unable to complete the
full week. There are 500 men living in
the camp and if the conditions are such
as described by the hon. Gentlemaninhuman-they would rise in righteous
indignation and revolt, and they would
be right.
The hon. Member has put his case
forward, but I think he has been misinformed; at least it would appear to be
so when his statement is compared with
the information which I have gleaned
after a personal inquiry into the circumstances under which these men are
employed and live.
I have already stated that 73 men
went from the city of Belfast.
We were
anxious, however, to do something for

twelve men, of whom two have returned.
At the time I made my inquiries 65 of

SUPPLY OF CANADIAN OATS.
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if he
has been able to procure a further supply
of Canadian oats for Northern Ireland;
if so, when will they be available, and if
there has been any avoidable delay.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Representations have
been made to the Ministry of Food with
regard to supplies of Canadian oats for
Northern Ireland, and it is hoped that
with the seasonal re-opening of the St.
Lawrence River supplies may become
available, subject, of course, to
exigencies with regard to shipping and
freight. In the past comparatively small
quantities of Canadian oats were brought
into Northern Ireland since the home
production of oats was adequate for our
requirements.

England and delivered to farmers here,

COST OF FEEDING STUFFS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that
meals mixed in Northern Ireland cost
£2 per ton more than meals mixed in
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The prices at
which practically all individual feeding
stuffs and all mixed meals may be sold
are governed by the provisions of the
Feeding Stuffs (Maximum Prices) Order,
1940, which applies to the whole of the
United Kingdom. Some time ago it was
the case that certain of the meals mixed
in England were being sold at prices
somewhat lower than certain meals
which were prepared in Northern Ireland. It must be realised, however,
that there can be no standardised price
for any particular class of mixed meals
since the price will depend upon the cost
of the individual ingredients of the
mixture. Consequently, it is impossible
to make a comparison between two
classes of meals unless one has complete
information as to the nature and proportion of the ingredients.
The high price of certain of the
mixtures prepared in Northern Ireland
was due to the inclusion of highly-priced
ingredients such as home-grown oats
and home-grown barley, not then covered.
by the Maximum Prices Order. A
maximum price has since been fixed for
home-grown oats, and the Ministry has
recently issued a new licence under
which compound cakes, compound meals
and mixed meals may be prepared, and
which excludes the use of the more
highly-priced ingredients. In consequence
of this action there has been a considerable reduction in the prices at
which mixed meals prepared in Northern
Ireland are sold to farmers, and I am
not aware that prices of mixtures are
now out of alignment with corresponding
prices in Great Britain. If the hon.
Member has any particular case in mind
I should welcome the evidence.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked

drawn to statements made at a recent

in connection with food rationing, to the

that conditions and customs in Northern
Ireland differ in many respects from those
in England, he would make representations to the Ministry of Food to give the
necessary authority to the Food Controller
for Northern Ireland to initiate and
operate a more workable scheme.
I understand that representations made
by the Belfast and North of Ireland
Grocers' Association with reference to the
application of food rationing machinery
to Northern Ireland and, in particular,
to the practicability of substituting a
certain form of card for the ration books
now in use, have been submitted to the
Ministry of Food and are at present
receiving consideration from that Department.
The final part of the question accordingly does not arise.
Mr. BROWN: Will you allow me to

Mr. NIXON: There is just one point
in connection with the Education Vote I
want to refer to. I raised it on a question, but it was not debated. On that
occasion the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Education made a genuine
mistake because the hon. Lady said in
reply to a supplementary question that I
was a member of the Belfast Corporation,
and that I could raise it there. Of course
I have not been in the Corporation for
the last four and a half years. But the
particular point was raised on a question
and admitted in reply. It is a most outlandish thing considering the state the
country is in at the present time. It
does not involve a censure of the Ministry
except that the Ministry might take steps
to put the matter right.
Fourteen years is the school-leaving age
for children attending school, but they are
not allowed to drop out when they come
to fourteen. They have to finish the term
which sometimes may be a week or a
fortnight or three weeks or a month. It
is not very long. Supposing it was a
month-and that is about the outsideand you take five days of the week that
means about twenty days. Those twenty
days would mean nothing at all to the
education of the child. There is a lady
Ways and Means-

Report Stage
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
who lives in Urney Street and her name
is Mrs. Bailie. Her husband is in France;
he joined up at the outbreak of war. Mrs.
Bailie has seven children, the eldest of
whom attained the age of fourteen. He
was offered a job in a mineral water
establishment. I know it is a job he
could take up. He could not take up a
job in a factory, but he could take this
job. Mrs. Bailie applied to let the boy

the job would not be available. What
the child would earn in connection with
the mineral water factory would really
be wanted with the rising cost of living
for the upkeep of Mrs. Bailie and her

The application which was made to
the body called the School Attendance
Committee was refused. Mrs. Bailie
came to me and I wrote as nice a letter
as I could setting out the circumstances,
which I need not exaggerate, and pointing out that by no stretch of imagination
could it be said that the extra education
the child would get would be of benefit.
The committee turned that down. Their
administration is not subject to the
Council at all, because if it were that
decision would have been reversed. This
is nothing to me at all. I flatter myself

the serious and considered attention it
should get.
more, the explanation the hon. Lady

I do not accept that as being true. I

was there many a time when a hardship

was done when there was no war. The

I heard Lord Haw-Haw the other night
talking about cases, but I feel they were
not as bad as this case. I have referred

the attitude of the people in my constituency-Lord Haw-Haw will not affect
them or myself-let me say we want the

enough to do away with them. Further-
I have stated exactly what happened,

Fourteen years is the school-leaving age,

I
say that these empty, brainless snobs

There are at least two clergymen. I hope

I was
on that committee, and I had

say this
practice should be stopped. This is the

They are all gone from round about
Urney Street.

Now I come to the real facts of the
case. I know the Imperial Government
is spending a million pounds a week-50
millions all told-in endeavouring to keep
down the cost of living. My complaint
is not what the producer gets; my complaint is as to the difference between the
retailer's price and what the producer
gets. The weight of complaints comes
from the producers, that is the farmers,
the men represented by the hon. Member
for North Derry. They say having regard to the retail prices they are not
adequately paid. That is my complaint,
and that is caused by overstaffing and by
interference. I am not the author of
that. It is the people in the trade and
business who state that the butchers,
the farmers and shopkeepers. The
Grocers' Association made the complaint

on to the cost of living and that could

the Motion. It was not to launch out in
an attack on the Government. We did

Regarding the question of munition and
armament factories, we had a statement

Already we have two potato factories in

The development of the flax crop is a
matter of extreme importance to the linen
trade. The linen trade is providing Great
Britain with its second most important
exporting commodity by which the Allies
are buying munitions in America. Therefore it is our duty to take special steps to
assist the linen industry. I would go so
far as to say that I approve of a suggestion made in the Belfast Press this week
that the linen industry should be subsidised to enable it to increase its exports.
I would approve of this Government going
to the British Government and saying,

linen we export to America to enable
munitions to be bought, in lieu of the
fact that we did not get one penny of

14 MARCH 1940
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 14th March, 1940.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DELAY IN PAYMENT FOR
LIVESTOCK.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that in
many cases sellers of livestock to the
Government in purchasing centres under
the Livestock Control Scheme are not
receiving payment for a fortnight and
over, and whether he will arrange that
such delays in payment are ended.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): It is not a
fact that the cases in which the period
stated by the hon. Member has elapsed
have been numerous. The normal interval between purchase and payment is less
than a week.
INTEREST ON LOANS TO
FARMERS.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that the
interest of five and one-eighth per cent.
charged on loans to farmers for the
purchase of seeds, fertilisers and implements is rendering the scheme of little
or no value, and whether he will consider the granting of interest-free loans.
under this scheme for the duration of
the war, or the reduction of the interest
to the same rate as in Great Britain.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It is not the
case that the rate of interest to be
charged to farmers for loans for seeds,
fertilisers, etc., is restricting the number
of applications for these facilities. On
the contrary, the response has, in fact,
been unexpectedly large.
For obvious reasons, I can hold out
no hope either of my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, being able to
arrange a lower rate or of interest-free
loans as suggested by the hon. Member.
As the hon. Member is aware the rate
of interest on such loans in Great
Britain is 5 per cent. and in Northern
Ireland 5 per cent.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister
tell us why loans should be 5 per cent.
in Northern Ireland and only 5 per cent.
in Great Britain?
The
MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Andrews): As a matter of fact it.
shows how excellent our credit is that we
are able to borrow and lend not only
to farmers but to others at within per
cent. of what the British Government
can do.
Mr. MINFORD: Are we not part and
parcel of Great Britain, and why should
we have to pay more on the money we
borrow than in Great Britain?
Mr. ANDREWS: It is only per
cent. more—a mere trifle. It only means
on most borrowings a difference of 7½d
over a period of six months.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply, is it a fact that last summer the
Government borrowed at 33 per cent.,
and at the present time when the war is
on the Imperial Government are able to
get money at 3 per cent.?
The hon. Member
Mr. ANDREWS:
does not understand-
Mr. NIXON: I do understand.
Mr. ANDREWS- -the system of borrowing. We have had to borrow from
time to time over a considerable number
of years, and we are actually paying interest on some of our loans at the rate of
5 per cent. It is true that the rates of
interest are low at the present time, but
it would not be fair to the taxpayers that
we should lend at a lower rate than we
borrow at. We have got to take the average of the borrowings when we come to
fix the rates we charge.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement that I do not understand, as a matter of fact is it not the
Minister who does not understand when
he pays 33 per cent. for money that can
be got at 3 per cent.?

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
PAYMENT OF DROVERS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that
drovers employed in connection with the
livestock control scheme are complaining
of the treatment they are receiving, one
Newry drover, who had been sent to a
purchasing centre in County Armagh,
being given 7s 6d for his day's work and
had to pay 4s 7d bus fare, 4s for his keep
for the night before, as there was no bus
to get him there in time in the morning,
and 1s 6d for his dinner, so that instead
of receiving anything for his day's work,
he was 2s 7d out of pocket; and whether
he will ensure that travelling and subsistence allowances are granted in such cases
in future.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not aware
of any dissatisfaction among drovers
employed in connection with the meat and
livestock control scheme. Such drovers
are casually employed, as required, and
their remuneration is that ruling for
droving work in the particular district
concerned. Neither myself nor my
Ministry has received any complaint from
any drover.
I have no knowledge of the case referred to by the hon. Member, but if he
will let me have fuller particulars I shall
be glad to make inquiries as to it and
communicate the result to him.
In general, drovers are employed locally
and, therefore, no question of travelling
or subsistence expenses should normally
arise.
GRADING OF CATTLE AND SHEEP.
on
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to a resolution passed
unanimously at a meeting of farmers and
fruit growers held in Portadown
Saturday evening under the auspices of
the Ulster Fruit Growers' Marketing
Association and the Portadown Branch
of the Ulster Farmers' Union, expressing
keen dissatisfaction with the present
arrangement under which the grading of
cattle and sheep is carried out by
Government officials in Northern Ireland,
instead of by the panel system as in Great
Britain; demanding that the system be
changed forthwith, and that the grading
be carried out by practical and experienced men as in Great Britain; and
whether he proposes to take any action in
this matter.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's question is in the affirmative, and to the
latter part in the negative.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask is there not
in addition to the panel operating in
Great Britain a liaison officer in the
person of a farmers' representative who
appears at the grading centre and can be
called upon by the producer to make
application to the grader for a test?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have not
made any further inquiries in regard
to that.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Will the right hon.
Gentleman make some inquiries to find
out if that is so?
Sir BASIL BROOKE indicated assent.

BROADCAST.
to
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
reason why in his recent B.B.C. broadcast on the increased tillage campaign
in Northern Ireland he referred
various crops, including wheat, potatoes,
barley, oats, narrow-stem kale and
cabbage, and made no mention whatever of flax, in spite of the fact that
the linen industry will depend increasingly on home-grown flax and provides

7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime

Whig" of 8th March, 1940, signed by
Viscount Castlereagh, M.P., expressing
The PRIME MINISTER: I read the
letter referred to, which was apparently
written under a misunderstanding of the
situation. Black-out is a matter affecting
the whole United Kingdom, and instructions regarding its application reach this
Government through the usual channels.
I may mention that the Committee of
Imperial Defence, with whom my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, was in touch on the outbreak of
hostilities, emphasised the importance of
the whole of Northern Ireland being
covered by the regulations. It will be
readily understood that as we here have
pledged our utmost and ungrudging support to the Imperial authorities we must
bear, in the interests of national security,
with any inconvenience caused by the restrictions imposed. As, however, the
days are now lengthening rapidly I hope
the difficulties and discomforts wil!
become less onerous.
I have also seen the other statements
to which the hon. Member refers. The
question of centrally controlled lighting
has been considered very fully and the
objections found to be insuperable. In
large industrial areas the position is that
there is, as a rule, a dual system of street
lighting, partly electricity and partly gas.
Whatever the possibility of central control of electric supply, it is impracticable
to extinguish gas lighting, since the street
lights are fed from the same main as the
household supply. The dangers of gas
poisoning on the resumption of supply,
when so many taps might not have been
turned off, are such that the suggestion
could not be adopted.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
thank the noble Lord for his very
courteous and informative reply and to
say that that type of reply is worthy
of the highest admiration?

diagnosed as suffering from

2. Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what provision is made or can be made
for persons normally healthy and strong,
but who have become almost stone deaf
and are unable to find employment in
consequence.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are
several voluntary agencies in Northern
Ireland who interest themselves in making
provision for the training of deaf persons
and assisting them in finding employment.
In addition boards of guardians are empowered under Statute to send deaf
persons to any institution established for
the deaf and to contribute towards the
cost of their maintenance therein.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Price Regulation
Committee for Northern Ireland, like all
similar committees set up by the Board
of Trade under the Prices of Goods Act,
has been constituted so as to provide for
the representation of industrial, commercial, co-operative and labour interests.
The members of the Northern Ireland
Committee were appointed by the Board
of Trade, partly from nominations made
by the Trades Union Congress and other
organisations, and partly from nominations made by the Ministry of Commerce
at the invitation of the Board.
In
formulating nominations the
Ministry endeavoured to provide for the
representation of each interest generally
rather than sectionally. Obviously it was
not possible to include representatives
from all of the workers' organisations,
nor to provide for representation on a
territorial basis. I do not know whether,
in submitting nominations to the Board
of Trade, the Trades Union Congress
consulted any of the organisations referred to by the hon. Member. None of
them, however, was consulted by the
Ministry of Commerce.

SHORTAGES OF MUTTON.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of sheep killed in the Belfast
Abattoir since 1st March, 1940, and the
number killed there in the corresponding
period of 1939; whether it is a fact that
Belfast traders who, before the Control
Scheme, bought on the average 20 to 40
sheep a week are now unable to obtain
more than one or two sheep a week;
whether heavy losses are being inflicted on
such traders and serious shortages of
mutton caused to their customers by the
working of the Control Scheme; whether
compensation will be available to recoup
the traders for such losses; and whether
he will represent to the competent
Ministry at Whitehall the necessity in the
public interest of such relaxation of the
regulations as will permit Belfast traders,
in cases where the Ministry cannot supply
their requirements, to continue to obtain
from Eire their accustomed supplies of
sheep.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The number of sheep
killed in Belfast Abattoir from 1st-15th
March, 1940, was 1,508 and in the corresponding period in 1939 I am informed
that 3,969 sheep were killed.
There has been a shortage of sheep for
retail purposes and it is the case that
retail butchers have not got their usual
supplies. The object of the Ministry has
been to allocate the sheep available
amongst the various butchers, giving
preference, of course, to those with
hospital contracts. During the past three
weeks no fat sheep have been shipped to
Great Britain and all supplies of mutton
available have been distributed to
butchers in Northern Ireland. I cannot
see how heavy losses have been suffered
by traders simply because they have not
mutton with which to supply their customers. The rationing of meat is on a
monetary basis and does not give any
guarantee of the class of meat which will
be supplied. Traders have ample supplies
of meat with which to supply their
customers.
The question of compensation does not
arise, therefore, since naturally the
Ministry cannot distribute to butchers
what it has not got and is unable to buy.
Traders are quite at liberty to bring sheep
from Eire for sale to the Ministry in
Northern Ireland. It has to be remembered, of course, that no fat stock can
now be sold for slaughter for human food
to anyone other than the Minister of
Food or his agents and no one can
slaughter animals for food except the
Minister of Food or his agents. It has to
be pointed out, too, that traders who
bring sheep from Eire for sale to the
Ministry and subsequent slaughter by
the Ministry can get no guarantee that
they will get all or any of the sheep so

slaughtered for sale in their own retail
shops.

equitable distribution of available supplies and whilst mutton is at present

the supplies of meat are ample.

PRODUCTION COSTS OF MILK.
8. Mr. BYRNE (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he can state if it is a fact that production
costs of milk supplied by milk producers
and audited by Messrs. James Baird
& Company were submitted to the Joint
Milk Council when asking for an increased price for milk; and whether these
figures were taken into account by the
Ministry's representatives on that Council
when fixing the price.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: A statement
was submitted to the Joint Milk Council
on behalf of milk producers in support
of a recent application for an increase in
the price of milk. I am not in a position
to say whether or not it was audited by
the firm of accountants mentioned.
The hon. Gentleman can rest assured
that the Ministry's representatives on the
Joint Milk Council have given most careful consideration to all representations
made to them in connection with milk
prices.
DISADVANTAGES OF MILK
PRODUCERS.
9. Mr. BYRNE (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
he can state if it is a fact that owing to
the disadvantages under which milk producers are labouring there is a tendency
for these people to go out of the milk
business and thereby endanger the milk
supply, and whether in the national
interest the dairying industry should not
receive more encouragement from His
Ministry than it does at present.
As regards milk for human consumption, the Joint Milk Council has authorised an increase of 3d per gallon on the
price paid to producers to meet increased
costs of production. This increase became
operative on the 19th November and
continues until the 30th September, 1940.
As a measure of the extent of the assistance granted to Northern Ireland producers it may be stated that in Great
Britain the increase granted to producers
operated only as from the 1st January
and was fixed at the rate of 3d per
gallon for January and February and
24d per gallon for the remainder of the
period ending September, 1940.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am satisfied
that there are adequate supplies of milk
available to meet the needs of the
community.
As regards manufacturing milk, the
Ministry has, since April, 1934, paid by
way of assistance to producers the sum
of £804,000. The special circumstances
created by the war are receiving close
attention at the present time.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask the
right hon. Gentleman is it a fact that if
the producer gets a higher price for his
milk the consumer in the city of Belfast
will have to pay more for his milk?

have taken steps to see that farmers are

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I an
aware that some Regional Education

The Education Act of 1923 recognises
agricultural education. as a form of
education separate and distinct from
elementary education, and the control
and provision of instruction in agriculture has been entrusted by Parliament
to the county committees of agriculture
acting under the Ministry of Agriculture.
The Ministry of Education, therefore,
has no power to sanction the teaching of
the subject in public elementary schools.
This, however, would not prevent the
use of a suitable reader on the subject,
and the Ministry is prepared to consider
any such reader which may be submitted
to it, and, if it considers it suitable, to
sanction its use in public elementary
schools.

GOVERNMENT POLICY REGARDING
VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether, in view of the prevailing outcry in Great Britain at the
disastrous results of the absence of definite
religious teaching in the schools, the
Government will reconsider its policy of
denial of any aid from public moneys
towards the necessary routine repairs of
the voluntary schools and denial of any
aid beyond 50 per cent. towards the building or reconstruction of these schools, and
whether she will place all the elementary
schools on an equality as they are in Eire
to-day and were in Northern Ireland before 1921.
Mrs. PARKER: I cannot accept the
implication contained in the hon. and
learned Member's question that definite
religious teaching is given only in the
voluntary schools in Northern Ireland and
not in the provided and transferred
schools. In all provided and transferred
schools as in voluntary schools-a period
of at least half an hour daily, or its
reasonable weekly equivalent, is provided
for the purpose of religious or Bible instruction, and I am glad to say that I
have no reason whatever to think that the
religious or Bible instruction given by the
teachers in provided and transferred
schools is any less thorough and effective
than that given in voluntary schools.
The grounds on which the hon. and
learned Member relies, as a reason why
the Government should take steps to increase the amount of aid at present available from public funds in connection with
the necessary repairs to voluntary schools
or the building, enlargement, reconstruction and equipment of such schools, do
not, therefore, in fact, exist.
DECLINE IN SCHOOL POPULATION
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can state what
effect the year-by-year decline since 1933,
now totalling 14,329, in the average
number of elementary school children has
had on the number of schools or staffs.
Mrs. PARKER: On the 31st December, 1938, the number of public elementary schools had fallen by 114 and the
number of teachers by 216, compared
with the position at the end of the year
1933. I should say, however, that these
decreases must not be ascribed solely to the
decrease in the school-going population.
The decrease in the number of schools is
due almost entirely to the pursuance by
the Ministry of its policy of amalgamating
small neighbouring schools when a suitable opportunity arises and when the
amalgamation is in the interests of educational efficiency and public economy.
The decline in the number of teachers is
also due in part to the same cause, though
it is mainly due to the decrease in the
number of pupils.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Old Age and Widows' Pension Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In the many debates which have
taken place in this House the spokesmen
for the Government have always made it
perfectly clear that it was not lack of
sympathy with the pensioner class, but
lack of means, which prevented the
Government from introducing legislation
to improve the position of the old-age
pensioner. The undertaking was given.
and repeated more than once that whatever changes were made or improvements.
introduced in Great Britain, identical
changes would be introduced by our own.
Government. I have, therefore, the very
greatest pleasure to-day in moving the
Second Reading of this Bill. I do not
propose to weary the House with an exhaustive examination of the measure.
Mr. NIXON: You will not weary us
in well doing.
Mr. GORDON: I always knew the hon.
Member knew scripture from his youth
up, and that is an indication and an
incentive to me to proceed. An explanatory memorandum has been circulated
with the Bill, and the question of pensions has been discussed so often in this
House that I will restrict myself at this
stage to merely mentioning some of the
more important aspects of the measure.
The first important question which the
Old Age Pension Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
insured contributor will ask is: What
changes are made and who will benefit
by this Bill I am introducing. In the
first place it lowers to 60 the age at which
a woman insured in her own right becomes entitled to a pension. It also gives
the right to the wife of an insured man
who is in receipt of a 65 pension to become entitled to a contributory pension
when she attains the age of 60. We expect
that 3,500 insured women and 2,800
wives will become entitled to an old-age
pension of 10s per week when the Bill
comes into operation on the 1st of July
next.
I now come to a very important part
of the Bill which provides that a supplementary pension based on the needs of
the household may be paid to any old-age
pensioner.

The proposals in the Bill have the
merit of meeting adequately every case
in which there is real need, at the same
time having due regard to the economy
which it is the duty of each one of us
to practise in the national interest at
the present time, both in our public and
private capacity. The Bill is a lengthy
one owing to the fact that many consequential amendments of the Insurance
Acts are required, and the Unemployment Assistance Act has to be adapted
and modified to make it applicable to
the new supplementary pension scheme.
So far as health insurance is concerned
the Bill follows established precedent in
linking up the provisions in Northern
Ireland with the corresponding provisions
in Great Britain. Health insurance is in
fact established on a United Kingdom
basis, and the Government of Northern
Ireland has, accordingly, arranged with
His Majesty's Government at Westminster that the Special Suspense Fund
established under the Great Britain Act
will be extended to Northern Ireland by
Order in Council. Into this fund will be
paid the reserves which the approved
societies will no longer require to meet
the cost of sickness and disablement
benefits to their women members over the
age of 60, and out of it will be paid the
special sickness payments to which
women over 60 will continue to be eligible
during the transitional period in accordance with regulations to be made under
the Acts.
The disposal of the balance in the fund
is left for the future decision of the
Parliament of the United Kingdom, but
if it should happen to be diverted from
health insurance purposes we have an
understanding that there will be
equitable distribution of it as between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

I now want to say a word about the

There is nothing worse than a household means test, because it means that in
order to get a few shillings the earnings
of everyone in the house, including people
who are no relatives of the pensioner, will
be thrown in. Often people give shelter
and a room and a bed to some pensioner
who is perhaps no relative at all. The
household means test brings them all in.
Nobody wants it. That is where the whole
thing is wrong. If we can get the means
test without the household means test,
perhaps we could not say so very much,
because I know that people who are well
off would come in if there were no
test. I want the Government to draw a
distinction between the household means
test and the means test. That is where
the whole damage is going to be done,
and that is where many people have
already suffered. Some old people are
afraid to apply for anything because a
son's wages or a son-in-law's wages, or
a daughter's wages, or the wages of
someone else who does not belong to
them at all, are going to be taken into
account, and an inspector is going to be
sent round to the works to find out the
earnings. It is a monstrous proposal,
and, without being critical, I sincerely
wish that it could be dropped, or that

there a limit?

It is only by dealing in a modern way

considerable extent.

Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This Bill is one of
the series of emergency Bills arising out
of the present abnormal conditions, and,
as hon. Members will see, its operation
is limited to a period ending within a
fixed time after the end of the present
emergency. The Bill is a fairly lengthy
one, containing as it does some
sections, but, in fact, practically all the
provisions it contains have been approved
in principle by this House in connection
with previous legislation on "Rent
Restrictions."

one.

In the first place, it continues the

at the moment controlled, but which
would go out of control on 1st May next,
without any variation
alteration
whatever, and, in the second place, it

to a maximum limit of £75 poor-law
valuation.
or
control in the manner I have indicated
is generally admitted as an emergency
necessity. The general policy of the
Government is to maintain a reasonable
level of rents by the supply of an
adequate number of houses so that the
inflation of rents will be prevented by
the operation of the law of supply and
demand, rather than by any artificial
means. I need hardly point out that
this policy secures the provision of
houses built in accordance with up-todate ideas, thus raising the general
level of housing conditions in the
Province, which, of course, could never
be secured by any method of rent
control.
I do not think that I need occupy the
time of hon. Members at any very great
length in setting out the reasons which
have influenced the Government in
taking these steps, for I think that the
desirability of continuing and extending
In pursuit of this policy the Government, since it was set up, has secured
the provision of no fewer than 36,467
houses by the payment of £2,959,000 by
way of subsidy, and, in addition, 3,978
labourers' cottages have been built since
1921 at a cost to the Government of no
less a sum than £355,000 as a contribution to loan charges, which would otherwise fall upon the local authorities.
War conditions, however, have necessitated the suspension of this policy.
Owing to the shortage of timber no new
houses will be erected during the present war, and, further to this, there has
been a large percentage drop during the
last twelve months, not only in the
number of vacant houses in the Province,
but also in the number of new houses
erected, and as time goes on a further
drop in the number of vacant houses is
bound to take place.
Thus, I think, it will be agreed that
the demand for houses is going to exceed
the supply, and, indeed, already, as I
am sure many hon. Members are aware,
demands for increased rents are being
made for subsidy houses which are now
coming out of control. I might mention
one instance of houses previously let at
7s 9d, for which a demand of 11s 10d
has been made.

hon. Member will agree with me that
as the rates of Belfast have fallen

Turning now to the details of the

There is another important matter
that is not dealt with in this Bill.
Nothing has been done about key
money, and that is a very vicious
practice that operates in Belfast. You
have landlords associated with your
Party who are robbing the poor day in
and day out. We have had to take them
to task on several occasions and make
them pay back the money they took in an
indirect way for the possession of
vacant houses. There is no provision in
this Bill to deal with that evil of demanding key money. The Minister is
not stupid and never was, nor is he
sleeping. He may sometimes look as if
he was, but he knows what is going on as
well as I do, because the majority of cases
of this kind I get from his own Division.
He knows that this vicious system is
operating day in and day out, and he
has made no provision in this Measure
to safeguard the tenants. Why has he
not done so ?
It is all very well to say that under
the law as it stands no landlord can
charge a fee for the tenancy of a vacant
house. That may be the law, but the
people who are concerned in demanding
key money do not go out of a house and
leave it bare. When the new tenant goes
into the house he will find one or possibly
two old bedsteads and an old sideboard
which could not be removed because it
would fall to pieces, and he is told he is
paying a fee of £10, £15, or £20 for
the tenancy as a part-furnished house.
What he is really paying that money for
is for entrance to the house. That is not
done directly by the landlord; he is too
cute for that. He was brought up in a
good school. He gets the outgoing tenant
to do this little bit of masquerading
business. He says to the outgoing tenant,
"Leave these articles in the house, and
on your recommendation I will accept

The outgoing tenant does the business

I know the Minister will agree with me
when I say that in all these Acts there
are the greatest anomalies. First I should
say this. A substantial part of the income
of the Government and of all local
councils, comes from property. All local
councils levy rates directly on property.
Out of the rates the Council have to
make a contribution to the Exchequer.
Sometimes they call it an education
levy, but it does not matter what they
call it the contribution has to be made
to the Exchequer. In addition, there
is a lot of property in the form of ground
rents, and that looks to be ready money
until you are getting it. The incometax on those rents is, I think, 8s in the
£, and the person who owns ground rents
gets 12s instead of 20s. I am not complaining about that. I am showing the
way all things are largely supported by
property.
There is a type of house in Belfast
let at 3s 9d, 3s 10d, or 4s a week. That
rent includes the rates. Last winter
there was hardly one of those houses to
which the plumber was not sent at the
expense of the landlord, and maybe the
plumber was in more than once. A
year or two ago there was a heavy snowstorm that brought down all the spouting. Certainly, there are streets of
houses from which the people who own
them get nothing. It would pay those

up to £140 got what built the houses.
Those men who got the property built

Nobody who knows anything about

Some day
day or other the Government

1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister

Unemployment Assistance Board and the

whether he can give the number of
meetings of this Board during the past
year and since its inception.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The average unemployment
figure for the year 1924 was 40,359 out
of an insured population of 260,500; for
1925 59,299 out of 269,000; and for the
last twelve months 73,413 out of 350,500
insured persons. The hon. Member will
realise that the extension of insurance to
agricultural workers and to younger age
groups between the dates mentioned has
resulted in a considerable increase in the
number of insured persons, and that the
provision of unemployment assistance and
the "franking" procedure has also led to
the registration of many workers who did
not formerly attend the exchange, so
that the figures are not comparable.
As regards the second part of his question, the information is as follows:-

MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND
PIG PRODUCERS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if it is a
fact that it has now been established
that the present Minister of Agriculture
and his Permanent Secretary, with the
assistance of the Pig Industry Council,
have deprived producers of pigs in the
period September 3rd to September 27th
last, of a vast sum of money, and, if so,
what steps he proposes to take in the
matter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have been asked to
reply. The answer is in the negative.
It was the agreed intention that Northern Ireland should be excluded from
the operation of the Order fixing pig
prices made by the Board of Trade on
September 3rd. A recent action in the
High Court of Justice in Northern Ireland has shown that the form of the
Order failed adequately to carry out this
intention.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply that his Ministry was going on an
assumption that the Order did not apply
to Northern Ireland, is the Minister's
assumption sufficient justification for
attempting to deprive the farmers of
Northern Ireland of thousands of pounds
due to them?
Owing to the stress of events in the
first weeks of the war the Ministry of
Agriculture did not receive a copy of the
Order for some time, because it was not
thought by the Ministry of Food to apply
to Northern Ireland. As a consequence
my Ministry acted on the presumption
that the Order did not apply, and had no
opportunity of considering whether the
terms of the Order correctly carried out
the agreed intention in this respect.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The word I
used was "intention". It was the agreed
intention that this Order should not
apply to Northern Ireland. But the
wording was framed in such a way that
actually, according to the High Court
decision, it does apply.
Mr. NIXON: So that the Minister's
subsequent statement shows an attempt
to negotiate behind backs with the Board
of Trade to keep the Order from
applying?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
will realise that there are many questions
on the Order Paper, and if I allow
supplementary questions to such an extent
we will not get through the questions at
all and it would not be fair to other
Members. Therefore, I appeal to hon.
Members to reduce their supplementary
questions as far as possible. They should
make them questions of fact according to
procedure.
Mr. BROWN: Will all producers of
pigs sold at that particular time receive
the same benefit now as received by the
plaintiff in that action?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I should like
notice of that question.

Mrs. PARKER: The decrease in the

PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

with their case"; whether this statement

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The answer is
in the negative.

TRADING ACCOUNT.
15. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The total
amount of levies collected by the Pigs
Marketing Board from pig producers for
the 12 months ended 31st March, 1940,
is £87,025.
The amount of loss incurred by the
Board in trading during the same period
was approximately £73,994, the deficit in
the trading account at the 31st March,
1940, being £52,076.
The continuance of a levy is necessary
to liquidate the outstanding deficit of
approximately £11,000 in the Board's
fund, excluding investments in curing
factories.

the Board be increased if they have to
