RENTS OF BUSINESS PREMISES.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether it is the intention of
the Government to introduce legislation
restricting the rents of premises used for
business, trade or professional purpose,
for the period of the war, in view of the
acute and widespread distress owing to
war conditions among the tenants of such
premises.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply. The
answer to this question is in the negative.
As the hon. Member is aware, business
premises were only brought under control
for a limited period, from the 2nd July,
1920, to the 24th June, 1921, the necessity for such control being due to
abnormal circumstances which do not
exist at the present time. Having regard
to the number of business premises at
present unoccupied, the Government is
of opinion that the rent of such premises
would be best regulated by the law of
supply and demand.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Minister
realise that a great many of the tenants
of these houses who had been able to
make ends meet at the beginning of the
war now find that it is quite beyond their
power?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
think the point raised by my hon. and
learned Friend is due to the amount of
rent charged. I think it is due to other
circumstances caused by the present war.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister to give further consideration to
this question, or has he spoken the last
word on it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes. I have
gone into the whole matter very carefully,
and I have already informed the hon.

COURT OF REFEREES' DECISIONS.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

MR. LESLIE BURGIN'S VISIT
TO BELFAST.
13. Mr BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the total
cost to the Exchequer of Mr. Burgin's
visit to Belfast; what benefits Northern
Ireland unemployed are to receive by
this expendiure; whether it is a fact that
only certain newspaper representatives
were invited to attend at the conference;
whether other newspaper representatives
were excluded, and if so, can he state the
reason and by whose authority this
decision was given.
The PRIME MINISTER: I propose
to reply to this question which has been.
addressed to my right hon. Friend.
The total cost to the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland of the arrangements
made by the Government in connection
with the reception of Mr. Burgin and of
the Press party is estimated at approximately £150.
The object of the visit was to enable
the Minister of Supply to investigate at
first hand the capacity and resources of
Ulster in plant and man power, with a
view to determining the extent to which
we could contribute still further to the
national war effort. In addition to the
factory which the Ministry propose to
establish for the production of shells, Mr.
Burgin promised that further orders for
munitions and armament work would be
placed and he also gave the assurance of
continuity of contracts for linen and
textile products. It would, moreover, he
said, be the duty of the local area
organisation of his Ministry which he
established on his arrival to explore the
possibilities of sub-contracting work being
allotted to small firms in provincial
districts.
With regard to the last part of the
question, invitations for the Press tour
were extended to all newspapers published
in Northern Ireland and to other newspapers selected by the Ministry of Supply.
No Press representatives were present at
the conference between Mr. Burgin and
the deputations received by him on the
28th March.

debars the teaching of any distinctive
religious doctrine in either a provided
or a transferred school is strictly enforced.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF

Ministry has seen the newspaper report
of the discussion at the Belfast Education Committee to which the hon. and
learned Member refers.
by example and precept to inculcate

part of the teachers to endeavour both
or
The Education Act of 1930 provides
that no teacher in a provided or a transferred school may be required as a condition of appointment or holding office
to teach any religious catechism
religious formulary which is distinctive
of any particular denomination. There
is nothing, however, in this or in any
other enactment which debars the teaching of distinctive religious doctrines in
provided and transferred schools. Indeed
under the Education Act of 1923 it is
the duty of the Education Authority to
afford opportunities for catechetical
instruction according to the tenets of the
religious denomination of the parents of
children attending any provided or transferred public elementary school, and for
other religious instruction to which those
parents do not object, and those clergymen or other persons to whom those
parents do not object must be allowed
access to the children in the school for

at times to be arranged in accordance
with regulations of the Ministry..

3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state, in
addition to the £22,355,000 paid by the
Imperial Government to Northern Ireland
since 1921, the total to date of the land
purchase annuities paid into the Northern Ireland Exchequer which
allocated by the Imperial Parliament to
Northern Ireland, and the totals to date
since the Unemployment Reinsurance
Agreement of the contributions from
Northern Ireland to the Imperial Government and of the payments by the
Imperial Government to Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The total net receipts into
the Northern Ireland Exchequer since.
1921 in respect of the land purchase
annuities handed over under the Government of Ireland Act to our Government
by the Imperial Government were
£7,267,794. The total Northern Ireland
contribution to Great Britain between
1925 and 1940, which is the period for
which the hon. and learned Member
desires information, was £13,588,000.
During the same period the payments by
the British Government to Northern
Ireland were £13,599,000, which includes
amounts in respect of the Unemployment Insurance Agreements, and part of
the Special Constabulary grants required
to restore and maintain law and order.
I feel it necessary to point out that
the particular years which my hon. and
learned Friend has selected are clearly
liable to create a wrong impression as to
the correct position, seeing that they
leave out of account years in which large
contributions were made by this Government to the Imperial Exchequer, and in
which no Unemployment Reinsurance.
payments were made to our Exchequer.
The true position was shown in my reply
to his question last week.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister if in this pitch-and-toss policy
in regard to the Re-Insurance Agreement Northern Ireland always stands to
win in recent years?
Mr. ANDREWS: Does the hon.
Member, I wonder, object to the Agreement?
Mr. CAMPBELL: Am I at liberty to

SOURCE OF EDUCATION
EXPENDITURE.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is a fact that over
90 per cent. of the £2,000,000 expenditure by the Regional Education Committees on provided and transferred
school buildings comes from taxes and
less than 10 per cent. from rates.
Mrs. PARKER: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply to this
question.
The charges on loans sanctioned by
the Ministry to meet capital expenditure
incurred by local education authorities on
provided and transferred schools are
spread over a number of years, usually
about 50 years, and the amount of such
charges varies from year to year.
The grant-in-aid of the expenditure of
such authorities payable by the Ministry
under the provisions of Section 76 of the
Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
is not earmarked for any particular
service or item of expenditure, and I am
not, therefore, in a position to state
definitely the percentage of the loan
charges which falls on taxes and rates
respectively, without a considerable
amount of investigation.
I am of opinion that the information
which would be obtained as a result of
such investigation would not be in any
way commensurate with the time and
labour involved.
I might, however, say that the grantsin-aid of expenditure payable by the
Ministry to Education and Regional
Education Committees in respect of the
financial year 1938-39, the last year for
which audited accounts are available, and
the grants in respect of the attendances
of students and the incremental portion
of the salaries of teachers represent 60.4
per cent. of the gross expenditure (including loan charges) of such committees.
in that year.
The amount due in respect
of that expenditure from derating grants
and underated hereditaments was 11.8 per
cent. and 18.2 per cent. respectively.
It should be remembered that under
the provisions of the Finance (Northern
Ireland) Act, 1934, a contribution from
local rates is payable to the Exchequer
towards the cost of educational services.

Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Continuance of Rent
Restrictions Acts).
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I beg to move to
add the following new sub-clause :
"(2) In computing whether any and,
if so, what increase in the rent of a
dwelling-house to which the said Acts
apply is permissible under paragraph
(b) of sub-section (1) of section two
of the Increase of Rent and Mortgage
Interest (Restriction) Act, 1920 (which
paragraph relates to increases of rent
corresponding to increases in rates),
the amount of any allowance made to
the landlord, whether under sub-section
(5) of section seventeen of the Local
Government Act (Northern Ireland),
1934,
or under any local enactment
relating to allowances given where
rates are paid by the owner instead of
by the occupier, shall be treated as
part of the amount payable by the
landlord in respect of rates."
The object of this Amendment is to
secure that the discount allowed to the
landlord, where he pays his rates
punctually, is not passed on to the tenant.
There was an anomaly whereby if a
landlord paid his rates and got discount
he had to pass it on to the tenant.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

Education (School-leaving Age) Bill (S.).
Order for Second Reading read.
Mrs. PARKER: As hon. Members are
aware, the raising of the school-leaving
age would have become effective in July,
1940. It is now my duty to move the
Second Reading in this House of a Bill
postponing still further and for an unspecified period the operation of the
Education Act of 1938.
for its introduction and adoption was
briefly but adequately explained by the
Minister of Education. It is only necessary for me to emphasise the two principal reasons for the proposed step.
This proposed measure comes to us from
another place where the obvious necessity
The first is that similar legislation has
already become effective in Great Britain
and I need not point out the necessity for
keeping in line with them in this matter.
The second reason is that if there were
no further postponement large capital
expenditure would have to be incurred in
order to provide extra school accommodation. Apart from the almost insuperable
difficulty of obtaining building materials
such outlay would be quite out of the
question at a time when the Government
is curtailing and asking all public bodies
to curtail all but the absolutely essential
expenditure. I am sure that my deep
regret at the stern necessity for this Bill
will be shared by all. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill
be now read a Second time."

to strike any note of opposition to the
Bill, but I think this is the first opportunity which the Parliamentary

of a Bill in this House.

AFFAIRS OF THE TRANSPORT
BOARD.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if Mr.
D. L. Clarke, chairman of the Transport
Board, in his evidence before the Joint
Select Committee on the transport problem, swore that the evidence tendered to
the McLintock Committee by Sir Wm.
Wood and the railway managers was
"very inaccurate, misleading and unreliable"; whether, in alleged proof of
this charge, Mr. Clarke proceeded to give
instances in support of his allegation, and
whether he further charged Sir Wm.
Wood with making "a direct misstatement" on the occasion in question. (See
Report of Joint Select Committee).
Whether the Government liability in respect to this Board is £3,000,000, plus
£250,000 for the financial year just
ended; whether he will state the total
amount paid by the Government in respect to, or on behalf of, this Board up to
the end of the last financial year, and
whether the Minister will inform the
House as to what the Government intend
to do about the matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. As to the second part, I am to
refer the hon. Member to the answer given
by the Minister of Finance to the hon.
Member for Central on the 11th April.
As to the final part, the whole question
of transport is at present receiving the
careful consideration of the Government.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the first
part of the Minister's answer to the effect
that it is in the affirmative did the
Minister during his legal experience ever
before know of one gentleman of standing
actually call another gentleman of standing a liar or practically a liar as in this
case?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It depends
entirely on the method.
Mr. NIXON: I never heard of it.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the Minister aware
of the fact that the Transport Board,
which is adding to its losses by £250,000
a year, is still buying transport concerns
and thereby adding to the liability?

2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

fertilisers, implements, etc., namely, 5
per cent.

GARAGES AND ARMY REPAIR
WORK.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he has made any
representations with regard to the claims
of Northern Ireland in connection with
the report that repair shops at garages
all over the country may soon be engaged in repairing mechanical casualties
from France, including tanks, Army
lorries, cars, and motor-cycles; whether
it has been decided to parcel out a percentage of the repair work to motor
traders at home instead of having it all
done at the Army servicing depots; and
whether he can give the House the result
of such representations.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I would refer the hon.
Member to the reply which I gave on
20th February to the question on the
same subject addressed to me by the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh. For the
reasons which I stated, I do not consider
that I would be justified in suggesting
that mechanical casualties from France
of the kind mentioned in the question
should be transported to Northern
Ireland for repair. I would add, however, that among the matters at present
under investigation by the Northern
Ireland Area Board recently constituted
by the Minister of Supply is the practicability of utilising such facilities as our
garage repair shops are in a position to
provide.
Mr. BROWN: Arising out of the
Minister's reference to the Board, might
I ask him to make representation, so
that the provincial areas can get representation on the Advisory Committee of
the Board.
PROVINCIAL AREAS AND
INDUSTRY.
5. Mr. BROWN: I beg to ask the
Prime Minister, whose illness
we all
regret, whether the Government have considered the claims of the provincial areas
to a greater share in industrial enterprises both in war and peace, in view
of the fact that all the advanced industrial nations are now convinced of the
disadvantages of having their industries
centralised in a few big cities, and that
in Great Britain a Royal Commission on
the Distribution of Industry had just
issued its report recommending that
definite measures should be taken to disperse industry as evenly as circumstances
will allow, and whether that
mendation will be kept in mind by the
Government.
recom-
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
The answer to the question is in the
affirmative. The new industries legislation passed by the Parliament of Northern Ireland was specifically designed to
attract new industrial undertakings to
whatever centres offered the maximum
facilities for a successful development,
and the assistance given by the Government under the provisions of that legislation has not been confined to any one
area.
As regards the placing of Government
contracts for war material, the hon.
Member will realise that the first consideration must be the suitability of such
facilities as at present exist at any particular centre. Every area is assured of
receiving consideration by the Imperial
Service Departments charged with the
task of procuring supplies of war-time
requirements.

materials; and whether the Government
will consider the lifting of the ban, as
far as possible, on civil building in Nor-

thern Ireland, to reduce the huge unemployment roll in the building industry,

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been

ACCEPTANCE OF FAT SOWS AND

11. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if it
is a fact that his Ministry, acting on
behalf of the Ministry of Food, is refusing to accept pigs of the following
description, viz., fat sows and boars, and,
if so, whether it is in the national interest
that these animals which are no longer
required for breeding purposes should
have to be retained on the farms, thereby
using up valuable feeding stuffs which
are required for other fattening stock.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's question is in the affirmative. I might
explain that despite feeding stuffs difficulties an unduly large number of fat
heavy pigs have been offered for sale
during recent weeks, and difficulty has
been experienced in disposing of them.
The Minister of Food has, therefore,
suspended the purchase of fat sows and
boars throughout the United Kingdom
during the fortnight commencing April
15th.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Hire-Purchase Bill (S.).
Order for Second Reading read.
share my satisfaction that the Bill is
now before the House, and I believe they
will join with me in making every effort
to expedite its passage to the Statute
Book.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Bill, to which the
House is now asked to give a Second
Reading, follows the Hire Purchase Act,
1938, which came into force in England
and Wales on the 1st January, 1939. It
was the intention of the Government to
introduce the present Bill at a much
earlier date, and I regret that the
outbreak of hostilities, which brought
with it a train of emergency legislation, should have inevitably caused its
introduction to be delayed. I feel
sure that hon. Members will, however,
can
a
Hon. Members will be aware of the
wide range of goods which
be
bought on the instalment system. The
purchaser who is not in a position to
pay the whole of the price at once, or
who prefers to spread the cost over
period of time, can generally avail himself of these facilities to buy, not only
necessities, but luxuries also. Motor
cars, cycles, wireless sets, musical
instruments, as well as essential articles
of household furniture, and gas and
electrical fittings can often be bought by
hire purchase, while in some parts of
Great Britain the system extends to livestock and rolling stock. In America, I
am told, there is even a credit system by
which tourists can take a cruise or a railway journey upon paying a first instalment and the balance by easy stages-an
extension of the system which, fortunately, perhaps, has not so far much
prevalence here. But there is no doubt
that hire-purchase business in the
United Kingdom has attained vast
proportions, and has come to affect a
very large section of the population.
It is generally recognised that the
great bulk of business transacted on the
instalment plan is carried on in a perfectly honourable way in accordance with
the best traditions of commercial practice. It is fortunate that this is so, since
hire-purchase has become so widespread
in recent years, and has proved its value
to so many people. It has been obvious
for some time, however, that the system
is open to certain abuses. On the one
hand there have been harsh dealers not
always just in the treatment of their
customers, and, on the other hand, there
have been hirers whose carelessness or
ignorance has sometimes encouraged the
activities of unscrupulous dealers. Το
remedy the state of affairs in Great
Britain a Private Member's Bill was introduced into the British House of
Commons and was welcomed by all
parties. Members of every shade of
political opinion contributed in a
friendly and constructive way to evolve
the Act which is now on the Imperial
Statute Book. The Government of
Northern Ireland is now introducing a
Hire Purchase Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.j
similar measure, and the Bill before the
House has already received consideration
and approval in another place.
Although in Northern Ireland purchases by instalment are probably less
numerous and narrower in scope than in
Great Britain, the practice is on the increase, and it is accordingly desirable
that the safeguards which operate in
England and Wales for the just conduct
of this business should not be denied to
Northern Ireland. I should also like to
emphasise particularly the desire of the
Government that the law governing commercial practice in Northern Ireland
should be on the same plane as that in
other parts of the United Kingdom to
which our economic life is so closely
bound.
There is no need for me to dwell
at length on the particular abuses
of hire-purchase and credit-sale practice
with which I expect hon. Members are
familiar. The Bill is of necessity largely
concerned with legal machinery and
technicalities into which it is not necessary to go at the present stage. Broadly
speaking, the effect of the measure
should be to make the hirer more aware
of what he is undertaking when
he signs his agreement; and, by defining
certain rights and duties of hirer and
owner, the Bill is intended to ensure
that the agreement, when signed, shall
be carried out in the most sensible and
just manner. It will suffice, I think, if
I draw attention now to those main provisions designed to remedy abuses which
have become apparent in the operation
of the system.
Clause 2 provides for the disclosure by
the owner to the hirer, in writing, of
the price at which he can purchase the
goods for cash, and also for a written
note or memorandum of the agreement
in which the salient features of the arrangement must be set out together with
a note of the hirer's rights in the matter.
where a hire-purchaser has more than
one hire-purchase agreement with the
same owner, and is unable to maintain
instalment payments on all of them, he
may decide towards which of the agreements the payment he can make shall
be applied; and if he fails to do this the
payment will be applied to the various
agreements proportionately. Under
Clause 11 once a hirer has paid one-third
of the hire-purchase price on any article
the owner may not proceed to recover
possession otherwise than by court
action. In this way the circumstances
of each case can be thoroughly investigated, and some of the more glaring
abuses prevented, notably the ruthless
recovery or "snatching back" of the
goods by the owner, and the forfeiture
by the hirer both of the goods and of
the money he has already paid.
Clause 5 is designed to remedy a
number of abuses which have crept into
the system, among them the right
of entry into premises in order to take
possession of goods. Probably the most
important provision of the Bill is to be
found in Clause 9 and those immediately
following it. Clause 9 provides that
Clause 15 puts an end to another wellknown abuse of the system—the linkedon contract by providing that where a
further agreement is made between the
same parties after one-third of the hirepurchase price has been paid, the provisions of Clause 11 to which I have just
referred shall operate as regards the
further agreement also. I am confident
that hon. Members will support the
general purpose of this Bill and, at a
later stage, give careful consideration to
the details of its provisions, so that those
classes of the community whom this Bill
so closely affects may be assured that
their best interests will be safeguarded
when the Measure becomes law. I beg
to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: It is better late than
never. When I pressed on the Government twelve months ago to introduce this
measure they failed in their duty to the
people whom this Bill is now sought to
safeguard. Are you doing anything to
protect the interests of these people from
the date on which this Bill should have
become operative in Northern Ireland?
Are you doing anything to keep this Bill
зtep by step with Great Britain? Those
are the two salient points I want
answered. First, if you are not doing
anything to recoup these people who have
suffered by the failure of the Government
to introduce the Bill earlier, then I say
an answer must be forthcoming from the

right hon. Gentleman. In the second

what I want to know. I am in agreement with the principle of the Bill. This
being an impoverished area we have
never had sufficient purchasing power to

cannot see why the working classes should

The right hon. Gentleman stated, I

one gets into that circle it is pretty difficult to get out of it. No matter what
I may say it will never make black appear

here a notice which appeared in one of
our papers advertising for a qualified

he must be competent in every respect
and highly efficient in the matter of

This man must know every point of law
and how to get on to every point of law
so as to reclaim for the owner the goods
that were purchased under a hirepurchase agreement. This man was to
get £3 a week. This proves that the
repossession of goods is very extensive in
Northern Ireland. I have known cases
where the people had no reasonable opportunity to meet the payments, and they
were compelled to pay the fees of the

has happened in the city of Belfast.
I am only speaking for the borough of
Belfast as I know it. I have seen the

word black. That is this combine of

people safeguarded and protected from
these notable gentry in the furniture

amended. I hope the right hon. Gentleman will see his way to revert back to

Then, again, up to a certain figure mentioned in the Bill the right of possession
is given to the owner. I object to that

have the right to enter my home and
take away the goods which he says are
his property. He should first proceed
through the court for an order.
going to oppose that part of the Bill.

Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move: "That
this House views with alarm the sending
of men to work in Great Britain while
industry declines in the provincial areas
of Northern Ireland, and is of the opinion
that the sending of men to Great Britain
to work is not likely to bring prosperity
to this area, and that it is causing unnecessary hardships to families and dependants, thus indicating the inability of
the Government to supply work for the
unemployed, their only hope being the
conscription of our man power to work in
Great Britain under very trying conditions."

side of the House. The opportunity was
lost, and where are we to-day? We have
in Northern Ireland an employable
capacity of 24,000 people in shipbuilding,
engineering and aircraft manufacture.
That is the peak. But we have an
employable number up to 35,000, and we
cannot find work for them. Men do not
go to England, Scotland and Wales in
order to keep away from their wives and
families; they do not go voluntarily. They
go there in order to be in a position to
produce sufficient income to keep themselves, their wives and families in a state
of decency and comfort. Not a bad idea.
But look at what they lose. Family life
is broken. The discipline exercised by
the father is entirely gone. The mother
is left in charge of the household. There
may be five, six or seven boys, and no
woman without the assistance of her
husband can exercise the discipline that
some boys require. The family touch is
lost.
That is too big a sacrifice to make.
Family life should be kept intact by
employing the husbands at home. It
may be said we have not got employment
for them. This motion condemns the
Government for their failure to provide
work. The Government could have had
this work if they had wanted it, but
because of the system under which they
are operating in Northern Ireland they
think it better to have surplus labour in
order to keep down the wages level of the

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): In the main
estimate for the Ministry of Finance
there is a net increase of £11,600;
£4,300 more. is required for salaries. This
is due to the replacement of officers on
active service and those seconded to the
Imperial Government. Of this £3,700
is recouped to us by the Imperial
Exchequer.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £114,780 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge that
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1941, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Finance." (Note-£57,000
was voted on account.)
There is a net increase of £2,500 in the
cost of the administration of Ulster
Savings Certificates. There now exists
an Ulster Savings Committee for which
provision is required for a full year as
compared with a four months' period in
1939-40. As hon. Members are aware,
the Committee is straining every nerve
to ensure a maximum response in this
area, and this involves a certain amount
of additional expenditure. Since the introduction of the National Defence issue
of Certificates in November last the
average weekly sales have increased
from approximately 4,200 to over 54,000,
and over 150 savings groups have now
been formed. To date 40,000 people
have subscribed £860,000 in this new
Defence issue of Savings Certificates, of
which 75 per cent. is lent to the Imperial
Government for war purposes. Because
of this arrangement a substantial part of
the cost of administration is borne by
the British Exchequer to the extent of
some £8,500. In addition, the Imperial
authorities have agreed to bear the full
cost of advertising the campaign in
Northern Ireland.
The office of the Registrar-General
requires an extra £3,000 to meet the cost
of maintaining the National Register.
The whole of this additional expenditure
is recovered from the Imperial Government and will be found in the appropriations-in-aid. Our entire population has
been registered by using the applications
for ration books as a basis-a very convenient and economical way of dealing
with this problem. 1,273,000 identity
cards have been issued (a figure which
excludes soldiers and sailors and inmates
of institutions) and the willing and valuable co-operation of local authorities in
every district is very much appreciated.
The work of the Registrar-General's
Office in connection with the verification
of the ages of those joining H.M. Forces
and their families has greatly increased

are willing to do a little bit extra for

further exploration and excavation of

Oral Answers to Questions.
DOWN LANDOWNERS AND
COMPULSORY TILLAGE.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
all owners of land in County Down have
complied with the Compulsory Tillage
Order; and, if not, whether he can state
the names of the owners who have been
exempt from this Order, and the reasons
for their exemption.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): With regard to the
first part of the question, I think the
hon. Member will realise that it would
be impossible for me at this stage to say
if all owners of land in County Down
had complied with the provisions of the
Compulsory Tillage Order. I can, however, say without hesitation that farmers
in County Down, and indeed throughout
Northern Ireland, have been practically
unanimous in their response to the
Tillage Order.
As to the second part of the question,
I will make available to the hon. Member for inspection the complete record
of exemptions and partial exemptions
granted in County Down. I think it desirable to add that no exemption was
given without the closest scrutiny, and that
practically all were given on the ground
that if strict compliance with the Tillage
Order had been demanded milk production for the towns would have been
seriously interfered with. In most cases
partial exemption only was given. This
means that where it was felt that the
applicant for exemption, although engaged substantially in milk production,
could still, owing to the number of dairy
stock carried, do some tillage he was
required to do so.
PIG INDUSTRY COUNCIL.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, in view of the fact
that his Ministry is taking steps to elect
representatives of the curers on the Pig
Industry Council, he will in the near
future consider the question of allowing
the pig producers to elect their own
Board, so that through this Board the
pig producers will have the opportunity
of electing their own representatives on
the Pig Industry Council and not continue to be disfranchised indefinitely.
In
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No, sir.
view of the fact that the principal
functions of the Pigs Marketing Board
are now in abeyance as all pigs are purchased by the Ministry of Food, I do not
consider it necessary to provide for an
election of members to that Board during
the present national emergency.
Mr. NIXON: If the functions of the
Board are in abeyance are the members
of the Board being paid and, if so, why?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: There are
certain minor functions-not the functions normally carried out by the Pigs
Marketing Board.

TRANSPORT BOARD.
3. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the £250,000
guaranteed during the year ended the
31st March last in respect of loans to
the Transport Board is in addition to or
is included in the sum of £3,000,000
already guaranteed.
The MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): The
total amount guaranteed is £3,000,000,
and the sum of £250,000 is included in
that amount. No further guarantees
have been given or asked for.
4. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
the Transport Board is adding to its
losses by £250,000 a year and is still
buying transport concerns and thereby
adding to its capital liability.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
fact that the Transport Board is
incurring losses of £250,000 a year.
The published accounts of the Board for
the year to 30th September last (a copy
of which I understand was sent to each
Member of the House) show that the
Board earned an operating profit of
£7,693, in place of an operating deficit
of £76,206 in the previous year.
After charging interest, there was a
net deficit of £97,131, consisting
entirely of interest not earned.
The Board inform me that they are
not buying any transport concerns, nor
are they taking over any such concerns,
other than those which they are
pelled to take over under the terms of
the Act.
com-

making a profit why is it the Ministry
has to extend the guarantee to another
£250,000.
Mr. NIXON: It is all that misleading
word "operating".

have dealt with that in my answers to

refuges and incidental works, and

Turning to Subhead B, there is a

With regard to Bann drainage, as I
stated last year when introducing this
Public Works and Buildings 952
Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
Estimate, the channel improvements
remaining to be completed are being
carried out with the Ministry's own plant
and by direct labour. The war has
slowed down progress to a certain extent
as lighting restrictions prevent the
operation of the plant except during the
hours of daylight. Given reasonable
weather conditions, however, it is hoped
to have the whole scheme completed in
about eighteen months.
In contrast with the winter of 1938-39,
last winter was, from a drainage point
of view, dry until the end of January.
On the 29th of that month, however,
after snow and a rapid thaw, the heaviest
discharge on record passed down the river
and reached almost a million c.f.m. at
The Cutts.
The highest level reached by Lough
Neagh was on January 31st and February
2nd-53ft. O.D., or 6ins. below the commencement of flooding. In pre-contract

PRICE OF PIGS SOLD IN
SEPTEMBER.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
result of his consultations with the law
officers of the Crown regarding the position of all those who sold pigs in Northern Ireland between 3rd and 27th
September, in view of the decision of the
Lord Chief Justce for Northern Ireland
in the case of Swain v. The Producers'
Bacon Company (Collin Glen), Ltd.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
30 APRIL 1940
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir. 1
must, first of all, point out that it is not
the province of my Ministry to interpret
the legal effects as between buyers and
sellers of orders made under the Defence
Regulations in regard to prices. That is
entirely a matter for the courts to decide
and it would obviously be improper for
the Ministry to attempt to usurp the
functions of the courts.
In the particular instance to which
the hon. Member, refers, the question of
the application to Northern Ireland of
S.R.O. 1061, made by the Board of
Trade on 3rd September, 1939, has recently been the subject of a decision by
the Lord Chief Justice for Northern
Ireland. My Minstry has no reason to
question, and no desire to question the
soundness of the decision given by the
Lord Chief Justice, but I am advised
that equally the Ministry has no power
to tie the hands of any individual curer
who may be advised by his own legal
advisers that he is legally entitled on any
grounds to resist the claim of a producer
for higher prices than those received by
him during the period 3rd to 27th
September.
Mr. BROWN: Has the Minister overlooked the fact that the Lord Chief
Justice made it perfectly clear in his
decision that this case was a test case,
and the public were led to believe that
payment would automatically follow to
those who sold pigs at this particular
time?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think the
answer I have given is correct, and it is
the answer I have been advised to give
to the question.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether in view of the
fact that his Ministry misinterpreted the
Board of Trade Order fixing the prices of
pigs he is not prepared to assist pig producers to get the full prices they are
entitled to.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think the
hon. Member or any producer who wishes
to have the position clarified should consult his own legal adviser.
PAYMENTS FOR PIGS.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has seen in
the Press the report of the case of
Messrs. John Dinsmore & Sons against
the Pigs Marketing Board, and whether
he can state why it is that so many pig
producers in Northern Ireland have now
to resort to the Law Courts before they
can get for their pigs the price to which
they are legally entitled.
Mr. BROWN: I give notice that I shall
raise this matter on the Adjournment.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have seen
reports in the Press of the case to which
the hon. Member refers. With regard
to the second part of the question, I am
afraid the hon. Member is exaggerating
the position. I am aware of only two
instances in which pig producers have
recently taken legal proceedings in connection with payments for pigs sold by
them.
Mr. GAMBLE: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, is it a fact that
there has been more litigation over the
price of pigs since the dissolution of the
former Pigs Marketing Board than there
was during all the years that Board was
looking after pig producers?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The fact is
there is a war on and certain Orders
have been made which have received
different interpretations.
That is the
reason.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is the Minister prepared to give all the assistance to pig
producers to get the full prices for their
pigs, or does he think the producers must
take individual action to get that full
price?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It depends on
what the hon. Member means by all
assistance. If they bring up particular
cases they will be considered.
Mr. ELLIOTT: If every pig producer
who has not received the full price has
to undertake litigation, it will mean a
great deal of litigation.
Mr. BEATTIE: A paradise for the
lawyers.

of Agriculture, as representing the

SUPPLY OF SEED BARLEY.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
quantity of seed barley purchased by his
Ministry, the quantity disposed of to
date, and whether the surplus (if any) not
required for seed will be available to stock
owners in Northern Ireland for feeding
purposes.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The quantity of
seed barley purchased by my Ministry was
3,200 tons; the quantity disposed of to
date is 1,570 tons; if there is a surplus
at the finish the question of its utilisation
for feeding purposes will be considered.
Alternatively such a surplus may be held
over until next year. This would be quite
practicable because the seed is of such
a high quality that it could he held over
without any material loss of germinating
power.

barley which is at present in Northern

SLAUGHTER OF FAT CATTLE.
9. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture. whether now that the
slaughtering of fat cattle is under Government control it would not be more
economic to have such slaughtering of
all Northern Ireland cattle carried out
in Northern Ireland, and ship the
carcases across to Great Britain instead
of the live animals, thereby conserving
shipping space; and whether, if this was
done, it would not also be possible to cure
all hides in this country and establish
one or more tanneries in Northern Ireland
to deal with such, and thereby give more
much needed employment.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Apart from
any other considerations, it would not
be practicable to put the hon. Member's
suggestions into effect in view of the
existing restricted shipping facilities from
Northern Ireland ports, and of the fact
that those facilities do not include the
necessary equipment, including refrigeration, for the proper carriage of dead meat
in quantity.
Mr. BROWN: Is it a fact that a great
deal of shipping space could be saved by
erecting these tanneries and erecting
factories to make boots and shoes from
the product of these tanneries in Northern
Ireland? Does the Minister not consider
that would save shipping?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes. But first
of all you have got to kill your beast,
and the difficulty of the hon. Member's
suggestion is that beef butchered here
could not be shipped to England under
present conditions.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Minister say
that more shipping is required to send
dead animals than to send live animals?

Hire Purchase Bill.
Considered in Committee.
———
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
CLAUSE 1 (Application of Act).
1. This Act shall apply in relation
to all hire-purchase agreements and
credit-sale agreements under which the
hire-purchase price or total purchase
price, as the case may be, does not
exceed-
(a) where the agreement relates to a
motor-car or railway wagon or
other railway rolling stock, the
sum of fifty pounds,
(b) where the agreement relates to
livestock, the sum of five hundred
pounds, and
(c) in any other case, the sum of two
hundred pounds,
and in this Act the expressions "hirepurchase agreement" and "credit-sale
agreement" shall be construed accordingly.
Mr. MINFORD: I beg to move in
paragraph (c), leave out "two" ("two
hundred pounds") and insert "one."
This Bill as originally introduced in
the Senate closely followed the English
Act except for certain adaptations.
When this Bill was before the Standing
Committee in the Imperial Parliament
some Members suggested that the amount
Hire Purchase Bill-
Committee

HOUSE OF COMMUNS
[Mr. Minford]
be limited to £50 and others suggested
£150. As a compromise a sum of £100
was agreed to. I think I am right in
saying that the Bill could not have got
through the British House of Commons
only for that compromise being arrived
at. It was generally agreed that £100
was a good limit to allow any person to
engage in the hire-purchase system. The
figure was also agreed to as being a protection for the working people of Great
Britain. I suggest that to increase the
£100 to £200 would mean bringing in
the more moneyed class. This Bill is to
protect the working people from being
fleeced by hire-purchase concerns whose
reputation is not of the best. If the
£200 is inserted in this Clause instead
of £100 it means that the Bill will not be
as good as the English measure. The
£100 was accepted by both sides in Great
Britain after a long discussion, and the
Bill would never have gone through but
for that compromise. The intention of
the Bill is to protect the working classes.
If the moneyed class wanted this Bill
there would be no use in having a maximum limit at all. As the £100 has been
accepted in Great Britain I do not see
why it should not be agreed to here.
Northern Ireland being part of the
United Kingdom it is only right and
reasonable that we should go step by
step in this policy. Another thing is
that if the £200 is retained hire-purchase
agreements here would be on a different
footing to those in Great Britain. In
the interests of the working people I ask
the Committee to accept the amendment.
I hope they will agree with me.
£100 and £200. (Hon. Members:

Mr. ANDREWS: The House will
remember that in their Interim Report,
circulated a short time ago, the
Valuation Committee recommended the
postponement of the general revaluation
due to take place next year. Clause 1
of the Bill gives effect to this recommendation. Apart from other considerations, it will be appreciated that
during the war is not an appropriate
time to carry out a revaluation intended
to last for five years, and it has been
postponed in Great Britain. Machinery
for dealing with the annual revision of
valuations will, of course, be maintained
to enable the re-assessment of property,
the value of which may change.
required the Ministry of Finance to
ascertain the cost of annual revision in
the second year after each general revaluation, and this sum was to be
regarded as the standard cost of annual
revision for the separate years in each
quinquennial period.
Clause 2 is concerned with the contribution to be made by counties and county
boroughs towards the cost of the annual
revision of rateable property. In the
1932 Act, Parliament laid down the
principle that from the date of the first
general revaluation. local authorities
should contribute half the actual cost of
annual revision. In order to fix the sum
to be paid to the Exchequer the Act
In the present five-year period general
revaluation came into force in 1936-37,
and the standard year was, therefore,
1937-38. The cost of annual revision in
this standard year was found to be
£17,000, and as the law now stands local
authorities were liable from 1936 onwards
to pay half this amount, that is £8,500,
instead of the £3,405 which they have
paid since 1932.
Shortly after the cost in this standard
year became known the Valuation Committee was set up, and as one of their
terms of reference was to consider
"whether the whole basis of paying for
valuation ought to be revised SO as
to combine the costs of annual revision
with those of general revaluation" action
to recover the higher contribution from
local authorities was delayed pending the
report of the committee.
As stated in their interim report,
circulated a short time ago, the committee
decided to suspend consideration of this
and other questions during the war. The
Government felt that it would be unfair
expect local authorities to fulfil
retrospectively their obligation under the
1932 Act which would be £8,500 per
year. Accordingly, after consultation
with representatives of local authorities
I have agreed to take statutory power to

Hon. Members will observe that

roughly. I can best illustrate this position by two or three examples.
Part of the saving is due to the
stopping or curtailment of services which
are not of immediate food production
value, such as the purchase of land for
forestry purposes, improvement of livestock, grants to agricultural shows, etc.
The Agricultural (Emergency Provisions) Act which was passed when war
broke out empowered the Ministry for
the period of the emergency to take over
the staffs of the County Committees of
Agriculture. Those staffs were transferred
to the Ministry and became Civil
Servants and their salaries amounting to
£12,000 which were shown in Vote 2
now disappear from that Vote.
On the other hand the salaries of the

in Vote 1, and as their services, amongst
others, are mainly engaged upon the
tillage campaign, the cost is recouped as
an appropriation-in-aid from the appropriate Imperial Department, namely, the
Home Office.
Again, hon. Members will note under
the heading Marketing and Food Defence
Division a very substantial increase in
the staff of this section from 94 to 243.
It is this staff which, amongst other
things, is responsible for the administration and control of such new services
as livestock and meat control, pigs and
bacon control, butter, margarine, oils
and cooking fats control, fertilisers and
feeding stuffs control, and so on, services
Broadly speaking, the work of my
Ministry in this anxious and exacting
period of war may be divided into two
sections-first, increased food production
from our own soil, and, secondly, the
purchase of the produce produced from
our soil, the resale of it, and its carriage
and distribution down to the retailer.
With regard to increased food production, as the Committee is aware, the
Ministry are operating under powers
delegated to it by the Secretary of State
for the Home Office under the powers
conferred upon him under the Defence
Regulations. The plans prepared during
the period of stress preceding the war
provided for the ploughing up during
the first year of the war of an additional
area of two million acres in the United
Kingdom-a total which has been fulfilled by the farmers of the United
Kingdom. Of the total of two million
acres Ulster was allocated 150,000 acres.
our
In the first days of the war it became
clear to me that if we were to play our
full part, and if we were going to bring
agricultural community through
what was manifestly going to be a period
of great stress and difficulty, it would
be necessary to plough up much more
than an additional 150,000 acres. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do not think
it is necessary to point out that our agricultural income is mainly derived from
livestock and livestock products-80 per
cent. Another point that should be
borne in mind is that the livestock population is very much greater. There is
a
greater concentration per acre in
Ulster than any other part of the
United Kingdom. Accordingly, I set
out to get at least 250,000 additional
acres under the plough. As the Committee are aware, we have achieved that
aim. More than 260,000 acres of old
grass land have already been turned over
by the plough. Crops of oats, barley
and flax have been sown or are in process
of being sown on this new tillage area.
Some idea of the magnitude of this
task may be gathered from the fact that
Ulster's contribution to the increased
tillage campaign is equal to that of
Scotland-it is 70 per cent. more than

the
allocated task. Moreover,
additional acres ploughed in this, the

Is going to be the position from

There is one point I would like to
mention before I leave this matter. Sometimes the Ministry have been accused of
being asleep and not taking the strong
action they should take. Let me tell the
Committee that at the beginning of the
war, and with the concurrence of my
right hon. Friend, the
Friend, the Minister of
Finance, we bought all the pedigree flax
seed available in Canada. The result has
been that our farmers have been able to
purchase that seed at a reasonable price.
It has meant that the cost of the raw
material for the spinners, when that flax
is scutched, will be considerably lower
than otherwise. More recently still, as a
result of a promise which I made to the
farmers that I would not see them plough
up the land and have them short of seed,
and again with the concurrence of the
Minister of Finance, we went into the
grain market and bought, as a Ministry,
the barley which I thought would be required to be sown in this country. The
result of that action is that the farmers
here have been enabled to buy their
barley at the same price as the farmers
on the other side of the water. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I could not, even if it were necessary
I should do so, give the Committee an
adequate idea of the enormous amount of
organisation which has been put into this
tillage campaign; to mention one item
only, the provision of the necessary
tractors, the training of the operatives,
anticipating and calculating the needs for
machinery, securing supplies and distributing is a romance in itself. But at
least I can do this, express my thanks
to the staff, outdoor and indoor, for the
way they have risen to the occasion. I
should like also to thank the County
Committees of Agriculture. The country
owes a great debt to them for the unselfish way they put the whole of their
resources and machinery at the disposal
of my Department, and for the backing,
support and voluntary work which members of the committees have given to this
big effort; and, last but not least, I
would like to express my indebtedness to
the War Committee of the Farmers'
Union. The hon. Member for Derry
was president of the Union for
most of that time. I should like
to say what a great help they were
to me. We were able to discuss many
difficulties and were able to rub off many
edges that might have created trouble in
the country. On the whole, as a result
of the team work manifested everywhere
by farmers, county committees, staffs,
Ulster Farmers' Union, labourers and
everybody else, we have succeeded in
doing a work which we can well be
proud of.
There is a second phase, but I do not
propose to go into details because it
would take far too long and would not
give an adequate picture. I would like.
to deal with the activities of the Ministry
in the purchase of food and its distribution to the retailers. They affect not
only the farmers but also the consumers,
and therefore are of importance to all of
us. In the purchase of farm produce
and its resale and distribution to the
retailer the Ministry is acting as the
agent of the Ministry of Food. It is
the Minister of Food who fixes prices,
distributing margins and hence the price
at which the products are sold to the
community, and my Ministry, which
carries out the orders, operates the
machinery, and in some instances devises
it.
Since the 15th of January my Ministry
has been purchasing all the cattle, sheep
and pigs for slaughter in Northern
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Estimates
Ministry of Agriculture
[Sir Basil Brooke]
Ireland; those required for the feeding
of our own population are slaughtered in
17 abattoirs staffed and operated by the
Ministry, and the meat distributed to
every butcher in the country. The cattle,
sheep and pigs are presented at 97
purchasing centres and depots, carriage
of all these animals to their destinations
in this country and to England and
Scotland has to be arranged and paid for
by the Ministry. I think the Committee
will admit that this truly gigantic
change-over has been accomplished with
remarkable smoothness and efficiency,
and I venture to think that our people
are getting better quality meat than they
ever did before. I have only heard of
one major complaint-there have been
many minor ones of any substance,
namely, a temporary shortage of mutton.
There is this point to remember, that
formerly a considerable amount of
mutton came from the South of Ireland.
There is no import of mutton from the
South of Ireland at the present time.
Now we have to supply not only His
Majesty's soldiers stationed in Northern
Ireland but the ships of His Majesty's
Navy when they call in our harbours.
They have to be revictualled. If we have
a temporary shortage of mutton it is
caused chiefly by those two reasons,
namely a lack of import of mutton from
the Free State and what the Forces
on the other hand are taking. It has
been suggested that we should ship
more beef carcases and in return import
mutton. Considering the difficulties of
shipping at the present time I do not
think any reasonable person would care
to add to those difficulties. I would
remind those who make such criticisms
that in a week or so we shall have more
mutton and lamb than we can consume.
Before leaving the livestock and meat
scheme I should like to mention one
further aspect of it. The centring of
our meat supply in 17 abattoirs has had
two great advantages. First it has provided our community with a complete
meat inspection system covering the
whole supply of the country, and ensured
that our meat is handled and transported
under greatly improved conditions.
Secondly, it has eliminated an enormous
amount of waste. All the products not
utilised for human food are now available in quantities which enable them to
be converted into animal feeding stuffs,
industrial products and fertilisers, and
it can now be truthfully said that each
animal is being used from its head to its
hoof.
And now I must content myself with
one further illustration. The Ministry,
on behalf of the Ministry of Food, is
purchasing all the butter produced in
this country or brought into it. It is

What of the small farming community?
My constituency, practically speaking, is

They are just as willing to increase food

realise that the subsidies or other financial assistance given to the large farmers
will not reach them for the simple reason

struggling farmer and his family. He is

of Agriculture allows the number of
those farmers to diminish then our

They are the unorganised section of

devoted to the training of land girls?
I trust not, and I hope we shall be given
an assurance that this extravagance-for

Now I want to refer for a moment to

him every support possible in his efforts.
When I referred to this matter on a

Therefore I cannot see any difficulty on

boots and shoes to be made. from the products of Ulster tanneries. These matters
are of very great importance, and if the

I should like to say a word or two about

be impossible for us to have. the same
kind of panel as they have in England;
but we could have a farmer and a

Mr. MINFORD: I rise to tender my
congratulations to the Minister of Agriculture and to the Ministry for
successful way in which they have tackled
the great task that is entrusted to them.
I think the fact that 260,000 additional
acres have been put under the plough is
something of which the right hon.
Gentleman has every reason to be proud.
Going among the farmers as I do, I
know that the farmers are very grateful
to the Minister for the consideration he
has extended to those who were not able
in every way to comply with the requests
of the Ministry. The Ministry have met
people in such circumstances in a way
that has made them very grateful.
Prior to the war farmers were not
getting fair treatment, and it is worthy
of comment that it took the war to show
to the people of Great Britain the importance of agriculture. The farmers
have already risen to the occasion, and
I can assure the Minister of Agriculture
that they will do even better to help
the country in this time of national
emergency. I, like other hon. Members,
was struck by the number of officials for
whom provision is made in the Estimates.
I asked myself what these men do. The
answer is that the Ministry have undertaken the colossal task of administering
up to £12,000,000 for livestock and food,
and it takes a big staff to carry out a
task of such magnitude. It has been
suggested that umpires should be placed
over the men who are employed in
grading livestock. In principle I agree;
but I must say that the inspectors, in
my opinion, have carried out their work
in a way of which we should be justly
proud.
Speaking as a farmer who has put
stock on the market for a good many
years, I must say that one sometimes
came away without having got what one
expected. My experience of the graders
is that they are doing their job very well.
We all remember the old method of
bartering, and I believe that if the choice
between barter and having their stock
graded by the Ministry's inspectors were
put before the farmers, they would prefer
the grading.
Regarding the supply of sheep, I know
that there must be a line of demarcation.
One of my friends in a provincial town.
had entered twelve sheep, and then he
thought he would send twenty. The
twenty were graded, but he was very
much annoyed when the inspector, finding that only twelve had been entered,
insisted on his taking eight back with
him. I should like the Minister to make
a note of that incident. I think that
was going beyond the ordinary limits of
red tape. If there had been a glut in
the market I could have understood it,
but at the present time hospitals and
other institutions are complaining about
a shortage of mutton. Within a month
or six weeks there will be an enormous
number of lambs all over Ulster. My
experience is that the three saleyards in
Belfast are filled from door to door on
Monday, and it is really impossible to
deal with the position, unless the
Minister is going to ration lambs or limit
the sale to a certain number week by
week. In pre-war times the seaside
resorts took quite a number of these
lambs. I believe that, even with the
war
on,
we in Ulster and in Great
Britain have not lost our courage, and
that the lambs will be taken as usual.
The hon. Member for Pottinger said
that the levies were being taken out of
the pockets of the farmers, and that the
farmers passed on the cost to the consumers. I think that is not a fair statement, because the hon. Member knows
perfectly well that the farmers are
getting only a reasonable return for their
labour. I think the consumers have no
right to grumble, for they are getting
their supplies at a just price. During
Estimates-

Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
the last war prices soared to great
heights, and I am delighted that in the
present struggle the State has stepped in
and enabled the distributors to buy food
at reasonable and just prices. I Ι am
quite sure that the Minister of Agriculture here will get into touch with the
Imperial Minister and with the Minister
of Food from time to time, in order to
decide how much it is necessary for a
farmer to get in order to give him a
return for his labour.
We are all out to do our best to produce as much food as possible, in order
that the people may be fed during the
war. In regard to one remark made by
the hon. Member for Pottinger, I should
like to say, as an ordinary citizen, that
if there is going to be any shortage it
should not fall upon the Royal Navy, the
Army, or the Royal Air Force. I have
never met any man or woman who has
experienced a shortage of food to the
detriment of his or her health. I really
think that the people do not quite realise
that there is a war on, because they are
getting as much food as they require, or
at any rate as much as is good for them.
Some people say that the farmers are
If in the past the farmer
grumblers.
grumbled, he was unfortunately compelled to grumble; but I believe that
agriculture has now been put on a sound
business basis. Agriculture fell so low
prior to the war because we had allowed
our men to drift from the land. The
farmers were unable to pay the farm
workers as much as they could earn in
other industries. I am pleased to know
that the Government have established a
Wages Board, because the agricultural
labourer is entitled to as good wages, as
good hours, and as good holidays as the
men in any other industry. If the
Minister carries out that promise to the
labourers, I am quite satisfied that he will
also give the farmers a fair return for
their labour, in order that they may pay
good wages to that deserving class of
people, the agricultural labourers.
Someone has spoken about the possibility of a great shortage of labour at the
harvest. On that point I may say that,
if I need men, I communicate with the
Employment Exchange at Ballyclare or
Antrim, and I find there is no difficulty
in getting men, so long as they are offered
reasonable wages. The men may not be
as well versed in agricultural matters as
is desirable, but my experience is that if
they are paid reasonable, decent wages,
and if consideration and patience is
shown to them, they turn out pretty
good chaps.
I was amazed at the statement made
by the hon. Member for South Armagh
regarding the Cookstown School, that between £4,000 and £5,000 was spent in
order to train six girls to drive tractors.
That, of course, is absurd. Everyone
interested in agriculture knows of the
good work that has been done at the
Cookstown School in training girls to
make good butter and to look after
poultry. From my own experience of
this school, I can say that it has done
good work among the young women in
the rural parts of this area. If we curtail the activities of such schools, we will
lose the valuable experience of those who
have been entrusted with the care of those
institutions.
I should like to see a potato factory
established in Northern Ireland. I remember that we had three or four bad
years when the Ministry of Agriculture
was under the right hon. Gentleman's
predecessor. I raised the question of trying to have a factory established at that
time, and was told that if potatoes
should happen to rise in price it would
be difficult to supply the factory. But
we are now living in war time, and if
we had a factory going for three, four or
five years, it would be well worth while.
I think that to take potatoes from here
to Wisbech and bring them back in the
form of
potato meal is wasting very
valuable space in our ships. When we
are fighting on two fronts we require all
the space possible for the use of our
If the surplus were
Fighting Forces.
made into potato meal here it would save
transport across the water and would
also act as an inducement to farmers to
grow more potatoes. We are growing
larger crops to-day, but the people are
not eating SO many potatoes. The
potatoes could be turned into most
valuable food for cattle. It is not a
question of the cost of inaugurating a
scheme; we must look far beyond the
initial cost. Now that the land has been
tilled we must go through the ordinary
tillage routine by growing root
or
Ministry of Agriculture

Estimates-

potato crops. If the land is not to be
put back into grass, farmers will have
to get a reasonable price for their
produce.
If the Minister could induce the
powers that be to build a factory in
Northern Ireland it would encourage the
farmers to continue agriculture. The
farmers from a patriotic point of view are
at present tilling their land. We must,
however, remember the unfortunate
repercussions of the last war. In 1918
prices were good, while in 1919 and 1920
they were better, but we all look back
with horror to those years when the
price of farm produce was at a very
low level. If a potato factory were
erected it would give confidence to the
farmers. Farming is the basic industry
of any country, and the war has made
people look to the farmers to produce
food. The farmer asks for nothing
unreasonable. He wants a fair return for
his labour.
I should now like to refer to the statement made on the Adjournment yesterday by the Attorney-General in regard
to pig prices in Northern Ireland from
3rd September to later on in the same
month. Without any disrespect to the
Ministry or the Attorney-General I am
still convinced that something should be
done to stop this talk of injustice
to the producers. The learned Attorney-
General in reply to me yesterday said
that I had suggested that the Minister
had misinterpreted the Order which
came from the Board of Trade, and that
I was saying the Ministry should be the
legal advisers of the farmers. I never
suggested any such thing. What I did
suggest was that if the Order was misinterpreted-I do not say it was done to
try to injure the farmers-it is the duty
of the Minister, especially after the
Collin Glen case had been decided by the
Lord Chief Justice, to enter into some
arrangement whereby the farmers will
receive the money to which they are
entitled.
The Collin Glen factory owners have
written to a gentleman I know stating
that he may expect to hear from them in
a very short time regarding the prices of
the pork he sold during September. I
agree with the hon. Member for South
Tyrone that the curers and factories are
sheltering behind the Ministry. No one
suggests that the Minister
or the
Ministry tried to do the farmers out of
that money during that particular time,
but the farmers believe they are entitled
to the price paid by the English curers
during that period and which was denied
to them. Nobody is going to blame the
Minister for that.
I should like to ask the Attorney-
General, who is a shining star in the
legal world, is it British justice to
suggest that because an order was misinterpreted-it has been proved to have
been misinterpreted by a court presided
over by the Lord Chief Justice-farmers
should be denied the amount of money
to which they are justly entitled? It
would have been better for the Ministry
to have taken legal advice on the matter.
One official said bluntly and boldly that
this Order did not apply to Northern
Ireland. I am not finding fault with
the Minister or the officials. A mistake
has been made and the sooner it is
remedied the better.
During the past six months pig producers have gone through an anxious
time. They have done their best to produce pork notwithstanding the fact that
they did not know where the feeding
would come from. I should like along
with the hon. Member for South Tyrone
to hear a pronouncement in regard to the
policy of the Ministry of Food in Great
Britain. Are they trying to bring in
sufficient food to keep our livestock
going? I listened to a broadcast by the
Minister of Food or the Minister of
Agriculture sometime in September, and
he told the farmers of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland not to sell one animal
off their farms, and not to lessen their
stock, not even to one hare. I hope that
is still the policy.
or
In conclusion, I should like to congratulate the Minister on the splendid
work that he and his staff have done and
are doing. In regard to the land fertility,
compulsory tillage, cattle, other
schemes, I have always found the officials.
courteous in the extreme. I hope the
Minister will have the confidence of the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I should like
to deal very briefly with some of the
points raised by hon. Members. The

from one will find that eventually it does

from the pocket of the consumer. His
further statement that the Ministry of
Food is making money out of the consumer does not bear any semblance of
As the hon. Member for
accuracy.
Antrim has pointed out, the Ministry of

It is, I think, one
million per week. So far as I am aware
no butter has been sent in any form,
camouflaged or otherwise, to a soap
factory. I would suggest to the hon.
Member for Pottinger that he should,
privately, let me have any information
in his possession, and I will then look
into the matter.
As some hon. Members wish to leave I
will deal with the points raised by them
as quickly as I can. The matter of chief
interest is the legal decision in the Swain
case. Of course the House has heard the
explanation given by the Attorney-
General. I do not intend to deal with
the legal side of the matter because I
am not in a position to do so. The
position is this. On the 3rd of September an Order was made by the British
Government that producers of fresh pork
might feed their pigs for a longer period
and thus turn them into use for bacon
purposes. That was the Order. As hon.
Members are aware we have no producers of fresh pork in this country. In
consultation with my Ministry it was
intended by the Ministry of Food that
that Order should not apply here. At
that period a new contract system had
come into being, and we felt until we
saw exactly how matters stood that it
was no use having an Order that did
not apply to more than half of one per
cent. of pig producers in this country.
In the writing out of the Order the words
"Does not apply to Northern Ireland"
were omitted.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Thank goodness.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I sympathise
with the hon. Member in that expression
of joy.
It has been decided by the court
that the producers are entitled to certain
moneys, but the Order was not intended
to apply to Northern Ireland for the
reason I have given. It boils down to
what I, as Minister, should do to help
them. I am anxious that every producer should get as much money as possible, but, quite honestly, legally I
cannot do it. It means that each producer or curer has to decide whether he
will go to the court and accept its
decision. That is how the position lies.
I hope in this brief explanation I have
made the position clear.
Another point raised was in connection
with the scrapping of the livestock
schemes. So far as that matter is concerned it is only pushing an open door,
as I am with the hon. Member every
time. The livestock improvement scheme
has been going on for some 40 years. It
was started in Ireland under the old
Department, and has been increasing
ever since. I have not finished with the
battle for that money, and I hope I may
be successful.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: When it comes
to grants for shows I am treading on
different ground. The plan adopted by
my Ministry, in conjunction with the
Ministry of Finance, is only to spend
money which is of immediate benefit for
war purposes. That is the position in
regard to shows.
Another point of considerable importance was with reference to referees
for the grading of cattle. As the hon.
Member for North Derry so ably put it,
I may say we have consulted and talked
over this question for the best part of
the last five or six months. In theory it
is perfectly right that there should be a
referee, but in practice it is an extremely
difficult thing to work out. If the
grading was inaccurate, or if the grading
officers were making big errors in favour
of the Ministry of Food or the farmers,
there would be a case for a referee, but,
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
1 MAY 1940
in fact, the actual grading error, in
spite of the vast number of animals,
varies from one-half to two per cent.
That is a very small thing indeed.
One farmer I admit may be unlucky and
another may do rather better than he
should. But when you come down to
the practical side of it as to how you are
going to appoint a referee then you
come up against a very real difficulty.
The difficulty is this, that if the Ministry
appoint the referee they pay him and,
therefore, that paid referee would be
just as much under possible suspicion as
the Ministry's officers at the present time.
If on the other hand the farmers agree
to appoint a referee and pay him themselves, it would be very doubtful if the
Ministry of Food would agree to a
referee paid by any outside body deciding
whether their officers were right in their
decision or not. What I have never
succeeded in getting from the farmers is
this. Supposing you do have a referee
and supposing you made an appeal and
the actual carcase is weighed, would the
farmer be prepared to refund to the
Ministry if in fact the carcase weighed
less than the Ministry's official declared
it to weigh. I have never got any clear
statement on that.
It is a thing bristling with difficulties.
Some Members of this House who have.
not been to these centres do not realise
the enormous rush there is in trying to
get the work through in time.. Very
often the veterinary officers start at 8
o'clock in the morning and they are quite
often at it until late in the afternoon.
If you are then to have a referee looking
at each animal you are going to about
double the time, and they would never
get through the work. So that although
in theory one has sympathy with the idea
of a referee, in practice we have not found
any means of working it out.
I would say increase the, livestock. It is
purely a matter for the individual himself. I cannot assist him. The only thing
I can say is by the work of the agricultural community, from the Ministry right
down to the farmer himself, increasing
the acreage as we have done, the chance
of increasing livestock is greater than it
would have been if we had not done so.
Then various hon. Members have asked
me whether I can give a definite statement as to whether livestock should be
increased in this country or not. Now,
if anybody asked me if the war was going
to be over to-morrow or in the next ten
years it would be just as easy to answer
as to say whether livestock should be
increased or not. Each man must decide
on his own. Nobody could possibly say
what the feeding stuff position is going
to be. If on his own farm a farmer has
plenty of stuff that he had not last year
The Member for South Down raised
the question of forestry, and complained
that less money was to be spent on
forestry. The principle I pointed out a
few minutes ago applies to that, that
no money is being spent on anything
which is not directly producing food for
war purposes. That is really the governing factor. The arguments he used are
perfectly sound. One ought to invest for
the future. But there is such a heavy
expenditure necessary for the war that I
think it is advisable at the moment to
hold back, merely completing the planting of such trees as have been purchased
and wait for better times before carrying
on planting.
So far as the Cookstown school is concerned I think the article he read from
"John Bull" referred to the effort we
made to start a reserve land army, that
is to say, ladies who were prepared to go
through a course of farm training at
Cookstown and were also prepared to go
back to their homes or take on a job
immediately. That scheme did not work
out. It will be appreciated that during
war time every scheme must be thought
out and every effort made to meet all
possible difficulties that may arise in the
future. The same thing applies to Cookstown, where we tried the experiment of
getting ladies to take up this work. It
did not work out. We have now reverted
to the old scheme of poultry.
My Ministry are considering very carefully the question of labour for the
harvest. In a matter of a month or so
I hope to be in a position to know exactly
what will be required and how we intend
to meet it. All these points have been
thought about and we are not leaving
anything to chance so far as we are able.
As to the potato factory, I have already
told the House in answer to a question
that my Ministry are negotiating on that
point and I could not state anything
more at the moment. I would just like
to say in conclusion that I appreciate
very much indeed the references which

2. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
