I would refer the hon. Member to the
answer given to the hon. Member for
South Tyrone to a similar question asked
by him on the 5th March last.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I assume the
hon. Member refers to the concession recently granted in Great Britain enabling
a farmer to haul to and from the railway
station under a 5s tractor licence produce
grown on or requisites for the farm
occupied by him.
Since that answer was given I have
received full particulars regarding the
concession granted in Great Britain from
which it is clear that it was granted owing
to the fact that local transport difficulties
had caused many delays in getting produce away from farms. I am as yet by
no means satisfied that similar conditions
prevail here, but I am at present considering representations that have been
made to me in connection with the concession to which the hon. Member refers.

7 MAY 1940
Second Reading
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Industrial Assurance and Friendly
Societies (Emergency Protection
from Forfeiture) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): One class of legislation which it
has been found necessary to bring into being
since the outbreak of war comprises certain
measures framed with the intention of
preventing undue hardship to members of
the public who, through no fault of their
own, find themselves, owing to circumstances arising from the war, unable to
discharge certain financial commitments.
The Emergency Bill to which the House
is now asked to accord a Second Reading
is of this character. As its title indicates, it is designed to give protection
from forfeiture to certain classes of
policies of assurance.
Under the measure
now before the
House it is proposed that this protection
will not be extended to any policy which,
exclusive of bonus, covers an assurance
exceeding £50 in amount or upon which
less than two years premiums have been
paid or which has been effected on or
after 1st September, 1939.
Subject to these limitations, the Bill
applies to (a)
(a) policies of industrial
assurance, which as hon. Members will be
aware is the business of effecting
assurances upon human life, premiums in
respect of which are payable weekly as a
rule, and are received by means of doorto-door collection; (b) policies. of
assurance upon human life effected with
collecting societies, not being policies of
industrial assurance; and (c) policies of
assurance upon human life, in respect of
which there are separate premiums,
effected with registered friendly societies.
other than collecting societies.
dorsed or a notice will be served on the
applicant to the effect that it is a policy
protected by the Act. If, on the other
hand, the application is refused the
applicant will have the right of appeal
against such refusal to the Industrial
Assurance Commissioner.
It is inevitable that some owners of
policies by reason of circumstances
arising directly or indirectly out of the
war will be unable to continue paying
the premiums. The object of the Bill is
to ensure that such persons shall have
an opportunity to inform the assurance
company or the society of the circumstances and make an application for the
protection of the policy. If the company
or society, as the case may be, admits
the application the policy will be en-
The details of the procedure, which
includes notice to the policy-holder of his
rights of application and appeal, are
clearly set out in Clauses 2 and 8 of the
Bill.
When a policy has received the protection of the Act, the assurance will remain
in force notwithstanding the fact that no
A
further premiums are being paid.
company or society may thereafter appeal
to the Commissioner for the protection
to be brought to an end, and if the
Commissioner is satisfied that the owner
of the policy is no longer unable, by
reason of circumstances arising from the
war, to pay the premiums on the policy,
he will make an order for the ending of
the protection. If no such order is made
by the Commissioner, the protection will
extend to a date to be appointed by
Order in Council and thereafter there
will be a period of three months' grace.
Such are the main provisions designed
to prevent hardship to policy-holders.
Hon. Members will agree that it is only
just that consideration should be given
to the companies and societies affected
by these modifications in normal practice.
As a set-off, therefore, against the nonreceipt of premiums upon a policy under
which a claim arises before the expiration
of the period of grace, the company or
society will be allowed to deduct the
amount of the outstanding premiums,
with interest thereon, or, if the policy
is one of endowment insurance, its
period of maturity may be postponed and
the period of contribution extended.
In the case of a whole-life policy
which remains in force at the expiration
of the period of grace, if the premiums
in default have not been paid or tendered
before the expiration of that period, the
amount assured by the policy will be
reduced by the sum produced by multiplying the amount of these premiums by
the factor specified in the Schedule to
the Bill.
This measure is in terms almost
identical with those of the Industrial

Assurance and Friendly Societies (Emergency Protection from Forfeiture) Act,

I trust that hon. Members will lend

The life policy
policy is deposited with

or protection is being made if such cases

That is the only point I wish to raise. I

Member referred to the fact that

industrial insurance companies or friendly
societies. There should be provision in

those people formerly served their country

the largest number.
out in that direction I think I am justified

Wednesday, 8th May, 1940.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOUR FOR AGRICULTURE.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what steps
the Government propose to take regarding
the problem of extra labour for dealing
with the cultivation and harvesting of
the crops to be sown and planted in the
260,000 additional acres ploughed up in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have been asked to
reply. The whole question of the extra
labour which may be required for the
harvesting of this year's crops is at present receiving my close consideration.
PRICE OF PIGS IN SEPTEMBER.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that in
the recent case over pig prices of Swain v.
The Producers Bacon Co. (Collin Glen),
Ltd., it was sworn in evidence by the
manager of the defendant company that
when he telephoned Stormont to find out
the position of the firm the advice he
received was not to pay any other than
the old price until it was otherwise determined, and whether, in view of the fact
that the Lord Chief Justice for Northern
Ireland has now decided that the Board
of Trade Order of 3rd September last,
fixing a new and higher price applied to
Northern Ireland and given judgment
accordingly for the plaintiff in the case
mentioned, he will now withdraw this
advice and make it clear that the Ministry
would welcome an effort being made to
have all producers concerned throughout
Northern Ireland paid the amounts to
which they are entitled under the judg
ment of the Lord Chief Justice in the
Swain case at the earliest possible
moment.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir. As
I have already explained to the House
it was the agreed intention of the
Ministry of Food and my Department
that this Order of the 3rd September
should not apply to Northern Ireland.
It was some time after the 3rd September
before a copy of the Order was seen by
my Department, which had, therefore, no
opportunity of considering whether the
terms of the Order actually applied to
Great Britain or to the whole of the
United Kingdom.
With regard to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question, I have nothing
to add to the statements I have already
made on this subject.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether,
when a copy of the Order referred to was
received by the right hon. Gentleman's
Department, it was immediately submitted to his legal adviser, or whether
the Ministry took on them to interpret
it themselves?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I could not
answer the hon. Member definitely as to
whether it was immediately submitted,
but it was fairly soon afterwards.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether it
was only after the legal advisers had been
consulted that the Ministry discovered
that they had made an error in this
matter.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No, sir. No
error was made. It was a question of the
Ministry not having received the Order
to see if it should apply and, therefore,
as an arrangement had already been made
by the Ministry of Food that the Order
should not apply, naturally that continued on.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is it not a fact that
if when the Ministry received the Order
referred to it had been submitted to the
legal advisers of the Government this
whole business would have been made
right?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is in the nature
of a hypothetical question.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): It has been my custom,
when presenting this Estimate in past
years, to review briefly, for the information of hon. Members, the trend of international trade and to indicate the part
which Northern Ireland plays in the
maintenance of that trade. The Committee will appreciate. the circumstances
which render it undesirable for me to
follow that course on this occasion.
When introducing last year's Estimates
I referred to the serious reduction in the
value of linen goods exported in 1938 as
compared with 1937, due in a large
measure to world unsettlement. The
whole situation during the last four
Estimates-

Ministry of Supply
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
months of 1939 was so completely altered
that no useful purpose would be served
by quoting comparative figures of linen
exports as a whole in the years 1938 and
1939, but it may be said that linen
exports generally in 1939 showed an
increase in both quantity and value.
Partly due to the same cause, the exports
of linen piece goods to the United States
of America in 1939 far exceeded both in
quantity and value those for 1938, this
increase being particularly noticeable
during the last four months of the year.
I do not need to remind hon. Members
how vitally important it is to maintain
these and all other exports to foreign.
countries, and particularly to the United
States, during the present crisis.
Special efforts are now being directed
towards the intensification of export trade,
and the part which Northern Ireland can
and must play in this endeavour will be
recognised by the, forthcoming visit of Sir
Andrew Duncan, the President of the
Board of Trade. Sir Andrew's visit
must of necessity be of short duration,
but he has made arrangements to confer
with members of the various export
groups and sub-groups which have been,
or are in process of being, set up by trade
organisations in Northern Ireland in
accordance with the recommendations
made by the Export Council. The
formation of these export groups is
designed to provide the maximum
stimulus to the national export drive,
and the members of the groups will, I am
sure, welcome the opportunity of discussing their problems with the President
of the Board of Trade personally. Sir
Andrew will also meet other representatives. of our industrial community while
he is in Belfast, and I am confident that
his visit will help in the solution of some
of the problems encountered and encourage our industries to exert still
greater efforts in the campaign to develop
our overseas trade.
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope the visit will be
more fruitful than Mr. Burgin's.

Mr. BARBOUR: We have no reason

appreciate that the productive capacity
of the linen industry will in the immediate future depend to an increasing extent on home-grown flax, and in this
In common with other Departments,
the scope of my Ministry's activities has
been greatly enlarged under present
emergency conditions. Normal statutory
functions continue to be discharged without interruption, while new duties have
been undertaken, not only in the interests of Northern Ireland itself, but
also on behalf of Imperial Departments
whose functions cover the whole of the
United Kingdom.
My Ministry, which maintains close
contact with the various service departments, is now represented on the new
Area Board of the Ministry of Supply.
The main object of this organisation,
which includes in its membership representatives of each of the service departments, is to ensure the fullest use of
the present emergency of the productive
capacity and the man power of Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members will appreciate
that I am precluded from giving detailed
figures of contracts placed, but during
the three years prior to April, 1939, it
was estimated that Government contracts
placed directly in Northern Ireland were
valued at £12,250,000. Since the outbreak of war, ever increasing use has
been made of our industrial capacity by
Government contracting departments.
Hon. Members will recall the impressive account of contracts placed given on
the occasion of his recent visit by Mr.
Burgin, the Minister of Supply, who also
referred to further substantial contracts
pending. Even so, however, so long as
our employment figures remain substantial, no one can regard the position with
complacency, nor contend that we are
making our maximum possible contribution towards the national cause. Hon.
Members will, however, appreciate that
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce 1098
8 MAY 1940
one of the principal difficulties with which
we and the new Area Board are faced at
the present juncture, is the absence from
the reservoir of available labour of any
substantial number of workers skilled in
engineering and other trades essential to
the production of warlike requirements.
War under present conditions, especially the form of economic warfare which
the Imperial Government are prosecuting
with ever increasing intensity, must inevitably create difficulties for trade and
industries established on a peace-time
footing. These difficulties are particularly evident in meeting the demand of
our industries for raw materials at a time
when shipping space and supplies must
be used to satisfy, in the first place, the
essential requirements of our armed
forces.
The system under which priority is
given to essential requirements is operated
through the control of raw materials by
the Ministry of Supply. Attached to the
Central Priority Department of that
Ministry are a number of priority subcommittees, composed of representatives
of Government Departments, who consider the various claims to priority of
supply, and recommend the procedure
necessary to exercise such priority.
Northern Ireland was in a peculiar
position in that many of its requirements
did not come under the supervision of
the London Departments which were represented on the committees. In these
circumstances an arrangement was made
with the Ministry of Supply whereby my
Ministry has been appointed under the
priority organisation to represent the
requirements of Northern Ireland not
covered by Imperial Government Departments. Through the close contact with
the Ministry of Supply which has thus
been established, my Ministry is in a
position not only to safeguard the special
requirements of essential activities which
come under the supervision of the Northern Ireland Government, but also, where
necessary, to advise Northern Ireland
firms on the procedure for obtaining raw
materials required to complete work
undertaken on behalf of Imperial
Government Departments.
that flax control is undertaken mainly
by the industry itself, working in close
contact with the Ministry of Supply,
allocations within the industry itself
being undertaken by committees representative of the industry. In many cases
my Ministry has been able to assist
Northern Ireland interests where questions of priority have arisen, and I am
satisfied that under this system Northern
Ireland is receiving her full share of
available supplies of raw materials for
essential purposes. These new control
arrangements now embrace such essential
commodities as timber and iron and steel,
and generally all such raw materials as
come under the supervision of the
Ministry of Supply.
Special consideration is being given to
our linen industry to enable it to carry
on its valuable trade with overseas
countries. Hon. Members will be aware
In addition to this work my Ministry
has also found it necessary to undertake
certain additional work on behalf of the
smaller industries of Northern Ireland.
For example, our woollen industry, which
in peace-time conditions did not experience the need for the establishment of a
trade association, was compelled by the
strict control of raw material imposed by
war-time conditions to devise. at short
notice an organisation through which wool
could be rationed to manufacturers in
Northern Ireland. In these circumstances my Ministry, in co-operation with
the wool control of the Ministry of
Supply, undertook to provide the
necessary secretarial assistance to the
Wool Rationing Committee which was
created to serve this purpose.
It is not infrequently a matter of some
difficulty to draw a line of demarcation
between the functions of my Ministry
when acting as agent on behalf of the
Ministry of Supply, and when engaged
in furthering the interests of the industrial and trading community in Northern
Ireland. It is in these circumstances
that only in respect of the Ministry of
Supply's wool rationing scheme have we
made a charge against that Ministry for
recoupment of my Ministry's expenditure.
In common with the whole of Great
Britain, Northern Ireland has experienced difficult conditions in the matter
of coal supply and distribution during
the winter months, owing mainly to the
exceptional severity of the weather in
Great Britain over protracted periods.
Fortunately many of our industrial concerns had laid in exceptional stocks of
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
coal last summer, and the more difficult
winter period is now happily behind us.
I am hoping that ample supplies will be
available in the near future, and when
that stage
is reached industrial and
domestic consumers alike will be welladvised to lay in the maximum possible
reserve supplies.
By arrangement with the Mines
Department, the administration of coal
control in this area is dealt with by my
Ministry. The cost of carrying on this
work will, of course, be recovered from
the Mines Department under the usual
administrative arrangement.
My Ministry is also providing, on
behalf of the Board of Trade, the secretarial and accommodation facilities
necessary for the administration in this
area of the Prices of Goods Act, 1939.
The main objects of this Measure are
the prevention of profiteering and the
control of the vicious spiral of soaring
prices and increasing wage demands,
which, if unchecked, will contribute to
the serious evil of inflation.
The classes of goods covered by the
orders issued thus far under the Act are
those articles of general consumption
which enter into the cost of living for
the man of modest means, other than
articles the prices of which are already
controlled by other Departments, such as
food. The Act is intended to apply not
only to the retailer but equally to the
wholesaler, merchant and manufacturer
of the price-regulated goods. The consumer will be protected from exploitation,
but there will be no unfair interference
with the legitimate interests of the
trader.
spread apathy on the part of the public.
Hon. Members will be aware of the
arrangement whereby a senior officer of
my Ministry has undertaken the duties
of divisional food officer for Northern
Ireland under the Ministry of Food rationing scheme. In this position he has the
assistance of officers drawn from the staff
of several other Northern Ireland Departments, the salaries of himself and his
staff being born on the Vote of the
Ministry of Commerce and recoverable
from the Imperial authority.
The machinery for enforcing the Act
consists of a Central Price Regulation
Committee in London and 16 local committees, of which one is in Northern
Ireland. The Northern Ireland committee is composed of 15 members recruited on a representative basis. Inspectors are not employed so that the
proper working of the Act depends on
the co-operation of the public who are
invited to present their complaints to the
committee. So far, I am glad to say,
the volume of complaints in Northern
Ireland has been small, and I trust that
this state of affairs indicates the fair
dealing of our traders and not any wide-
Turning now to the normal functions
of my Ministry, I should like to refer,
in the first instance, to the results
achieved by the legislation passed in
1937 for the attraction of new industries
to Northern Ireland-legislation which,
like its counterpart in the special areas
of Great Britain, has been largely in
abeyance since the outbreak of the war.
Assistance was granted in 35 cases involving an ascertained commitment of
£4,013 5s Od per annum by way of site
and rent grants, and loans to the amount
of £232,500. Such instalment repayments of these loans as have already fallen
due have been promptly met, and in
one case when the total amount of the
loan could not be profitably employed
owing to the outbreak of the war, a
substantial amount was repaid in one
lump sum. Notwithstanding the difficulties of the time the employment given by
these concerns has risen from 968 in
December, 1938, to 2,280 in December,
1939, and now stands at 2,616. These
figures take no account of the employment afforded by the undertakings which
received the smaller measure of assistance
provided by the earlier Act of 1932.
In the field of industrial assurance, I
am happy to say that there has been a
substantial decrease in the number of
complaints made by policy-holders during
1939, while the latest available figures
continue to record a steady increase in the
premium income of the companies and
societies engaged in this class of work.
Another feature is a definite fall in the
total amount paid out by way of surrender value. This may be taken as an
indication that fewer people were forced,
owing to stress of circumstances, to terminate their contracts and would suggest
that, during the period under review,
there was greater prosperity among that
Estimates-

class of the community which favours
this form of thrift. The Imperial Parliament has passed legislation to protect all
holders of industrial assurance policies,
who, as a result of the outbreak of
hostilities, find themselves unable to
meet their premium payments. As hon.
Members will be aware, we propose to
make similar provision here, a Bill to
that end being now before the House.

Turning now to fisheries, I am glad
to say that there has been a substantial
improvement in the position of our
coastal fishermen. Although the quantity
of fish landed showed only a slight increase, the better prices ruling during
the year resulted in a considerable increase in value in 1939. The herring
catches increased slightly, while the
average value per cwt. was 11s 8d as
compared with 6s 7d in 1938. A considerable quantity was cured at Ardglass, but the outbreak of war prevented
the export of the greater part of the
cure to the usual markets. A large part
of the surplus has, however, been disposed of locally in recent months. From
October until the end of the year the
Portavogie fleet reaped a rich harvest at
the inshore herring fisheries at Maryport, and it is estimated that the
average earnings for each member of the
crews over the period were in the neighbourhood of £100. Hon. Members will
be interested to learn that a number of
our County Down fishermen, with commendable foresight, have seized the
opportunity afforded by this period of
prosperity to discharge their obligations
to my Ministry on account of fishery
praiseworthy effort are being sympathetically considered.
There were heavy landings of whiting
at Ardglass during the winter months,
the local fleet being augmented by
Danish seine net boats from Lossiemouth.
One result of the war has been the
absorption of a greater proportion of
the home-caught fish by the Northern
Ireland market. Our salmon fishing
during 1939 showed a considerable improvement over the two previous years,
which, as hon. Members may recollect,
were exceptionally poor, and there was
also an increase in the takings of trout.
During the past winter the stocks of
breeding salmon and trout were well
above the average, and conditions in the
rivers were for the most part favourable
to spawning. There has been an increase
in the quantity of eels caught in Lough
Neagh, and exports were approximately
30 per cent. more than those for 1938.
in
In concluding this brief review, I
should like to pay a well-deserved tribute
not only to the fishermen, but to the commercial community as a whole, who during
a period of difficulty have in general given
of their best. There is, I am glad to say,
the records of my Ministry, ample evidence
of the readiness with which industrialists,
traders, and consumers alike have cooperated with the authorities in the
smooth working of the restrictions
rendered necessary by the. present emergency. I beg to move.

Reference has been made to Mr.
Duncan's coming visit to Belfast. I do
not object to these gentlemen coming over
here on what might be called holiday
trips as long as they come at their own

the case.
Mr. Burgin, the Minister of
Supply, came here recently, and orders
for war work were supposed to be bulging
out of his pockets. One actually slipped
from his waistcoat pocket, an order for
so many shells, and he made such promises
that we thought there would not be an
unemployed man in Northern Ireland in
three months' time. I want to know
from the right hon. Gentleman what Mr.
Burgin's visit has done for Northern
Ireland so far as relieving unemployment
is concerned.
It is quite true that he has given a few
orders to those who were already in work,
but that was not the sole object of my
desire to get Mr. Burgin over here. It
was to get from him something for
those who have been out of employment
for so many years. We have ample
employment for those who are engaged in
the type of work Mr. Burgin requires,
but we have no work for those who are
unemployed. We were full up with
work on orders like those he left here.

There is the question of Mulhouse
Works, which I understand is going to be
taken over by a firm in this city. What
is going to be done with Mulhouse
Works? Is it not a fact that in that
factory there is going to be carried out
the same type of work as is at present
being done at that firm's own works. If
you had Mulhouse Works open to-morrow
could you man it with the skilled men
necessary for the class of work Mr.
Burgin requires to be carried out in the
interest of the State? I say you could
not. We want work suitable for our unemployed, and we can have it if we get
the assistance of Great Britain. Great
Britain has found work suitable for her
unemployed classes. She has placed
many thousands of people in employment,
as the latest unemployment figures show.
We in Northern Ireland have got to send
our labour across to Great Britain, and
our men have got to readapt themselves
to the class of work Great Britain puts
them to.
Why are we not thinking of our own industries? Are we going to be the lame
dog for Great Britain all the time? We
cannot afford to be the lame dog; we
have too large an industrial population.
We want something that will keep our
people in employment not only during
the war but after the war.
At the present time we are helping to build up industries in Great Britain. The Minister
of Labour said yesterday that the
difficulty here is the provision of
machinery. That is absolute bunkum,
and well he knows it. Machinery is not
the handicap, because there is not a
factory that has been established in
Great Britain in the last six months that
has not been equipped, and if Great
Britain can get the machinery we can get
it too. I had to smile when that statement was made by the Minister of
Labour. If that is all the right hon.
Gentleman can get from Mr. Ernest
Brown he would be better staying at
home and leaving the money he spends
on visits to London in the pocket of the
Minister of Finance.

I come

fair share of this money which the
Imperial Government is giving in subsidies for flax development. I claim that
we in Ulster are the pioneers of flax
growing in the United Kingdom. It is
only within the past few years that England has started to grow flax, with the
exception of a small area for seed purposes, but to-day they are developing the
industry to a considerable extent.
As regards flax development, we should
all do our best to increase production in
this Province. I am afraid that in Great
Britain they are playing a much more
important part in the development of flax
growing than we are in Northern Ireland,
because in Great Britain they have

the Flax Development Committee will
take steps to see that we have mills of
the same kind established in Northern
Ireland. I suggest that application
should be made to the Imperial authorities to give. to Northern Ireland a grant
for building such mills here, because
to-day flax is an essential national asset.
The Imperial Government gave a subsidy
to have these factories built in Great
Britain, and as we are part of the United
Kingdom, I see no reason why we should
not claim our share of any such subsidies
and build a factory here.
Although I do not envy the people on
the other side having these factories, we
should take every care that they do not
filch from us this old industry of flax
growing which our forefathers took such
a pride in developing. It used to be said
that there was no place where flax could
be better grown or linen better spun
than in Northern Ireland. But times
have changed, and to-day flax can be
grown in Great Britain as well as it can
be grown in Northern Ireland, and linen
can be made in England as well as here.
I hope we shall retain our position in
spite of the competition from Great
Britain. Once we have defeated Hitlerism
we may get an export trade we have not
had before, and I hope the Minister will
take notice of the suggestions I have
made.
As regards the Ulster Office in London,

redundant at the present time. We

PEAT RESOURCES OF NORTHERN
IRELAND.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government will
take steps to develop the peat resources
of Northern Ireland in view of a possible
coal shortage.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
The answer is in the negative. Various
schemes for the large scale exploitation
of peat as a fuel have been laid before
my Ministry from time to time. Unfortunately, such schemes depend upon
the existence of large areas of deep peat
unobstructed by earlier workings and
free of tree stumps and roots. No such
deposits are to be found in Northern
Ireland on an extensive scale.
I may also remind the hon. Member
that our Northern Ireland peat deposits
are not public property. Large areas of
turbary have been allocated, under the
provisions of the Land Purchase Acts,

In the Budget statement which I made

under the constant menace of violent and

No one can prophesy with any degree of

be continued until the security of
Britain and France with which is
bound up the safety and freedom of
small nations-is assured beyond doubt.

The capacity of our manufacturers and

For obvious reasons it would be unwise for me to review in detail the

made here to the national effort. In

the nation is reaping the benefit of the

The Budget-

Minister's Financial Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
Hon. Members will see that motor
taxation brought in over £200,000 more
than I estimated in my supplementary
Budget. I am afraid I allowed myself
to be unduly influenced, when arriving
at this estimate, by those who maintained
that the increased tax would drive cars
off the roads. If it had not been for
the necessary petrol rationing there
obviously would not have been much
change in the number of cars in use.
Hon. Members will also notice, that we
have received a provisional payment of
£600,000 from the Imperial Government
towards meeting our excess war transferred expenditure. in accordance with
the arrangement which I explained to
the Committee last October. The total
revenue last year was £18,204,542, and
the total expenditure was £16,084,924,
thus we had a balance of £2,119,618.
The provisional Imperial contribution
which emerges for last year is, therefore,
£2,000,000 as estimated. I anticipate
that the final figures of reserved taxes
will show a considerably increased
revenue over the provisional figures, so
that this provisional Imperial contribution for last year will, I am happy to
say, be substantially increased; the
surplus for the past year to be transferred
to our Reserve Fund being £119,618.
Expenditure, 1940-41.
I now turn to the position of our
finances for the current
year. The
figures to which I shall be referring are
those contained in the last column of
Tables II and III of the White Paper.
I shall deal first with the estimates of
our expenditure.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Under the head of Consolidated Fund
Services the item of £215,000 for interest
on borrowings includes for the first time
provision for meeting a full year's interest
on our 33 per cent. Stock which was
issued last year in order to meet our
transport guarantees. In addition, I
have found it necessary to allow a larger
sum for interest in respect of temporary
borrowings on Treasury bills owing to the
increased rates of interest prevailing in
the short-term market as compared with
last year.
The next item of £323,000 makes full
provision for our sinking funds to meet
the interest liability on savings certificates and to provide a perpetuity revenue
in place of the existing land purchase
annuities when that item of revenue
disappears.
The figure of £457,000 represents the
estimate of the sum to be paid to the
Road Fund from the yield of motor
taxation—that is, the estimated yield of
the motor vehicles duties after retaining
in the Exchequer, in accordance with the
Statute passed by Parliament last year,
half the proceeds of the duties on private
cars and motor-cycles.
In view of the existing commitments of
the Road Fund and of the various statutory and loan charges which fall to be met
from the fund, my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Home Affairs does not anticipate that the existing revenue of the
fund will permit him to pay any new
grants during this financial year, and
this has already been explained to representatives of the local authorities with
whom I have much sympathy owing to
the unavoidable difficulties in which they
have been placed in this connection.
The remaining Consolidated Fund services are provided for at a figure of
£172,000, which includes a provision
towards meeting Exchequer liabilities in
respect of commitments entered into
under the Loans Guarantee Acts. The
total amount of the provision for Consolidated Fund services stands, therefore, at
a figure of £1,167,000.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Estimates already issued of expenditure on Supply Services amount to
approximately £12,284,000, which is
some £542,000 less than the final
Estimates for 1939-40, owing mainly to
anticipated decreases or savings in expenditure on unemployment, air-raid
precautions, agricultural and educational
services, and public works and buildings.
Since the outbreak of war I have
caused each item of Government expenditure to be considered in relation to the
necessities of war finance. The test
applied has been this: Is the particular
item essential to help to carry on the
war, or is it necessary in order to maintain some important service in the civil
life of the country? If the item of peacetime expenditure does not satisfy one of
these requirements it has been disallowed,
Minister's Financial Statement 1158
The Budget-
21 MAY 1940
or else it has been drastically reduced. It
will interest hon. Members to know that
as much as 78 per cent. of our voted
expenditure is on social services, such as
unemployment benefit and assistance, oldage pensions, health insurance benefits
and education; 17 per cent. on police,
Special Constabulary, civil defence, agricultural and other services. Less than
the remaining 5 per cent. is spent on
administration costs, which include the
salaries of Ministers, Members of Parliament and civil servants. Hon. Members
will, therefore, appreciate the difficulty of
making further substantial economies. As
regards the former I will say nothing; as
regards our civil servants, I deplore the
attacks which are from time to time made
upon the service, which are unfair, discouraging and ill-founded.
Mr. NIXON: Are you looking for
criticism?
Reserved Services.

£52,000 over the amount required for
last year.
The major part of this increase occurs under the heading of Post
Office, which is estimated to cost
£1,312,000.
In addition, there are the items (which
do not appear in Table II) representing

of the "new" land purchase annuities

prior to the transfer of services to this

Hon. Members will be glad to learn that
this will enable our Imperial contribution
for that year, namely 1938-39, to be
finally fixed at £1,300,000 in place of the

Finally, I have provided as a charge
on the revenues of this year a sum representing a payment that will fall to be
made to the United Kingdom Government during the year as an adjustment
of the Northern Ireland residuary share
of reserved taxes in respect of an overpayment for the year 1938-39. The final
figures of revenue and expenditure in
that year are now available, and they
show that a sum of £72,000 is required

SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.
I now have to consider what margin
should be allowed for Supplementary
Estimates for charges which will arise
during the present year, and for which
no provision has been made in the Estimates already presented to Parliament.
Hon. Members know the paramount
importance of concentrating the maximum
possible of our financial resources on the
prosecution of the war. It is, therefore,
only possible for me to make provision
for further expenditure in respect of
services of an urgent and vital nature. I
am happy, however, to be able to allow
a margin for meeting the full
cost this year of the new legislation for improving the position of
old-age and widow pensioners. I am

I now come to certain new proposals
affecting the revenue and expenditure of
the current year. I propose to introduce
a clause in the Finance Bill to put goods
vehicles driven by gas on an equal footing
with other goods vehicles. This will be
done by taking power to ignore the container for holding gas, or the plant for
producing the gas, in computing the
weight of the vehicle. I feel that vehicles
of this type which do not run on petrol
should, in present circumstances, be encouraged in every way.
I also propose that members of the
fighting forces who are home on leave
from service overseas or afloat should be
exempted from motor licence duty on
their own cars or motor-cycles, for a short
period on payment of a fee of 10s in the
case of a motor-car, and 2s in the case of
a motor-cycle.
A clause will be included in the
Finance Bill which will extend to the
estates of merchant seamen killed in the
war, the relief from death duties which,
under existing legislation, operates in the
case of members of the armed forces. A
similar exemption was in operation
during the last war and is intended to
come into force in Great Britain this
year.
I am also taking this opportunity to
announce that I propose to refund the
stamp duty payable on solicitors' certificates and other documents in certain cases
where the solicitors are serving with H.M.
Forces or are killed while so serving. I
anticipate that these concessions will not
cost more than £500 per annum, and can
be met within the existing estimates,
which I have given to the Committee.
I am sure that hon. Members will welcome
these concessions to members of our
fighting forces and merchant services.

Before arriving at the provisional
Imperial contribution and surplus for the

Exchequer which have resulted from the

scheme will be established without delay
on a sound and economic basis.
The
general position is being very carefully
considered by the Government, and we
have, of course, to take account of the
effect which the war is having on transport conditions generally.
The second concerns our war-time expenditure. I have already reminded
hon. Members that last year the British

taking directly on
approved expenditure on our Consolidated

as in other spheres, Ulster is playing at
helpful part in this national emergency.
Hon. Members will be relieved to know
that I have no more figures to impose
upon them to-day, but as this is my
second war budget and as it is necessarily
permeated by the war needs, I cannot
close without adding one more thought.
The glorious valour and endurance of our
sailors, soldiers and airmen, combined
with the unselfish industry of our civilians
must result in the ultimate triumph of
the high and noble cause for which this
war is being waged by our Empire and
our Allies, and in the establishment of a
just and enduring peace. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to extend
congratulations to the right hon. Gentleman on the Budget speech which he has
delivered to the House. It is only in
keeping with the record of the right hon.
Gentleman in the respective departments
which he has passed through. He tried
to give this House a clear appreciation
of the working out of this Budget, which
we all understand to be the guiding
factor of Parliament for the year to
come. I do not know that I can go into
the Budget statement as presented in the
manner I would like to do, because I
have no superability in my mental makeup whereby I could grasp all the figures
and all the details of the statement
already made. But I will endeavour to
bring before the House one or two points
which struck me as very important.
that the element of complaint is not a
personal one. I had my mind made up
to ask that this be treated as a breach of
privilege, but I could not produce the
publication in time. That is my reason
for making my comments on the Motion
for the passing of the Budget.
Before proceeding to do so, I regret
to have to make reference to an important point, but, nevertheless, it must
be done in the interests of the Members
of this House and in the interests of good
conduct. This morning my attention
was called to the fact that this statement
which we have just heard at this time of
day, appeared in the London district at
10 o'clock this morning-the Budget
statement which is supposed to be secret,
which is held to be so important that
Ministers of the Crown have been dismissed from office for the least leakage.
I was acquainted this morning that there
was a leakage of this Budget statement
from the London Office. Now, we
appointed a trade officer to the London
Office in the person of Sir James Cooke-
Collis. I feel that this is so important
at the moment that we must take cognisance of this position as created, and I
want the House clearly to understand
What actually happened. The Minister might as well have not made any
speech so far as the Press of Great
Britain and the world is concerned,
because the Press Association in London
has already got that statement into the
respective offices of their subscribers, and
they were able to get that through a
paid servant in the Ulster Office. I
refer to the London Press Officer. He
has made a fool of the Minister and a
fool of this House, and also of the entire
Press of Ireland. The Minister knows
very well the seriousness of such a leakage.
Certain interests might very well
make financial gain out of it. A Minister
of the Crown at Westminster was dismissed with ignominy for a similar breach
of confidence a few years ago. I and
every Member in this House await a
statement from the Minister as to what
action he proposes to take in the matter.
I suggest that some drastic action is
necessary.
This is just another example of the
autocratic behaviour of the so-called
Trade Office in London, which has never
confined its activities to trade matters at
all, but simply proved to be a vehicle
for political propaganda. Its activities
have proved an embarrassment not alone
to civil servants, but to the journalists of
the Province. To-day either consciously
or unconsciously the Minister has insulted the members of the Press Gallery
of this House. He made an arrangement
with them. And I know they appreciated his courtesy in the matter. Under
this arrangement the journalists were to
get advance copies of the Budget statement on condition that no publication
should take place before the Minister had
concluded his speech. They were called
to Stormont at 12 o'clock this morning
and asked to sign undertakings to that
effect. In other words, they were made
fools of because the London Office-the
so-called trade office-had already taken
it upon itself to circulate copies of this
document to the news agencies in London
early this morning thereby undermining
the accredited representatives of these

I now come to the Budget statement as
we have heard it. I want to make this
very clear. Are we in this House really
in earnest in giving our full support to
the overthrow of the Nazi Party? Are.
we serious? If we are, let us examine
our own position and find out have we
done our shore towards that overthrow.
Let us find out are we endeavouring to
do our share; in other words, pull our
weight all the time. If we are not, then
it is time we were putting our house in
order. I have been regarded as one
belonging to the extreme element, as
being, perhaps, one who would trample
down constitutional law. I know certain
Members on the other side. would put me
down as that type or brand. I have as
much respect for constitutional law as
any Member of the Committee.
I went through the last war and the
war previous to it. I have watched the
efforts of the Ulster people in response
to the many calls made by the Government. Since last September I have been
going through various areas in the
Province, and I can find no enthusiasm,
no inspiration, no great desire for conversation. That is brought about, in my
opinion, by the method under which this
Government is working. The Government seems to establish itself as the sole
authority for the conduct of war affairs
in the Province. It is not taking into
its confidence anyone outside a certain
circle, and the people who are anxious
and willing to throw their whole weight

The PRIME MINISTER: Yesterday
I was regretting my age. Many years
ago I was able to say with a clear
conscience that I would not ask any man
to do anything which I was not myself
prepared to do, but to-day all I can say
is that I cannot ask any man to do what
I would not have done at his age. The
hon. Member who has just sat down has
raised a point which I am very glad to
be able to answer, and I hope it will
clear the air not only in this assembly
but outside.
In the year 1899, when the South
African War broke out, it will be recalled that there was no conscription in
the United Kingdom. In 1914, when
the last Great War broke out, there was
again no conscription in the United
Kingdom. The men on both of those
occasions were raised by a drive through
the north, south, east and west of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. When I
say drive I mean an intensive recruiting
campaign. It will be remembered that
bands paraded the streets, meetings were
held in towns and villages throughout the
country, and posters were exhibited at all
points asking men to join up to save the
country. I did something myself in
regard to that recruiting campaign, and
I only wish that my health permitted me
to do more, to-day.
What are the real facts of the case?
Let us consider them. When the present
war broke out, far from withholding the
offer which Ulster could make to the
joint cause, I wrote to the authorities
and promised them all the help we could
possibly give. At the invitation of the
then Prime Minister I went to London
to discuss with him how all along the line
Northern Ireland could be best employed
in this particular campaign. Knowing
something which I did not know they
knew a great deal that I do not know
even to-day-the authorities in Great
Britain came to the conclusion that while
conscription should be introduced into
Great Britain, it should not apply to
Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Quite right, too.
The PRIME MINISTER: While they
are able, by pressing a button, to get
another million or two million men of a
certain class in Great Britain we cannot
do that here, and what I have been pressing for is that they should treat Northern Ireland in exactly the same way as
the whole of the United Kingdom was
treated in 1899 and 1914.
Mr. BEATTIE: But have they not
treated us the same way as then?
The PRIME MINISTER: No.
Mr. BEATIE: Oh, yes. The Boer
War and the last war.
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member knows quite well that compulsory
service does not apply in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is so.
The PRIME MINISTER: If the hon.
Member goes to England or Scotland at
present he will not find a recruiting campaign being carried on. There are no
posters exhibited, no bands marching
through the towns and villages, and no
flags flying. Nothing of that kind is
being carried out as all the recruiting is
being done by conscription. In Northern
Ireland, to which conscription does not
apply, I hold it is necessary for the
British Government to authorise the
Army to start a vigorous recruiting
campaign. If that were done I feel confident that the response would be as great
as it was to the appeal made in the years
to which I have referred.
It must be remembered that subsequent

to-day is one which has naturally caused
many of us to be perturbed, and no one

prevailed throughout Europe and the
world, and over which unfortunately
they have no control.

Mr. JOHNSTON: I rise to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon
his Budget statement, and particularly
on the size of the Imperial contribution,
though like other hon. Members I should
like to know if the amount is sufficient.
Ulster people up to the present have
done all that they have been asked to
do. They have raised all the troops they
have been required to raise; they have
made, every contribution they have been
asked to make. They are anxious to do
everything they can to help in the prosecution of the war, but they do not know
what to do, and they are not told. Why
should it be necessary for the Ulster
people to press the Government to take
further action? Why should they not be
led and told what to do? If they are
told what to do, they will do it willingly.
The only trouble is they do not know
what to do, and they are not told. What
we lack is drive. If you have a driver
you will have followers, and you will have
action. There is no use in talking
nowadays; talk will not win the war. I
wish to say that Ulster is not doing all
that it is capable of doing at the present
time. We know what is happening in
France to-day; we know the seriousness
of the situation. We must have leadership. If the Government tell the Ulster
people what to do, it will be done. They
will contribute in money and in men and
in everything else towards the winning of
the war. I do not want to say anything
further. It is the duty of the Government to tell us what they want us to do.

has been made the rule in England, and

it is under those conditions we are carrying on, all we can do is submit ourselves

Major HALL-THOMPSON: In spite

I cannot but feel we owe it to those

I believe that if a recruiting campaign

what happened the last time might

has got to be won, and I take it it must

In reference to another matter, I may

been endeavouring and will endeavour to

definite answer to certain questions. We
wait and nothing happens. In about
three weeks time you get a letter from
London to repeat you are willing and, if

If we are going to win this war let us

do. I am prepared to do my share and
the men I have under me are prepared
to do their share, and will do it well.
But I hate this delay and overlapping.
Surely our Government have some say
in the matter. If they have not, well,
it seems to me a hopeless business. We
ought to be taken more into the confidence of the Government. We constantly see in the papers that something
is going to happen. Many things I see
in the papers I personally do not agree
with at all, but we are told this is real.
Another thing. The Government
preaches about economy. We all want
to economise. I have got to economise.
Firms have got to economise and yet
they get four or five-page circulars, and

office. If that sort of thing is going on
there must be other departments in which
great economies could be effected. I sincerely trust the Government at this time
will take every step to economise and
reduce staffs where possible. Thus they
will help others outside to do their best
and give them every encouragement.

I think it is up to this Government,

from Southern Ireland. All honour to

Section 65 of the Unemployment
Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1936,
provides that, in the event of any Order
being made by the Minister of Labour
for Great Britain on the recommendation of the Unemployment Insurance
Statutory Committee for the amendment
of the Unemployment Insurance Acts in
force there, his Grace the Governor may
by Order in Council apply to Northern
Ireland the provisions of any such Order.
The Committee concluded that the conof interest and
sequential reduction
sinking fund payments would release
from the fund an annual sum sufficient
to raise from 3s a week to 4s a week the
rate of dependant's benefit payable under
the general scheme of unemployment
insurance in respect of each of the first
two dependent children. The Committee
also found that the agricultural
account there was a disposable surplus
sufficient to justify an increase of
dependants' benefit equivalent to that
proposed under the general scheme, and
recommended that there should be the
same increase in dependants' benefit
under the agricultural scheme as under
the general scheme.
on
The report of the Unemployment
Insurance Statutory Committee on the
financial position of the Unemployment
Fund in Great Britain at the 31st
December, 1939, disclosed that for the
calendar year 1939 the income of the
account relating to the general scheme
of unemployment insurance had exceeded
expenditure by such a substantial amount
as to justify the Committee in recommending that part of the accumulated
balance should be used to make a reduction of £37,000,000 in outstanding debts.
In order to give the desired effect to
this arrangement the Committee further
recommended that the maximum weekly
amount of agricultural benefit payable to
any one applicant should be increased
from 33s to 35s a week. With the
approval of Parliament an Order was
made by the Minister of Labour in
Great Britain on the 5th April, 1940,
increasing rates of benefit in accordance
with the Committee's proposals from the
11th April, 1940, and the provisions of
that Order were applied to Northern
Ireland from the same date, by the Unemployment Insurance (Increase of
Benefit in respect of Dependent Children)
Order (Northern Ireland), 1940, for
which the approval of the House is now
sought.
It is estimated that expenditure on
these increases will be approximately
£55,000 a year. Of this sum, £25,000
will be met from savings in interest and
sinking fund charges resulting from a
repayment of debt on the Northern
Ireland Unemployment Fund amounting to £840,048. This repayment of
£840,048 is the insured population proportion of the repayment of £37,000,000
on the debt of the Unemployment Fund
in Great Britain recently carried out.
Of the balance of £30,000, which must

will be repaid by Great Britain under

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): This has been a year of crisis.
Twelve months ago we had reasonably
fair prospects of improving trade conditions, but the horizon was soon overcast with clouds, and in September the
hurricane of war burst upon us. That
at the moment is the dominating fact.
To it everything else must be subordinated. All the energies of the
country must be directed towards securing the maximum effort in our war aim.
Injuries (Civilians) Scheme has given to
the civilian population here the benefits
of the scheme of compensation for war
injuries which has been made available
for civilians in Great Britain.
I was prepared to give, as usual, a
full account of my stewardship for the
year, but, in view of the news we received to-day, I feel that the Committee
would not wish to hear me review the
past at any great length. I will therefore just briefly remind hon. Members
that last autumn we passed a considerable amount of legislation to enable
us to simplify our procedure to meet
war-time conditions, and to ensure that
persons who lost their employment
owing to the war were not left destitute.
I should also mention that the inclusion
by the United Kingdom Parliament of
Northern Ireland within the Personal
I personally interviewed Mr. Brown,
the former Minister of Labour in Great
Britain, in order that a larger number of
openings should be made available for
young men who are anxious to receive
the necessary training. He very kindly
agreed to do this, and as a result we are
placing 100 of these volunteers in the
training centres at once, and more, I
expect, will follow at an early date.
I should say a word here about the
number of the unemployed. At the
beginning of 1939 the live register showed
94,783 unemployed. It fell steadily until
in August, 1939, it was 63,113, and we
expected further reductions; but the
impact of war destroyed our hopes; the
number rose by 1,500 in the following
month and continued to rise until in
January last it reached 83,655. Bad as
this was, however, it was 11,000 lower
than it had been a year before.
February showed a
welcome fall to
81,784. A further reduction of 9,738
took place in March. In April the
registers showed another decrease of
4,397, thus reducing our unemployed
figure to 67,649; that is to say, a fall of
16,006 in the three months.
Hon. Members will understand that
there has been less demand for some
trades owing to war conditions, and in
others there has been some difficulty
about the supply of material, which it
would not be in the public interest for
me to discuss here. We are, however,
making every effort to remedy these so
far as is possible.
I shall now turn to the Estimates
themselves which total £5,962,963 as
compared with £6,245,833 last year, a
net decrease of £282,870. It will
probably be convenient if I take the
Votes in order, and I shall refer to the
items in which there are substantial
increases or decreases as compared with
last year.
Vote 1 provides for the
expenses incurred by my Department in
the administration of the schemes for
which it is responsible. The net sum
required is £72,905, which is £30,565
less than last year.

of war. We are doing considerably less
inspection and investigation and less
keeping of records and detailed accounts
than before the war; (3) a consequential
reduction in the travelling expenses of

Mr. BEATTIE: It is not my intention

I desire to make only one comment.
The Minister and his Parliamentary
Secretary have now to get wide awake.
There is no justification whatever for the
large numbers of unemployed in Northern Ireland. They are urgently needed
for work of national importance. These
two gentlemen must immediately find useful work for those idle hands. Having said
that, I am sure that all the Members on
each side of the Committee will give
them a helping hand if they are called
upon to assist. Perhaps I see the
position in a different light to other hon.
Members, but I am prepared to make
sacrifices in the national interest. In
Northern Ireland we have at our disposal many rusty hands which should be
brought back into industry to do work of
urgent importance. The right hon.
Gentleman need not put forward the
excuse that the lack of machinery or
skilled labour is the obstacle to work
coming to this part of the world. We
can have the machinery and the workmen.
The last thing I wish to say is that
it is a standing disgrace to see every
morning 1,500 skilled tradesmen standing outside the union door seeking
employment and unable to obtain it. I
want that position changed. During the
last war a position of a similar kind was
changed. The Parliamentary Secretary
is aware that within twenty-four hours
we reorganised our forces and readapted
skilled labour from one unit of employment to another. There is no earthly
reason why 1,500 of our highly skilled
workmen should be standing idle when
they are anxious to perform work which
is of vital importance to the country.

DEFENCE OF THE SIX COUNTIES.
PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Lord Glentoran).
The PRIME MINISTER: As I
promised the House I was prepared to
make a statement bringing up to date
the situation so far as our home defence
is concerned, subsequent to my visit to
London, my consultations with the
Ministers concerned and with the
War Office. After my colleagues and
I had
had carefully considered all the
points that arose from that visit
and from subsequent communications
from the other side, we issued to
the Press, as we invariably do as soon
we have a publication ready, the
following statement:-
as
Arrangements have been completed
with the Imperial authorities under
which the Royal Ulster Constabulary
and the Ulster Special Constabulary
have undertaken the duty of home
defence, in addition to their normal
constabulary duties. An additional
section of the Special Constabulary, to
be called the Ulster Defence Volunteers, is also to be formed, whose duties
will be confined to home defence.
The new section will consist of male
British subjects resident in Northern
Ireland who voluntarily undertake to
serve therein without pay and are
accepted for such service.
Members will not be required—
(a) to give whole time service; or
(b) to live away from their homes; or
(c) to enrol for a period exceeding the
period of the present emergency;
and the service of any member may be
determined by competent authority at
any time, or at his own request by
fourteen days' notice in writing given
by him.
Recruitment will be undertaken by
the county commandant of each
county, who will make local arrangements for the enrolment of volunteers,
through the sub-district commandants,
within the establishment which may
be prescribed. The numbers required
Prime Minister's Statement 1258
Home Defence-
28 MAY 1940
in each sub-district will vary according
to the circumstances existing in each
particular area, and the sub-district
commandant will give notice throughout the area for which he is responsible
when he is in a position to accept
recruits.
Service in the new section will be
entirely voluntary, nor will any
additional payment be made to members of existing constabulary forces in
respect of home defence duties.
It may be in the recollection of the
House that some time ago I ventured to
predict that the time would come when
home defence would be a regular fourth
arm of the service and that it would
probably be of a permanent character.
It has now come upon us very much
sooner than even I anticipated. The
necessity to-day is very real. There are
many in this country who still find it
difficult to picture the peril in which the
country stands, and our duty then is to
play our part completely in the protection of our own home country. It
would be perfectly unthinkable to have
to bring over here, unless as a very last
resort, troops that are required elsewhere in order to protect our citizens.
We ought to be able gradually and
slowly to develop our own resources to
the extent that we, should be able to do
for ourselves.
fact that our agricultural produce for
the other side and ourselves goes into a
common pool in this time of danger. As
I say, agriculture has played a hundred
per cent. part, and I defy anybody to
criticise it.
I have had much heart searching
during the past number of months as to
the proper attitude to take to steer
between all the difficulties which confront
this country along with the Mother
Country, and I have come to the conclusion that with regard to all the
activities in which we are engaged, with

are almost 100 per cent. complete and

country have nobly played their part in
rising to meet all requirements. Therefore, when one hears grumbling and
criticism, and sees a certain amount of
nervousness which affects a community
at all times of stress like the present we
score all that off and point to the
can
The next question that arises is with
regard to the vast manufacturing that is
going on. My hon. Friend (Mr. Grant)
has explained that naturally under the
new modern conditions of mechanised
labour we are left with more unemployed
than we would like to see. I have visited
these places myself. I have seen the
manufacture of aeroplanes and visited
other establishments where great work is
being done in the making of munitions.
I went into one place and got into conversation with a man who had been in
an ordnance factory in England and who
had the specific duty of passing the
shells which were being turned out.
I asked him what proportion of those
shells had to be cast when they passed
through his hands, and he told me that
they were 100 per cent. perfect. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Those encouraging remarks from the men in
charge of the duty of seeing that no
mistakes are made are very comforting,
but naturally many of our people do not
quite understand the efficiency that is
being displayed not only in our yards.
but in the manufacture of munitions.
Take the next point. Could we absorb
more of the unemployed in connection
with these matters? Of course we
could, if the tools were available for
them. It is very easy to cast all sorts of
aspersions upon the Government, and
upon my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Labour. You may have very many
men out of employment, but if you are
going to employ them you must have the
tools which they can take up and use.
You may have a certain number unemployed at the moment, but if as a result
of the disaster on the Continent, from
which flax comes, there is suddenly a
stoppage of the supply for our great
mills, hon. Members surely will not turn
round and accuse my right hon. Friend
of failing in his duty in not having these
girls or, in some cases, men in employment. Surely they will not blame him.
for so many people being out of work.
The number sways to and fro, and no
one can say from day to day what will

The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
hon. Member knows as well as I do that
since newspapers were started there has
anonymous correspondence. We
know what value to place upon it. At
the same time, it is well that it should

not got the power to compel anyone to
join any of the branches of His Majesty's
Forces. Therefore, in the Ulster area,
we have to rely on voluntary recruiting.
Then some of those who have gallantly
gone out to the front tell us that they are
disappointed because the Ulster boys at
home are not filling up the gaps in their
ranks caused by casualties.
I am sure it goes to the heart of each
one of us when we think that where there
is an Ulster unit Ulster boys cannot keep
it up to full strength. I had a long talk
with those in the War Office, because I
could see where the point arose which had
created so much of this difficulty. That
was that whereas in the other two wars
to which I referred the other day there
was a strong and energetic recruiting
campaign throughout the whole of the
United Kingdom, there has been nothing
of the sort done this time in the Ulster
area where only volunteers can join the
Army. The authorities have, however,
promised me very shortly to correct that.
I think they are going to do all they can
to open depots in various parts of the
country where those desirous of responding to the call will have no difficulty in
joining up.
Then we go from that point, that is
those joining our three regiments-the
Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers, the Royal

Another very important point in connection with that is very easily explained.
The response to such a volunteer call will

We come next to the new force which

Fortunately we were in a better position

Royal Ulster Constabulary, making in

The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SUPERVISION OF REFUGEES.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government will,
whilst affording every possible hospitality
to genuine refugees from Holland,
Belgium or France, take effective steps
to ensure that there are no Nazi Fifth
Columnists amongst these refugees; and
whether he can state. if measures will be
taken for the proper and adequate supervision of all refugees.
The PRIME MINISTER: The
answer is in the affirmative.

Powers Act just passed by the British

The PRIME MINISTER: The
Emergency Powers (Defence) Act, 1940,
the Act to which the hon. Member
refers, applies to the whole of the
United Kingdom. The Act extends the
powers of His Majesty in Council to
make Defence Regulations making provision for requiring persons to place
themselves, their services, and their
property at the disposal of His Majesty.
An Order in Council has been made

to Northern Ireland, be in the hands of
the Minister of Labour for Northern
Ireland, who will have powers similar
to those being conferred upon the
British Minister of Labour in relation to
Great Britain.
I am not yet in a position to say how
far it may be necessary to exercise these
powers in Northern Ireland, but I can
assure the hon. Member that the nature
of the action taken will be determined
by reference to the supply of labour
necessary in order to enable industry to
fulfil the nation's war requirements.

the net total of the two Votes of this
Estimate was £2,329,560; for this year
it is £2,287,342-a decrease of £42,218.
Vote 1-for £66,735-shows a decrease
of £3,597 as compared with last year.
This Vote, of course, is for the expenses
of the headquarters and inspectorial staff
of the Ministry, and it would not be
right that I should pass from it without
referring to the retirement last year of
Mr. Bonaparte Wyse, who had been
permanent secretary of the Ministry for
more than 12 years.
He was well known, I am sure, to
every
Member of this House. He was
that very rare thing-a first-rate administrator, an expert educationist, and a
broad-minded man of the world, very
human, and very sympathetic with education authorities, managers and teachers
in all their conundrums and in all their
difficulties. He was continually receptive of new ideas and anxious to grasp
and appreciate the point of view of all
with whom he came in contact. His
profound experience was always at the
disposal of those concerned with education in Northern Ireland and he laboured
unceasingly for the intellectual and
cultural advancement of the pupils in our
schools.
I am glad to pay this tribute to
one whom I held in high esteem, and who
is greatly missed by everyone in the
Department.
When the Ministry of Education for
Northern Ireland was established the
Government was fortunate in having at
hand to help in the setting up of the new
system three acknowledged Irish experts.
-Mr. Wyse for elementary education,
Mr. Houston for secondary education,
and Dr. Garrett for technical instruction,
Estimates-

Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker.]
and these with the assistance of mature
and experienced chief inspectors were
able to implement our new education
charter with sympathy and appreciation
and to lay a foundation of administrative
practice and precedent which would serve
as a model to others. These men have
now passed from the service and with
them the first chapter in our new educational system in Northern Ireland has
been brought to a close.
And so we are turning the first page
of the second chapter-which will be
written by their successors-by the men
who have profited by their training. I
think it is only right to point out that
these successors have taken over in
difficult times, and I do not think it
would be out of place for me to speak
of the devotion to duty which they have
shown, particularly since the outbreak of
war. It is well to give thanks for services rendered at the end of a long
journey, but it is also well to encourage
by grateful appreciation and to speed on
the way those who are at the beginning
of the road, and I believe the House will
agree with me in offering this encouragement.
Several of our principal officers are on
war service-many others have been lent
to other departments both here and in
England. The Committee will realise
that the loss of these officers in times like
these constitutes a serious strain on the
staff of the Ministry and particularly on
the Permanent Secretary, nevertheless,
we have considered it our duty to release
them if they can contribute effectively
to the general war effort whether as
combatants or in other departments. At
the same time my officials are not forgetting that our paramount duty is the
administration of education, and that
those who are left behind must see to it
that the interests of the children in our
care are safeguarded no less carefully
than in the normal times of peace. As
I have explained, we are much below our
normal establishment, and that combined
with the fact that several officers are at a
lower place in the incremental scale than
their predecessors accounts for the
decrease of £3,597 in Vote 1.
hon. Members will see from page ix

our children have been able to

The premises of Stranmillis Training
College were taken over by the military
authorities when war broke out, and the
hostel at Balmoral Hall, for men
students, has since been temporarily
acquired by the Petroleum Board. We
were fortunate enough to be able to obtain
reasonably satisfactory accommodation at
Portrush, and while, of course, it is not

our own buildings, yet as chairman of

personally testify that the principal of
the College and his efficient staff, as well

altered circumstances that there is no

training may suffer by the temporary
migration from Stranmillis.

When I introduced the Estimates last

reached, because they show that, although

rolls, that reduction was very much

I pass now to Sub-head C-Grants and
other expenses for secondary education.
Last year I asked the Committee for a
provision of £209,150 for this service and
I reviewed briefly the development of
secondary education in our area since
the establishment of this Government,
showing that the numbers in attendance
at the schools had more than doubled,
and that the financial contribution by
the State had trebled, within the past
sixteen years.
I ask now for £217,000
under this sub-head. I am happy to
announce that development still continues and that the numbers in attendance have again increased considerably.
Most of this increase is normal, but there
is evidence that part of it is due to the
presence our secondary schools of
children who formerly attended schools
in Great Britain. We are glad to
welcome these pupils and we hope that
neither they nor their parents have any
fault to find with the standard of our
education in Northern Ireland.
There is one matter in connection with
secondary education on which, with the
permission of the Committee, I should
like to comment briefly. It is a matter
which has been brought up on various
occasions in this House and elsewhere,
and it is important. The Ministry
is still very seriously concerned
the fact that a large number
children each year delay their transference from the elementary school to the
secondary school until after their fourteenth birthday; our latest figures show
that of a total of 3,199 new entrants to
the secondary schools 785 were 14 years
of age or more. Now if there is one
point on which all educationists
agreed, it is that the child whose parents
wish him to derive full benefit from a
secondary education should go to his
secondary school certainly not later
than the age of 13. He will take
his junior certificate examination at
or 16, and as the course is
one that should not normally be
done in less than 3 years, comprising as it
does subjects many of which are not

I turn now to technical instruction-

There are many more matters in connection with the Estimates on which I
might speak, but I feel that this is no
time for speeches. The Ministry of
Education is not a "War" Ministry; our
first duty is to ensure, so far as we may,
that the education of our children shall
proceed unimpaired and that there shall
be no falling back that is not absolutely
unavoidable. Nevertheless, we contribute
what we can to the general effort; not a
day passes that does not bring with it
some new problem touching on the war
and the schools-food propaganda, assistance to the farmer during school holidays, war savings groups in the schools,
classes for the care and maintenance of
agricultural implements, special workshop classes in the technical schools,
salaries of teachers on war service and so
on, while before us there is always, of
course, the question of evacuation.

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to raise a point
in connection with the Pensions Account.
Assuming a man has attained the age of
63 and his wife has attained the age of
60 has the wife to wait until the
husband, who is the insured person,
attains the age of 65 before she gets the
pension? If so, she has to wait until
she is 62 before she receives it. That
point has occurred to the minds of many
insured contributors who are
over the
age of 60. It has been put to me
repeatedly by workmen from the Queen's
Island and other industries. I feel it is
a great hardship that the wife of the
insured person must wait until her
husband reaches the age of 65 before she
qualifies for the pension.
Let us take the case of the spinster.
She on her own qualifications gets the
pension at 60. At the moment we have
wives who are older than the husbands.
The husbands are, say, 59, and the wives
are, say, '64. The wives of those men
cannot get the pension until their husbands reach the age of 65, which means
they will be 70 before they receive the
pension which they are entitled to get
at 60. I knew many anomalies would
arise, and this is one of them. I
feel myself the right hon. Gentleman
will have some trouble with the applications he will receive, because my advice
to everyone who comes to me-and they
do not come in ones or twos-is to get
their claims presented and then the
answer would appear on the notice they
get stating whether they would receive
it or not. I know they will not receive
it. The law does not permit them to
receive it. That being so, there will be
many disappointments throughout Northern Ireland when the true effect of the
reduction of the pensionable age to 60
years works out in practice.
