R.U.C. AND THE ARMY.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether he was acting on the
advice of the Law Officers of the Crown
in London when he stated in the House
on the 28th May, that members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary and the "B"
Specials must all re-attest and then they
become legal combatants and incorporated
in the Army, and whether he can state
the reason why members of these forces
were not allowed to enlist since the
beginning of the war.
The following question also stood upon
the Order Paper :-
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if any call
to enlist in the Fighting Forces has been
made by the Government to the Regular
and the Special Constabulary, such as
was made by the authorities to the Royal
Irish Constabulary in the last war.
Since my statement to the House last
Tuesday regarding the combatant status
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
and the Ulster Special Constabulary when
used for the purpose of resisting armed
invasion of Northern Ireland, I have
been informed by the Army Council
that-
The PRIME MINISTER: With the
hon. and learned Member's permission I
propose to take the first two questions
together.
It appears to the Council that the
Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
Ulster Special Constabulary and the
additional section of the Special Constabulary which is to be formed will,
if they are employed for the purpose of
dealing with invaders, become members
of the Armed Forces. They must,
therefore, comply with the requirements of Article 1 of the Hague Rules,
that is to say they must:-
(i) Be commanded by a person responsible for his subordinates.
(ii) Wear some fixed distinctive sign
recognisable at a distance.
(iii) Carry arms openly.
(iv) Conduct their operations in accordance with the laws and customs
of war.
The Council understand that the
several categories of the Ulster Constabulary if employed for the purpose
of repelling invasion will come under
the command of the appropriate
military commander as soon as they
are called upon to take part in any
warlike operation.
It must be emphasised that nobody
can at one and the same time form
part of the armed forces and of the
peaceful population, and once members
of the Ulster Constabulary Forces have
appeared as combatants they cannot
thereafter claim the status and immunities of members of a purely civil
force.
In view of this statement no reattesting or other formality will be required in the case of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary or the Ulster Special
Constabulary.
As regards the last part of the question,
I would inform the hon. and learned
Member that, recognising the onerous
duties which will devolve on our regular
police forces, the Imperial Government
has included all full-time members of

and whether the honest answer referred

propose to take the next two questions

The PRIME MINISTER: With the
hon. and learned Member's permission I
I have seen the statements to which
the hon. and learned Member refers,
regarding the enlistment of Ulstermen in

The PRIME MINISTER: There again
these are matters dealt with entirely by
His Majesty's Forces. We have no
knowledge given us of those who turn up
at the recruiting office and are refused
for any reason. I am quite sure in this
emergency that any man who can pass
the physical test will certainly be taken
into the ranks somewhere. I can hardly
believe what the hon. Member states.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
there is a representative of the Ministry
of Labour in the recruiting office and
when a candidate tenders himself for
enlistment that representative is referred
to to see if the man is registered on the
unreserved services? Is it not a further
fact that in each of the two cases I
brought before this House the Minister
finally made arrangements for the unemployed man to get into the Army by
changing his registration? And what is
the sense of keeping thousands of men
idle, many of whom are willing to join,
on the bogus ground that they are in
reserved service?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Grant): I would like to
reply to that question. It is a fact that
the responsible Ministry in Great Britain.
has issued a list of reserved occupations,
so an officer of the Ministry of Labour
has to appear in the recruiting office and
if a particular applicant for recruitment
is on the reserved list there is no power
to accept him. That is a matter entirely
for the Imperial authority.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply and seeing we stand or fall by this
war which we all have at heart, is it not
time to make representation to have that
ridiculous rule done away with and allow
all unemployed men who want to join
to join?
The PRIME MINISTER: My right
hon. Friend the Minister of Labour is at
the present time in London discussing
with Mr. Bevin these and other questions
affecting labour generally.

He will have a rather more difficult
task to perform than we had in 1914.
Criticism is often directed against recruiting to-day and comparisons are drawn
between recruiting then and now. I do
not know whether anybody in the House
is old enough to remember that I myself
was appointed by Lord Kitchener as the
recruiting officer for Ulster with Colonel
Thomas Hickman for the Ulster Division.
It must be borne in mind that in those
days there were no reserved occupations.
To-day men throughout the countryside
are, I presume, busy to a degree producing the crops necessary to provide us with
food, but in those days all those men
were ready for the call and were not
classed by the Government as being in a
key industry.
Then there are also the great shipyards.
To-day, of course, there is the increased
employment necessitated by the construction of aeroplanes. All those men in
1914 were free to join, and they did join.
But to-day they are key men in reserved
occupations, and the reason for that is
the same reason that prevails in the rest
of the United Kingdom, namely, that
the fighting men cannot fight without the
necessary weapons of war, and also that
we cannot carry on this war unless our
people produce enough food to save the
country and to save the shipping which
is so much required for transferring our
Dominion and Colonial warriors from
their part of the world to the home
country.

All these men are classed as in

with whom, as I say, I am in the closest

At the same time there are other things

very lonely hillsides and elsewhere, and
what might happen to them in case an

the advice to be spread abroad that that
water should be drawn the night before

firebugs become active sometimes a bucket
of water will put out a fire which otherwise might spread and cause a great deal
of damage.
In our Own smaller working-class

There is one important matter I would

elusive creature, rumour. Really the

One man tells another in a whisper and

get a friend to go to him and trace the

It may be within the knowledge of

These are solemn days. A hundredfold more than in other wars the Angel
of Death is, in John Bright's phrase,

victims from all ranks, from the homes

We have been told about the defence

I feel that our shores could be better

I refer to the possibility of invasion from

certain things must be done, because in

maintained.

Coming now to the various services
administered by my Department, I am
happy to say that law and order has been
The disloyal minority have not, of
course, neglected to take advantage of the
opportunities given by the outbreak of
war to intensify their efforts, both by
direct action and by propaganda for the
purpose of creating disorder. Their
efforts have been, and, I suggest, will
continue to be frustrated.
The efficiency and discipline of the
constabulary forces has been maintained
at the usual high standard which they
have accustomed us to expect from them.
The manifold war duties arising out of
the lighting restrictions, the regulations
concerning aliens, and the defence regulations generally, have placed on them a
severe burden, in addition to normal
peace-time activities. Moveover, it was
considered necessary immediately on the
outbreak of war that the responsibility
for policing the Belfast Harbour estate
should be taken over by the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. Thanks to the willing cooperation of the Belfast Harbour Commissioners this was accomplished without
friction, and the new arrangements are
working with the greatest possible
efficiency. The force as a whole, as I
expected, has cheerfully accepted the
additional burdens thrown upon it.
A special word of praise must be
accorded to the Special Constabulary.
The re-introduction of the system of
night patrols by members of that force
has been no small factor in the preservation of the peace and the maintenance of
law and order in the " black-out," particularly during the long nights of the
winter period. The Special Constabulary
has also proved to be an invaluable
reservoir upon which the Government can
draw to supply the necessary reinforcement of the regular police for the purpose
of guarding vulnerable points against
sabotage, and the many other duties
requiring the services of additional men
which arise out of the war.

of suitable accommodation, in the maintenance of a satisfactory dietary, and in

Air-raid precautions services have made
steady progress, and whilst it would be
foolish in days such as these to congratulate ourselves that all emergencies have
been provided for, it can, I believe, be
stated that good use has been made of
the time which has elapsed since the war
began to develop and perfect many
measures which will be of the utmost
value in protecting the population from
the worst effects of attack by hostile aircraft when we have to meet it. It would,
I think, be wrong not to give expression
to the gratitude of the Government and
my gratitude to my hon. Friend the
Member for St. Anne's, my former Parliamentary Secretary, for his energetic and
skilful leadership in this matter.
One particular feature of our precautions I should like to refer to at some
length. Last summer, plans were made
for the evacuation of children from
Belfast in the event of air raids. At that
time everyone feared that such attacks on
the civil population might well be an
early experience of a war. In Great
Britain this feeling was so strong that
evacuation was carried out even before
war had actually been declared. We, in our
more remote position, felt justified in waiting a little to see how events would shape,
and the civil population has so far been
spared this barbaric form of warfare.
This fact, and the difficulties and discomforts of evacuation, which the action.
in Great Britain made obvious, had then
caused a certain revulsion from the idea
of evacuation. In order to find out the
views of parents of children in these circumstances, and to be in a position to
bring up to date the plans made last
summer, my Ministry recently instituted
a new registration of children for evacuation. It was made clear that the children
would not be evacuated unless the Government was sure, from the course of events,
that they were in actual and imminent
danger, and parents were asked to state
what they would wish the Government
to do for their children in such circumstances. The comparatively close connec
tion of Belfast to the rest of the Province
enabled us to introduce into our plans a
feature which has not been common elsewhere, namely, to ask each parent who
has friends or relatives in a country
reception area to nominate the person
with whom his children should be billeted.
The response to the new registration
has not been as complete as might have
been hoped. This is probably due to the
causes which I have just mentioned, for
the response to a corresponding new
registration in Great Britain seems to
have been even less encouraging. It is
scarcely necessary to emphasise how unfortunate it is that parents should have
treated the question in this manner; the
immunity which we have enjoyed cannot
be attributed to any humanitarian
scruples on the part of the King's
enemies, and we will not be out of the
wood until their power to deal an underhand blow is finally destroyed. No child
is going to be evacuated until such blows
begin to fall, but, on the other hand, no
one-not even the Ministry of Home
Affairs can make satisfactory plans to
move large numbers of people unless he
has a fair idea of the numbers who are
going to be moved.
However, a substantial number of
parents have realised the position and
registered their children; upwards of
20,000 children have been registered, of
whom about one-half have taken advantage of the privilege of nominating their
own hosts. The revised plans for the

PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Mr. Barbour).
The PRIME MINISTER: It is within
the knowledge of everyone how seriously
the situation has developed since we met
last week, and how it points more
and more to the utmost possible precautions being taken on the home front
in the event of an attack upon our island

too happy to pay this tribute because
sometimes I find the words of hon.
Members which go out of this House

all time in our history this is one when
people should have as much guard on
their tongues as possible in order not to
The
cause any feeling of nervousness.
nerves of many people are undoubtedly

homes scattered here and there. It is

[The Prime Minister]
home. As has been frequently stated in

In the midst of their great difficulties
they had, almost instantly, to improvise some force to cope with the new
danger revealed in our last debate on
this subject. At the same time we
ought to be ready to protect our country.
I am glad to be able to inform the

the volunteers of loyalist Ulster enrolled
and what we asked on this day last week
has been accomplished as I stand at the
box to-day. That is a very remarkable
feat indeed, not so much from the fact

but from the point of view of the
magnificent organisation which permitted
a revolutionary movement of that kind
to be carried through with such
rapidity and smoothness. We have today, as I promised, doubled our force,
and we have armed the men. They are
out to-day guarding the people in all
parts of the Province.
I cannot, after what was said to-day,
pass over this matter without paying
tribute to the man on whose shoulders the
organisation chiefly depended-Sir Charles
Wickham. I am going to speak of him
not as a valued servant of Ulster, but as a
close friend for whom I have a very
high esteem and one who can, I think, be
ranked with those men who have served
Northern Ireland in this Government for
nearly 20 years and pulled us through
some very difficult times.
It is very easy to cast aspersions upon
any man, but I do not know anyone who
has with such dignity, spirit and power
carried on with his ordinary constabulary
duties, at one time with the "A" Specials,
"B" Specials and "C" Specials, and now
with a vast number of "B" Specials and
the new Ulster Volunteers without, so far
as I can remember, making one mistake.
in guarding the country, and seeing to it
that the law was observed, and that those
who did not observe it were brought before the proper authorities. I am only
I should like to point out one or two
things in connection with this matter. It
has been stated, I think by one of the
hon. Members, that it would be
much better to have recruited a larger
force. That will be done. Those of us
who have to decide these matters think
it would cause great disappointment to
men anxious to join if they were enlisted
and then had to lie off for a long time
before being called up. If that were
done the charge might be made against
the Government that these people had
offered their services and had been turned
down. The real meaning of this is that
we must extend along the lines which
carry not only the voluntary services of
our people, but also the necessary equipment. I do not wish to exaggerate the
situation with regard to arms and equipment. But I am afraid the hon.
Member's suggestion to start off now and
have an arms factory would not be
feasible. The delay would be such as to
make it of little avail in the present
emergency.
When I heard last night at midnight
the statement of President Roosevelt
speaking on behalf of the great American
nation, where he said he would pour out
with both hands all the equipment necessary to help the Allies over here I
immediately said, well, when it reaches
the other side in the first instance it will
give me an opportunity at any rate of
claiming a share of that, so that as our
requirements here for home defence
increase, in case danger comes upon us
suddenly and unexpectedly we will be
able to go on and on, and I hope in the
end, if the necessity arises, we will be
able to arm every solid loyal man in

Ulster so that it cannot be said we were

We are, as you all know, in great danger

to say absolutely nothing that would in
any way help the enemy, which is not

force? Why not place arms in the hands

was the way to secure two rifles in order
to be able to help the parachutists when

occur in England is it not prudent on our
part to take the utmost precautions that
nothing of the kind should occur here?
co-operation between their Government

is this, so little of a lead have the people

operate in Northern Ireland as in Great
Britain, and will be made retrospective.

APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT
PRESS OFFICER.
2. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Finance whether in view of the
necessity for curtailing expenditure he
can state why the Government propose to
appoint an assistant Press Officer at
£450 per annum; whether it is a fact
that there is already a Press Officer at
Stormont whose salary is £750. per
annum, and another at the London Office
whose salary is £650 per annum, with an
allowance of £150 a year, and whether
in view of the fact that little or no
news regarding Northern Ireland appears
in the English Press he will consider the
advisability of doing away with these
positions instead of increasing them.
Mr. ANDREWS: The decision to
appoint an assistant Press officer arises
from an agency arrangement entered
into between the Ministry of Finance
and the Ministry of Information. Additional duties require to be performed for
the Imperial Department, which will be
responsible for half the salary of both
the Press officer and of the assistant
Press officer.
The position of the Press officer in the
London Office is on an entirely different
footing, and it is considered that there
is justification for the duties of a propaganda nature which he is performing
and which have been frequently approved
of by hon. Members.

OVER HERRINGS.

3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether there is to be any
scheme in Northern Ireland similar to
that of the British Ministry of Food for
taking over, during the period June to
August this year, the whole of the cure
of herrings at the principal Scottish
fishing ports, so that if all the herrings
cannot be sold for the home market the
Ministry of Food will buy the surplus
from the fishermen.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am in communication.
with the Ministry of Food regarding the
practicability of extending the scheme to
cover the Northern Ireland herring fishings. The hon. Member will, of course,
appreciate that the scheme can only come
into operation if there is a surplus of
herring available for curing. The ques
tion of whether a surplus will arise will
depend not only on the presence of large
shoals of herring but also on the participation of visiting drifters in the
Ardglass fishing. The herring catch is
unpredictable, and landings at County
Down ports may be entirely absorbed by
the fresh market or for kippering which,
it is anticipated, will be carried on this
season to a substantial extent.

EXCHEQUER AND FINANCIAL

Considered in Committee under

Motion made and Question proposed:
That it is expedient-
(a) to provide for the issue out of
the Consolidated Fund to the
Civil Contingencies Fund of sums
not exceeding in all the sum of
one hundred thousand pounds;
(b) to provide for the transfer from

Fund of the sum of twenty-one
thousand and sixty-three pounds
eighteen shillings and five pence;

Finance to purchase by agreement
Northern Ireland Transport Stock
and to borrow money for the
purpose of giving effect to any
such agreement;
(d) to enable provision to be made
by regulations for certain matters
as respects Ulster Savings Certificates; and
(e) to extend the period of office of
existing Comptroller and
Auditor General.-(Governor's
recommendation signified.-Mr.
Andrews).

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): I can quite understand hon.
Members feeling that in the serious times
we are passing through our efforts should
be entirely associated with matters affecting the war. On the other hand, hon.
Members are aware that local affairs
must be carried on. As regards this
proposal affecting transport, I would like
to make it perfectly clear that this is a
first step taken in accordance with the
recommendations not only of the
McLintock Committee but of the Select
Committee of this House and the
Senate; a first step that has got to be
taken before the transport position
generally can be dealt with. To deal
with transport is a most difficult matter,
as those hon. Members who formed the
Select Committee and who sat considering the matter for many months, themselves very well know.
The difficulty of dealing with the problem was also greatly increased during the
war, because the war has brought about
different conditions affecting transport to
a very considerable extent. I am glad
to be able to say that both the Board
and the railways have been doing considerably better since the war began.
That improvement may be of a temporary nature, but, on the other hand,
I am glad to say it has, to some extent,
affected the financial position of the
Board and the railways in a favourable
direction. Why do the Government now
propose to purchase this A and B Stock?
It is doing so because, as hon. Members
will appreciate, the A and B stockholders
are part owners of road transport in Northern Ireland, and before we deal with
the matter as a whole these stockholders
have to be dealt with. In dealing with
the property surely we cannot be blamed
for carrying out the recommendations of
the Committee to which I have referred.
Mr. NIXON: One of the recommendations.

which, as I have said, it is absolutely
necessary should be carried out before the
major problem is dealt with no matter what
the solution may be.. When introducing this
Resolution I said that the proposal was
not to hand over cash to these stockholders, but in lieu of the present stock
which they hold to give them 32 per
cent. Northern Ireland Government
stock. We have not, fortunately, to go
on the market at the present time in
order to deal with the matter. That
clearly sets out the position. If this provision was not carried out a serious
position might arise in connection with

must be remembered that these stockholders have rights and privileges under
the Transport Act. If they were to enforce those rights and privileges, as they
are entitled to do, it would be found before many weeks passed by to be very
detrimental to the interests of transport
generally in Northern Ireland.
The hon. Member for Pottinger requested me to make the position in reference to the Civil Contingencies Fund
clearer. That fund exists for the purpose that when this House is not sitting

The first object now is to help Great

The very

munitions, the building of ships, the

FINANCIAL SECRETARY'S
RESIGNATION.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I have to
inform the House that I have sent in my
resignation.
Mr. SPEAKER: If the hon. and
gallant Member is making a personal
statement, as he informed me he intended
to do, he should ask leave of the House.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: By leave of
the House. I have to inform the House
that I sent in my resignation as Financial
Secretary to the Minister of Finance on
Thursday, the 13th June. On Sunday I
flew to England, as it seemed to me the
sands were running out. I make no
secret of the fact that I was in Whitehall. The sands have run out. The
danger to this country is certain and cannot long be delayed.
The Government here, as at present
constituted, is by nature of its personnel,
its lack of drive and initiative, and utter
lack of what war means-I here except
certain Members-is quite unfitted to
sustain the people in the ordeal that we
have to face. I wish to quote a statement of the Prime Minister.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. and gallant
Member must realise he is making a personal statement now. He must not
debate any subject.

state the number of persons convicted
of drunkenness due to the drinking of

convictions of persons for drunkenness as

what are commonly called "Toney wines."

Member to the report of the Select Committee on Adulterated Wines, in which it

troduced to-day I am fulfilling one of the

To my mind it is absolutely wrong

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Before
entering on the points raised in the
debate I would like to say that it was
with great regret I left the Ministry of
Finance in which I had worked for three
years. During that time the Minister
and I never had a cross word. We
worked together in great harmony, and
I want it to be perfectly clear that my
resignation had no concern either with
the Minister or Ministry. At the same
time I would like to point out that I
always found the members of the Civil
Service with whom I worked efficient,
loyal and hard working. I take the
earliest opportunity to say what I think
of their services, and for which I thank
them. It was with great regret I left
the Ministry, but I felt it my duty to
do so. The public may be assured that
there were no differences between the
Minister of Finance and myself.
I would now like to deal with some
of the points raised by the hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's. In
doing so I realise that as Financial
Secretary I bear my share of responsibility for any Estimates introduced. The
Minister of Finance has, of course, the
chief responsibility, but I do not want
to escape any responsibility in the matter.
I would like to divide my answer to the
hon. and learned Member's points into
three. The first thing I want to deal
with is the question of Sprucefield, which
loomed largely in his remarks. He says
that two or three years ago I introduced
an Estimate for £3,000 for an improvement in the men's accommodation. I do
not think the hon. and learned Member
Second Reading

HOUSE OF COMMONS

is aware of the facts, otherwise he would
not have put up the case he did.
At the time I introduced the Estimate
in the House Sprucefield did not belong
to the Government, and nobody in his
senses would estimate or go in for extensive buildings on a place which did
not belong to him. We come down to
what was sanctioned this year for improvement of the quarters at Sprucefield.
The Minister of Finance, the Inspector-
General, the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's and myself, as well as
some others, went and inspected the place..
We spent the greater part of a day there.
After a full examination we came to the
conclusion that the living quarters were
not fit for human habitation. We set
the architects to make a close inspection,
and after consultation it was decided that
new quarters should be built. It was impossible to build new huts as there was
no timber, and we, came to the conclusion
that the job should be done properly
once and for all. The cost of the actual
building comes to £5,633. In addition
to accommodation for nine men this is
a depot in which the stores of the police
are kept. Nearly every day of the week
at least eight or nine men go there and
have dinner, and extra accommodation is
required for them. I fail to see why the
police should not be. allowed to have a
room in which to sit in the evenings when
they have had their meals.
So much for Sprucefield. The hon.
and learned Member in his speech quoted
figures covering the years 1934 to 1939-40.
I may say straight away that there is no
doubt at all that the figures he quoted
are accurate and cannot be controverted,
because they have been taken from the
Estimates. But you have to remember
that those figures are the effect. What
was the cause? I would remind the House
that in 1931 there was a crisis and
economy cuts were made, and the
Government reduced their expenditure
for the two or three years following.
Then as things got better it became the
policy not only of the Government here
but of the Government in England to
encourage employment by giving more
work.
Imperial Government decided to replace
the old and bad post offices. I have not
got the figures-it is impossible to carry
them in my head, but I had them under
review quite. lately. The expenditure
both by this Government and the
Imperial Government rose very considerably, in some cases nearly 50, 75, or 100
per cent. To carry out this work the
staff obviously had to be increased.
That is the answer to the hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's. The
policy was to give more employment and
do more building. There had to be an
increase of staff. So much for the
criticism on broad lines; it is not for me
to go into the details.
The Government decided to replace all
the condemned police barracks, build new
labour exchanges, and so forth, whilst the

The PRIME MINISTER: I apologise
for having asked you, sir, to call the
House together. I think all Members are
satisfied that the critical situation in
which we stand was sufficient justification. I am treating this as a war
Measure, and one of the utmost importance. I thank the Committee which
was set up for the suggestion they made
and their recommendations, one of which
in connection with this Ministry is being
adopted as quickly as possible by the
Government. I thought at one time the
Committee would find it difficult to set
to work as quickly as they did after the
first meeting, but I congratulate them
and thank them most heartily for helping the Government in this difficult
matter. As they cover all sides of the
House it means, I presume, that the Bill
will be passed through all its stages very
rapidly.
The object of the Bill is, of course, to
concentrate in one department under a
Cabinet Minister all matters essential to
public security, civil defence, and the
protection of persons and property.
Immediately after the Bill is passed it
will be necessary to have an Order in
Council defining the functions of the new
Minister, but I can say that there will be

requires in order to secure adequate

civil defence shall be. transferred to the
new Minister as soon as possible.
The Clauses can be gone through, of
course, one by one, and any questions asked
will be answered either by my hon. Friend,
the Attorney-General, who is with me,
or by myself, whichever finds it convenient. The Clauses are all really selfexplanatory, and I do not think it will

SECURITY OF TENURE FOR
TEACHERS.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she can state if any
further progress has been made by the
Ministry to give security of tenure to
Public Elementary School teachers due to
the declining school population.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I am
very glad that the hon. Member has
afforded me this opportunity of stating
what the Ministry has done with a view
to lessening the risk of unemployment
amongst teachers.
The Ministry's action has been taken.
under three heads:-
First, a considerable reduction has
been made in the number of students in
the Training Colleges.
Secondly, there has been the temporary
regulation by which salary is not withdrawn from an assistant in a school other
than a large school until the end of the
sixth consecutive quarter of insufficient
average.
of course, governed by the Education Act
of 1935.
Thirdly, the Ministry has written to
the Regional Education Committees and
also to the cardinal and bishops of the
Roman Catholic Church, the Diocesan
Board of Education of the Church of
Ireland and the Elementary Education
Committee of the General Assembly on
the subject. The powers of the Regional
Education Committees in the matter are,
I am glad to say that the replies have
been, on the whole, encouraging. The
Ministry is aware that diocesan panels of
unemployed teachers are at present kept
by the cardinal and the bishops of the
Roman Catholic Church, and that, as a
rule, vacancies are filled from these panels,
The Elementary Education Committee of
the General Assembly is at present
setting up a panel for Presbyterian
teachers, and it is understood that the
question of setting up a single panel for
the four Church of Ireland dioceses is
about to be considered.
It is hardly necessary for me to say
that the Ministry will gladly welcome any
action which it is practicable for Education Authorities and the Churches to
take, by the establishment of panels or
otherwise, with a view to securing that
teachers who lose employment owing to
insufficiency of average shall be transferred to vacancies elsewhere as quickly
as possible. Further than this, however,
the Ministry has no power to go.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the hon. Lady could she not give the
House an assurance owing to the importance of the teacher now to the child that
any teacher threatened with loss of
position due to falling averages will be
retained for at least the duration of the
war.
Mrs. PARKER: I am afraid I am
not in a position to give that assurance,
but I will look into the particular point
raised by the hon. Member.

1. Mr. WARNOCK asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that the
Northern Ireland Divisional Food Office,
after consultation with the Government
of Eire, has issued ration cards, covering
all descriptions of rationed foods, to
residents in Eire along the entire Border
to enable such residents to come into
Northern Ireland to purchase such foods;
whether the Government of Northern
Ireland was informed of, or was a party
to such consultations, and whether he
will make representations to the proper
authority to ensure that our essential and
rationed supplies are retained for the
use of the people of Northern Ireland
and not made available to residents in a
neutral country.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
I understand that the Ministry of
Food in London entered into an arrangement somewhat on the lines described
by the hon. and learned Member. I am
also informed that the primary object.
of the arrangement is to enable retailers
in the city of Londonderry to retain
some portion of a trade across the Border
which has been theirs for many years.
The control and rationing of foodstuffs, as the hon. and learned Member
will be aware, is a matter for the
Imperial Department concerned, and the
Government of Northern Ireland was not
consulted by the Ministry of Food before
making the arrangement referred to with
the Government of Eire. The arrange
ment is, I understand, on a reciprocal
basis, inasmuch as, in certain circumstances, retailers in Eire can
registered by Food Control Committees
in Northern Ireland and thus supply
customers in Northern Ireland with
rationed foodstuffs.

the instructions given by the Minister

RECENT BANK RAIDS IN
BELFAST.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state
why the recent bank raids in Belfast
were not anticipated by the police
authorities and why provision was not
made for due protection.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The hon. Member will appreciate that the police cannot be expected to have foreknowledge
of the precise time and place of all contemplated crimes.
Due protection must always be a compromise between the special risks inherent in certain cases and the requirements of preserving the general security
of the community as a whole.
Steps, which the hon. Member will not
expect me to elaborate, are being taken
to minimise the risk of occurrences in the
future of incidents similar to those to
which his question refers.
Mr. NIXON: Why were these steps not
taken in time? In all cases of trouble
in Ireland there have been bank raids,
and in view of that why were the raids
not anticipated and steps taken accordingly as the banks are open for only four
hours? Is it not a fact that some
months ago about 30lbs. of gelignite was
stolen from a brickyard? Why were
steps not taken to have the gelignite put
in a proper place?

pleased to furnish him with a copy of

So. I feel this is a very important

What he has done in the past does not

He may be everything that his followers.
think he has been in the past, and I pay

One thing has been done which I, as a
member of the Civil Defence Committee,
resent very much. The evacuation
scheme was put into operation without
the necessary courtesy being extended to
members of the Committee. The Committee met on Tuesday and the Cabinet
decision was made on Monday. They
had not the courtesy or the decency to
inform the Committee that evacuation
was to take place the following Sunday.
No one wished the evacuation scheme to
be a greater success than I did. I saw

see it a huge success, but the least I
expected was that the Prime Minister
Iwould inform us that certain things

3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

drawn by Sir Charles Blackmore when he

The PRIME MINISTER: In the
absence of my right hon. Friend I propose to take, this question.
At the time of his retirement Sir
Charles Blackmore, who was transferred
from the Imperial Civil Service to that
of the Government of Northern Ireland
on the 1st August, 1921, was in receipt
of a salary of £1,750 a year. His total

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
This undoubtedly cast upon the labour
market numbers of people, through no
fault of their own, and through no fault
of the employers, but through the action
of the Government in restricting production. Unemployment created under
conditions of that character with an increased cost of living necessitated something being done to meet an abnormal
situation of that kind, and the Government decided to introduce a Bill similar
to that passed by the United Kingdom
Parliament.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Unemployment Insurance
Bill now in the hands of hon. Members
is a small Bill but a somewhat important
Measure, and while it may not reach the
pinnacle hoped for by some hon.
Members, it is a real attempt to deal with
a situation which will become more
evident as the war continues. The
Imperial Government has imposed restrictions on non-essential industries,
and due largely to a shortage of raw
material one of our main industries, the
linen trade, though engaged to some
extent on war work, has had to curtail
production.
The Bill is a short one, and I propose
to be brief in my explanation. The
question now arises: What does this Bill
propose to do? First, it proposes to increase the benefit under the general
scheme and under the agricultural
scheme on the 1st August, 1940;
secondly, it proposes to increase the
maximum weekly rate of agricultura!
benefit from the 1st of August; thirdly,
it proposes to increase the weekly contributions of all insured workers over 18
years on the 5th August; fourthly, it
proposes to change what is called the
continuity rule from the 1st August,
which I will explain later; and lastly, to
bring into insurance workers whose
salaries are under £420 per annum on
the 2nd September. Those are the main
changes proposed in the Bill.
Under the general scheme an increase
of 3s a week is proposed for men and
women, and also for young men and
young women who are maintaining dependants. Other young men and young
women will receive a weekly increase of
2s. Under the. agricultural scheme the
Bill proposes a 3s increase in the weekly
rates of benefit for men and young men
who are entitled to benefit for their
dependants and also a 2s increase for
other young men and women and young
women, and at the same time an increase
in the weekly maximum of agricultural
benefit to 41s. a week.
As hon. Members are aware, no
increases have been made in the benefit
rates for adult claimants since the war
started, and as I explained earlier, the
increases now proposed have taken into
account the rise in the cost of living
during recent months.
For the classes whose benefit rates are
increased, the Bill proposes an increase
in contributions. The general scheme
1729 Unemployment Insurance Bill-
23 JULY 1940

Second Reading
contributions will be increased by 1d from
each of the contributing parties, namely,
employer, worker and the State; and a
corresponding increase of d all round
will be made for agricultural scheme contributions. This latter increase will hold
good until 5th July, 1942, after which
date there will be a further increase of
d. No change is proposed by the Bill
in the contribution rates for persons
under 18 insured in either scheme.
Clause 3 of the Bill deals with the
continuity rule. The position at present
is that any three days of unemployment
within a period of six consecutive days
shall be treated as continuous unemployment and shall count for benefit purposes.
The Bill proposes to substitute two for
the three days, which means if a person
is unemployed in any two days out of six
consecutive days those two days shall
count for benefit purposes. This change
will lessen the inducement to refrain from
doing more than three days' work in any
six days, and should encourage workers,
particularly those in casual employment,
to take additional employment when it is
available in the week. Hon. Members
will appreciate that this change does not
involve any alteration in the existing
waiting period of three days, which remains unaffected by the Bill.
An important alteration which the Bill
seeks to effect, and one which I am sure
will be welcomed on all sides of the House,
is contained in Clause 4. At present
the income limit for unemployment
insurance is £250 a year.

a step which would be likely to add to the

CLASS VIII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF PUBLIC SECURITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £43,294 be
granted to His Majesty for the service of
the year ending the 31st March, 1941,
to defray the salaries and expenses of
the Ministry of Public Security."
The CHAIRMAN: With the leave of
the House I will allow discussion on the
three Resolutions to take place on the
first one.
Then the other two will be
put formally.
I
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott):
would have wished that my
first
appearance before this Commitee seeking a grant of public funds had been
occasioned by circumstances more propitious than those which find me here.
For the first time within living memory
this country stands in danger of invasion
by a powerful foe. Within less than a
year the war against Germany has passed
through many startling phases. We
have seen people after people overrun
and subdued-for the time being-by
the armed might of Hitler, after being
corrupted from within by every form of
propaganda and by every means that
could hinder and weaken their opposition to the enemy's military advance.
To-day the United Kingdom and the
Empire beyond the seas stand alone in
arms against the enemy-the last obstacle
in the path of his ambition, the bulwark
of those ideals towards which mankind
has struggled throughout the ages and
towards which mankind will surely turn
again, and quickly, if we but hold the
torch aloft. To-day, in this Province, we
are ranged with the rest of the garrison
and that-and no less-is our duty and
our privilege.
I understand it is the custom in this
House for a Minister on the presentation
of the annual Estimates to give the Committee an account of the work of his
Department over the preceding twelve
months, and to inform the Committee, as
fully as possible, of the policy being
followed as respects those matters of
public administration with which his
Department has been entrusted.
It is with this background that I
present these Estimates to the Committee,
and it is against this background that I
would ask the Committee to consider
them.
So far as this Ministry is concerned,
however, I feel sure that hon. Members
will not expect from me an exhaustive
review of this nature. For one thing, the
Ministry is but a month old; for another,
the Estimate is in substance, and indeed,
for the most part, in form, supplementary in character. Again, while there
is no desire to keep the Committee in
ignorance of what my Department may
be doing or intends to do, may I remind
all that these are difficult times; the ears
of the enemy are wide open and there are
many matters which cannot prudently be
entered upon with the detail which might
reasonably be expected in happier circumstances.
At the same time the Committee is
entitled to know, and I am prepared to
give them the broad lines of the policy
that is being followed and the nature of
the objects on which will be spent the
substantial sums for which I am now
asking.
The activities of my Department may
conveniently be considered in two
separate groups; first, what I might call
the security services; and then the
services of civil defence. In the first
group the security services-I put all
those matters affecting the preservation
of law and order and the maintenance of
public security. Here let me make it
plain in view of certain circumstances
which have arisen inside the House and
not outside it that I am not a Minister
of Defence. The defence of this part of
the United Kingdom against enemy
attack is the business of the armed forces
of the Crown, over whose disposition and
employment neither this Government nor
this Parliament has any jurisdiction, but
the closest touch is maintained and the
friendliest relations exist between the
heads of the three services in Northern
Ireland and our own Government, and
the assistance of the civil departments is
at the disposal of the service authorities
whenever they may require to call upon
1791 Supplementary Estimates-
Ministry of Public Security 1792
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
it. To this end a small standing committee, presided over by Sir James Cooke-
Collis, has been established. On this
committee is a representative of the
General Officer Commanding and of each
of our own Departments most likely to
be concerned, SO that proposals of
the military authorities requiring the.
collaboration of the civil departments can
be disposed of and put into effect with
the expedition that the present situation
demands.
Parliament has given me power in the
Ministries Act to make. Orders for the
preservation of the peace and the maintenance of public security. The Orders
already made deal with the banning of
processions, the prohibiting of church bell
ringing except as an alarm and then only
on the orders of a military or police officer,
and restrictions on the sale of maps. I
do not suppose that any of these measures
has caused much serious inconvenience to
any section of the community, but if
the emergency grows graver or if a more
complete review of the situation suggests
that such a course is necessary, the public
must expect, and be prepared to accept,
more inconvenience and heavier restrictions on their normal habits, their
freedom of movement and their amenities.
I shall endeavour not to make Orders unnecessarily, but I am sure hon. Members
and the general public will realise that
in these days, more than ever before, the
security and safety of the community
must be the supreme consideration.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
So far as internal security is concerned,
the existing emergency has added to the
difficulties which are. always present and
to the already numerous duties of the
police. I need not, however, stress the
special importance of maintaining law
and order in these times, but I think I
may say on behalf of every officer and
man of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
that it is their most anxious desire in
these arduous days to discharge their duty
in a manner worthy of the high traditions
of the. Force and of the confidence which
the public has in it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That confidence is valued
and valuable, but active co-operation is
always needed as well, and, to-day, with
a common danger threatening all, I trust
that every citizen will make it his duty
to keep his eyes and ears open and to
support and help the police in every
possible way.
The Committee will probably expect me
to make, some reference to the recent recrudescence of activity in the Province
by armed parties, described as members
of the Irish Republican Army. Outrages
such as the burning of a food store would
be felonious enough in times of peace,
but when the country is fighting for its
life they constitute a menace to the
national effort and the national safety as
grave as any form of treason. We shall
use all the resources at our disposal to
combat the activities of these gunmen and
to bring them to justice. This last outrage is by its very nature aimed at the
whole community, for men, women and
children of every class and of every creed
must eat. I trust the label "I.R.A.”
will blind no one to its true character.
It would be folly to think of this occurrence merely as another episode in the
so-called war of Irish freedom. It is a
blow struck for the enemy, and only those
who are ready and willing to help the
enemy can have had part in it.
And now let me say something of the
progress that has been made with the
formation and training of the Ulster
Defence Volunteers. The circumstances
that gave rise to the establishment of a
Local Defence Volunteer force in Great
Britain existed in no less degree in Northern Ireland. We had not, however,
the chain of Territorial Associations
which form the administrative basis for
the movement in Great Britain. But
we found ourselves with an organisation
complete and ready to hand, and, accordingly, with the full approval of the War
Office, the Government decided that the
new force should grow up round the
nucleus of the county organisation of our
Special Constabulary.
I may add that while this decision was
taken before the formation of my Ministry I have no doubt from what I have
seen that the expedient has been justified by its results and that nothing like
the progress already made could have
been achieved in any other way. The
response for recruits has been most satisfactory. The numbers enrolled now
amount to over 23,000. In many
districts the establishment could have
been filled twice or three times over.
Rifles and ammunition are available for
those enrolled and have been issued to
most of them. Uniforms are in course
1793 Supplementary Estimates--
Ministry of Public Security 1794
24 JULY 1940
of being distributed, and up and down.
the country the members of the force are
hard at work, not only fitting themselves
for their role, but in many cases already
carrying out their appointed tasks. In
a relatively short time much has been
accomplished and the enthusiasm and
hard work of all who have brought this
to pass are worthy of the most hearty
commendation.
The work of organisation and training
is, however, not yet complete and all
concerned have still much strenuous
effort in front of them. It must be
recognised that the ultimate purpose of
this force is a military one and the aim
and object of this Ministry must be to
do all in its power to ensure that when
the time comes for the military authorities to assume control of it the force will
be a well-tempered weapon worthy of
the part it is to play and of this
Province. In this connection I am happy
to say that the force has received, and
is receiving in increasing measure, the
guidance and help of the Army authorities. The full-time services of a number
of Army officers have been placed at the
disposal of the force to help in training
and administrative duties, and we have
also obtained the services of N.C.O.'s of
the regular Army as instructors in drill
and musketry. The help so rendered and
the friendly co-operation of units in the
various areas have already been of
immense assistance in the formation of
this new auxiliary force. For this I wish
to express my warmest thanks and also
the hope-indeed, my belief-that, in
the hour of need, the help so freely given.
will be returned with interest.
I
ment's work-the civil defence servicescommonly referred to as "A.R.P."
have deliberately used the phrase "less.
picturesque," for within the past couple
of months there has been a tendency for
trained personnel to gravitate from the
A.R.P. services into the new Defence
Volunteers. I can only deplore this
tendency in so far as it has resulted in
irregular and inconsiderate transfers from
one service to the other. The safety of
life and property in the community may
depend just as much on the warden, the
ambulance driver, the first-aid worker,
the auxiliary fireman and the member of
the rescue squad as on the volunteer who
shoulders a rifle. The Defence Volunteers
form a valuable auxiliary of the regular
Army, but the A.R.P. workers are our
first-line troops against the ravages of
aerial bombardment.
Undoubtedly the volunteer movement
has proved attractive to those to whom
a military pursuit presents an appeal,
especially when it can offer the added
advantage that members of the force are
able to do their soldiering in their spare
time and in the neighbourhood of their
own homes, but while welcoming the
response to the call for recruits for this
force, and appreciating its high value, I
cannot from the subject without also
pass
commending the claims of the regular
fighting services, especially to the younger
sections of our manhood, who are not
employed in essential national services
and are otherwise free and fit for wholetime duty.
I shall now pass to a less picturesque
but no less essential side of my Depart-
In connection with this problem it is
but right that I should acknowledge that
many of those who wished to transfer
have been guided solely by a desire to
serve in the capacity which seemed most
useful and that many others for the same
reason have expressed a desire to do active
duty in both services. It is impossible
to formulate any rule which will be satisfactory in all cases, but I have directed
that no person in an A.R.P. service shall
transfer to, or be accepted in, the Defence
Volunteers unless released by his superior
officer for the purpose, and I have adopted
some
generally applicable the principle
adopted in Great Britain of "one man,
one job." It must be remembered that
combatant and non-combatant services
cannot be combined at pleasure and
further that, in any given district, the
need for both services may arise and the
personnel of each may be engaged at the
peak of their effort at the same time.
While I feel this principle is sound it is,
of course, appreciated that in
districts, generally rural, there may be
overlapping as, for example, when
wardens and volunteers do the same
patrols; and that in some cases A.R.P.
posts and personnel may require a guard.
But in instances of these types the
difficulty ought to be overcome by the two
services working in close co-operation and
by attachments for the performance of
specific duties rather than by attempting
a definite fusing of duties on the part of
the individual.
Before turning to the actual Estimates
I should note one other general considera-

tion as it has an important bearing on the

When the A.R.P. Estimates for this and
last year were passed the position was
such that Northern Ireland seemed to be
at the extreme range of hostile aerial
attack and beyond the reach of land
operations. All that the situation
appeared to demand was provision against
the possibility that Belfast and its
immediate neighbourhood might from
time to time be the target of enterprising
bombers. Outside that obviously vulnerable area there seemed little cause for

next March, practically nine months. The

try of Home Affairs, and this saving will

For these reasons it has been my first
preoccupation during the weeks that have

All our trained A.R.P. personnel are

and practice are necessary.

The presentation of Estimates, such as
these, focusses attention on the kind of
help which money will buy. I fully agree
that this is no time for waste-waste was
never a greater vice than at present-but,
at the same time, protection must be provided in an adequate form. I do not
think the figures I have given are in any
way excessive having regard to what has
to be done, and they are certainly not
beyond the standard of expenditure
which exists in Great Britain. That form
of protection, though valuable and well
worth while, is not enough in itself. Our
security demands the co-operation of
every man, woman and child in the community, a united front with all prejudices laid aside; all animosities buried;
all sense of self-importance forgotten.
The present is no time for petty differences. The bomb is no respecter of
persons, neither is it sensible of any fine
distinctions of class or creed. The job
we have in hand demands the strength
and energy of us all. As a people we
have the strength and the energy, and I
am confident that whatever the trials
before us we shall not prove unworthy of
the common cause. I beg to move.

asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether lawn mowings from golf courses
in Northern Ireland are being made into
silage for feeding purposes as is being
done in some cases in Great Britain, and,
if not, will he take suitable steps to have
the good example of Great Britain in
this matter followed in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The hon.
Member can rest assured that this and
related feeding stuffs questions are constantly under the consideration of my
Ministry.
With regard to the special question of
silage from lawn cuttings there are prac
tical difficulties, and I am handing the
hon. Member a copy of detailed advice
given by my Ministry on this subject.
The following is the copy referred to:-
SILAGE FROM LAWN CUTTINGS.
If lawn cuttings are available in
sufficient quantity they may be made
into silage by following the method
described in the Ministry's leaflet No.
101. In order to make good silage it is
necessary that the green material be
available in such quantity as to enable
filling to proceed regularly until the silo
is filled or the stack completed. Enough
cuttings would have to be available to
permit a layer of at least three feet deep
--
85-17
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

25 JULY 1940
to be filled into the silo every second
day. If the material were filled in
shallower layers or at longer intervals the
portion at the top would have reached too
high a temperature and be damaged
before the next instalment is added.
The surface area of the silo or pit in
which the silage is being made will, of
course, influence the depth of layer made
by a certain quantity of material. Where
relatively small amounts are available
the best plan would be to make the silage
in a concrete pit which is divided up into
comparatively small compartments. Each
compartment should be filled and sealed
off separately. The size of the pit and of
each compartment will depend on the
amount of cuttings which are available
every second day.
This will, however, be a rather difficuit.
procedure and will need care if good
silage is to be made. Except a considerable quantity of cuttings is available
every second day it is doubtful if it would
be worth while to attempt the making
of silage.

Mr. BROWN: In the Estimates there

munitions will be required. We should
once more reconsider the question of

the Estimate. We were all thrilled to

on the wireless last night. We should
be thankful to God that in an emergency
we have men like Lord Beaverbrook
coming forward and giving the benefit of
their undoubted talent, dynamic personality and boundless enthusiasm. Lord
Beaverbrook gave the splendid news that
3,000 planes a month are coming to us
from America, and he went on to say
that our real source of supply depends
on home production.
That has been recognised in more places
than one. The proposal was put forward
in this House a short time ago by the
hon. Member (Rev. Professor Corkey).
The proposal was that if it is not possible
for us to induce the British Government
to set up for their benefit and ours a
munition factory, or a number of
munition factories, there was no reason
why our Government should not proceed
with such a scheme on their own and

of great assistance to the State and
Empire if we utilised some of the money
from that extra taxation in the erection
of a number of munition factories.

linen. He did not ask the trader to
commit an offence. That is, I think, the
mistake the Government is making.
This is not like asking a trader to give
him Irish linen. In this particular case
the inspector asked the trader to do what
would be committing an offence if the
trader did it. The trader did it and
committed and offence, and so did the
inspector.
According to our instructions in the
police that was an unworthy way of
making a case.
For instance, I, as a
policeman, was never allowed to go into
a public-house during closing hours and
ask the publican to give me a glass of
whisky. I knew that would be an
offence. If the publican did that and I
prosecuted him I would have been dismissed. It would be just the same if
I went to a spirit grocer and asked him
to commit an offence. I only draw
attention to the difference between the
two cases for the Minister and every
other person to see. In the old days it
was never allowed. It was considered
unworthy and I think there has been a
misapprehension about it on the part of
the Minister of Commerce. He thought
it was much the same as the case I have
illustrated, but it is entirely different. I
will leave it at that because I do not
think it would be followed up.
This man left in as much meat as would
do his customers for the week-end. He
closed his premises on the Friday and
opened again on Saturday in order to sell
the meat in accordance with the requirements of his customers. The customers
did not turn up on Saturday-they may
have been on holiday-and he found that
the meat was likely to be left on his hands.
If he had kept the meat until the following Monday it would have gone bad. He
found he could not send it back, and he
sold it to people who were ready to buy
it. An inspector walked in and caught
him, and he is now expecting a summons.
This man wrote to me and I handed his
letter to the Minister of Finance's Secretary. I know the matter will receive
careful consideration. I regret the Minister is not as well as we should like him
to be. This is a matter which should be
looked into. If you read the letter you
would see that it is very hard for a
butcher to keep fresh meat.
He is supposed not to take it unless it is fresh, but
he has to take what he gets, and he does
not know whether it is fresh or not. He
has no guarantee that all the meat will
be taken by the people who have the
coupons, and it is not likely that it will
all be taken during the holiday season.
In the interests of the trade the matter
should be considered in order to see that
no grievance arises. I will leave it at
that.
There is another matter which affects
the. Minister of Agriculture. I did not
give the Minister notice, so I will not
press the matter.
A butcher selling meat
must receive coupons, but he has no
guarantee that the people. will take the
meat. Very often they do not take it
and it is left on his hands. There is a
way of sending it back, but that cannot
always be done. I got a letter from a
butcher-I do not know the man-which
I sent to the Minister of Finance, as I
thought he was the proper authority, and
I knew it would receive careful attention.
According to his letter this butcher is a
very straight man. You will recollect
that the 12th of July fell on a Friday.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: There may be

Supplementary Budget.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): In days gone past it used to
be frequently said that the Chancellor of
the Exchequer, whoever he happened to
be, had one big day in the month of
April and was afterwards forgotten all
about for the rest of the year. Things
have changed. As Minister of Finance
this is my fourth Budget statement in
fifteen months, and before the financial
year comes to an end there may be
another.
ment of world peace on an enduring
foundation. It is inevitable that finance
should play a vital part. We all recognise that everything is at stake-freedom,
justice-
Mr. BEATTIE: There is no freedom.
This deplorable war must bring us
victory which will lead to the establish-
Mr.
ANDREWS - Christian civilisation, and, in fact, the continued.
existence of our Empire. I feel confident, therefore, that
that there is no
sacrifice, however great, which the taxpayers of Northern Ireland are asked to
shoulder that they will not willingly
bear, in order that victory shall be
secured at the earliest possible date.
My duty to-day is very much simpler
than when unfolding an annual Budget.
I have nothing to do to-day with the year
that has gone. In my Budget Statement
in May I disclosed how the actual expenditure had corresponded with the
Estimates for 1939-40, and I also referred
in detail to the savings that we hoped
to make in our normal peace-time expenditure during the current year. It is
therefore unnecessary that I should give
this information a second time, and consequently my task to-day is mainly confined to showing how the increases which
the Chancellor of the Exchequer has
recently imposed, and which automatically
apply to us so far as our reserved revenue
is concerned, affect our finances. It is
also, of course, necessary for me to inform the Committee as to how I propose
to deal with those transferred taxes
which are in our own keeping to deal
with.
Dealing first with the reserved taxesthe increases in income-tax and surtax
announced by the British Chancellor
will increase the revenue from these taxes
in Northern Ireland by £700,000 this
year, and £970,000 in a full year. These
are very large sums. The changes in
the duties on beer, tobacco and wines
will increase our reserved customs and
excise revenue by £228,000 this year,
and £348,000 next year, The Committee will recall that, as I stated in my
last Budget, the purchase tax is to be
regarded as a reserved tax, and will be
administered by the Imperial authorities for the United Kingdom as a whole.
Accordingly, it becomes necessary to
attribute to Northern Ireland its share

will give for the yield of this tax depend upon the date upon which it is
brought into effect, the number of
articles to which the tax will apply and
the rate of the tax itself. On the
assumption of a United Kingdom yield
from this tax this year of £40,000,000,
I am budgeting for a yield to Northern Ireland of £680,000, which is 1.7
per cent. of the total yield.
I
I now come to transferred taxes.
intend to submit to the Committee this
afternoon a resolution to increase the
rate of estate duty by 10 per cent. in
the pre-1939 scale for estates exceeding
£10,000. This will bring our estate
duty rates into line with those which are
now operating in Great Britain, and is
estimated to produce another £15,000
this year and a somewhat larger sum in
the full year. Hon. Members will be
aware that in his recent Budget the
British Chancellor of the Exchequer increased the rates of entertainments
duty. Hitherto the scales of duty in
Northern Ireland have been different to
those in force in Great Britain; on some
seats the tax was heavier and on others
lighter. I now propose, in accordance
with our general policy, to bring our
entertainments duty rates, as from 6th
October next, into line with those
operating in Great Britain. In some
cases this will mean a small increase in
the tax on the price of admission, and
in others a small reduction in tax. The
net effect of these changes, however, is
estimated to increase our revenue this
year by £16,000 and by £35,000 next
year. In view of the different conditions
here no change will be made in the
existing law exempting outdoor sports
from tax, although these sports are
taxed in Great Britain. These increases
in taxation, which I have outlined
to-day, are necessary to provide Ulster's
share of war expenditure, and I therefore ask hon. Members on both sides of
the House for their kind support.
I am now in a position to give to the
Committee a provisional figure for the
Imperial contribution this year. The
contribution which I announced in my
previous Budget was £4,500,000, and
the estimated surplus was £140,000.
The increases in income tax and surtax
which I have referred to are expected to
yield £700,000, and in Customs and
Excise duties £228,000. The token figure
which I am taking for the proceeds of
the purchase tax is £680,000.
Turning to transferred taxes, the
increase in the rates of estate duty is
expected to yield £15,000, and those in
entertainments duty £16,000. All this
adds up to a total of £6,279,000. From
this figure I have to deduct £150,000,
which is the gross increase on our
Exchequer this year of the new
Unemployment Insurance Act. This
further extension of the unemployment
insurance code I regard as a peace-time
service and, accordingly, as a legitimate
charge against the Imperial contribution.
After deducting the £150,000 from the
£6,279,000 I am left with £6,129,000,
of which £6,000,000 is the provisional
Imperial contribution for the year and
£129,000 the margin for surplus. I am
sure that the Committee, and, in fact,
Ulster people generally, will be very
gratified to know that we in this part of
the Kingdom are in a position to provide
this substantial sum towards war
expenditure.
In addition, when considering our
financial war effort, it should be remembered that Ulster people have already
lent towards the cost of the war through
Defence Bonds £1,150,285. In Ulster
Savings Certificates (National Defence
Issue) there has been raised £1,591,025,
making a total of £2,741,310. I am glad
to be able to
announce to-day that
instead of handing over to the British
Exchequer 75 per cent.-as up to the
present we have done of the amount
raised through Ulster Savings Certificates, I propose, as the response to our
effort has been so satisfactory, to pass
to the British Exchequer from the 1st!
April last, 90 per cent. of the total raised
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-as I
have reason to hope that 10 per cent.
will be sufficient for our own present
requirements. It should also be borne
in mind that Ulster people have invested
large sums in War Loan and other
Government securities, including both
Post Office and Trustee Savings Banks,

Committee
although it is not possible to say exactly

I have also received from Northern
Ireland citizens the sum of about
£55,000 by way of interest-free loans for
transmission to the Chancellor of the
Exchequer. This is only a part of the
total sent by our people direct to the
British Treasury. Some of our citizens
are paying their Income Tax a year
ahead and voluntarily doing without the
rebate on interest made in such cases.
To illustrate the spirit behind all this I
would like to quote an anonymous letter
which I received a few days ago—
"Dear Sir-Please find herewith
Postal Order value 10s. I propose to
send you this every four weeks, being
2s 6d per week which I wish to contribute to the expenses of the war. It
is a small sum, but every little helps.
I will do this provided I can keep my
work until the end of the war.
Yours truly,
'VICTORY FOR BRITAIN.'"'
That is the generous, patriotic and unselfish spirit which will win the war.
I wish to express the Government's
gratitude to all these citizens and many
others who are also helping the war effort
in unknown ways.
It is therefore clear that in the domain
of finance, as well as in other directions,
Ulster is playing her part. A just cause
cannot be a lost cause, and sooner perhaps than some people expect the usurped
power of the blood-stained dictators will
give way, and, in the words of Abraham
Lincoln, "government of the people, by
the people, and for the people" will be
again restored throughout all Europe.
I beg to move.

One day last week I put down a
question about the appointment of an
inspector under the Explosives Acts, a

who must be about 70 years of
age. The
Minister of Home Affairs, in reply to

in the public interest to state that. It

70 years of age is not the person to
appoint as an inspector. Explosives are
used in Northern Ireland only for
quarrying purposes, and yet we must pay
for an inspector.
These quarrying explosives were, always
looked after by the police, and the duty
of the police they were not doing it
lately, but I think they are now-is to
see that the explosives are kept in a safe
place, safe as regards accidents and safe
also from raiders; to ascertain the
quantity of explosives sold to the
quarries and the quantities used; and to
keep a check on them. The police will
still do that. I was an inspector myself
once. I had a big appointment from
Dublin Castle, and all I had to do was to
visit the quarries occasionally, and to
see what explosives they had and where
they kept them. Now apparently we
have to have some inspector high up. I
do not know how this appointment came
to be made, but I do know the clubs had
something to do with it.

The PRIME MINISTER: That depends on the Chair. The reason I rise is
to explain this matter in a few words.
This debate has taken a different

and I thought it would. On the one
hand the question of unemployment has
been raised, and on the other the. advis
ability of cutting into the contribution

What are the real facts of the case?
Before I go into them I should remind
hon. Members that it is only a short time
-two or three months-since I foretold that an increase in the unemployment figures was bound to take place
when the supplies of necessary flax from
continental countries ceased to come into
the country for our mills to manufacture
into linen for export abroad. Hon.
Members will bear in mind that my forecast made two or three months ago was
correct, and already the stocks in hand
are beginning to run out. The consequence is that flax-spinning mill
owners and linen manufacturers generally
are feeling that there is not sufficient raw
material for them to keep their mills
running full time.. Those mills are not
Government concerns; they are owned by
private individuals whose anxiety at all
time is to work at full steam ahead and
to produce as much as possible of the
goods which are well known throughout
the world and which are wanted abroad
in order to help the dollar exchange.
Which one of my hon. Friends here can be
blamed for a situation like that? Latvia,
all the Balkan States, Russia itself,
France, Belgium, Holland and all those
countries which supplied us prior to the
war period with the raw material we
required are now cut off.
Mr. NIXON: What about Ottawa?
The PRIME MINISTER: Ottawa and
Canada generally, I understand, like
other parts of the Empire, are endeavouring to supply us with flax, but unfortunately the flax that is grown there, and
the flax that is grown in New Zealand,
is not exactly the type that we require
here.

I now come to the alleged inactivity
of the Government with regard to
flax. Some years ago, just after I
had the honour of being appointed Minister of Agriculture, a question arose as to
whether it was possible to bring in a flax
scheme based on the usual marketing
schemes such as pigs, eggs, milk, etc. It
should be obvious to the House that no
Government could pour out public money
to produce a raw material unless there
were some condition attached to it. The
condition which we suggested was that
the flax produced in this country should
be paid for according to grade; that is
to say, if a particular type of Russian
flax made 12s in Russia, or when it
reached Northern Ireland, then flax of a
like type raised in this country should be
paid for at a similar rate. For technical
reasons I understand that is an extremely
difficult matter in reference to the spinning trade, because it requires all sorts
of flax. A particular grade which might
suit one mill might not suit another.
There was no possibility, so far as I
could see, of arriving at any satisfactory
scheme whereby a quality qualification

could be provided for the payment of flax
here.
I am quite sure that no Member of this
House would agree to pouring out money
for the purpose of producing flax here if,
after it had been produced, it was found
to be of no value. The scheme, as the
Minister of Finance has already told the
House, fell through. The Government
decided that the best way to deal with
this very difficult question was to set up
the Flax Development Committee, to see
what were the best methods of producing
flax in Northern Ireland. One of the
difficulties of flax production was the
tremendous cost of handling from the
moment it
was sown until sold as
scutched fibre. Any Member who has
looked into the work of the Flax
Development Committee will realise that
it has been of extreme value, and I trust
it will put the flax industry on a proper
footing.
There were certain hitches in the
negotiations over prices for the time
being, and my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, and myself met the
spinners and discussed with them the
possible prices. I pointed out at that time
that unless a price which was comparable
with the price being paid for other
produce was paid then there would be
very little flax produced. I went over
to London on two different occasions. I
found it extremely difficult to convince
the Ministry of Supply of the very
obvious fact that the difficulty was that
they were calculating on the cost of production which did not arise. As well as
my memory serves me a level price of
21s or 21s 6d was fixed at the beginning
of February or the end of January. At
all these negotiations the Ministry of
Supply had pointed out to them the fact
that every week they delayed in fixing a
price which we thought was comparable
to that given for other farm produce
meant that hundreds of acres less flax
was being sown. Anybody who has any
knowledge of flax knows that in order
to produce it the ground has to be
ploughed rather shallower than for other
crops. That is the reason for the delay.
That was the pre-war position. On the
declaration of war my Ministry, with the
concurrence of the Ministry of Finance,
wired to Canada and bought all the
pedigree seed available. That was the
first step we took. Then came the question as to how the farmers were to be
paid. Hon. Members will recollect that
at that time the prices for farm produce
were being increased. The reason was
that unless prices were raised production
of food would fall to a very dangerous
level, and the consequence was that if the
price of flax was not raised to something
approximating the other produce of the
farm there would be no flax, unless
farmers were ordered to grow their usual
acreage. In my opinion that would be
a very drastic thing to do, and it was
much better to offer a financial inducement. If a farmer felt he was a flax
grower and knew something about it he
would not like an official of the Ministry
going round and saying he had grown 70
acres at the beginning of the war. The
House will forgive me if I am not completely accurate in my history, but it is
very hard to remember. The Flax Committee dealt with the Ministry of Supply
with regard to prices. I believe I am
right in saying they suggested to the
Government that as they were appointed
flax controllers it would be better if the
Government did not interfere in the
negotiations which had been taking
place. I think that is the correct story.
The House will see that the Government before and since the war started
acted in as strong a way as possible in
order to get the one essential price which
is the only inducement. The Government is not to blame for the lack of flax
at the present time.
