Mr. WARNOCK: It is always a great
pleasure and I think everyone in the
House will agree that I do not pay
fulsome compliments-to listen to the
Minister of Agriculture, because he does
try fairly to answer the points put to

we are palmed off with something that is
not an answer. It is a great pleasure,
therefore, if the argument you have put
up is met with reasoned argument. You
may agree or not, but that is the right
way to deal with Parliamentary procedure.
The Minister of Finance to-day has
dealt with the question of an Imperial
contribution. I sometimes have a quiet
laugh to myself when he talks of
Imperial contribution because it is not a
contribution at all. It is a tax which
has got to go over to the British Government, and we do not contribute it in
the sense. which contribution really
means. We do not willingly of our own
volition give this money to England.
England imposes upon us certain taxation, allows us a certain amount for our
needs, and takes the balance. You may
call it a contribution if you like, but it
is nothing of the sort. It is the amount
of money England extracts out of this
country. That point is not of very much
importance. But there is a matter arising
from this question of a contribution
which is of very great importance and
which has been stressed by two or three
Members this afternoon.
but we are making a contribution in the
wrong way. It is not in money we ought
to be making this contribution. We
cannot afford this draining of the lifeblood of this country by paying a sum
of £6,000,000 annually to England. And
if we continue to do it we will be faced
inevitably with a poor country far more
deeply impoverished than ever before.
Our contribution from this country
should not be in money but in men. In
this way of pouring out money we are
making ourselves less and less competent
to carry on the unequal struggle which
we have carried on for so long. And
yet, on the question of unemployment
raised here to-day, if we continue to
pour out the lifeblood in this way the
unemployment position after the war will
be something terrible to contemplate,
because we will have unemployment
running to astronomical figures and no
resources out of which to meet it.
The Minister of Finance-I am not
speaking of the present occupant of the

of this Government agreed to the.
Revaluation Act under which Northern
Ireland was revalued and taxed for
income tax purposes on the same basis
as England. That dealt a death blow to
the financial structure of this country.
This country is a poor country. It has no
coal and no mineral resources worth talking about so far as we know. I will be
dealing with that in a moment. It has
no primary production except agriculture, and it is utter nonsense to suggest
that this country can maintain itself and
make a contribution of £6,000,000 per
annum to any other country.

I have looked over in the past few
days the legislation which has been passed
in this House for the past two years,
and I say deliberately that the only useful function that this Government can
perform at the present time is to have
work for its people. There is nothing else
they can do. All our legislation, particularly during war time, is virtually duplicating English legislation. Every Act
of Parliament is simply a reflex of the
English. No original legislation has been
passed in this House for some considerable time and there is no likelihood of it.
The only function you have is administration. You have the Minister of
Labour. He does not create employment.
It is not the function of his Ministry.
If employment is not there he feeds the
unemployed. It is not his function to
create employment. I do not believe this
Government have done one single thing
to create a demand for labour in this
country. The Minister of Labour and
the Minister of Commerce administer the
affairs of their Departments and the
Minister of Finance administers his
Department, but there has been no
original effort on the part of the Government. Their sole duty, and the only
useful function they can perform, is to
see that this country gets employment
and more of it. I have said time after
time that was the function of the
Minister of Commerce. He should
orientate himself or go out.
There is one contribution I would like
to see this country making-a contribution of men for the forces. The
Government have left this matter too
late. It was said from the front Government benches "We do not want recruits."
Now when recruits are wanted they are
not coming forward in anything like the
number required. I believe lack of
leadership on the part of the Government

my house to some young troops stationed

are walking about the streets?" There

FLAX CULTIVATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."
-(Mr. Grant).
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Ministry
aimed at 50,000 acres of flax and hoped
that it might reach 60,000 or 65,000
acres. The actual acreage for the present
season is about 45,000. With regard to
plans for the future my Ministry is at
present engaged in considering the tillage
campaign for 1940-41, and flax will be
included. As soon as the matter has
been finally settled the House will be
informed.
Mr. BROWN: I wish to refer to a
matter which was discussed here to-day
-the serious position of the flax industry
which has brought about an increase in
our unemployment figures until they now
stand at over 71,000. There is not much to
be gained by holding an inquest as to
why this is so, but I should like to know
the position. In the first place will the
Minister of Agriculture tell us what
acreage of flax was aimed at in the
current season, what acreage was sown in
the current year and what his plans are
for the coming season?
Mr. NIXON: I know the Minister
cannot make a second speech, but I
should like to know if he is considering,
in conjunction with the Eire Government,
the very rich flax-growing Ulster
counties of Donegal, Monaghan, and
Cavan. There is quite a large amount
of flax being grown in those counties at
the present time. I know it is not to a
certain extent the concern of the
Minister, but so far as we are aware the
flax grown
there comes to the mills of
Northern Ireland and, therefore, would
be valuable to our workers. The Minister
has no jurisdiction in Eire, but perhaps
he could enlighten us as to the position.
there just in the same way as he keeps
his eye on flax coming in from any other
country on the Continent but which is
not available at the present time. I
understand there are large supplies of
flax in the Ulster counties I have
mentioned, and that the prospect of increasing the supplies is very great, provided prices, etc., are right.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I understand
the Ministry of Supply made arrangements with the Eire Government for a
certain acreage to be sown with flax. I
think it was 1,000 or 1,600 acres, but
that is purely guess work on my part.
The question of flax production is a
matter for the Ministry of Supply. They
buy all flax, whether in Northern Ireland or in Eire. I expect some similar
arrangement will be made with the Eire
Government for the season 1940-41.

Workmen's Compensation (Supplementary Allowances) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Bill to which I am asking
the House to give a Second Reading
follows what is largely an agreed measure
between the T.U.C., employers' representatives, and the Imperial Government,
so that I feel there is no need to apologise
for introducing what is in effect Copy
of the British Bill.
The Imperial Government appointed a
Royal Commission, under the chairmanship of Sir Hector Hetherington, in
December, 1938, to examine the whole
structure of workmen's compensation
with a view to overhauling the entire
system. That work has been interrupted
and was for a time suspended, but I
understand the Commission is now
functioning.
It has long been a cause of great dissatisfaction that the scales payable under
the existing Act were inadequate and
Since
required substantial alteration.
the inception of workmen's compensation
in 1897 the general structure of the
scheme. has remained practically the
same, although there has been amending
legislation from time to time. This Bill
is purely an interim Measure, which seeks
to provide a temporary war-time scheme.
for easing the lot of injured workers by
providing them with supplementary
allowances.
In framing this Bill two important
principles have been prominently kept
in mind. First, that in order to be
capable of being brought into speedy
operation under war-time conditions it
must be simple and as free from administrative complications as possible, and,
secondly, it must not impose an undue
burden on industry. Therefore, the
method proposed, bearing those principles in mind, is that there should be a
supplementation of the weekly rates of
1905 Ways and Means-Report

7 AUGUST 1940
Adjournment
compensation for any injured worker,
with a further addition for the man with
young children up to 15 years of age.
Let me explain how these supplementations operate:
Take a totally incapacitated man with three children
whose normal wages were £3 per week.
He receives the ordinary compensation of
£1 10s; his supplementation is 5s;
two children at 4s, 8s; one child 3s,
making a total of £2 6s, a difference of
14s between compensation and his normal
earnings. If the worker is receiving compensation at a reduced rate because his
incapacity is only partial, then the allowances paid to him are proportionately
reduced.
In both instances the aggregate of
compensation and allowances is subject
to an overriding maximum of seveneights of the loss of earnings. The subsection dealing with this point is designed
to secure that a workman's total of compensation, plus allowances, will still fall
short of his normal wages.
These proposed scales of allowances
were the subject of a considerable amount
of discussion in Great Britain. In April
a Bill was introduced in the Imperial
Parliament containing proposals which
were more limited in extent. That Bill
was not universally acceptable, and in
view of the undesirability of proceeding
with a contentious measure in these
critical times it was withdrawn. The
present proposals were substituted as a
result of consultations held between the
Government, trade unions, and employers, and, I think, fairly meet the
difficulties which have arisen through increased cost of living.
There is one point on which I would
like to assure the House. There will be
no means test attached to these allowances. The procedure for claiming will
be found in Clause 3 of the Bill.
A declaration may be required from the
workman giving a few essential particulars, and to assist him in proving, if
necessary, his marriage and the ages of
his children Clause 4 provides for certificates being obtainable at a cheap rate.
I think these are features which will commend themselves to every Member of the
House.
Clause 7 the Act is to come into operation on the 19th August it is designed
not only to apply to accidents which may
arise after that date, but also to accidents
which have occurred since 1st January,
1924, provided weekly compensation is
still payable.
The only other matter to which I need
make reference is that, although under
I wish to commend this Bill to the
House, not as a sweeping measure of
social reform, but as a measure destined
to confer benefits of a substantial
character on those who have had the misfortune to meet with an accident while
engaged in industry. I think it is a real
attempt to remedy a grievance that would
have become more apparent as the war
continued, and I have reason to believe
I will have the wholehearted support of
every section of the House. I beg to
move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not wish to make
any long comment on the Bill. I think
it is opportune and that it will do good
in the direction in which it tends to move.
I hope if any further changes in circumstances appear the Minister will not be
late in bringing forward another Bill to
supplement the amounts contained in this
Measure. We in the labour movement
have looked for this Bill as far as the
compensation is concerned. I am beginning to wonder how far we can travel for
further supplementation of allowances.
under Bills previously passed by the
House. I wish the Bill speedy progress
through the remaining stages.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. CAMPBELL: Before the House
rises this afternoon I crave leave. to refer
to a matter, or rather two matters of
administration. In the Belfast and
other danger zones during the present
emergency men of different views are cooperating in schemes for the safety of the
people the common people-in the event
of air raids. I think that is highly commendable.. Co-operation of that kind
ought to be encouraged in every way, and
I would feel it bitterly and sorely if anything occurred to chill that co-operation,
but in the ranks of a number of these
people co-operating in that invaluable
way apprehension and alarm are being
caused by police raids on the homes of
unoffending persons in Belfast. The
raids have been made on the homes of
those who are doing their bit honestly
and hard towards air-raid precautions,
towards improving them, and in their
indignation complaints reach Members
of this House. It is our duty as Members
to give reasonable. expression to those
complaints in this House, so that a
remedy may be found and means adopted
to try to prevent things of that kind
recurring. These men in their indignation talk as if they were on the verge of
giving up their jobs.
Over 900 men in the two Nationalist
constituencies of Belfast and areas bordering on those constituencies are taking
part in this work. About 1,000 or 1,100
in other Nationalist areas in Belfast are
also unselfishly throwing themselves into
the work, and their services will be
invaluable for the protection of the civil
population in a time of emergency. A
high percentage. of our people live within
the inner and vulnerable belt of Belfastdistricts bordering on the docks and on
the river, and very many of them are
interested in this matter of air-raid precautions. These men, who do not get a
penny for their services and work of
public utility, feel sore and even bitter
when their poor homes are invaded, in
some cases without a scintilla of justification, by a posse of police. If there must
be searches it is desirable in the public
interest that they should be sensible
searches and not made harum-scarum.
Day after day we have complaints in
our papers and those across the Channel
of the system peculiar to the Nazis
with their Gestapo and contempt for the
liberty of the individual. Some folk not
far
away are of that type of mind. We
cannot complain of the police. The police
have their orders. They must obey their
orders, but one does wonder in some cases
what is the sinister machinery that puts
the police in motion.
I hope things are not coming to the
pitch when quiet citizens, though they
may be of the Nationalist shade of
politics and may not be in every respect
agreeable to authority, are to be exposed
to the perils of domiciliary search and internment. In time of war encroachments
on personal freedom are inevitable, but
raids made on the strength of tittle-tattle
or on the spiteful stories of unscrupulous
enemies-
Mr. BEATTIE: Anonymous letters.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Or
anonymous
communications coming from sources that
do not bear the least reputation for
credibility-raids made on the strength of
that kind are a danger to the community,
which it behoves this House to watch. It is
a danger to be watched with jealousy and
to be checked with promptitude. Parliament and public opinion across the water
have just been aroused by an outcry of
corresponding mischief there, and I was
glad to see the very sensible speech of the
Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
laughing practically off the stage the silly
campaign for what was called the Silent
Column. Malicious tale bearers who put
innocent neighbours in peril are odious
and pernicious creatures. Bad weeds do
grow, and they are apt to grow apace.
accusers are.
Here is an executive armed with
arbitrary powers.
Against an internment order an internee has no chance
to defend himself in
a public court
of justice. There is no ventilation
of his case. There is no judge to see
fair play. He does not know who his
He has no opportunity as
he would have in an ordinary court of

If he appeals his appeal goes to a secret
tribunal. They may be admirable men.
I do not say a word of complaint about

understand, are permanent officials of the

strike an ordinary person as rather
strange.

8 AUGUST 1940
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 8th August, 1940.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved "That this House at its rising
this day do adjourn until 4 o'clock on
Thursday, 15th August, and that after
the report of the Royal Assent to Bills
agreed to by both Houses, Mr. Speaker
do adjourn the House, without Question
put, until Tuesday, 10th September."
-(Mr. Minford).
BILL PRESENTED.
Truck Bill,
"to restrain legal proceedings under
the Truck Acts, 1831 to 1896, in respect
of certain transactions heretofore effected
which might lawfully have been effected.
in another form, and to remove doubts as
to whether persons employed under
contracts rendered illegal by those Acts
are or were to be regarded for purposes
other than those of the said Acts as
employed under contracts of service,"
presented by the Minister of Labour
(supported by the Attorney General and
Mr. Grant); to be read a Second time on
Thursday, 15th August, and to be
printed. (Bill 20.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Workmen's Compensation (Supplementary Allowances) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLAUSES 1 (Supplementary allowances to workmen entitled to weekly payments), 2 (Provisions as to redemption),
3 (Requirements as to furnishing of
information), 4 (Proof of age and
marriage), 5 (Provision with respect to
schemes applying to workmen suffering
from silicosis), 6 (Consequential adaptation of Assurance Companies Act, 1909),
and 7 (Short title, construction, commencement and application), ordered to
stand part of the Bill.
TITLE agreed to.
Bill reported without amendment to
the House and read the Third time.
Ordered, That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate and desire their concurrence.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.
Adjournment.
Resolved "That this House do now
adjourn." (Mr. Minford.)
Adjourned accordingly at
Ten Minutes after Three
o'clock until Thursday,
15th August, in pursuance of the Resolution
of the House of this
day.

PROBLEM OF UNEMPLOYMENT.
5. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is prepared to set up
a Committee of the whole House to sit
either in private or public session to
investigate the problem of unemploy-
The PRIME MINISTER: In view of
the changes in the employment situation
both in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland due to war conditions. I do not
share the hon. Member's belief that a
Committee of the. House would be likely
to assist materially in directing Ulster's
available workers into the channel of war
or export production.
My colleagues and I are maintaining
the closest contact with Ministers in
charge of Imperial Departments responsible for supplies and armament production, and I am hopeful that as a result
of further developments increasing
numbers of our workers will be absorbed
into employment. Efforts, moreover, are
being directed towards making available
additional raw material for the linen
industry with a view to increasing the
export of linen goods, while other
industries are also being actively assisted
in the development of overseas trade.
I may add that the Government is at
all times prepared to examine carefully
any concrete suggestions from hon.
Members designed to further Ulster's war
effort and thereby increase the employment prospects of all workers irrespective
of the period of their unemployment.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I would remind the hon.
Member that the published monthly
returns of unemployment furnish
analysis of the duration of unemployment
amongst those on the live register, but
it would involve a disproportionate
amount of labour to extract information
of the previous occupations in which particular categories of unemployed were
engaged.

Finance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): It is my duty to-day to
move two Finance Bills. The first one
now before the House is required to give
legislative effect to the proposals which
I outlined in my Budget speech in May
last. The second will provide for the
taxation changes made in my supplementary Budget.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid, if the
right hon. Gentleman will allow me, he
will have to follow the rules of procedure, that is, deal with the Finance
Bill before the House, and, subsequently perhaps he can make his remarks with reference to the second Bill.
Mr. ANDREWS: I quite approve of
your ruling, and I certainly was not
going to go further than to make this
preliminary announcement that I have
two Bills to take on this occasion, the
first dealing with the Budget proper
and the second with the supplementary
Budget. I then was going to proceed,
I hope with your approval, to deal with
the first Bill first.
Clause 1 of this the first Bill to which
I have referred provides that when the
weight of a goods vehicle is being arrived
at a gas container or the plant for producing gas shall not be taken into
account. In the same way no duty will
be charged in respect of a trailer used
for carrying a gas apparatus. I am
sure hon. Members will approve of these
provisions because of the desirability at
the present time of taking every means
to save petrol.
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
10 SEPTEMBER 1940
Clause 2 will enable members of His
Majesty's Forces on leave from service
overseas or afloat to use their cars or
motor-cycles for a short period on payment of a small fee-10s in the case
of a car and 2s in respect of a motorcycle.
The remaining Clauses relate to death.
duties, and with the exception of Clause
7 are intended to strengthen the existing law against evasion of various kinds.
Clause 3 is a somewhat technical Clause
designed to prevent a particular type of
evasion, too common. A life interest in
property is liable to estate duty provided.
it continues uninterrupted until death.
As the law stands, if the interest is surrendered no claim for the payment of
duty can be made. This Clause will stop
this loophole.
Clause 4 will ensure that duty is
chargeable on property which is transferred to a relative in return for a life
annuity or other periodical payment
made to the deceased during his lifetime.
Clause 5 expands the definition of
"property" to make certain charges and
debts liable to duty. Clause 6 brings
within the estate duty code certain
interests ceasing on or before death.
Clause 7 is intended to grant to the
estates of merchant seamen killed from
war causes the same relief from death
duties as operated in the last war, and
as already applies to members of the
armed forces under existing legislation.
Clause 8 will enable British Government
securities to be free from death duties in
Northern Ireland in the cases where
they are also exempt from British death
duties. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be

came into power. One branch was at that

When you went into the office proper

I said, "I will not come back." I sat

my

The Minister made a point about

Finance (No. 2) Bill.

Mr. ANDREWS: This Bill provides
for the taxation changes announced in
my supplementary Budget last month.
Clause 1 imposes an increase of 10 per
cent. in the pre-1939 scale of estate duty
for estates exceeding £10,000. Clause 2
provides that where an interest in expectancy has been mortgaged, duty will
only be payable at the rate in force at
the date of the mortgage. Clause 3 puts
our entertainment duty rates, as from the
6th October next, on the same scale as
will come into force in Great Britain on
that date.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Hon. Members are aware that our rates
in the past have been different from those
in the rest of the United Kingdom. The
new scale will therefore mean a small
reduction of duty on
some seats and
slight increases on others. I am gratified
that all these proposals have been
accepted by our community in a splendid
spirit. That is another proof that Ulster
people are fully willing to share the
burdens necessarily associated with the
winning of this deplorable war, which
was forced upon us by an aggressive and
brutal foe. I beg to move.

"That this House views with dissatisfaction the existence in Northern
Ireland of 68,287 unemployed persons,
and urges upon the Government the

When this Motion appeared on the

Prime Minister announced to this House
that it would certainly commend itself

the Government would most certainly
accept it. I was thereby encouraged to

as follows:-
(1) A great land reclamation scheme,
to be preceded by the immediate extension
of the Ministry of Agriculture's Land
Improvement Scheme of unemployment
relief grants towards the cost of labour
obtained through the Labour Exchanges.
for the clearing of scrub, drainage of
land, etc., to all owners or occupiers of

our own Government here have been
doing their utmost to take up the slack
in local employment.
Hon. Members will realise that we are
at war in the economic as well as the
military sphere, and in this, as in other
aspects of the war, we are working as an
integral part of the United Kingdom.
The policy adopted by the Imperial
Government on the home economic front
is to produce the maximum and consume
the minimum, a course which entails
severe limitation of internal trade.
National productive capacity on a wartime basis is devoted to two main
objects. First, the manufacture of
armaments and munitions, ships, aeroplanes, tanks, textiles for the armed
forces, and in general as much of the
equipment for a nation under arms as
can be produced at home. I need not
enlarge upon what Northern Ireland is
doing, and can
can do, in this respect.
Secondly, the manufacture of goods of
all kinds for export abroad. Fine linen
and whisky, and a host of luxury or
semi-luxury goods must be exported in
exchange for armaments and essential
imports, principally from the Americas,
where our reserve of foreign exchange
must be maintained.
The turning over of productive capacity
to war work and export trade means
inevitably that home consumption of
luxuries and semi-luxuries must be
limited: This is being done largely by
means of a series of Orders made by
Imperial Departments under Defence
Regulations. The principle underlying
the Piece-Goods and Made-up Goods
Order, and the Limitation of Supplies
(Miscellaneous) Order, issued by the
Board of Trade, is that the supply of
Unemployment

certain goods on the home market shall
be restricted to a fixed proportion of the
quantity of such goods supplied in the
year previous. These Orders naturally
raise innumerable problems and difficulties for the business community in Northern Ireland, and they often entail a
certain amount of hardship, the reason
for which may not always be immediately
apparent. Yet the exigencies of national

trade in the goods effected has previously

that only within the past fortnight my

which have led to the freeing of
additional supplies of raw material for
our linen industry, and also an arrangement which eases the position of our
export trade.

Then I come to the matter of mineral

the facts? In 1925 a Commission was set

mont to examine the mineral resources of
our country, and subsequently a Blue

Two or three years ago a further
Commission was set up to go into the

supplies of ore..

DEPENDANTS OF INTERNEES.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider
the plight of internees' dependants, and
whether help can be rendered by nonpolitical bodies to give the dependants
aid without any interference from civil
authorities, and whether he realises the
plight of those dependants whose breadwinners have been interned.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am afraid I find
it somewhat difficult to understand the
purport of the hon. Member's question,
but if it is to inquire whether the Government is prepared to give financial
assistance to the dependants of persons
who have been interned under the Civil
Authorities Act, the answer is in the
negative.
With regard to the second part of the
hon. Member's question, I can only say
that the authorities will not interfere in
any way with the disbursement of its
funds by any body, provided it is within
the law.
give outdoor relief to dependants of these
men who are interned?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

the right hon. Gentleman is he prepared.
to recommend the poor-law authorities to
PRISON SHIP IN
STRANGFORD LOUGH.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can give an
explanation as to the interning of men
on a troopship in Strangford Lough;
whether he has given due consideration
to the prevailing war conditions and
dangers to which these internees are exposed; whether he is aware of the anxiety
of the dependants of those interned, and
whether he will have such a method of
internment abolished.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It was
essential that additional accommodation
be found for the internment of disloyal
citizens of Northern Ireland. As this
accommmodation could not be obtained
elsewhere a ship was procured and is at
present stationed in Strangford Lough. I
am quite satisfied with the precautions
which have been taken to ensure the
safety of those on board. The answer
to the last part of the hon. Member's
question is in the negative.
R.U.C. HOLIDAYS.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will issue an
order under which all ranks of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary will in turn get their
full holidays as a statutory right, as in
the case of civil servants; whether he'
will consider the reorganisation of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary Representative Body so as to provide for its personnel being composed of representatives
of the House of Commons who shall
report direct to the Minister.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): I have
arranged with my right hon. Friend to
answer this question. Civil servants are
not entitled to holidays as a Statutory
right. The granting of leave of absence
from duty within the approved scales is
in all cases, both in the Civil Service and
in the Royal Ulster Constabulary, subject to the exigencies of the public service,
and I am sure the House will agree with
me in insisting that this principle must
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
be maintained. The answer to the second
part of the hon. Member's question is in
the negative. The purpose of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Representative Body
is to represent the views of the members
of that force. Moreover, the Statute
under which the Representative Body is
established requires that it shall consist
of representatives elected by the members
of the force from amongst their number;
and that it shall be entirely independent
of and unassociated with any body or
person outside the force which it represents.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
right hon. Gentieman does the answer to
the question mean the Government refuses absolutely to allow the police force
to organise in a body or association or
trade union?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The answer to the
question is simply a paraphrase of the
Statute under which the representative
police body is formed.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the police body
has no democratic control at the present
time, no representative body?

BELFAST SANATORIUM.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of years which have elapsed since
the Belfast Corporation first proposed to
extend or build a new sanatorium, and
the total amount spent on plans, visiting
sites, etc.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The ship was
obtained on charter by the Government
of Northern Ireland from the Ministry of
Shipping, but as the terms of the charter
have not yet been finally settled between
the Government of Northern Ireland and
the Imperial Government, I regret that
I have no information at present regarding the total cost or the weekly cost of
the ship. The owners of the ship are the
British India Steam Navigation Co. It
would not be in the public interest to
disclose the numbers, either of the crew
considered necessary by the Naval
Authorities or of the officials considered
necessary by the Ministry to control the
internees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Belfast
Corporation first proposed extensions to
the existing sanatorium in the year 1932,
the first plans being selected at a competition in 1934, and the final plans being
ready in 1936. As the hon. Member is
aware, the site at Whiteabbey was not
considered suitable for the proposed extensions, and the Corporation in 1936
took steps to investigate the possibility
of acquiring a site for the erection of a
new sanatorium.
The amount spent on plans for the
improvements at Whiteabbey and of
visiting proposed sites for the new
sanatorium totals £10,088.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that reply
does the £10,000 include the travelling
expenses of the committee in pursuit of a
site, and is the £10,000 more or less than
the Minister gave here in a somewhat
similar answer on a former occasion, and,
further, is the Minister aware that there
were public allegations of attempted
bribery in connection with the acquisition
of the site wherever it is to be.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
Member puts a further question down I
will endeavour to give the information.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
that reply is it not true to say the right
hon. Gentleman acquiesced with regard
to these plans and no protest was made
by the Government in regard to the
building at Whiteabbey although the
Government turned the site down after
the Corporation had been dealing with it
two or three years.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As a result of
an inquiry the Ministry of Home Affairs
turned the site down having regard to the
views expressed by the inspector.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is it not true to
say the Government passed the plans and
approved of the action of the Corporation
up to the last minute?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

Mr. MacDERMOTT: The scale of
issue of clothing to Class "B" Special
Constabulary does not include waterproof
coats, except for men mobilised for fulltime duty.
During part-time service the scale
period of wear of garments is four years,
except for the greatcoat, where it is
eight years. The men are entitled to
receive replacements when they have
completed the period of wear, and the
age of uniforms in possession of the men
is therefore not greater than the period
stated above.
On being mobilised for full-time duty,
"B" men receive an immediate additional
issue of uniform, as follows:-One frock,
one pair of trousers, one greatcoat, one
waterproof coat, one cap and one forage
cap. After six months continuous
mobilised service they receive a replacement issue of frocks and trousers.
The number of "B" men mobilised for
full-time duty in Belfast is 388; of these,
only 180 have, so far, received waterproof coats, owing to supply difficulties.

the deficiency will be remedied.

LAND IMPROVEMENT SCHEME.
11. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Finance whether in order to assist in
promoting the success of the "Grow more
food and flax" campaign, the Government will consider an immediate extension of the Ministry of Agriculture's
land improvement scheme of unemploy
ment relief grants towards the cost of
labour obtained through the labour exchanges for the clearing of scrub,
drainage of land, etc., to all owners or
occupiers of land irrespective of their
valuation, or whether they are exclusively or partially engaged in farming.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): Up to the present the Land Improvement Scheme in Northern Ireland
has been confined to bona fide farmers, including those persons substantially engaged in farming as well as engaged in
some subsidiary business. Grants towards
labour costs are given under the scheme
on the following basis:-
(a) 75 per cent. grant to farmers
whose valuation does not exceed £150.
(b) 50 per cent. grant to those
whose valuation is below £250.
Persons who own land with a valuation in excess of £250, which, of course,
means a very large property, are
obviously wealthy and should, therefore, be able to carry out the work
themselves. Accordingly, I would not
feel justified in subsidising them out of
public moneys, much of which comes
from the poorer sections of the community in the form of indirect taxation.
In present circumstances I have already
agreed to waive the bona fide farmer
Oral Answers

condition and, further, in case there
should be anyone with a valuation exceeding £250, who may not have the cash
available at the moment to carry out
necessary improvements, I am prepared
to lend on reasonable terms the amount
required.
I may add that as far as tile drainage
is concerned, grants will be given without any valuation restriction as in Great
Britain.
Mr. BROWN: Will you permit me to
thank the Minister for the concession he
has granted, and to express the hope that
he will see his way to grant the other
concessions also?

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Truck Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): It will be within the recollection of hon. Members that on the 1st
May I intimated the Government's
intention of introducing a Bill corresponding to a Measure of the Imperial Parliament for dealing with a very
limited, but none the less important,
problem arising out of a decision of the
House of Lords in a case which had been
brought under the Truck Acts.
I think, therefore, I am justified in asking this House to regard it as an agreed
measure.
To enable hon. Members to appreciate
the purpose of this Bill, perhaps I should
say a few words about its origin. The
Truck Acts date back over a hundred
years to a time when serious abuses had
arisen which called for correction. Their
main purpose was to secure that a worker
should receive the full benefit of his wages
and not be compelled to accept payment in
kind or to make his purchases in shops
belonging to his employer.
On that occasion the hon. Member for
Pottinger asked me to make sure that
the rights of workers would be adequately
safeguarded, and I told him to trust me.
I am now able to reassure the hon. Member, and the House generally, on that
point, for the British Bill was discussed
with the T.U.C., who gave it their blessing. Moreover, the Bill passed through
all its stages in the Imperial House of
Commons in little more than an hour,
and has since reached the Statute Book
without a single amendment or division.
The Act of 1831 stipulated at the outset that the entire amount of a worker's
wages must be actually paid in coin, and
that any payment made by delivering
goods to him should be illegal, null and
void. It also provided that a worker
could recover from his employer so much
of his wages as had not been paid in
coin, even though he had received payment in kind.
Section 23 of that Act, however, contains some exceptions. An employer
may supply medicine or medical attendance, fuel, and (to miners) materials and
tools; he may supply provender for the
workman's horse, he may let him a dwelling and he may also supply food prepared
and eaten in the employer's house.
Further, he may make a deduction from
the worker's wages for the articles or
service supplied if the charge does not
exceed their real and true value, but
always provided that the worker has first
consented in writing.
In the now famous case of Pratt v.
Cook the workman had received for a
number of years 53s per week plus meals
valued at 10s per week. The effect of
the House of Lords' decision, I understand, is that, while it would have been
quite legal for the employers to have
contracted in writing to pay the man
63s and to deduct 10s for the food, it was
illegal to contract to pay 53s plus food to
the value of 10s, although the net result
to the worker would have been the same.
Under that decision the fortunate Mr.
Pratt was able to recover some £400.
Others may be tempted to follow his
example and it is the view of the Government, as it was the view of the
Imperial Government and of the T.U.C.
that the possibilty of claims of such a
Truck Bill

Finance Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
nature-claims without real meritinvolves a risk of serious injury to good
industrial relations.
The interpretation of the Truck Acts.
is not always a simple matter. Some
idea of their complexity is given by the
fact that, in the Pratt case, a judge
found in favour of the workman, the
Court of Appeal, by a majority, found in
favour of the employers, while the House
of Lords, again by a majority, reversed
their finding. It is understandable,
therefore, that other employers may unwittingly have made illegal contracts and
the effect of this Bill is to restrain legal
proceedings as regards the past where the
contract could readily have been cast in
legal form without any material difference to the worker.
That is the purpose of sub-section 1, of
Clause 1, and I wish to stress the fact
that it deals with past transactions only.
No restraint will be imposed on proceedings arising from transactions taking
place after the Bill becomes law. Employers will have to see in future that
their contracts comply with the law as
interpreted by the House of Lords.
The only other matter to which I need
refer is that dealt with in sub-section (2).
This is put in as a safeguard for the
worker. If a contract of service infringes
the Truck Acts and is, therefore, illegal
there is a possibility-I will not put it
any higher than that-that, for example,
insurance contributions paid in the
ordinary way in respect of employment
under that contract might be regarded
as invalid. In such circumstances the
man might be deprived of benefit or his
widow of her pension. That would
manifestly be unjust. The sub-section is
accordingly designed to make it clear
that the Truck Acts stand by themselves
and that the fact that a contract of
service is rendered illegal solely because
of a breach of those Acts is not to affect
the validity of the employment for any
other purpose.
I beg to move, "That the Bill be now
read a Second time."
Question proposed.
I took the right hon. Gentleman up
right. One Clause is designed and
intended to restrain proceedings for
certain acts committed prior to the
introduction of this Measure.
Mr. GORDON indicated assent.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister indicates
his assent. That is like saying to a thief
that he has taken a certain amount of
"prog," he has it on him, but by virtue

in respect of that "prog" which he has

It is a very dangerous principle to protect something which has been illegal
by passing a Bill. I do not care whom
it affects. It does not alter my opinion
about it to tell me that it is in the

What was illegal yesterday and subject to

DEBATE ON MOTION.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move:
"That this House demands that the
Government take immediate steps to deal
with the unemployment situation in
Northern Ireland; to stop the use of
public funds for the service of officials
engaged in private matters, and to prevent the use of all official motor-cars
for individual convenience."
I move this Motion because I feel that
this House could not spend too much time
on the question of unemployment. My
criticism of the House in the past has been
that it has spent too little time on the
question of this evil which has existed
in this part of the world for at least 20
years. The present Government has been
in office for 19 years, and for at least 16
years of that period I have repeatedly
made representations to it, either by way
of motion or other methods, or in
discussion on the Estimates, to try to get
something done for the unfortunate
The world is changing very fast. The
policy of the present Government seems
to be like the laws of the Medes and
Persians-unalterable. It is prepared to
pursue its course in a derelict ship over
waters which that ship is not able to
withstand, and sooner or later a tragedy
is bound to befall the vessel in which we
are sailing. The Government was handed
over a very heavy responsibility when it
took up office in this Northern area. I
sympathise with any Government,
whether Unionist, Liberal, Labour
Socialist or Nationalist, on whom such a
heavy burden falls when taking over office
with a roll of at least 120,000 unemployed.
and no prospect of world trade recovery
whereby the industries of this area might
be brought into useful production. The
Government were to be sympathised with
because of the position at that time, but,
as I have already said, times have
changed, men have changed, production has changed, but the Government remain the same for ever.
That is my reason for trying at this
late hour of the day to instil into them
some inspiration, whereby they might
make an endeavour to grapple with this
very serious and cankerous disease that
has been in our midst for the past 20
years.
With my experience of the last war, I
thought that when this war became
stabilised it would require all the man
power of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the Dominions. It is quite true
to say that at the moment the Dominions
are fully employed in the production of
national requirements for the furtherance
of our war aims. England, Scotland and
Wales are also fully employed, but we in
Northern Ireland never seem to be in
the running to employ our man power
fully in the war effort of Great Britain.
If we
were in the same position as
England, Scotland and Wales, we should
not have 70,000 unemployed. My statement may be challenged by someone who
would say that three-quarters of a million
people in England, Scotland and Wales.
are unemployed. But there is a big
difference in the classification of the
people who are unemployed in England,

Lord, the Prime Minister, we will still
have the unemployment problem. There
are thousands of hands waiting.
The noble Lord complimented the
Member for Down and is prepared to
accept his Motion. Everything said by
the Member for Down has been said by
the Member for Pottinger and myself for
the last 15 years.
Is not that so? No
action was taken and there will be no
action taken as long as the right hon.
Gentlemen are in the land of the living.
It is not my intention to talk this matter
out. The Member for Pottinger is
anxious to have a vote, and therefore I
will sit down. But I appeal to the noble
Lord to let the cat out of the bag as soon
as possible. It is something like Hitler's
secret weapon. I appeal to the noble
Lord to let us know exactly what is going
to be done inside the next two or three
weeks. If he brings forward anything
that will help the unemployed I will be
the first to give him credit for it.
Mr. MINFORD: The time is very
short, and I have some comments to
make.
Mr. BEATTIE: I was wishing to
move, "That the Question be now put."
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the hon.
Member would wait two or three
minutes. That Question can be put at
half-past Six. The hon. Member for
Antrim has been trying to speak for
some time.
Mr. MINFORD: I am sorry I have
only two or three minutes to speak. I
agree with the hon. Member in deploring the unemployment in Northern Ireland. Might I suggest to the Prime
Minister to form a committee of this
House to go into every detail of unemployment. I believe it could do much
to solve this problem. For instance, at
the present moment we have spinning
mills idle for want of flax, and we have
farmers prepared to grow flax if they
get encouragement. I believe the
Government would do well to establish
a committee in this House to go into
this problem. There is no good in
making speeches here unless we can talk
across a table. I suggest that the Prime
Minister should establish a committee of
this House to see what can be done.
The only way to solve the question is to
give the farmers of Ulster inducement to
grow food and flax..
We know that in war-time the production of food is of the utmost importance.
The farmers have risen to the occasion
during the past year, I am sure, to the
satisfaction of the Prime Minister, and
I can assure him they will rise doubly
high if the Government only help them
and keep the pledge they gave. I am
sorry I had only a minute to speak, but
if you want to put the closure on I am
content with making that suggestion to
the Prime Minister.
Question, "That this House demands.
that the Government take immediate
steps to deal with the unemployment
situation in Northern Ireland," put,
and agreed to.

MESSAGE TO AIR MINISTER.
Mr. SPEAKER: At the request of
Members on all sides of the House I
sent the following telegram to Sir
Archibald Sinclair, Air Ministry,
London:-
"At the unanimous request of the
Members of the House of Commons,
Northern Ireland, I beg to send you
this expression of the intense admiration we all feel for the wonderful
and magnificent initiative and gallantry of the Royal Air Force."
In reply to that I received this:-
"The tribute of the House of
Commons of Northern Ireland to the
gallantry and initiative of the Royal
Air Force is an encouragement to us
all in these stirring and strenuous
days. It will be gratefully received.
by all ranks of the Royal Air Force
to whom I am sending it at once."

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The hon. Member is
noticeably incorrect in his suggestion that
this year's flax acreage in Northern Ireland was 20,000 acres less than that aimed
at by my Ministry. The acreage aimed at
for Northern Ireland was 50,000 acres,
and of this 46,500 acres were secured. As
regards the acreage for 1941, the figure
of 100,000 acres has been mentioned as
the aim of my Ministry, which acreage, I
may perhaps mention, was only attained
during the last war over the whole of
Ireland after four years' intensive effort.
I have every confidence that I shall be
able to secure the acreage suggested for
this year,
but the hon. Member must bear
in mind that a considerable area of flax
will be sown in Great Britain and Eire
next year and that the amount of flax
that can be produced is limited by the
quantity of suitable seed available. The
hon. Member may rest assured that every
acre for which seed is available will be
sown.
It must further be remembered that
the extent of the export trade in any
commodity is determined by the price at
which the goods can be sold. In this
connection I would like to sound a note
of warning because in the view of the
Imperial authorities flax is already at a
dangerously high price.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, it is true that
my Ministry is heavily engaged during
the present emergency, but I have not
yet seen anything to make me believe
that either of the bodies mentioned by the
hon. Member is in a position to undertake the task of securing the desired increase in flax production with anything
like the effectiveness of my Ministry.

workers in scutch mills within the scope

Before proceeding to explain the provisions of the Bill, I should first like to
apologise to the House for the somewhat
limited time which we have been able to
allow for its discussion. The urgency of
the matter arises from the fact that the

moment. I trust that hon. Members will
accept this explanation of what might at

hurry legislation through the House.
fixed for his scutched crop. This question
of net return is clearly of first importance
if we are to secure that expansion of the

The proposal for regulating wages of
workers employed in scutching is contained in Clause of the Bill. Members
will be aware that the prices payable to
the farmers for scutched flax are fixed by
Order, and now range from 20s to 25s
per stone according to grade. Having
thus fixed the prices to the farmer, it
remains to ensure that these prices are
not renderd illusory by any disproportionate increase in the charge which the
farmer must pay for the scutching of his
flax. That charge is in turn based on the
rate of wage which the scutch mill owner
pays to the workers employed in his mill.
If that wage is to remain a matter of
bargaining and voluntary agreement
between employer and workers in each individual mill, there will be risk of disputes with consequent delay and dislocation in the processing of a commodity
which is of first importance for war purposes as well as from the point of view
of the export trade. Difficulties of this
kind arose in the last war. All the
arguments point to the desirability of
fixing a uniform rate of wage on a basis
fair to all concerned and which will
permit of the scutching charge to the
farmer being fixed at a stable figure, thus
helping to standardise the net return
which the farmer may expect on the prices
I have already indicated that all the
interests concerned, including the representatives of scutch mill workers, mill
owners and farmers, are unanimous as to
the desirability of fixing the wages and
charges to which I refer. There remains
the question of the appropriate machinery
for determining these wages and charges.
So far as wages are concerned it was felt
that the simplest method was to amend
the Agricultural Wages Act so as to include scutch mill workers within its
ambit. There is already substantial agreement between the mill owners and workers
as to what would be an appropriate rate
of wage, and I feel confident that the
Agricultural Wages Board, if and when
the matter comes before them, will give
full weight to the recommendations of the
parties primarily concerned.
It will be clear from the wording of
Clause 1 of the Bill that in delegating to
the Agricultural Wages Board the func
tions of fixing wages of workers in scutch
mills, we are not proposing to classify
such workers for all time as agricultural
workers. They are to be placed in that
classification simply and solely for the
purpose of the Agricultural Wages Act.
A special sub-section (2) to Clause 1 is,
in fact, inserted to preserve the right to
insurance benefit at industrial rates of
workers who would ordinarily be entitled
to such rates, but who for the special
purpose of the Bill will be deemed to be
workers in agriculture.
Concurrently with a determination by
the Board in regard to wages, the charge
to be made by the mill owners to farmers
for scutching can be fixed under the
powers already existing. These charges
bear a very precise relation to the wages
paid.
Clause 2 of the Bill covers an amendment agreed to by representatives of
employers and workers relaxing the provisions of the Agricultural Wages Act in
relation to the statutory half-holiday.
Section 2 (2) of the Act provides that the
Agricultural Wages Board shall, so far
as practicable, secure a weekly halfholiday for agricultural workers. Experience. has shown that in many cases
2089 Agricultural Wages Bill-

both workers and employers would prefer

Many older workers in particular would

satisfactory to both workers and

would provide the Board with the necessary discretionary powers to regulate this

If agreed to by the House the amendment

1. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The hon.
Member appears to have been misinformed; the Ministry has not written to
education committees telling them to
terminate specialised classes for unemployed in technical schools. I am aware
that a report to that effect did appear in
the Press, but it was corrected a few days
later.
I should explain that the Ministry
recently wrote to education committees
giving the dates for the termination of
existing courses and pointing out that it
was proposed to arrange further courses.
Such courses, indeed, are in operation at
present and I need hardly say that it is
the desire of the Ministry of Education
that every effort should be made to continue such courses as may be requested
by the Ministry of Labour.

DISALLOWANCE OF UNEMPLOY-
MENT ASSISTANCE.
3. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Labour
whether he will make inquiries
regarding disallowances imposed by the
Appeal Tribunal in Armagh Area Office
of the Unemployment Assistance Board
for periods in excess of six weeks; whether
this procedure is in accordance with the
regulations; whether he is aware that
claimants allowed by said Appeal
Tribunal as "Available for work" were
only granted for periods of one and two
months; and whether in view of the acute
unemployment situation in Armagh area
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers
[Mr. Beattie]
he will consult with the Board with a
view to longer periods being allowed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Unemployment Assistance
Acts make no provision for limiting the
period of disallowance of an applicant
who is held not to be within the scope of
the Acts. Such a disallowance accordingly holds until such time as the
applicant may show that he again fulfils
the conditions. It is always open to the
Appeal Tribunal, in making an award,
to indicate a period after which it considers the award should be reconsidered.
The Appeals Tribunal is an independent
body and it would not be proper for me
to seek to influence their decisions.
The employment situation in Armagh
is constantly under review by the Assistance Board, but it is understood that the
majority of cases the hon. Member has
in mind are those of applicants who
refused to accept employment elsewhere.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is there no consistency
in the regulating of these appeal
tribunals; is it a fact that uniformity of
disallowances has been recommended by
the right hon. Gentleman, and is it a
fact that the Armagh area is the only
area that gives a lesser amount than six
weeks.
Mr. GORDON: No. I think the hon.
Gentleman is under a misapprehension.
When a man fails to show that he comes
within the scope of the Act he is turned
down until such time as he shows that he
comes within the scope.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
unavailability for work excludes completely a man or woman from receiving
any assistance from the Unemployment
Assistance Board, and is it a fact that
men and women must have a period of
employment before they become entitled
to consideration by the Board?
Mr. GORDON : Yes. The hon.
Gentleman is quite correct.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of that fact
why then the inconsistency in the Armagh
area as compared with Belfast? Why are
allowances only granted for a period of
six weeks while in Belfast they are
granted for an indefinite period?
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
is labouring under a misapprehension. If
he can bring before me a case of that
character which is treated differently from
the city of Belfast he can rest assured I
shall have the matter investigated.
Mr. BEATTIE: Very good.

UNEMPLOYMENT INQUIRY.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he will set up a Select
Committee of the House to go thoroughly
into the whole question of unemployment in Northern Ireland, or, alternatively, will he adopt the suggestion in
a leading article in the "Northern
Whig" that the time has come to appoint
a Minister specially charged with the
duty of organising Northern Ireland's
economic war effort.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am prepared to set up a Select Committee of
this House to inquire into the unemployment situation as it is affected by matters
within the powers of this House.
With regard to the last part of the
question, as far as is compatible with
the constitutional position, I will assume
responsibility for the general conduct
and co-ordination of Northern Ireland's
economic war effort.
I may mention that I am involved at
this very moment in delicate negotiations, the nature of which cannot be
made public, but the successful outcome
of which I hope will lead to the mitigation of unemployment in our midst.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
thank the noble Lord for his reply?
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the noble
Lord if he can give the House any intimation of the terms of reference for
this Select Committee?
The PRIME MINISTER: Not at the
moment. Later on I will be able to
acquaint the House of the terms of
reference.
Mr. MINFORD: May I thank also the
Prime Minister for his reply. I was one
of those who mentioned the matter last
week.
Mr. SPEAKER: The sentiments are
very nice.

over again that in this grim national
struggle in which we are engaged agriculture has an important part to play.
Mr. Hudson, Minister of Agriculture,
speaking in the British House of Commons on 11th July, 1940, a little over
two months ago, said:
______________
Tens of millions of people on the
Continent of Europe will face in the

perish, but British agriculture, with
modern methods, modern science and
the necessary enthusiasm and drive
can and will play a very large part
indeed in saving the people of this
island from suffering a similar fate.
Is a drastic reduction in prices, I ask
you, coupled with increased costs of production, the way to stir up enthusiasm
and get the drive which Mr. Hudson
considers so necessary at this time in our
national life?
Speaking at Nottingham on February
17, Sir Samuel Hoare, then the Home
Secretary and agriculture's representative
in the War Cabinet, said:
:-
We must grow more food at home.
That is the great constructive plan
that lies open to us. Look at the
advantages. First we make fuller use
of our natural resources which the
Almighty has bestowed on this island.
That is good husbandry. That is
sound economy.
Next, we get better food, fresher
food, more nourishing and healthier
food for ourselves and our children.
Then, by growing more at home we
need to buy less from abroad. We
effect a saving in our stocks of gold
and foreign exchange. We can use
more of our resources to purchase the
raw materials that are needed to make
war.
And, finally by this economy and by
no other can we hope to emerge from
this war, in one respect at least,
sounder, better off, wealthier, than we
went into it, for we shall have welltilled fields where we grew thistles,
ploughland where we had moorland,
and a prosperous countryside where we
had a region of rural distress.
So let us turn to agriculture. Let
us give our minds to the soil. That
is where we shall secure the best and
swiftest results.
Sir Samuel added that the Government
did not under-estimate the difficulties
which farmers faced in consequence of
the war, and he continued:—
I do not forget their feelings of
doubt and resentment for the way in

down after the last war. That must
never happen again.

Governments never seem to realise the
importance of the agricultural industry
until the nation is engaged in war-it
was the same in 1914. Then farmers
were asked to increase their output, to
plough and dig for victory, and they
did. They were told that never again
would their industry be neglected; never
would it be allowed to fall into a state
of bankruptcy and despair, but as soon
as the Armistice was signed in 1918 these
promises were all forgotten and agriculture was again relegated to the
bankrupt position, from which during
the four years of war it had been
temporarily rescued.
When we entered on the present
struggle in September of last year agriculture was again called to the fore.
More than ever was it necessary for the
farming community to "go to it." They
did, and promises were again made to
them, but unlike the war of 1914-1918
these promises are not even kept until
the war is over. Before the present war
is well under way we find the promises
made to agriculturists are again broken
and the food of the nation is endangered
thereby.

In June last the British Government
intimated its desire to see a substantial
increase in agricultural wages and the
establishment of a minimum agricultural
wage of 48s a week in England and Wales
-that involved in respect of England and
Wales an increase of 10s a week.
England and Wales the new wages rate
came into operation on July 1st.
In
At the same time that the Government
announced its intentions with regard to
agricultural wages it gave to farmers an
undertaking that the prices of farm produce would be increased to cover fully the
increased wages costs, and that these increased prices would be applicable to the
crops then shortly to be harvested.
Accordingly at the end of June it was
announced that the guaranteed price for
wheat would be advanced from 10s to
14s 6d per cwt.; the maximum price for
oats from 11s 6d to 14s 6d per cwt.;
mutton and lamb prices increased by an
average of 2d per lb. over the whole year.
Pig prices were raised from 19s 6d to 21s
a score, or 117s 6d a cwt.
With regard to beef, the July and
August fall in prices was not brought into
operation. The announcement also contained two further important features.
First, that summer milk prices would be
increased by 1d per gallon, and that a
statement with regard to milk prices
would follow shortly.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes. The

All these upward price adjustments
applied to Northern Ireland in precisely

Scotland. Let me remind the House that

annum, whereas the price increases represented an additional income to the farming community of approximately
£36,000,000. That was the announcement
made in June. The September announcement made certain adjustments that is
the reason for this Motion-and I should
like members for agricultural constituencies to follow these quite closely.
In the first place, a minor alteration
was made with regard to oats, which
really strengthen the farmer's position.
The maximum price for the 1941 crop was
reduced from a figure of 14s 6d a cwt. to
13s 6d a cwt., but, at the same time, the
standard price which the farmer is
guaranteed was raised from 9s to 12s 6d
a cwt.
Flax prices, as I have already announced, have been increased by 2s 6d a
stone in respect of the present crop and
the 1941 crop, and these prices will be
subject to review in the event of any
increase in the cost of production.
Winter milk prices to the producer,
beginning on October 1, are being increased over the corresponding winter
prices for 1938-39 by 7d per gallon for
the months of October and November;
8d per gallon for December and January,
and 7d per gallon for February and
March. This applies both to liquid and
with certain minor exceptions to manufactured milk. I am
sure the hon.
Member for South Tyrone will be glad to
hear that.
In pursuance of this policy the scale
of increases for cattle was modified falling
by, roughly, 1s 6d per cwt. each fortnight until they reach their lowest figure

With regard to potatoes, I fully agree

just secured the agreement of the Minister of Food to accept responsiblity for
these increased costs. In consequence of
this arrangement prices as from the 1st
of October will be as follows:-Growers'
minimum prices will be increased by 20s
per ton, whilst there will be further increases of 5s per ton on 1st November;
10s per ton on 1st January; 5s per ton
on 1st March, and 10s per ton on 1st
May. I think that is a very satisfactory
price and should give a proper return,
even on the first figure, where the average
cost of production is £30 to £31 per acre.
These prices will be operative from the
1st October. The prices of seed potatoes
will advance on the 1st February, 1941,
by 10s per ton.

future, would be better secured by a reorganisation of the Cabinet."

I do not propose to say anything
to-day except what the whole country is
saying, but I can crystallise what I am
going to say a little later on, by saying
that in the entire country practically all
over the Six Counties the same story has
been told, that this Government has been
too long in office and is in the main composed of tired and jaded men. That is
the text on which I am going to speak
to-day. I cannot but think that with
the material at our command within the
limits of the Unionist Party, we can
wield an instrument of Government far
more effective than that which we at
present enjoy. I think the instrument
which we are wielding at the present time
has lost its edge and has become blunt,
and the time has come for the introduction of new elements into the Government
for the purpose of bringing fresh minds.
to view the older political problems.
Before I begin to criticise the Government it is well I should say what I think
nearly everybody in the country is saying
about it. There are very few rightminded people in this country who would
withhold words of praise and gratitude
from the Members of the present Government. There can be no doubt in the
mind of any person that for a long period
of years they served this country faithfully and well, and in difficult and
troublesome times they showed courage
and resolution that ought not to be forgotten. They laid the foundations well,
but the time of which I am speaking is
the time when its members were in their
prime, ten or fifteen years ago, when they
were younger men than they are to-day.
My challenge now is that they have
served their day and generation and it
is time for them to make way for
younger, more virile and more active
men.
This Government has been longer in
office than any Government in the world.
Five of its Members and the Chief Whip
have been continuously in office for
twenty years. If they were each and
everyone of them the best men available
for their particular office I should still
very much doubt the wisdom of such a
prolonged period of office, because the
edge and the keenness they possessed have
disappeared with long familiarity. It is
Vote of Censure
Vote of Censure
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
not good in any country in any circumstances that the same men should remain
in office for such a long period. It is
not in the interests of good government.
So it has proved in this country. Experience in every country where democratic institutions prevail, has shown the
wisdom and necessity of constant and continual changes of personnel for reviewing
old problems from a fresh angle. It is
wrong that the one man should always
have the one problem. He views it from
the same angle and there are many blind
spots which would be appreciated if new
minds were brought in to regard it.
This is the common experience all over
the world.
There is an interesting example in the
outcry in America against the proposed
third term for President Roosevelt, the
idea at the back of which is that no
man should be more than ten years in
office. If it were not for the present
crisis President Roosevelt would have no
chance of being elected for a third term.
The Americans are wise. It is quite
right. But Northern Ireland is a law
unto itself in this respect. It has been
a bad one. When a person becomes a
member of the Government of Northern
Ireland he does not become a holder of
an office for a term: he becomes a tenant
for life. Nothing but death or illness or
promotion ever removes anybody from
that office. That is the experience of this
country for the last twenty years. Let
us recall any person who has been in
office. With the exception of my hon.
and gallant Friend (Lt.-Col. Gordon) and
myself, who resigned in disgust, is there
any Member of this Government who
ever left because of incapacity or failure,
or any other cause than death, old-age
or promotion? That is not right. That
is not government.
in any Parliament; in this Parliament I
think it is particularly bad. The
Opposition in this Parliament has been
numerically insignificant.
The spur
which is necessary to keep any Government, the best Government in the world,
up to the mark is lacking here. The
Opposition may do their best, but, as I
say, they are numerically insignificant,
and there is no possibility of any vote

struggle in which we find ourselves to-day.

How are we affected by these factors
of lack of keenness, lack of enthusiasm,
lack of energy? I think in this way.
When the war broke out Northern Ireland had always been an Imperial
Province and Eire stood, as I said before,
sullenly aloof and neutral. The political
position of Northern Ireland has always
been one of some difficulty, and here was
a heaven-sent opportunity to put us on
the top of the wave, to put us absolutely
100 per cent. right with Great Britain,
and to show the British people that here
we were willing to spend and be spent in
the Imperial service. There would have
been the contrast of Ulster on the one

herself into the battle with all the energy
that a proud people can command and
on the other hand the neutral and
dangerous situation in Eire. There was
a contrast to put before the British
people, and had that been done our
political position was safe for 100 years.
It would never have been forgotten. But
the opportunity was let slip.
members of the Government resigned
that any real energy was shown in the

two reasonably intelligent
We have had for a great many years
a vast army of unemployed. I think
that at any time during the past twenty
years we have been almost the worst
part of the United Kingdom from the

here. We were entitled to vastly more.

Our situation was geographically ideal,

entitled us to a vastly greater share.

as head of the Government. I have

In my view the Minister of Commerce is
the person who has failed in his duty in
this matter. It is not the duty of the
Minister of Labour to provide employment. He has many functions in the
way of administering the service and
placing labour when the demand arises,
but it is not, either here or in Great
Britain, the function of the Minister of
Labour to create employment. That is
the function of some other person, and if
it is not the function of the Minister of
Commerce it is nobody's function. In my
view he occupies the most important office
in the Government except that of the
Prime Minister. I think the only thing
we can do in this country is to look after
the industries by which the people live.
So far as any person can see the
Government have got no policy whatever
in respect of unemployment. We had
three speeches within the last three weeks,
two by the Prime Minister, one at a
meeting in the city and one in this
House, and one by the Minister of Commerce in the House. I hope I am being
fair; I do not think I am unfair when I
say that the Government policy is this:
We will stand by; we will allow the
natural ebb and flow of trade to govern
the numbers of our unemployed, and we
will pay unemployment assistance in one
form or another to those people who are
out of work.
Yesterday, no doubt in view of this
debate, the Prime Minister agreed to his
favourite strategy of setting up a Select
Committee. The technique is so familiar
as to be almost contemptible. When the
transport question arose two years ago
the Recorder of Belfast was appointed to
sit as a Committee; then there was the
McLintock Committee, and then there
was the Joint Select Committee presided
over by the Minister of Public Security.
The work of those three committees rests
in the archives of the House. When
matters were becoming critical about the
time of the resignation of the Financial
Secretary and myself another committee
was set up, the Defence Committee. Now
on the eve of this Vote of Censure when
the Government was naturally going to
be challenged on unemployment the
Prime Minister is engaged in very delicate negotiations and he sets up a Select
Committee. That will deceive nobody.
It may placate members of his party, but
it will not deceive the country, because
it has no reality. The Select Committee
may provide an excellent safety valve,
enabling Members to express their views,
but so far as helping to solve the unemployment problem is concerned it is a pure
waste of time and money. I hold that
view of practically every committee of
more than three people.
Who is to blame? The Prime Minister,
of course, must accept the responsibility
For two and a half years we have passed
legislation in this House, 75 per cent. of
which has been duplication of British
legislation and 25 per cent. has had to
do with internal administration. There
has been no Act put upon the Statute
Book during the lifetime of this Parliament which has really benefited the people
of this country. The only real thing this
Government can do at the present time is
to stimulate trade and commerce to provide work for our people, because that is
how we all live. It is the be-all and endall of our existence. It is not being done
by anybody, and it has got to be done by
someone. If it is not done by the Minister
of Commerce there is no justification for
the retention by him of his office. If the
function of the Ministry of Commerce is
to remain what it has been for the past
few years let us close it altogether. The
Ministry of Commerce can perform useful
functions, but does not. I know it acts
as Registrar of Companies and Inspector
of Fisheries and Weights and Measures,
but that is only administration. Is this
country a shilling richer in the last few
years for the efforts of the Ministry of
Commerce? Its direction is wrong, inept
and palsied. It must go. There ought
to be a re-orientation of the functions of
this Ministry. It ought to be on its toes,
and it is not.

In
Yesterday it was stated that a Select
Committee would be set up to deal with the
problem which I have outlined. A Select
Committee to my mind is merely a stopgap, and generally is the recourse of any
Government which is embarrassed.
Great Britain we. have recently seen many
committees abolished so that problems can
be dealt with quickly and efficiently.
While many committees in Great Britain
have recently been abolished here we are
starting another one. The Committee on
Transport has been referred to, but I do
not propose to deal with that.
What has brought about this lack of
work and feeling of frustration? A war
policy is necessary. Non-essential industries must go out of production and
subordinate themselves to war industries.
We find owing to taxation, lack of war
materials, and so forth, that non-essential
industries are suffering from unemployment. In Great Britain there is the
alternative-they turn over to war work.
Here we have, in the main, no new war
factories. In addition we find-the
Minister of Labour will correct me if I
am wrong-some 6,000 people in Northern
Ireland had to seek employment in
England during the last few months. It
is this practice which is causing the
anxiety and unrest.
The Prime Minister alluded to recent
happenings in Great Britain, and hinted
that the dispersal of industry might help
to solve this problem. I hope and trust
it will, but I would like to point out that
new industries are not transferred overnight and that it will take time, indeed
a long time, to get them going. Much
criticism centred round the Ministry of
Commerce, and I am afraid a good deal
of it may be justified. Let us examine
the facts. The Minister of Agriculture
in Northern Ireland is and has been since
the war started the agent of the Ministry
of Agriculture in England, with which
he has worked in the closest co-operation,
and the whole world knows the success
he has made of it.
The Minister of Commerce is different.
The Ministry of Supply saw fit to set up
its own organisation here outside the
Ministry of Commerce, and so we have
the Ministry of Commerce and the
Ministry of Supply area organisation. It
is extremely undesirable that there should
be two organisations dealing with supply.
I think the Ministry of Commerce should
be the direct agent of the Ministry of
Supply in England. If that were so we
would get much closer contact, and the
problems from which we are suffering,
instead of being dealt with by an
committee, which represents the Ministry
of Supply here, would be under one control. The right thing for the Government
to do is to try to get, as was done in
England, some outstanding outside man
to come and take control of this branch of
the Ministry of Supply.
