ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government Inquiries Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is a Bill which,
I am sure, will commend itself to hon.
Members. As will be seen from a glance
at the Bill, it is of a purely administrative character, and as its necessity may
not be obvious to those not versed in
complex Local Government procedure I
propose, with the permission of the House,
to say a few words in explanation of the
necessity for the present Measure.
As hon. Members are aware, my
Department is authorised under different
codes of Statutes, such as the Public
Health and Poor Law Acts, to direct the
holding of inquiries, but these powers are
in each case limited to matters arising
under the particular code which empowers
my Ministry to hold the inquiry. Matters
calling for inquiry and investigation concerning the administration of Statutes
dealing with other aspects of Local
Government administration frequently
occur, but my Department has no statutory authority in these cases to order an
inquiry or investigation, as the case may
be, even if it is perfectly obvious that this
should be done.
the administration of the Whiteabbey
Sanatorium. While an inquiry may be
fully warranted, it is very doubtful if
my
Department has any statutory authority
to hold the inquiry requested.
It is,
therefore, very desirable that my Department should be given such general powers
as will enable it, if it thinks fit, to cause
a sworn inquiry or investigation to be
held into any aspect of Local Government
administration.
As an example of the type of case to
which I have referred I would instance
the application which has been received
by my Department from the Belfast
Corporation for a sworn inquiry into
an
With regard to the Bill itself, it will
be seen that it is a very short one, and
authorises my
Ministry to order
inquiry or investigation into the administration of any enactment by any of the
local authorities referred to in Clause 1
of the Bill. For the purpose of such
inquiry or investigation the relevant provisions of the Public Health Acts are
incorporated in this Bill.
These provisions refer particularly to the costs of
the inquiry and to the powers vested in
the inspector, such as the power to compel
the attendance of witnesses and the production of documents. It is not proposed
to enlarge the powers of the inspector
beyond those already possessed by
inspectors in my Department.
I am sure that the. House will readily
admit the necessity for a Bill on the lines
referred to, and accordingly I ask the
House for approval to the powers now
sought. I beg to move, "That the Bill
be now read a Second time".

now read a Second time".

Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
object of this Bill is to continue until
the expiration of the year 1941 the operation of the Acts set out in the Schedule
to the Bill. If hon. Members will turn
to the Schedule they will find there are
only three Acts set out. The first is the
Harbours, Docks and Piers (Temporary
Increase of Charges) Act, 1920. That is
the Act which enables the Ministry of
Commerce from time to time to make
orders varying dock charges in order to
enable dock undertakings to be carried on
without loss. The second is the Local
Government (Emergency Powers) Act,
1921, which in case of failure or refusal
on the part of a local authority to
perform its statutory duties enables the
Minister of Home Affairs to appoint an
official or commissioner to exercise the
powers and duties of the local authority.
The third Act in the Schedule is the
Local Authorities and Jurors' Books
(Temporary Provisions) Act. With the.
provisions of this Act hon. Members will
already be familiar as it has been passed
in this House early in the course of the
present year. I beg to move.
Mr. AGNEW: There is one section of
this Act which I am very much interested
in, and that is the Local Government
(Emergency Powers) Act. We in Armagh
have had a commissioner for many years
and we feel that he has had a very long
term, and that it is near time the people
of Armagh had the right at least to elect
their own Council. I have repeatedly
asked when that would be allowed, and
I have been promised pretty often that
when the time was appropriate the
electors would be entitled to elect their
own Council. This has gone on for many
years and we feel that the town is quite
safe and competent now to deal with its
own local affairs in so far as re-electing
its Council, even though in the emergency
local government elections are postponed.
I would like the Minister to give due
consideration to the fact that Armagh
city will be entitled to govern itself by
its own elected representatives.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time".
Sir DAWSON BATES: So far as I
am concerned I will be very pleased when
I am able to dispense with the inspector.
I think on reconsideration the hon.
Member will realise that this is not a
suitable time to have elections. If it had
been it would have been another matter.
I think also he will agree that the town
has benefited very much from the
present inspector.
Mr. AGNEW: I do not wish to cast
any reflections on the commissioner.

Flax-growing is of small importance

cultivation but one of our greatest
industries. For that reason it deserves
special attention beyond the usual
control regulations.

it is right or wrong. They always felt

A few years ago we proposed to the
trade what, to our mind, was a perfectly
workable scheme, namely, that there
should be a guaranteed price for flax, and
that flax should be tied to the world price
of flax. That was turned down by the
trade. If the trade had adopted that
scheme it would have done away with that
lack of confidence that does exist amongst
farmers. So far as the Ministry is concerned, we could do nothing more, except
adopt the suggestion which has more than
once been put forward, that a subsidy of
£2 an acre should be paid. What
guarantee could there be that that £2
an acre would go into the pockets of the
farmers. If my Ministry was responsible
for that £2 an acre it would have to
stand up against any criticism which the
House might make as to whether the £2
definitely went into the pockets of the
farmers. There was no means of proving
that.
The third stage was the setting up of
the Flax Development Committee to the
cost of which the Government and the
trade contributed. That Committee has
been working out methods as to how the
production of flax in this country can be
improved and cheapened. I do not think
a Government could do anything else. The
responsibility for the raw material rests
with the trade and not with the Government.

enormous sums
He went on with his argument with

As for potato factories, I can see no

the Ministry of Food are certainly
not going to pay more than the

slightly more than the minimum
price that they will pay in any case for

Provided the farmers of this country are
getting the minimum payment or
slightly more than the minimum payment that is all that should be necessary
and all that should be required. I do
not believe it is sound policy to set up
an industry that is uneconomic.
The. Member for Antrim was anxious

back work here for the linen industry?
The arguments advanced by the hon.
Member for South Down are, as the hon.
Member for North Derry said, addled.
One can say no more.
Question put, "That this House views
with disappointment the inadequate plans
already announced in regard to the vital
and pressing need for greatly extended
efforts in connection with food and flax
in 1941, and urges the Government to
take immediate, vigorous and comprehensive action in this very important
matter."

truth? Can it be challenged with any

fair-minded men of every section not
acknowledge they know the position
here and have their eyes opened that
the report itself speaks the truth and
nothing but the truth.
This report was the result of investigations into a camp for unemployed boys
at Ballyrogan this summer. It is a
report of deep import to all who have
any concern for the whole future of this
Province. The gentlemen responsible for
the report are leaders, Protestant leaders,
in social service here in Northern Ireland.
The facts startled them and made them
halt and take note of what is going on
in our midst. Reading the report I think
it would occur to most minds that it is
written without bias and certainly with
a single eye to the welfare of the whole
community. Proofs of discrimination
against the youths we speak of, Catholic
youths, with regard to employment leave
no shadow or scintilla of doubt. The
report says:
With the instrument of propaganda
now in the hands of the Government it
is of urgent importance that the refusal
of many to employ Catholic boys should
be discouraged. It may be that
the form in which it is often stated
the cry of "Discrimination against
Catholics" is ill-founded, but it is a
powerful fact that the vast majority of
boys attending the Juvenile Instruction
Centre are Catholics.
That is a powerful fact.
The evidence of quite good boys who
have been constantly looking for jobs
and who have failed to get them in
works where at the least the majority
of workers are Protestants and where
Protestant boys are constantly taken
on is, to say the least of it, suggestive.
These are words of vital importance
coming from the source from which they
emanate.
We continue to neglect this problem
at our peril. One wonders if it is not
already too late
Prime Minister associated himself with
that unchristian and pernicious counsel.
Lesser lights are acting upon it.
Many of these lads have been found on
investigation to be clean, tidy, good
workers and above the average in
intelligence, but they are the victims of
cruel conditions. Rebuffed, turned away
again and again in their search for work,
some of them go so foolishly wild and
astray as to attempt to get their own
back on society.
The crucial question put to these boys is
"What school were you at?" The Minister of Agriculture urged more than once
a denial of employment to Catholics. The
The investigators report that some
of these lads firmly believe theyit is not confined to one section of the
community only-would be better off
under Nazi rule. Their attitude towards
the police is one of distrust and defiance.
The report says:
———
To them the police are all prejudiced against the Catholic areas of
the city. All laws were bad laws because they were English laws and every
moral argument was propaganda. This
is not to be mistaken as the source of
defiance and lawlessness which is
equally prevalent among Protestant
boys.
Then comes a striking passage:—
""
We cannot refrain from expressing
our concern at the similarity between
the spiritual, moral, intellectual and
physical state of the unemployed youth
of this Province to that which obtained
in Germany at the rise of the National
Socialist Party. In short, we are on
the brink of a revolutionary situation.
The investigators found that revolutionary sentiments were commonplace
amongst the boys, not only Catholic boys
but also others. "The children's teeth,
say the high-minded Protestant investigators, "are set on edge. We are
the victims of a ruthless logic of history."
Suppression is no remedy; force is no
remedy. Courageous administration on
the part of the Ministry, with courageous
discouragement of any kind of discrimination such as these investigators
found which would absorb unemployed
youth into Government aided work
would give some promise of good. Grants
for new works and the expansion of
existing work would help to avert danger
by checking the deterioration in morale.

Mr. BYRNE: It was stated that it

so and so; that they were called up for

think that is sufficient to show that there

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 8th October, 1940.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DISALLOWANCES IN ARMAGH
AREA.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state how many
married men were disallowed as "Not
Available" by Mr. Kinnear at the
Appeal Tribunal held in Armagh Area
Office on 25/9/40; whether Mr. Kinnear
is a retired civil servant in receipt of a
pension; whether he has sufficient local
knowledge to deal with cases in Armagh,
and whether the Minister is satisfied with
the disallowances imposed, and can he
give the House the contents of the chairman's written report on disallowances.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): At the sitting of the Appeals
Tribunal referred to, the cases of fifteen
men were dealt with: six were allowed;
eight were disallowed, and one case was
adjourned as the appellant did not
attend. Six of those disallowed were
married.
It is not the duty of a chairman of a
tribunal to submit a general report on
disallowances, but of course he records
his decision in each individual case.
The chairman of the tribunal on that
occasion is a retired civil servant in
receipt of a pension. He is also a
barrister-at-law, and, combined with
legal knowledge, has had long experience
in dealing with the administration of
social services generally in Northern
Ireland. By the Unemployment Assistance Act, the question of an applicant's
title to assistance is referred to officers
of the Board and to appeal tribunals,
whose decision is final, and I am satisfied that the provisions of the Act have
been carefully observed.
COST-OF-LIVING INCREASE IN
ALLOWANCES.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state what the
cost-of-living increase meant to the recipients of assistance in Great Britain,
and how it applied in the Northern
Ireland 1939 Act; whether one shilling
each for man and wife, one shilling for
dependent over 16, and sixpence for each
child under this age was applied by the
Unemployment Assistance Board of
Northern Ireland; whether he can explain
what the Unemployment Assistance Board
did actually apply to claimants, and
whether the increase was based on a percentage basis.
Mr. GORDON: Under the amending
Regulations, dated 18th December, 1939,
the rates for unemployment assistance
were increased by the amounts mentioned
by the hon. Member, the Regulations in
Great Britain and in Northern Ireland
being identical in terms and administered
on the same lines. The increases in
allowances were made by way of additions
to the basic scale rates (and not as percentage increases), but as the amount of
unemployment assistance may not ordinarily exceed the applicant's normal earnings, it was not possible to give the total
scale rates in every case.
Mr. AGNEW: Would it not be wise to
follow the step-by-step policy when
dealing with unemployment?
Mr. GORDON: That is exactly what
we are doing as I have said in my reply.
We are following identical lines
administration and in the amount of
benefit given to the applicants.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it not a fact that we
only applied a 10 per cent. increase and
not on the same basis as in Britain.
Mr. GORDON: No. The hon. Gentleman is wrong. As a matter of fact to
indicate the extent of the allowances paid,
out of 28,013 applicants in the week preceding Christmas last year, when the
increased amounts were paid, 20,022 or

Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact

LOCAL
DEFENCE
VOLUNTEERS.
6. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state if
the. Local Defence Volunteers are under
police or military control; whether industries and other concerns have their
own Local Defence Volunteer Force, and
whether that force is based on the. same
conditions as apply in Great Britain;
what form of oath is taken by men
enrolling in this force; whether it is a
police or military attestation; whether
the Minister agrees with the present
system of control and whether he will
have the Local Defence Volunteers
placed under competent military control.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
Local Defence Volunteers form a section
of the Ulster Special Constabulary and
are accordingly under the control of the
Special Constabulary authorities. As
has been indicated on several occasions,
however, the Force will, under existing
arrangements, come under the command
of the military authorities when used in
operations against the enemy. Detachments of the Force which have been
formed in industrial and other establishments are in exactly the same position.
The oath taken on enrolment is that
prescribed by the Special Constables.
(Ireland) Acts.
In answer to the last part of the hon.
Member's question I am of opinion that
the present system of control has enabled
the Force to make better progress in the
time which has elapsed since its formation than would otherwise have been
possible, and this is also the view of the
military authorities. So far as the
future is concerned, I fully appreciate
that the ultimate purpose of the Force is
a military one, and for this reason the
military bias which the training and
organisation of the Force is at present
being given in increasing measure will be
continued. I may add, further, that the
whole question of how best to fit the
Force for its ultimate object has been
the subject of recent discussion between
the General Officer Commanding and
myself, and I can assure the hon. Member that the Government will not
neglect to make any change, either in
organisation or control, which may be
considered advisable for the purpose of
making the Force better fitted for the
performance of its military role.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that if
the Government wanted the men they
could increase that Force by 200,000 in
one week?
LIGHTING OF POLICE CYCLES.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he can state
if it is by order that members of the
Police Force use their cycles without
complying with the lighting conditions.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Where a constable's duty requires him to display an
unauthorised form of light he may lawfully do so under Paragraph 3 of the
Lighting Restrictions. (Northern Ireland) Order, 1940.
Apart from this exception, members
of the Force must observe the same conditions with regard to the use of lights
as apply to other members of the community, and standing instructions to the
police so provide.
LOCAL DEFENCE VOLUNTEERS
OR HOME GUARD.
8. Sir NORMAN STRONGE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether the
title of Local Defence Volunteers has
been changed to Home Guard as in
England, and also whether it has been
approved that the Force in each county
wear the regimental badges of their
county regiment.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The official title
of the Force still remains "Local
Defence Volunteer Section of the Ulster
Special Constabulary."
The title "Home Guard Section"
would, I believe, be preferable, as it
would serve to emphasise the unity of
purpose which underlies the movement
throughout the United Kingdom; but I
have deferred making the change pending the consideration of certain other

I consider that a cap badge of uniform

county unit.

CONCERNING ONIONS.
11. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can make any
statement on the subject of onions.
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, sir. But it would
be helpful if the hon. Member would
indicate with some greater degree of precision on what particular aspect of the
onion he would like me to pronounce.
I am aware that the question of the
price of onions is receiving the attention
of the Northern Ireland Food Price
Regulation Committee.
Perhaps the hon. Member will let me
have a note of the points on which he
desires to have information.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister tell
us why in view of the promise that prices
would be controlled the price of onions is
now six times what it was before the war?
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister say
if half-cooked onions are a good, wholesome, and advisable food for any person
to take prior to going out to meet friends
or going into company?
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the Minister
state why no action has been taken by
the Government to ensure that onions
can be purchased at a price the workers
can pay? The price of onions in Northern Ireland to-day is monstrous; in fact
they are dearer than eggs, and the working people cannot get them.

Societies (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BARBOUR: This Bill is a war
time Measure designed to facilitate the
business of societies faced with certain
difficulties attributable to the present
emergency. Such difficulties may arise
under the societies' rules or under
statutory enactments.
The term "society" includes friendly
societies, industrial and provident
societies, building societies and trade
unions. A large proportion of the
business of such societies in Northern Ireland is carried on by cross-channel
organisations and it was, therefore, desirable that the. Bill should conform closely
to the Act of Parliament bearing the
same title passed at Westminster in the
present year.
The first Clause of the Bill makes
provision for meeting difficulties in complying with statutory enactments or with
the rules of a society. It empowers the
Registrar of Friendly Societies, on receipt
of an application from the management
committee of a society, to give what in
the Bill is called a "direction", if he is
satisfied that, by reason of circumstances
attributable to the. emergency, it is
expedient to do so..
Such a "direction" may dispense with
or vary any rule of the society or any
enactment requiring meetings of the
society to be held at specified times or
periods or at specified places. It may also
authorise the appointment of trustees or
Societies Bill
Administration of Police Force 2288
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
officers and the continuance in office of
any trustee
or officer whose appointment would otherwise have terminated.
A "direction" may further authorise the
making of amendments of rules by a
resolution of the committee of management or of a general meeting of the
society, and the exercise by the committee
of management of the functions exercisable by
a meeting of the society,
or by a sub-committee of the committee
of management of the functions exercisable by that committee.
In cases where, owing to force of
circumstances, the. committee of management has already been constrained to do
anything which could have been
authorised by a "direction", covering
authority for such acts is to be given
retrospectively by the Registrar.
Clause 2 enables the Registrar to give
a "direction" for the amendment of the
rules of any registered branch
friendly society.

Clause 4 permits a building society to

provided the written consent of the

The Registrar is also given a power of

the Registrar will have power under
Clause 5 to waive the requirement for the
consent of a two-thirds majority.
Clause 6 makes provision for the continuation of the membership of friendly
societies of members who by reason of
their service in the Forces of the Crown
may be unable to attend meetings or to
pay their contributions.

Administration of the Police Force.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move,
That this House demands that a
Select Committee be established to
inquire into the administration of the
Police Force, owing to the failure of
the said Force to give full protection
to life and property.
I put this Motion on the Order Paper
after many years' experience of the
management of the Police Force in Northern Ireland. To-day, I am going to
use documentary evidence compiled and
issued to me by the respective Departments who should know best how this
administration has been working during
the last nineteen years. Each of us is
aware that the Royal Ulster Constabulary
sprang from the Royal Irish Constabulary and were formed under Act of
Parliament in the year 1922. In forming that body it was very necessary and
important to have at their head one who
was fully qualified in every aspect of
police work so that he could take up from
where the old R.I.C. left off.
At that time it would have been very
difficult for me to make any criticism of
the leadership of the R.U.C., but nineteen years have elapsed, and I can now
review the administration during that
period. When the House hear the
official report of those nineteen years I
hope they will feel it their bounden duty
to compel the Government by vote to
have this small committee of inquiry into
the management of such a highly efficient
body of constables and non-commissioned
officers. There is no gainsaying the
fact that our constables and noncommissioned officers are the finest
material that any head could have to
work upon.
I pay that tribute to that

section of the Force. They have done

the higher ranks of the Police Force?
The administration is in the higher ranks,
and it has come to such a state as not
to be serviceable. I believe the years
have taught them that the administration has set back the higher ranks and
something immediate must be done to

There is one thing I see wrong in the

it does not reflect credit on the heads of

It is not possible to arrive at any fair

In 1935, a year which has already been
referred to, and one of very considerable
difficulty, the percentage of specially
reported cases in which persons were made
amenable was 45.6; in the following year,
1936, the percentage rose to 59.7; in 1937
it was 67.1; in the year 1938 it rose to
the extraordinary figure of 75.8; in 1939
it was 71; in 1940 the percentage is so far
70.4. When one recollects that the
figures for 1939 and 1940 cover the blackout period when crime is obviously more
difficult to detect, I think the House can
be satisfied that there has been no real
falling off in the efficiency of the police,
and that the very high standard it has
been worked up to has been well maintained.

It is because these manifestations in
the shape of robberies, obviously designed
The first series of raids occurred a few
days after I assumed office on the 28th
June, 1940. In the course of these. raids
the Munster & Leinster Bank, 93 Falls
Road, the National Bank, 98 Falls Road,
and the Northern Bank at the corner of
Percy Street were raided by armed men.
Over £3,000 was taken, and in respect
of that activity one person is under arrest
and awaiting trial. On the 25th July the
Bank of Ireland in Armagh was raided.
The raiders did not succeed in their
efforts, and at the present time six
persons are awaiting trial as a result of
action on the part of the police which I
can without any exaggeration describe as
a most gallant achievement. I should like
to hear a little more in a debate of this
kind as to what the police have done
rather than raking up all the small petty
points which can be thought of.
On the 20th September the National
Bank, Falls Road, the Munster &
Leinster Bank, Falls Road-both of
which had been raided before-were
again raided and five post offices were
raided as well. A total sum of £2,100
was taken. In respect of these crimes one
person is apprehended. In two of the.
cases the raiders came into armed conflict
with the police, and there is no question.
that had the police not intervened the
amount lost would have been much
greater.
I want to say a word about what the
police can do to cope with crime of this
kind. It is, as I have already pointed
out, crime of an organised kind flowing
from a conspiracy which is detrimental to

the State. In police duties one has to
keep the balance between protecting the
general public and protecting specific
persons and places. If one concentrates
on protecting specific places and persons.
the general public will suffer, and if one
concentrates entirely on general policing
specific places of importance and particular persons may suffer. A balance
has to be struck. It is not possible
to garrison every
bank in Belfast.
There are over fifty branches in Belfast
alone. There. are eighty post offices.
There are, in addition, many places which
form a tempting target for those who
want money. To employ static guards at
all these places would, as everybody
knows, immobilise a great part of our
police force.
The day on which the first raids
occurred it was obvious to everyone that
they might be the beginning of further
trouble. I went to the Inspector-General
for the purpose of suggesting that he
should get into touch with the banks at
once, so as to plan a course of campaign
in order to frustrate or make more
difficult further attempts. I found a
conference had already been arranged.
After that, conferences were held. I
interviewed a deputation from the banks
and the point of view put forward by
them was that as they were carrying
large stocks of money it was of national
importance that they should get some
degree of police protection over and
above that afforded to the ordinary
private firm. I agreed with that. On
the other hand, I pointed out to them
that they had responsibilities and
should do everything possible to ease the
burden of the police. They should take
every reasonable step in their power to
help the police in their endeavours to
curb this particular kind of crime.
told them that I would do all I could
to see that they were given every protection compatible with the other duties.
incumbent upon the police force.
Since that time I have done my best,
the police have done their best, and the
Inspector-General has done his best to
implement that promise. I pointed out
to them that other dangers had to be
looked into and considered as well as
raiding of a particular kind. I think
they appreciated that point. Very many
of the banks have entered into wholehearted co-operation and have taken
steps which I cannot go into. The hon.
Member for Woodvale who has a simple
remedy for everything is not quite right
in saying that his practical suggestion
was spurned. I cannot go further than
that. The principle behind it was not
spurned, and although every case and
every bank has to be considered on its
merits he is far from right in suggesting
that his remedy was spurned because it
was simple. The problem is not a simple
one, but any practical suggestion which
will be helpful in suppressing this
particular form of crime is welcome and
will be welcomed.
Of course I realise that all that was
necessary could not be done in a day. It
is unfortunate that at the time of the last
raids on 20th September, 1940, the two
banks, which had previously been raided
in June, had not then provided any internal protection. I appreciate that in
this connection the strength of the chain
is at its weakest link. I am not suggesting that the directorates of any banks are
not willing to help, but it is obvious that
some standard of protection must be taken
for the simple reason if some are protected and others are not, attention will
be paid to those which offer the easiest
path for the raiders.
I am considering at the present time
the best means of ensuring that those who
have money in large quantities will take
every reasonable step for their own
safety. I wish to make it plain that
while there must be co-operation in this
matter it does not mean that all the work
has to be done by the banks or post offices
or other similar concerns. I quite accept
that the police have a duty to perform in
this matter, and so far as I am able I will
see to it that that duty is discharged.

4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the steps
taken by the Government to alleviate the
distress caused by the alarming jump
in the numbers of unemployed in the
linen and textile industries from about
17,000 in April, 1940, to about 37,000 in
September, 1940.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. The increase in unemployment to which the
hon. and learned Member refers is due
mainly to the loss of Belgium and France
as suppliers of flax, and to the consequential prohibition on the use of new
flax, other than coarse tow, for any
purpose except essential war requirements. The spinning section of the
linen industry was, of course, most
adversely affected by this development,
although the weaving section also suffered
to a lesser extent.
The efforts of the Government have
been directed to securing the release of
flax and flax yarns for export orders, and
towards obtaining Imperial Government
contracts for the manufacture of both
linen and cotton cloth to make good the
inevitable loss of trade in linen goods on
the home market.
As the hon. and learned Member has
doubtless observed from recent Press
reports, valuable concessions have been
obtained in both these directions, as well
as in securing orders for the making-up
trades. It would be idle to pretend, however, that any remedial action within the.
power of either Government could fully
compensate the Northern Ireland textile
trades for the loss of output brought
about by the shortage of raw materials.

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The overwhelming majority
of farmers willingly and promptly pay
their annuities as a debt of honour. The
number which it was necessary to bring to
court in respect of the half-yearly payment in November-December, 1939, was
588, which is less than per cent. of
annuitants; it is not yet possible to give
the figures in respect of the payment due
in May-June, 1940, because the sessions
are still in progress.
There is in one district a group of small
holdings of especially poor mountain land
in the occupation of tenant purchasers
who are in arrear with the payment of
their annuities; the Ministry has been
reluctant to take ejectment proceedings in
these cases. Apart from these, the
number of holdings throughout Northern
Ireland whose occupiers are in arrear with
their payments and for which purchasers
have not yet been found is negligible.

For the second time within
generation, the British people have been
called to the profound and tragic sacrifices of war. These sacrifices are demanded, as in 1914-1918, in the name of
democracy and freedom; they can be
justified only as these noble ends are
made real and living things in the lives.
of ordinary men and women. The last
war exacted an immense toll from the
workers. High-sounding promises were
made to them in recognition of their
effort; promises which were only partially
fulfilled. There was advance, indeed,
but it was an inadequate advance. Our
democracy is still an incomplete democracy. The standard of life of millions of
our fellow citizens remains inadequate.
The educational opportunities of the new
generation are still incomplete. Even if
there be a deeper social conscience than
in the past, our society still remains, in
its essential outlines, acquisitive and
unequal.
For us a Socialist Britain is not some
far-off Utopia, but an ideal that can be
realised within our time. We seek a
society in which there is a just distribution of wealth, and where the essential
instruments of production are publicly
owned. Such a society will establish
that national minimum standard
of
living which is a vital test of civilisation.
It will abolish the irrational privileges
which disfigure our present order. It
will secure genuine equality, and a high
level, of educational opportunity. It
will make economic freedom real by its
ability to offer security and a rising
standard of life to the worker, both
urban and rural. It will make justice.
responsive to the needs of the many, and
not only of the few. It will care with a
new intensity for the health of the people,
and will nourish the opportunity for the
creative use of leisure. Because its
Socialistic principles are built upon a
faith in the power of reason, we can give
to science that place and
which
scope
capitalism frustrates.
I call
upon the Government to
recognise that the day of the old order is
done. We declare that only a bold
Socialist planning of the foundations of
our system can give us the faith and the
power to meet the claims of those who
will bring us victory. They are entitled
now to the assurance that they will not
make their sacrifice in vain. We therefore conceive of reconstruction in Socialist
terms. But our Socialism is built upon
a profound faith in the people of the
world and a determination to press for
necessary social changes upon the basis
of democracy and justice. We reject all
demands for dictatorship, whether from
the Left or from the Right. We take
our stand upon that faith in reason
which looks to the declared will of the
people as the only valid source of power.
So long as that will is nationally respected, we are confident that the historic
forms of Parliamentary democracy
provide a highroad along which the
nation can pass peacefully from
acquisitive to a Socialist society. We
warn the enemies of democracy, whether
open or secret, that the declared will of
the people must prevail. The majority
of the nation is entitled to be master in
its own house.

This matter must be of deep interest
to many Members of the House who have
never heard it put forward previously.
If only for the sake of showing Parliamentary courtesy they should listen to
what I am saying. To-day we plan for
the destructive tasks of war; we insist
that it is not less urgent to plan for the

The years since
1919 have taught us nothing if we have
not learned that the mere conflict of
private interests can never produce a

watchwords, therefore,
be COoperation, not competition; public

shows, the logic of the present system

We believe that the nation is ready for
a new social order, whose foundations
must be laid now. The people have come
to see that social justice at home is an
essential condition of enduring peace
abroad. The road to justice lies through
the gateway of democratic socialism. By
this road alone, the nation, at long last,
can enter fully into its inheritance.
Every problem of our society has been
intensified by the coming of the war.
None can be intelligently faced save in
terms of national economic planning.
Vested private interests must give way
to public needs.

[Mr. Beattie]
Clearly, in order to win the war, we
must use to the. full the resources of the
nation, and this cannot be done without
public direction and control. Already the
Government has been compelled to bring
some degree of order into the chaos of
capitalism. Knowing that the methods of
private enterprise cannot bring victory,
it has been forced, over an extending field
of industry, to direct what goods shall
be produced and what services rendered.
It has had to introduce controls of
various kinds. It has intervened with
subsidies to stabilise the prices of some
essential foodstuffs. It has undertaken
the bulk purchase of food imports and
raw materials. The Admiralty has been
made responsible for both naval and
mercantile shipbuilding. Sea transport is
under close control. The railways have
been partially unified. The supreme
interests of a nation at war compel the
adoption of planning measures by a
Government which, by natural inclination, repudiates planning.
Much of this necessary interference
with private interests, however, has been
half-hearted, ill-devised, and accompanied
by muddle and avoidable delay. There
has been none of that bold, effective, but
carefully-prepared planning which is the
Socialist conception. Hasty improvisation
is not enough, either in peace or war.
If the war is to be won with the least
suffering and hardship, Socialist principles must be applied. After 1918, there
was a hurried return to "business as
usual". We demanded then, and we
demand now, that war-time organisation
shall be undertaken in the full knowledge
that there can be no going back; that,
after the war, the national war effort
must be turned to the building of a new
world.
bring about a fairer distribution of

While planning for war, the Government must plan for peace and a new
society. Instead of regarding each item
of State control as a temporary infringement of the normal, the occasion should
be seized to lay the foundations of an
efficient economic system. Thus, the railways, the coal industry, and a substantial
part of arms production should be made
national services during the war, and the
public regulation of finance should be
strengthened and consolidated. In
allocating the financial burden of war,
there should be a definite intention to
So, during the present struggle, the
form of the new order will be emerging
from the old. The main outlines of the
new order are clear. Those key industries
and services, upon which the well-being
of the nation depends, must be transferred to public ownership. Financial
power is central to the whole economic
structure; therefore, the banks must be
subject to public control. The direction
of investment is a public trust to be
determined in the public interest; left to
the chance of private decision, it breeds
domestic waste, colonial exploitation, and
only too often, war. There must also be
public ownership and control of coal and
power, of the basic forms of transport,
and, on a steadily-increasing scale, of
the land. Without these first measures of
public ownership, effective planning in
the interest of the whole nation is impossible.
The industries and services so brought
under national direction will have to be
reorganised as a condition of their
efficiency, and this task will be pursued
with vigour. Those still in private hands
will be required to plan their structure
and methods; for the nation can no longer
tolerate the grotesque waste of manpower
and wealth which arises from unregulated
private ownership. Individual initiative
and ability must not be restricted, but
must be directed to the service of the
community.
There must be, also, that control of the
location of industry which is urgent for
the public health, for the preservation of
the countryside, and for a new life in the
distressed areas. In the laws relating to
workmen's compensation, the employment
of children and young persons, merchant
shipping, and shops and offices, a Socialist
conception of industry makes possible a
new approach to the definition of necessary standards, which, in the daily experience of countless workers, have been
too long delayed.
There must be a fuller recognition of
the functions of trade unions in the
national life. Just as their knowledge
and experience are essential to the proper
organisation of industry and agriculture
for war, so are they essential to a proper
organisation for peace. The trade union.

-as the experience of dictatorships has

Any great social change necessarily
requires a wise administration of the
national income, and no administration
is wise that is not founded also in justice.
We differ from its critics in its tests of
fiscal wisdom. These critics believe that

on luxuries. This view, Labour emphatically condemns. In common with
enlightened economic opinion all over the

urgent national requirements, as judged

It is both economically right and

The Parliamentary Secretary stated

Order Paper in the name of Mr. Brown:
war-time emergency measure, doubling

desirable reform and thus keep step by

CONTROL OF LOCAL DEFENCE
VOLUNTEERS.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if he is
prepared to consider the advisability of
placing the Local Defence Volunteer
Force under the Military Authorities in
Northern Ireland, so as to follow step by
step with Great Britain and have the cooperation of all sections of the community in their determination to resist
all forms of invasion.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott) rose.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was the Prime
Minister I asked.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I have been
asked by the Prime Minister to reply to
this question.
It will be remembered that the Local
Defence Volunteer Force was formed in
the face of a threat of imminent invasion
when every hour was precious and the
need for speedy organisation was most
urgent. It is impossible, however, to
raise an effective armed force quickly
without an administrative basis to work
upon. In Great Britain that basis
existed in a widespread chain of Territorial Army Associations which were
used for the purpose. Here we had not
that basis and in the circumstances it
was decided, after consultation with the
War Department, to utilise the Special
Constabulary organisation which existed
in each of our counties. For my own
part I do not know what else could have
been done to meet the urgency of the
situation effectively, and the general
officer commanding has informed me that
in his opinion the substantial degree of
progress which has been attained could
not have been reached in the time without the aid of the Special Constabulary
organisation.
I have adverted to the formation of
the force, because some publicity has
recently been given to the suggestion that
the method adopted sprang from political
and sectarian motives. Such propaganda
is unfounded, and it is either mischievous
Oral Answers

Oral Answers
22 OCTOBER 1940
or uttered in ignorance of the material
facts. From the beginning, the object
of this Government has been to do all
that lay in its power during a period of
unparalleled urgency and peril to raise
and arm a force which would be efficient
for its role. That role is neither more
nor less than the role of the corresponding force in Great Britain. It is, as I
have previously stated, a military role,
and for that reason I have constantly
been in discussion with the general officer
commanding Northern Ireland District,
with the object of promoting the military
efficiency of the force.
As I have said, our anxiety, as a
Government, is to make the force the
best possible weapon for its purpose, and
to this end we are, and have been, ready
and willing to facilitate in any way we
can such steps concerning the control,
the status and the organisation of the
Local Defence Volunteer Force as the
Imperial Government may consider
desirable.

intact from the onslaught that may be

will go on.

political dictatorship at present occupied
by the Prime Minister?
Everything possible to secure the full
efficiency of that force will be done, and
everything that the Imperial authorities
desire us to do for that purpose will be
done willingly.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: No, sir. It is
not a fact that this organisation or movement had a political origin. I have made
it quite clear in the answer given that
the, motive of this Government was to
promote a force that would meet an
urgency which existed and still exists.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman state. why the Government
refuse to walk step by step with Great
Britain in regard to the formation of

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I have given the

Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the great majority
of the members of the L.D.V. are anxious

if any damage is done to buildings the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been

I have seen the statement referred to in
the question.
The reason for the chartering of the
ship was that my Government was requested by the military authorities to
remove the internees from the prisons,
and it was at their suggestion, failing any
other available accommodation, that the
Ministry of British Shipping was asked
by their Home Office, at our request, to

The reference that appeared in the
Press, to which the hon. and learned
Member refers, suggesting that the
Ministry of Shipping had urgently requested the return of the ship, is evidently
based on some misunderstanding as no
such request has been received by the
Government.
The urgency of the matter necessitated
the question of chargeability being left
over until time was available to go more
fully into it, and my Ministry provisionally agreed to accept financial responsibility. As it is now at the request of

being evacuated, the British Treasury is
being asked to bear the entire cost of the
chartering and fitting out of the "Al

Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
give the information asked for by the
hon. Member in the first part of his
question.
The condition that a person must be
available for work in order to receive
benefit or assistance is laid down in
Section 24 of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1936,
and Section 31 of the Unemployment
Assistance Act (Northern Ireland), 1934,
and under both these Acts statutory
authorities have been established to deal
with appeals arising out of claims to
benefit or assistance. When an applicant
refuses work in Great Britain or elsewhere, it is for these authorities to
decide whether the disallowance has been
correctly imposed.
A disallowance on the grounds that
the claimant is not available for work is
not necessarily continued until he or she
has found work; it may be terminated
when the insurance officer (or the area
officer of the Assistance Board, as the
case may be) is satisfied that the
claimant has become available.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman where he gets
power in the Northern Ireland Unemployment Insurance Act to disallow any
person either public assistance or unemployment insurance benefit for refusing
work in Great Britain? The Unemployment Insurance Act for Great Britain is
confined to Great Britain, and our Act is
confined to the area of Northern Ireland.
The right hon. Gentleman may be right
in theory, but in practice does not "not
available for employment" mean
a life
disqualification?
Mr. GORDON: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: Pardon me. It

insurable employment before he is reestablished.

Mr. GORDON: No, the hon. Gentleman is wrong. The question of nonavailability arises where a person refuses
work and is offered work again and refuses it once more. Under the Unemployment Assistance Act the officer can
refuse that man benefit until he proves
that he is available. The only way he
can prove he is available for work is by

Act.

Mr. GORDON: Yes.

Mr. GORDON: Under Section 31 of
the Unemployment Assistance. Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, an applicant is
required to be "available for work". If
an applicant refuses to accept an offer of
employment he raises a presumption that
he is not holding himself so available,
and officers of the Assistance Board have
thereupon to decide whether, having
regard to all the circumstances of the
case, the applicant fulfils the conditions
of the Statute. The Act in question contains no provision limiting a disallowance
in such circumstances to six weeks, as in
the case of the Unemployment Insurance
Acts, when a disallowance is imposed for
refusing or failing to apply for work.
At the outbreak of the war, the Board
ceased, in the interests of national
economy, to keep detailed statistics of
disallowances, and it has consequently not
been possible to obtain the information.
asked for in the last part of the question.

SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY.
12. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether any experiments
have been carried out in the production
of sugar beet in Northern Ireland, and
whether in view of the fact that Great
Britain has eighteen beet factories and is
producing 500,000 tons of sugar per
year, he will consider carrying out some
experiments even on a small scale.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): A series of experiments was carried out by the Ministry
over a two-year period in five of the six
counties and at several centres in each
county. The average yield of sugar beet
was seven tons, the yields varying from
three tons to 11 tons. The results
showed that sugar beet requires conditions similar to those required for
mangels and that the crop will be a comparative failure on soils which are cold,
shallow or sour, or where the soil is unable to withstand drought.
Potatoes, it will be noted, give a
higher average yield per acre and even
at £3 a ton potatoes are a far better
proposition for our farmers than sugar
beet with the full subsidy.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
if he has overlooked the fact which has
just been officially announced that sugar
beet in Ireland had a record increased
yield of sugar content of 25.1 per cent.
as against 16.5 in Great Britain in 1939 ?
Mr. SPEAKER: The replies to the
remaining questions will be circulated
unless hon. Members give notice to the

FERMANAGH COUNTY
COMMITTEE AND PRICE OF OATS
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the fact that it was stated
at the meeting of the Fermanagh County
Committee of Agriculture on 12th
instant by the secretary, that as a result
of the tillage drive 24,000 acres of oats,
producing 18,000 tons, have been grown
in County Fermanagh to replace 30,000
tons of feeding stuffs for cattle; that
farmers are selling oats at 6s per cwt.,
and buying them back, ground in the
mills, at 16s per cwt.; whether a member of the commitee asked what was he
to do with the oats he could neither use
nor sell, and whether he will make representations to the proper authorities to
have a minimum price fixed for oats in
view of the fact that the fixing of a
maximum price only is of no benefit to
the farmers.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's
question is in the affirmative. I would
like to assure him that there is no farmer
in County Fermanagh so foolish as to
sell his oats at 6s a cwt. and buy them
back ground at 16s a cwt. In view of
the figure which the hon. Member has
given I should have thought it was
obvious to him that the extra acreage of
oats is still a long way short of making
up the deficiency in feeding stuffs.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, he seems to be
unaware of the fact that since the war
the standard price of oats has been
raised from 8s to 12s 6d a cwt.

INTERNEES ON HUNGER-STRIKE.
Mr. CAMPBELL (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether one of the three internees who,
as a protest of their innocence, have been
on hunger-strike in Belfast Prison for
over a week, Bennett, from Lurgan, is in
a state of extreme exhaustion and in
imminent danger of collapse, and what
steps are being taken in his regard.
Sir DAWSON BATES: A report which
I received from the prison medical officer
this morning intimates that this man is
in no immediate danger. His condition,
therefore, calls for no special action at the
moment.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the right
hon. Gentleman be prepared to allow an
independent outside doctor to visit this
man?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, the
medical officer in the prison is a very
efficient official.
PAYMENT OF "B" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY ALLOWANCE.
Mr. HENDERSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Public Security
whether he could state for what reason the
allowance to the members of the "B"
Special Constabulary was not paid at 1st
October, and would he state whether steps
will be taken to have these men's allowances paid out immediately.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: These payments
are made as soon as possible after the first
day of the quarter. They are based on
returns received by the Paymaster from
the counties, as to the services (drills,
patrols, etc.) performed by each man.
There were some queries on the Belfast
returns with the result that payments in
the Belfast area were not issued until
yesterday. Payments to men in all other
areas had already been made.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Education (Emergency Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): This Bill
which I have the honour to introduce is
a very simple Measure designed to give
power to all education authorities or
managers to afford air-raid protection in
the schools. It also deals with certain
other matters arising out of war conditions affecting education. Two categories
of schools are affected, those within a
prescribed area and those outside what
may be termed the "compulsory zone".
The Ministry considers that air-raid
protection must be provided for all
recognised schools and colleges in a
certain area comprising the County
Borough of Belfast and the strips extending from Belfast to Larne and from
Belfast to Bangor, and for one mile
inland. They also include some other
schools which are in close proximity to
possible "target points". An order will
be, made subsequent to the passing of this
Measure, defining these areas, and
making it the duty of the education
authorities concerned to provide air-raid
protection for all their elementary
schools, whether voluntary or transferred.
The Ministry will assist by grants of 65
per cent. of the cost.
In the case of secondary schools and of
the voluntary technical schools and training colleges the duty of providing protection is placed on the governing body, but
the education authority is empowered,
either to do the work or to give a grant
towards it. The Ministry will provide 50
per cent. of the cost. These grants from
the Ministry apply also in connection
with the post-war restoration to their
Education Bill—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
former condition of all the schools
mentioned. In the case of those schools
outside the prescribed areas, where the
education authority considers that airraid protection should be given, the
Ministry will offer no objection and will
give the same grants of 65 per cent. and
50 per cent. respectively, but there will
be no compulsion.
In order to save time the education
authorities which will be affected by the
compulsory order have already been
approached, and I am glad to say that
they have met us in a most reasonable
and helpful manner. Work is actually

approved for about 50 schools in Belfast,
and for 10 schools in County Down. At
most of these schools the work is now in
progress, and in some of them it has
already been completed. The House can
rest assured that nothing is being left.
undone that ought to be done, and all

school children who are in danger zones
in as much safety as lies in our power.
Certain schools in Belfast which
appeared to the Ministry
to be
structurally unsound for the present

I am glad to tell the House that, as a

I should like hon. Members to realise

to the necessity of safeguarding the position of the teachers, and we consider that
the double shifts will enable us to absorb
those who are affected.
expenditure is recouped in full by the

in Great Britain.
I should like to draw the attention of
hon. Members to Clause 5 of this Bill.
It represents a change in the Education
Act of 1939, the Act which dealt with
evacuation problems. Under that Act
any expenditure incurred by a "receiving" authority for educational services
was recouped by the "evacuating
authority" and where the latter's financial scheme for the year was thereby exceeded, a grant of 50 per cent. of the
excess was payable by the Ministry. This
is not now in accordance with the practice
in Great Britain where such additional
Apart from the question of air-raid
precautions and evacuation there is
another matter dealt with in Clause 7, to
which I wish to draw attention. Shortly
after the outbreak of war it was decided
to suspend grants under Section 10 of the
1930 Act. I think hon. Members are
aware that Section 10 dealt with the provision or equipment of new voluntary
schools, or the alteration, enlargement or
equpiment of existing voluntary schools,
and one half of the expenditure was given
in that connection. These grants were
only to be given in cases of extreme
urgency. However, there were a number

the schools is to carry on. There are
also other cases where applications had
been made for additional accommodation
before the war and where temporary
additional accommodation is now available. In both these cases Clause 7 gives
the Ministry power to pay half the cost
of temporary additional accommodation.
I may add that these grants will be made
without any condition as to the vesting
of the schools in trustees, which was a
feature of the clause in the 1930 Act. The
only condition will be that the school be
maintained and carried on as
a public
elementary school, for such period as the

hon. Member will agree that these are
absolutely just and reasonable proposals.
In the Bill there are also a few minor
educational adjustments, but these

broad outlines of our policy. Our main
object is to assist the education authorities
(and, through them, the voluntary
managers, and also the governing bodies.
of secondary schools) to give adequate

charge.

if we sat with folded hands and made no

Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move:
"That this House views with alarm the
serious plight of our blind pensioners,
and feels the necessity for setting up a
committee to inquire into the whole
matter in order to give a decent standard
of life to these pensioners; and is of
opinion that the Government should
adopt a step-by-step policy similar to
that in Great Britain whereby blind
pensioners are given a certain degree of
security."
In putting forward this Motion it is
my desire that we should give greater
practical help to blind pensioners. It is
regrettable that such pensioners were
omitted from recent legislation passed
whereby supplementary aid was given to
old-age pensioners and contributory
pensioners. The omission of our blind
pensioners from recent Acts was a serious
mistake. I am afraid that this Govern-

do in a matter of this kind, I think that

area. He said there was a certain amount

Ministry of Home Affairs, but I understand that these children have been

there is no risk of infection as they are

have no reason for alarm on this point.

STANDARD PRICE OF OATS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
present position in regard to the standard
price of 12s 6d per cwt. for oats; how it
operates; and what procedure farmers
must follow in order to obtain this standard price.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The standard
price of oats for the 1940 crop is 11s 6d
per cwt., and for the 1941 crop 12s 6d
per cwt.
A subsidy will become payable if the
price per cwt. of oats sold in the United
Kingdom during the seven months
September, 1940, to March, 1941, is less
than the standard price by threepence or
more, and will be at the rate of 14 times
such difference in respect of each statute
acre of oats grown.
If a subsidy becomes payable it will be
made in the same manner as in pre-war
years, namely, by sending out to each
producer an appropriate form of application.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE

Mr. MacDERMOTT: A supply of

the population of County Fermanagh
was issued by the Ministry to the local
A.R.P. authorities during the summer.
I understand that the local authorities
have already completed the distribution
of respirators in the urban district of
Enniskillen and in the villages of the
surrounding rural areas. Issues to the
population residing in the remaining lesspopulous areas is, I am informed, proceeding.

Council proposes to provide a number of

Hall for use as a shelter. The scheme

however, and the Ministry has been informed that some shelters have been
completed.

SHOOTING INCIDENT IN FALLS

16. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Public Security whether last
week in the Falls Road area police fired
on a lad who, when called on to halt for

some of the bullets penetrated a shop to
the imminent danger of the trader in
occupation, and whether the Minister can

substantially as stated by the hon.
Member, though I have no information
that the warning shot which penetrated
the shop window did in fact endanger the
occupier.
The police are enjoined to use the
greatest discretion in the use of firearms
in effecting an arrest, and I am satisfied
that on the present occasion the action
which was taken was justified.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
say whether on this occasion the bullet
perforated a scarf around this boy's
neck, whether he received a flesh wound
on the arm, and whether soon afterwards
his father, a decent old man, had to be

that the boy was fired at not, as I understand, for the purpose of hitting him,
but to stop him. When called on by

and law-abiding household need have, any
alarm on account of a visit by members

1930, to include such works as may be

Mr. HENDERSON: May I say I am
whole-heartedly in support of this Bill?
It is rather unfortunate that it is not

The.
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): May I
interrupt the hon. Member to point out
that this is not the Bill but the Money
Resolution?
Mr. HENDERSON: This is to provide
the money to enable the local authorities
to purchase the materials. Are you aware
that it is nearly impossible to get cement
in Northern Ireland to-day?
The TEMPORARY CHAIRMAN
(Mr. Beattie): Would the hon. Member
pardon me? The Parliamentary Secretary points out that this is not the Bill.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am referring to
the Money Resolution, and you must pass
this Money Resolution before you can put
into operation the matters contained in
the Bill. My contention is that it is
going to cost 78 per cent. more owing to
the delay of the Government. It is the
policy of the Government to wait, and
by the time this Money Resolution and
the Bill are passed another three or four
months will have elapsed without anything being done.
The provision of money for the education of the evacuated children amazes
me. It would have been far better if
money had been provided to see that the
children got suitable places to live in
instead of pig-styes. In some parts of
Northern Ireland they are accommodated
in homes that could not be classified
except as hovels of the filthiest and worst
description, filled with vermin of every
kind. Children from Belfast, in many
instances, returned from Eglinton and
other parts of County Derry; from homes
in which the dogs were eating out of the
pots the children's food was cooked in.
If this money had been utilised to get
decent homes it would have served a
useful purpose.
We told the noble Lord the Prime
Minister five years ago that there was
going to be a war and we told him to
take the necessary precautions for the
defence of Ulster as one of the outposts
of the British Empire, but he dilly-dallied
and did nothing. This scheme will now
cost from 80 per cent. to 90 per cent.
more than it would have cost had it been
undertaken nine or ten months
ago. It
should have been introduced at the same
time the scheme in Great Britain was
brought in. Then the people of this
country would have been properly protected and the children would have been
safer than they are to-day.
Although the Government are asking
for this money to provide air-raid precautions in the schools some of the
members of the rural district councils and
county councils, who have the handling
of it, will do nothing unless they are driven
to it by the Government. They are hopeless. There should have been a Clause
in the Bill under which the Government
took over the scheme. It could then
have been done cheaper than it will be
by these oid gentlemen who have nothing
to do but while away the latter days of
their lives. While I support this Bill
wholeheartedly I wish to protest against
the delay. It will cost the taxpayers of
this country thousands and thousands of
pounds because the Minister at the head
of the Department was not alive to the

Under Subhead B.1 a sum of £2,500
is required for the purpose of training

with a view to increasing the area under
flax in the 1941 season to 100,000 acres,

present season. It is expected that there
will be sufficient scutch mills available to
deal with the increase in the acreage,

apprentices by means of a course of training of not less than ten weeks, and until
such times as the trainees have attained

scutcher, that is the trainer, and the

tends to interfere with the right of a
democratic State. I am a bitter opponent
of any who try to tamper with or destroy
the democratic principle which I and the
party I represent uphold. Can I visualise
the world to-day as being likely to be a
safeguard for those democratic liberties
that we all hold dear? After thirteen
months of war I think all of us can only
come, to the conclusion that nothing in
this world is safe at the present time. I
remember the year 1933 when Hitler
became the Chancellor of Germany. The
German State at that time was
a well
organised State. There was something in
the region of 14 million people organised.
They had their established institutions for
looking after the welfare of the working
classes. They had everything that the
workers of any country could desire to
have for collective bargaining. By the
year 1935 the whole trade union movement had been destroyed and its property
confiscated. The Social Democratic Party
had been built up with a membership of
4 million working class people. The
leaders of that party were pursued and
finally detained. Some of them are still
living in prison.
The result of the work in that year
1933 and the reorganisation of the leading
lights of the German Government was the
destruction of everything that we in the
working-class movement hold dear, and to
prevent destruction of that kind coming
to this country or Great Britain I am
prepared to take any risk which I think
will tend towards a solution of a very

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Lord Glentoran).
Mr. CAMPBELL: Now that excitement has died down and, I take it, the
House is beginning to break up, there is
one matter which I am bound to bring to
the attention of the House and especially
of the hon. and learned Minister of
Public Security in the hope that some
remedy will be found for the state of
things to which I wish to refer. It has
been stated to me by people whose
opinions I respect that an earnest protest ought to be made against the raiding
of humble homes where peaceable, lawabiding people live. These people, on
whose behalf I speak, have no sympathy
with crime or criminals. They detest
crime and they detest criminals. They
are the victims of vexatious raids in the
dead of night, and some of these quiet
folk are being driven to desperation.
Doubtless the malevolence of some secret
enemy is the means of sending the police
roaming through the houses of these
innocent people.
My information is that the raiding has
eased off a little since last week, and
that there is not now such a general reign
of terror.
I am informed that there has been a
class of police imported into this district
of which I speak who look upon the
people there as enemies and who treat
them without civility and without
courtesy. These people in the Falls area
have every right to be treated as their
fellow-citizens in other parts of Belfast.
If the statements which have been made
to me, and which I accept, are correct,
it is small wonder that the locality is
seething with indignation and discontent.
The chief complaint of the people is
directed against the ceaseless harassing of
people of excellent character. They are
interrogated, they are searched; they are
asked for their identity cards sometimes
thrice within an hour. They are insulted
with impunity, and they cannot reply,
because they know if they answer back
they will probably be arrested. They
are afraid to venture out into the streets
before their neighbours, so they remain
indoors. Sometimes they go for a quiet
walk to the parks, but there again they
are met by detectives and questioned.
They are all supposed to be guilty until
they prove their innocence.
In this House recently some reference
was made to men who were interned, and
they were described as potential criminals. That was given as a justification
for keeping them in jail, not actual
criminals, not proved criminals, but
potential criminals. Every man in this
House is a potential criminal. I do not
except myself or the Minister for Public
Security. We are, in our own several ways,
not without imperfections on our heads.
If men are to be interned and kept in
prison on the basis of being potential
criminals the whole population of Belfast
may be in jail.
The streets are cordoned off at night in
the terror of the black-out. I wonder if
in the Malone Road a few individuals
were being searched the Malone Road
would be cordoned off and the inhabitants
submitted to a house-to-house scrutiny in
the black-out. I think not. One boy
was mentioned to-day in the course of the
question and answer. He was shot in a
busy main thoroughfare and without any
deep regard for the safety of passers-by
because the bullet actually penetrated the
shop of a neighbouring trader. The use
of firearms in that way is an extraordinary state of affairs in a quiet community. That is not done, by the Gestapo
or by the Russian Ogpu but by our own
police force. The scarf round the boy's
neck was perforated by the bullet, and
he received a gunshot wound in the arm
because he. ran and tried to get away. It
was only by the mercy of Providence that
he escaped being killed.

The truth of the matter is at the
present time there is a widespread conspiracy in Belfast and outside it on the
part of people who are, beyond all
question, organised against the State,
and not only organised against the State,
but prepared to support the enemy. And
they are armed. I think even the hon.
Members will agree that it is the
bounden duty of the police to find these
men and find the arms. That can best
be done with the full co-operation of
every member of the community. I
should like the hon. Members some time
to give expression to that duty on the
part of members of the community, both
those they represent and others, because
if there was full information given to
the police there would be less need for
raids. No one regrets more than I do
the inconvenience innocent people are put
to by raids.
As long as the campaign has to be
waged against this dangerous and subversive element and as long as the raids
prove useful they will continue. They
have proved useful. It is idle to suggest
that there is nothing under the surface
in the Falls Road district. Recent
occurrences which have been the subject
of debate in this House show that. Lest
it be suggested when I refer to a
dangerous conspiracy that I am drawing

Members to bear in mind that in the
area with which they are acquainted
within the last few days men stopped on
the street have been found with loaded
revolvers upon them. I am speaking
now of a period covered within the last
week, and not only that but we have
found articles such as were contained in
this haul in one house:-One Thomson
machine-gun, one
pistol of modern
German make, four pistols, three revolvers, two rifles, Mills bomb and 400 to
500 rounds of ammunition. When one
finds men going about the street armed
in the way I have described and when
one finds arsenals of the kind I have
mentioned, it is surely obvious that the

Police Raids in Belfast
police must leave no stone unturned to
see that the arms are got and that the
men on whom suspicion rests are apprehended.
Everyone knows that when you are
looking for a suspected man you do not
find him in his own house. One does not
find arms in the houses of suspects. More
often indeed they are concealed in the
houses of people about whom there is no
suspicion. One finds that the people who
are suspect will go into the houses of
people who are not suspect. It is evident
that every person who has the public
security at heart must feel that the sooner
these men who are members of this subversive organisation are rounded up the
better. I hope some time I will hear from
the hon. Members that they are strongly
of that opinion too. In the campaign
which the police must wage and which,
so far as I can see to-day, they will wage

raids must be very inconvenient for those
who are innocent, but if they are
innocent the raids should prove nothing
to worry about.
Why should the hon. Members not
come out into the open and advise all and
sundry, their Own constituents and
others, to do all in their power to help
the police to lay by the heels this conspiracy in our midst? Why should they
not end these raids by bringing the cause
for them to an end? If they do that
nobody will be more pleased than myself
when the raids finish, but to stop them
now would be to help the I.R.A. and
hinder the police.
So far as conduct of the police during
raids is concerned, I will be only too glad
if hon. Members will bring to my notice
any cases of insults being offered. I
believe, in courtesy at all times, and I
will not tolerate insulting behaviour on
the part of the police. I believe that
what the hon. Members have said about
these actions of the. police has been
grossly exaggerated. This is a matter of
importance because it is a matter of
public security, and I implore the hon.
Members not to spend so much time

all in their power to ensure that the
police have the community behind them.
In this way the war against the State
will be brought to an end.

1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether it is a fact
that a retired lady member of the
Northern Ireland Civil Service, who was
pensioned off from the Ministry of
Labour, has been recalled to his Ministry
and promoted to the rank of deputy
principal; whether he can state if any
serving civil servants were qualified to
receive this promotion, and, if so, on
whose advice this lady was recalled;
whether he can state the rank and salary
at date of retirement which this lady
enjoyed and her present scale of saiary,
and her age.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): A
woman civil servant who recently retired
on pension from the Ministry of Labour
has been recalled to the service as a temassistant in the Civil Defence
porary
Division of my Ministry.
The salary fixed for her present
appointment is £296 13s 4d per annum,
and this amount, together with the
pension that she is receiving, brings her
total emoluments up to £600 per annum.
This lady has not been promoted. At
the date of her retirement she was serving
in the grade of staff officer with a salary
of £650 a year.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether the made-up salary is not in the
region of a deputy principal's grade or
scale of salary at £650 and why is this
lady being paid £600.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I think the
salary paid is short of that of a deputy
principal. The reason this lady was
brought back was that there was no senior
woman in the Ministry, and as the
Ministry has many contacts with women's
organisations it was thought proper there
should be a senior woman official.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would ask the right
hon. Gentleman to answer the last part
of my question. How long was the lady
pensioned off from the Ministry of Labour
and what is her present age?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The lady was
pensioned off four months ago. With
regard to age I hope the hon. Member
will not put me in the ungallant position.
of having to reveal the age of the lady.
I can give him this information, that she
retired at the ordinary age of retirement.

civil servants to raise this matter on the

5 NOVEMBER 1940
PROMOTIONS IN ROYAL ULSTER
CONSTABULARY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he can state
the total number of promotions made in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary since the
1st September, 1939, up to 1st October,
1940, by competitive examination; the
number of promotions to the rank of
Sergeant, Head Constable, District
Inspector; and whether he can state on
whose advice promotions are made, and,
if not made by competitive examination,
what policy is adopted.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The total number
of promotions made in the Royal Ulster
Constabulary during the period 1st
September, 1939, to 1st October, 1940,
as a result of competitive examinations
was 25. The number of promotions from
constable to sergeant was 49; from
sergeant to head constable 11; and from
head constable to district inspector 3. In
cases where it was not practicable to hold
examinations, promotions were made by
selection, due regard being paid to
seniority and to the recommendations of
