10. Mr. WARNOCK asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that in
Great Britain men called up for military service are entitled by Act of Parliament to reinstatement in their jobs
on the termination of their service, and
that even in Eire a similar statutory
right exists for men joining the defence
forces there, and whether he can state
when and why the Government of Northern Ireland decided to deny to the
volunteers from Northern Ireland who
have joined His Majesty's Forces this
advantage which is enjoyed by the English conscript.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am
aware that under the Compulsory Service Acts applying conscription in Great
Britain provision is made designed to
safeguard the employment of those who
have been called to the Colours, and
similar protection is afforded members of
the Reserve, including those residing in
Northern Ireland.
No such provision has been made in
the case of volunteers in Great Britain,
and it is not within the powers of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland to legislate on the matter.
I am hopeful, however, that employers generally will afford every
facility to their workers to enlist in
H.M. Forces and that they will give the
same measure of protection to volunteers
as would have been given if conscription
had been applied in Northern Ireland.

his Ministry is compelling applicants
who apply for free milk to make a return
of the wages of their husbands who are

change has been made by his Ministry
different from the procedure followed by
the Ministry of Labour.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Eligibility for free
milk under the National Milk Scheme is
determined on the basis of the joint income of the husband and wife. In
regard to
houseapplications from
holders in Northern Ireland where the
husband is in employment in Great
Britain, it is recognised that it is not
always possible for the applicantusually the wife to make an accurate
statement as to the husband's earnings
at the time of application. Where, however, the Ministry is satisfied that the

action, a free milk permit is issued pending completion of inquiries on the

The procedure followed in regard to
cases where the husband is employed
away from home was adopted after consultation with the Ministry of Food. I
am most anxious that no hardship, to
children or anyone else, should arise out
of any methods of procedure, and should
be glad to consult with the hon. Member
at any time.

FACTORIES.
15. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state what
steps were taken by his Ministry, and
when they were taken, to obtain for Northern Ireland as part of the United
Kingdom, its share of the many sugar
beet factories, potato factories, flax
factories, and other similar factories
already erected, and in process of
erection, in Great Britain with state
assistance provided on an equal basis by
the taxpayers of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The hon.
Member can rest assured that the whole
question of the processing of agricultural
products is receiving constant consideration with due regard to Northern Ireland
conditions. I have already explained the
position in regard to sugar beet. The
position with regard to potato factories
has been discussed at full length on the
various Motions tabled by the hon.
Member. I have nothing to add to what
I then said. As to flax factories, I am
afraid the hon. Member does not
appreciate the position. The factories in
England exist solely for processing green
straw to the green fibre stage. This work
is being undertaken in Northern Ireland
by existing firms who are receiving a substantially higher price for their fibre than
firms in Great Britain as compensation
for the capital they are investing in this
new process. The hon. Member may,
therefore, rest assured that in these
matters Northern Ireland is being treated
strictly on a United Kingdom basis.
Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact that
I am not sure of any such thing I
propose to raise this matter on the
Adjournment.

Ministry and are selling them at a lower
price? Will he take steps to have potato
factories established so that these potatoes
may be used in the manufacture of feeding stuffs?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am fully
aware of the position with regard to
potatoes at present. My Ministry have
made representations to the Ministry of
Food with regard to that. With reference
to the other part of the question I should
say that where potatoes are processed in
a factory the cost goes on to the feeding
stuffs and we are used in this country to
feeding pigs from the pits. It would be
inadvisable to have the potatoes processed
through a factory.

an economical proposition in England
why not in Northern Ireland?
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister prepared to withdraw the statement that
these factories would pay £1 a ton for

Sir BASIL BROOKE: No, that statement is not true. The processing of
potatoes does not pay the farmer as well.
Mr. BROWN: Is it a fact that the
Minister is now contradicting a statement
made by Lord Woolton? I am prepared
to accept Lord Woolton's statement.

The amount payable to a pensioner

We now turn to the Lagan Canal.
Unfortunately this undertaking is unable
to balance receipts and expenditure, but
were it to be abandoned the burden which
would fall on public funds would be no
light one. Moreover, the canal undertaking, in addition to providing navigation facilities, acts as a useful means of
drainage, controls the level of the Lagan,
and provides water supplies for industrial
establishments. The £2,000 included in
the present Estimate is the sum necessary
to maintain the navigation in being until
the end of the financial year and, also,
to carry out certain repairs which I am
advised are essential. These works include
the building of portions of the wall of
one lock and the building of two new
culverts to carry streams and flood waters
under the canal. The remedial work
necessary has had the effect of interrupting traffic on the canal for a short period.

RATIONING OF FEEDING STUFFS
12. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is a fact that
in the proposed rationing scheme for
feeding stuffs, while provision is being
made for a supply for dairy cows, the
milk of which is to go direct to the liquid
milk market, no provision is being made
for the supply of feeding stuffs for dairy
cows, the milk from which goes to the
various creameries.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The answer is
in the negative. Feeding stuffs will be
made available under the rationing
scheme for all cows producing Grade A,
B or C milk, whether such milk goes into
the liquid market or is used for manufacturing purposes. Approximately 56
per cent. of the cows supplying milk to
the creameries come within this category. It will not, however, be possible
to make provision for cows supplying
ungraded milk which is not suitable for
sale in the liquid market.
The production of milk for this market is
fast becoming a matter of paramount
national importance and it is essential
that the available supplies of feeding
stuffs should be utilised to encourage
that production. Further, the hon.
Member will bear in mind that producers of Grade D milk are mostly
seasonal producers whose COWS are
mainly on the grass and who did not in
pre-war days purchase imported feeding stuffs to any appreciable extent. I
would also remind the hon. Member that
most of these producers have a much
larger quantity of home-grown oats
available for feeding as a result of the
tillage campaign.

course, is done in order that prices to consumers may be kept at a reasonable level

have always acted accordingly. In the

what is the most important statement

whole industry. The statement
our
reads:-
It was Mr. Alexander Proctor, the
noted Scots flax expert, who originated
the idea that flax growing in these
islands should be harnessed to sugar
beet production. The scheme has
much to commend it and this is an
opportune time to reconsider its advantages. It would offer the farmer two
highly remunerative crops, one root
and the other cereal. It would enable
farmers to bring old grassland speedily
into condition for beet and other root
crops, as flax disintegrates old turf
twice as fast as grain, and-unlike
grain-is immune to the deadly
attacks of wire worm, the plague of
old grassland.
Hitherto, the chief drawback of the
sugar beet industry has been its
inability to provide constant employment either for its works, its agricultural and even its clerical staff. The
incorporation of flax fibre production
with sugar production, argues Mr.
Proctor, should about halve the overhead costs of sugar production and
abolish these chief drawbacks of the
sugar beet industry. One-half to twothirds of the flax crop could be treated
on the farms where it is grown before
beet lifting and manufacturing begins.
That is the statement in the "Belfast
Telegraph." The hon. Member for
North Armagh referred to the Select
Committee on Unemployment. I am not
going to refer to that Committee in any
shape or form, directly or indirectly. I
have not done so, and shall not do so.
I read that statement for the purpose of
getting it on the records of this House.
I think if it is studied it will prove to
be the greatest boon that we have had in
regard to flax production in this country.
for many a long day. It will also prove
of the greatest benefit from the industrial
and economic points of view.
According to the Proctor theory, the
four winter months devoted to sugar
manufacture are the very months most
unsuitable for flax production, so that
there would be four months beet sugar
manufacture and eight months flax
production for the permanent staff to
attend to, making an all-the-yearround job. Thus would continuity of
central rettery and sugar mill employment be assured, and both crops
would be most economically dealt
with. Some eighteen sugar beet
factories are operated in England by
the British Sugar Corporation, and it
should rot require much inducement
to get the Corporation to join hands
here with flax production interests.

OFFER OF WORK IN ENGLAND.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that unemployed farm workers in Fermanagh are
now being offered industrial work in
England, and upon their refusal to
undertake duties in which they are quite
inexperienced, their benefit is suspended,
and they are also held in some cases as
"not being available;" whether work on
farms is not regarded in England as a
reserved occupation, and whether he
thinks employment in industrial areas
across the Channel a suitable situation for
such persons.
farm labourers are, with other suitable
workers, offered employment in Great
Britain on unskilled work of national
importance. Subject to the men being
physically fit, the work calls for no special
qualifications other than ability to use a
pick and shovel, and it is, therefore, well
within the competence of the average
farm labourer (many of whom are accustomed to take spell employment as general
labourers, or as road or quarry workers).
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Unemployed men registered as
I have no reason to think that unskilled
work in Great Britain of the kind now
being offered to unemployed farm workers
is unsuitable for them, and I may say
that these offers are made with due regard
to our
our own probable requirements for
farm labour.
Agricultural workers are reserved at
the age of twenty-one by the Schedule of
Reserved Occupations, but the purpose of
this reservation is to debar such workers
from being claimed by His Majesty's
Forces. Neither here nor in Great Britain
does it operate to prevent farm workers
engaging in other kinds of employment.
On the question of suspension of unemployment benefit, the hon. Member is
aware that the Unemployment Insurance
Acts lay down the disqualification to be
imposed in cases where suitable employment is refused.
It is also a condition for the receipt of
benefit that an applicant proves that he is
available for work, and it will be appreciated that where an applicant continues
to refuse offers of suitable employment,
the question as to whether that condition
is fulfilled is a matter which has to be
considered by the statutory authorities.

2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

frequent experience at the Enniskillen
Referee Court.
Mr. GORDON: It is not the case that
unemployment benefit must be continued
pending the decision of a court of referees
on the claims of applicants who refuse
offers of suitable employment.
Regulations made under the Unemployment Insurance (Emergency Powers)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1939, provide
that insurance officers can disallow benefit where offers of suitable employment
are refused.
It is not the case that six to seven
weeks frequently elapse between the date
of the suspension of benefit and the
hearing of an appeal by the Enniskillen
Court. In the few cases where there has
been any lengthy suspension of benefit it
has been due to delay on the part of the
claimants in lodging their appeals
against the insurance officer's decision.

Subject to their comparative suitability, single men are sent in preference
to married men; and married men
sent only to jobs that carry an allowance
of 3s 6d per night for seven days per

Since all benefit or assistance due is paid

The
MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have seen the Press
report to which the hon. Member refers.
I am aware that the restrictions which
the Imperial Government have been

yarns for the manufacture of hosiery for

Sir DAWSON BATES: The boys who

any
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether boys who are
committed to Malone Reformatory are
sent there with the primary object of
receiving such moral and other training
as will enable them to earn an honest
livelihood and become good citizens;
whether boys who have a good record in
the institution are subject, without
reason, to police visits and attention
after they leave the institution; and
whether the police have been supplying
lists of convictions against such boys, for
offences committed before committal, for
the express purpose of preventing them
from finding employment.
Up to the year 1936, when an application was made by a parent or other
person for the discharge of a boy from
Malone to enable him to enter employment, it had been the practice to ask
the police to make inquiries on such an
application, and amongst others they
invariably interviewed the proposed employer to see whether, in fact, the offer
of employment was genuine. It was
subsequently represented to the Ministry
by Mr. Watson, the Governor of the
School, that such police visits to potential
employers rather militated against the
chances of a boy obtaining employment,
particularly if it became known that he
had been an inmate of a reformatory.
The Ministry thereupon appointed
Mr. Rogers, the school welfare officer, to
undertake such investigation, and the
practice of bringing the police into such.
cases then ceased. So far the system
has worked very satisfactorily.
It is untrue to say that the police
supply lists of convictions against such
boys for the purpose of preventing them
from entering employment. What does
happen is that if a boy, who has been
previously an inmate of Malone Training
School, has the misfortune to fall into
the hands of the police after discharge
for an offence committed by him, the police
supply the court with a list of any previous convictions, including the fact that
he had been a former inmate of Malone
Training School, but this is done as a
matter of practice in the court proceedings and not for the purpose of preventing the boy from obtaining employment.
I am sorry that this question should
have been raised as it is the Government's one desire that every boy leaving
the Malone Training School should get
every chance to obtain employment and
become a useful member of the community.
Mr. NIXON: How can the Minister
make that statement about convictions
and offences when I had the courtesy

convictions were in fact supplied to the

9. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether, in view of the fact that
undue hardship will be caused to many
property owners in Northern Ireland by
increases of upwards of 50 per cent. in
income-tax on property under the British
Finance Act passed in June last, assessing
such tax on rentals instead of on the Poor
Law Valuation, which increases in Northern Ireland will be over and above the increases in the rate of tax, he will make
immediate representations to the British
Chancellor of the Exchequer for some
relief by way of increased repairs, allowances, etc., or, alternatively, whether he
will advise the Government to take steps
to have repealed the Valuation Acts
(Amendment) Act (Northern Ireland),
1932, as the object it was designed to
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): As the hon. Member is aware,
prior to the present financial year taxpayers whose income was derived wholly
or partly from rented property were in a
privileged position in comparison with
other taxpayers and I feel sure that there
is general agreement that that position.
should no longer be allowed to continue.
I could not, therefore, especially at a
time when money is urgently required for
war purposes, agree to make representations to the Imperial Government, or to
take any action which would place property owners in Northern Ireland in a
better position than their fellow-citizens
in Great Britain owning property of a
similar kind. The hon. Member can
depend upon me, however, doing my best
to ensure that N.I. property owners are
not placed at a disadvantage.
I do not consider that the repeal of
the 1932 Valuation Act would achieve the
purpose which the hon. Member has in
mind, for the following reasons—
(1) The owner of rented property
would receive no benefit since incometax on such property is now being levied
on the actual income arising from the
property.
(2) The rate position would not be
affected because the rate depends upon
the expenditure to be met by the local
authority.
I should, perhaps, add that a repeal of
the Act would reintroduce all those unjust
anomalies which existed as between
different ratepayers prior to the passing
of the Act.

wards we will take the Second Reading of

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.
Andrews) (who was received with
cheers): You, Sir, have already paid a
fitting, eloquent and touching tribute to
2667 Adjournment of the House- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Tributes to late Prime Minister 2668
[The Prime Minister]
our
the memory of one who was beloved by
us all. We meet to-day under the
shadow of a most grievous loss. From
assembly the commanding and
revered figure of Lord Craigavon has
departed, and with his passing a powerful and inspiring force has been withdrawn.
Only a week ago he was with usalert in mind, virile in debate, a born
leader, a gifted and distinguished Prime
Minister. With almost
almost overwhelming
suddenness we have lost his noble
presence. But there will ever remain
with us the memory of his firm and
friendly voice, his kindly eye, the hearty
clasp of his hand, the stability of his
judgment, the wisdom of his counsel.
was
Lord Craigavon was a great Ulsterman, a great Irishman, a great Imperialist. His love of country
innate, sincere and strong. It was the
key to his whole career-as soldier and
statesman, Parliamentarian and Premier.
That fundamental patriotism led him to
serve with gallantry in the South
African War, to take his part in the
work of the Mother of Parliaments
before this Parliament of Northern
Ireland was established; to shoulder the
responsibilities of leadership at one of the
most critical periods in Ulster's history;
to fight tenaciously for the principles in
which he profoundly believed. In him
Ulster saw an epitome of itself. He
was the symbol and embodiment of its
ideals.
When Lord Craigavon became the
head of the Government of Northern
Ireland nearly twenty years ago he was
confronted with difficulties that would
have daunted the hearts of lesser men.
He grappled fearlessly with a troubled
and complex situation, and overcoming
formidable obstacles, he led Ulster along
the path of ordered government and
peaceful progress.
This is a moment when political
differences
may be forgotten and controversy stilled. We in this House, to
whatever school of thought we may
belong, unite in paying our respect and
homage to a man whose life was devoted,
with singleness of purpose, to the service
of the State. Even those who did not
share Lord Craigavon's views readily
acknowledged the deep sincerity with
which he held them. To supporters and
opponents alike he was ever fair and
courteous. He strove always to keep the
debates of this House on the highest level
and to maintain the dignity and traditions of Parliament.
Those of us whose privilege it was
to serve under his leadership know how
unswerving was his fidelity, how valiant
his spirit, how far-seeing his vision. I
counted it an honour, as one of his
lieutenants, to be associated with him
in bringing Ulster through those years
of turmoil and peril and in building the
structure of the State on firm and lasting
foundations.
By instinct and training he was a
democrat. Repeatedly he declared himself a firm believer in a free Parliament
and a free Press. He was not insensitive
to criticism. He knew the sting of pain
that a harsh and unfair word could inflict.
Yet he was big enough to receive such
occasional wounds without complaining
and without bitterness. He bore no
malice, and never allowed political
antagonisms to quench personal friendships.
At no time during his long and distinguished career did Lord Craigavon
reveal his greatness more clearly than in
the last two years of his life. When the
storm-clouds were. gathering over Europe
and war was drawing near he boldly
assured the Imperial Government of
Ulster's support, whatever might betide
In doing this he rightly interpreted the
mind of the Ulster people. So, too, did
both Houses of our Parliament. At
length the storm broke, the conflict came
-and Lord Craigavon was ready to meet
it. During nearly fifteen months of war
he devoted all his energies to the task of
making Ulster's manifold contribution to
the war effort increasingly powerful and
effective. His confidence in the triumph
of our cause was firm and unshakable.
He has not lived to see the day of victory,
but he has left us a lofty example of
faith and resolute purpose.
Less than a month ago, speaking in this
House, Lord Craigavon
Craigavon used these
words:
"Northern Ireland, please God,
under the old flag, and under the King
and Constitution, will carry on."
Those words ring in our ears to-day, and
I would make them my own. Northern

Ireland will carry on. Within the British
Empire Ulster will play its part in the
post-war world, and will find its inspiration in the life and work of him whose
loss we mourn to-day.
Our hearts go out in tender sympathy
to Lady Craigavon and the members of
the family in their hour of sorrow. We
know that they will find solace, as we
do, in the thought that the one who has
been taken from them died, as he had
lived, a devoted and faithful servant of
his King and country, a true friend of
the people among whom he lived and
whose welfare was constantly in his
thoughts.
No one can adequately fill his place.
Those of us who follow him can only
pray to be given strength to carry on
his work and to follow his noble example
of public-spirited integrity and unselfish
devotion to duty. I feel that I am speaking for my friends on this side of the
House, and I would be gratified also to
feel that my words have met with the

opposite. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In taking up the task that Lord
Craigavon has laid down we feel that if

Mr. BEATTIE: This is one of the
occasions which Members of this House
do not like to meet very often. The
occasion of the passing
passing out of a
Member is in itself depressing, but when
it is a leading light of the House on
the Government side it certainly casts
a gloom and shadow over our whole
proceedings. I myself cannot go back
just as long as Mr. Speaker or the right
hon. Gentleman, the new Prime Minister, but I can go back a little bit into
British political history. When I met
the late Prime Minister first I think the
hon. Member for Duncairn (Mr. Grant)
was with me. Lord Craigavon was in
the position of Parliamentary Secretary
of the Pensions branch in the British
House of Commons, and on the formation of the Lloyd George Government
he took up another position that threw
me into direct contact with him in my
capacity as a trade union official. From
that period on to the end of the Great
When this Parliament was established
I did not succeed on finding entrance,
but on the second attempt I was successful. Since that time I had many conflicts with the Prime Minister and at
times one looking on wondered how those
conflicts and the things that were said
could easily be forgotten. Notwithstanding all the political conflicts I had with.
the late Prime Minister I never found
that he allowed them to remain in his
mind or that he held them over for time
everlasting. I have been at daggers
drawn with him across this Table, and
yet when I walked into the corridor
I found the man whom I had been
challenging ready to accept me in a
homely way and to engage in a friendly
conversation, so that you yourself felt
sometimes more hurt than the man you
intended to hurt.
I put that down to two things. The
Prime Minister was a big man, both in
stature and in every other way. He
did not allow small things to worry him.
One quality I appreciated about him was
that when he made up his mind
on any question he determined to see
it put into operation. He knew what
he wanted, and knew how to get it.
He did not get into conflict with the
rights of Members in this House. He
himself was the embodiment of the
Parliamentary institution. He believed
in every Member, no matter whom he
represented, getting the same free right
as the representatives of the largest
Party.
I feel to-day that the Government have
lost a stalwart in the interests of their
cause, a man who knew how to lead, how
to marshal his forces and how to attack
when attack was needed. Such a position
cannot be filled by ordinary Members of
the House. It has been stated many
times that leaders are not made but born.
I must say from my experience that Lord
Craigavon must have been a born leader
2671 Tributes to late Prime Minister HOUSE OF COMMONS
Tributes to late Prime Minister 2672
[Mr. Beattie]
because he proved his leadership in this
House on many occasions by defeating
many things I thought would have been
successful. I believe he was sincere in
everything he did. His whole objective
in life was to keep this part of Ireland
associated with the Empire and to make
the Empire feel that this Province was
really part and parcel of itself.
He was also desirous of making Northern Ireland play its part in the great
struggle now raging, and neither I nor
anyone else can say that he failed in his
objective. I say now that Ulster, though
a smail unit of the Empire, is pulling her
strength towards the victory which we
hope will come very soon. It is to be
regretted that he has not lived to see the
fruition of his labours to that end, and
we hope that we shall be spared to see
the culmination he so desired. I believe
that his brave endeavours to do his duty
must be appreciated by friend and foe.
By no one are they more appreciated
than by myself. I never in my life had
a private war with the late Prime
Minister. I want that to be clearly
understood. Any war we had was a
political war. I fought on political
ground and in a political way, and our
friendship remained when he left this
House on Tuesday last.
In conclusion, I wish to tender to Lady
Craigavon and her family my deepest
sympathy in the loss they have sustained,
the loss of a loving husband and father
who devoted himself to his home life. All
I can say is that although he is not present to protect her a greater Power will
give her that guidance and comfort which
she would have received from her departed
husband, but which she now misses.
The work that he carried on so successfully and so efficiently has now been
handed over to a colleague in the person
of the right hon. Gentleman the Minister
of Finance, and I hope I will be understood when I say that no better successor
could have been found. I do not say that
with five or six minutes' experience of the
right hon. Gentleman. There have been
conflicts between us in the past as severe
as those between the late Prime Minister
and myself. In my early days in this
House I was, perhaps, over-anxious on
some questions; I was, perhaps, overeager and unable to tolerate delay. At
that time the right hon. Gentleman was
Minister of Labour, and I have happy
recollections of those days. If the right
hon. Gentleman serves the cause of Ulster
in the same way as the late Prime Minister
did his associates and the members of his
party will have nothing to complain of.
I wish him every success in the very
heavy responsibilities which will devolve
upon him in guiding this Province from
to-day to the termination of the war.

Craigavon (Burial) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PRIME MINISTER: In moving
that a Second Reading be given to this
Bill, which is self explanatory, I feel
it is only necessary to say that I am
confident that it will be the desire of
hon. Members on both sides of the House
that the proposal contained in the Bill,
which I am sure would have been Lord
Craigavon's wish and which meets the
approval of his family, should be complied with and that he should be buried
in a plot of ground close to this building,
in the erection of which he took such a
particular interest and within the walls
of which he led this House with so much
acceptance, brilliancy and distinction for
so many years. We shall long cherish his
memory and mourn his loss. I beg to
move.

My dear Harry,

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): Of the
public elementary school teachers who
have completed their training within the
last three years, and, on 31st October,
1940, were available for employment as
teachers, 271 were women.
Of these, 115 were then in permanent
employment, 114 in temporary employment, and 42 were not employed. Of
those not employed, 32 (all of whom first.
became qualified in August, 1940) had
not received any employment as teachers.
On 31st October last, 20 men and 42
women teachers were unemployed.
Although the Ministry has not complete
information on the matter, it is probable
that all are unmarried; and, I may add,
for the Hon. Member's information,
that 48 of these teachers became qualified
only in August last.

1-PAY:
The onset of war conditions brought
about a vast increase in the police duties
in the area of the Harbour Estate, and
consequently responsibility for the
policing of the Estate was undertaken by
the Government of Northern Ireland,
after consultation with the Imperial
Defence Departments. It was decided
that the situation could best be met by
the formation of a new Royal Ulster Constabulary police district. The personnel
of this district consists of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, Special Constabulary, and
members of the Belfast Harbour Police.
The last-named are still the employees of
the Harbour Commissioners, and paid by
that body. All, however, are subject to
the Inspector-General for orders and
discipline.

CATTLE TRADERS AND THE
MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been called to the report in the Belfast
Press on the 13th instant of a special
Oral Answers

meeting of the Northern Ireland Cattle
Traders' 'and Stock Owners' Association,
at which resentment and indignation
were expressed by the chairman and other
speakers against a speech made by the
Minister describing as parasites those
engaged in an industry that has built up
a valuable export trade for Northern
Ireland; whether it is a fact, as stated at
the meeting, that the cattle trade in
Northern Ireland was practically ignored
on every occasion by his Ministry, and
that even representations to the Minister
were treated with scant courtesy; and
whether he will withdraw the undignified
epithet of "parasites" which he applied

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have seen the Press
report of the meeting referred to by the
hon. Member. It is not a fact that the
cattle trade in Northern Ireland was
ignored by my Ministry or that their
representations were treated with scant
courtesy.
With regard to the last part of the
question, it must be obvious that my
statement, to which the hon. Member
refers, did not and could not apply to any
of those who are engaged in the livestock
industry to the benefit of the farming
community.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
can he tell the House to whom the word
parasites was applied?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think the
hon. Member should be as well aware as
I am of what a parasite is.
Mr. NIXON: What does the Minister
mean by saying that the word complained
of could not apply to cattle traders who
are in the trade for the benefit of the
farming community? Would he state if
anyone in Northern Ireland is in a
position for the benefit of the community
or for his own benefit? I have never met
these people to whom the Minister refers.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: There are certain people to whom the description of
parasite applies-people who are not
conferring any benefit on the community.
Mr. BROWN: When may we look for
an end to all these blazing indiscretions
by the Minister in his speeches?
Mr. NIXON: Does that apply to Sir
Dudley McCorkell?

PAYMENTS TO SIR DUDLEY
McCORKELL.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is a fact that
when the former Pigs Marketing Board
was dissolved and Sir Dudley McCorkell,
Major Malcolm Speir and Colonel Patrick
were appointed by him to carry on that
work, an assurance was given by him in
this House that those gentlemen were
acting without any
remuneration;
whether it is a fact that immediately Sir
Dudley McCorkell ceased to draw his
salary of £300 per year as chairman of
the Pig Industry Council he was
allocated the same sum as chairman
of the Pigs Marketing Board without any
reference either to this House or to the
pig producers who must find the money;
and how was it he did not tell the House
this when he announced that as chairman
of the Pig Industry Council Sir Dudley
McCorkell had ceased to draw a salary
on the 30th June?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: On the 7th
March, 1939, I informed the House that
the three gentlemen I had nominated on
the new Pigs Marketing Board, namely,
Sir Dudley McCorkell, Major Speir and
Lieut.-Colonel Patrick, had intimated to
me their desire that their services, for the
present at any rate, should be accepted
without remuneration, and that I had
accepted this offer.
The chairman, Sir Dudley McCorkell,
served in an honorary capacity until the
30th June, 1940. After that date the
Pigs Marketing Board recommended that
he should be remunerated at the rate of
£300 per annum, and that recommendation was approved by my Ministry. The
question of reference to this House does
not, therefore, arise.
Mr. NIXON: Are these Boards being
invented for the purpose of putting
broken-down gentlemen on the salaried
list at the expense of the hard-pressed
public of Northern Ireland? Only I
have two more questions I would go
further than that.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do not agree
Iwith the hon. Member when he refers to
Sir Dudley McCorkell as a broken-down
gentleman. He is one of the most
valuable members of the community, and
the services he gives are worth more than
£300 a year to the pig producers of Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: Do you expect me to
believe that?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do not mind
whether you do or not.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the hon.
Member will resume his seat.
Mr. NIXON: I might. I know quite
well that I am out of order, but desperate
diseases require desperate remedies. I
shall resume my seat, but it is simply
because I have two questions.
Mr. SPEAKER: Will the hon.
Member resume his seat?
Mr. BEATTIE: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell the House whether this
is another £300 given to this gentleman
for another class of work or is it the
same £300 ?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The same
£300.

STUFFS.
Mr. BROWN (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether
representations in connection with the
proposed scheme of rationing of animal
feeding stuffs have been made to his
Department by the Northern Ireland
Pedigree Cattle Breeders' Association
and by the Northern Ireland Pig Producers Association; whether the reasonable requests they have made are to be
acceded to, and, if so, in what way;
whether his Ministry has also received,
in connection with the same subject, a
resolution from the Northern Ireland
Feeding Stuff Manufacturers' Association urging that permission should not be
granted to cross-channel firms or their

new business selling straight meals and
locally manufactured compound meals,
where formerly they only sold crosschannel compound feeding stuffs, as this
is contrary to the statement of the

continue through the usual channels; and
whether it is proposed to give effect to
this suggestion.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Representations
were made to me by the Northern Ireland
Pedigree Cattle Breeders' Association
regarding the provision of imported feeding stuffs for pedigree cattle under the
proposed rationing scheme. The Association was informed that arrangements had
already been made to supply imported
feeding stuffs for pedigree cattle.
No representations have been received
by my Department from the Northern
Ireland Pig Producers' Association, but
arrangements have also been made to
provide a ration of imported feeding
stuffs for all breeding sows and fattening
pigs.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I have received a copy of the
resolution referred to by the hon.
Member. Under the proposed rationing
scheme all merchants, including local
representatives of cross-channel firms,
will be in a position to supply all classes
of feeding stuffs. This will mean that
both the merchants and the agents will be
able to supply feeding stuffs which were

GROCERS' ASSOCIATION.
Mr. NIXON (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether any
decision has yet been made in regard to
the repeated requests of the Belfast and
North of Ireland Grocers' Association
that the Ministry of Agriculture should
terminate the payment by egg retailers
in Northern Ireland of the licence fee
and levy on sales of eggs, since no such
licence fee or levy is payable in Great
Britain; whether since 29th August,
1940, the controlled wholesale and retail
prices of eggs have been the same in
Great Britain as in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: In reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's question,
this matter is at present before the
Ministry of Food.
The reply to the second part of the
question is in the affirmative, if by "controlled prices" the hon. Member refers
to maximum prices, but I would point
out that the fixing of maximum prices is
designed to cover differential conditions
in different parts of the country arising
from factors such as transport. There
is thus no reason why maximum wholesale or retail prices in Northern Ireland
should always reach the same level as in
Great Britain-indeed the reverse is the
case since eggs sold in Northern Ireland
do not have to bear the carriage charges
that have to be paid on Northern Ireland eggs sent to Great Britain, where,
as the hon. Member points out, the same
maximum price applies.
Mr. NIXON: If there is no levy on
the sale of eggs in Great Britain why
should there be a levy here?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That matter is
being considered by the Ministry of
Food. Their decision may change the
situation over here.

In fact,
the hon. Member for Shankill has already
said he was glad I had the privilege of
welcoming their Majesties at the Ulster
House in London. Yes, I had that
privilege, and I am sure Ulster people
generally were very gratified that their
Majesties paid us the compliment of
showing their interest in Ulster in the
way they did. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) They were particularly interested
to see the canteen where our service men
are being entertained, no matter to what
branch of the services they belong.
I do not feel I would be justified in
dealing at length with the question of
unemployment, but the hon. Member for
Shankill has raised the question of Free
State workers coming in here and getting
employment, while Northern Ireland
workers are asked to go to Great Britain
and obtain employment there. He was
perfectly justified in raising that question, and he is quite entitled to have a
candid answer. These workers coming in
from the Free State are, I understand,
of two classes. One are skilled workers
who come here, not to replace anybody
but to do work which is urgently required
to be done in connection with our war
effort. Then I understand a certain
number, but not a great number, are
coming in who may be described as unskilled. These are not brought in by the
Government, but by private employers.
I deplore the fact that some private
employers are bringing them in while we
have unemployed unskilled workers here.
But the employers who bring them in
must accept the responsibility for their
own actions. It is not fair to place the
responsibility upon the Government.
As regards asking a certain number of
workers to go to Great Britain when there
is not work for them here, it is not fair to
put the responsibility upon the Minister.
of Labour. That responsibility must be
borne by each member of the Government, myself among the number. The
position is this. When the work is not
here-regrettably not here is it unreasonable, in order to help the war effort
of the United Kingdom, that these people
should be asked to go for a time to Great
Britain and there play a very noble and
very necessary part? Personally speaking, it is regrettable that the work, as I
have said, is not here. The point is,
when it is not here are these workers to
remain here in idleness or are they to be
asked to go to Great Britain to perform
useful work there in connection with the
war effort? That is the position candidly
and, I think, clearly expressed.
There is no one more anxious than I am
to see work in Northern Ireland for our
own people in our own part of the United
Kingdom. It is not the fault of the
Government that it is not here. Ever
since 1936, my predecessor and his colleagues, and myself and my colleagues,
have been doing everything possible to get
as much work here as we possibly can.
But it is a regrettable fact, and it cannot
be denied, that the difficulty is that there
is not sufficient flax to keep all our mills
here going full time. The flax is not
available, and it is has to be conserved,
such flax as is here, for the Government
requirements, and the result is that our
export trade is not permitted and the
home trade is only permitted, I understand, to a very limited degree. It would
be wrong if the flax was used for export
and then it turned out there was not
sufficient for Government requirements.
That is the position, and it is a very
regrettable position. The Government,
however, has no power to control it. The
fact of the matter is that over 80 per
cent of our flax came from abroad in the
past before the war.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am sorry, but

Mr. SPEAKER: The right hon.

The PRIME MINISTER: He most

The Prime Minister talked to-day

authorities are. I know that when the

It does not matter who is right or wrong.
I am not going into that to-day. When
a matter is upheld on that side and denounced on this side it is debatable. The
minute it is debatable it is no question
for a civil servant.
One of the things touched on here was
the Minister of Home Affairs.
His permanent Secretary gave an interview to
the Press with respect to the proposed
appointment of Mr. Allen. It was put

it was improper. The Minister knows it
was improper. One of the things the
Minister said, I think, on this day week

man-to send a letter to the Press in his

Furthermore, that is quite justifiable, but

that everyone
in Northern Ireland is

Government on a different status to what

and Vote in this House at a later date.
